News.title: Two charged over alleged plot to assist Iran in RAF Fairford incident
News.content:
Two British nationals have been charged over an alleged plot to assist Iran's intelligence service as part of the investigation into the incident at RAF Fairford in September.

Mohmed Ahmad Abdulkarim, 24, from Westminster, has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service under Section 3 of the National Security Act.

Nouman Essghir, also 24 and from Westminster, has been charged under Section 4 of the same act with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK on 22 August - weeks before he was arrested near the airbase in Gloucestershire alongside four other men.

The pair will appear at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Tuesday.

A major incident was declared after three suspicious vans were seen near the US-operated airbase on 27 September.

Dozens of residents were evacuated and a large cordon was put up in the area around the base. No explosive materials were found in the vans by police but a quantity of petrol was seized.

Essghir, from Westminster, was one of five men arrested near the scene in Gloucestershire on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act. All five were released on police bail the following day, but Essghir was re-arrested on 20 October.

A 25-year-old UK-Iranian national who was also re-arrested on that date on suspicion of assisting a foreign intelligence service has now been released without charge. He remains on police bail after his initial arrest on 1 October on suspicion of preparation of terrorist acts.

The re-arrests in October led to detectives interviewing Abdulkarim.

Eight men have been arrested as part of the counter-terror police investigation.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said the release of the five men on police bail in September had raised significant questions and speculation about the investigation for members of the public.

He stressed that tactics used by counter-terror police can appear "illogical" at times but said that "there will always be a good reason or rationale behind them".

"In this case, this decision-making has led to swifter progress, better evidence, and ultimately us securing the charges that I've announced today," he added.

US President Donald Trump at the time said he was "surprised" the men had been released, saying: "We would not have released them."

Taylor said counter-terror police had seen "a range of incidents in recent months that we believe have been directed by the Iranian state".

Iran has previously denied any involvement in the incident at RAF Fairford.

The base has been used as a forward operating location by the US Air Force (USAF) for decades.

In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base to the Middle East, after the UK approved a request for it to be used for defensive strikes against Iran.

After the incident in September the US pulled its bombers out of the base and returned them to America.

Trump said the aircraft were removed due to "some threats" to the base, without giving specific details.

News.title: Minimum wage increase set to slow for 18-20 year-olds
News.content:
The minimum wage is set to rise but 18-to-20 year-olds are expected to see lower increases than in previous years, the BBC understands.

Pay for younger workers will rise in line with the increase in minimum pay for employees aged 21 years and over.

However, the increase for younger workers is lower than that seen in the previous two years, when Labour raised the rate to meet a manifesto promise that it would remove "discriminatory age bands" with all adults entitled to the same minimum wage".

Chancellor John Healey will reveal the new pay rates in the Budget on Wednesday, while also announcing measures to give families what he is calling "breathing space" with the cost of living.

"The manifesto pledge on equalisation still applies but we were always clear it could happen over time," Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds told the BBC:

"Of course, you want not just good wages but good work, " he added. "It is a balance of making sure the pressures on the labour market are taken into account."

The Times reported that the National Minimum Wage for 18-to-20 year-olds is likely to rise by 3.9% from Â£10.85 an hour to around Â£11.27.

That is a smaller rise than the 26% increase the Labour government has put in place for younger workers since returning to power in 2024.

Even after the reported rise, the rate remains below the National Living Wage for older workers, which is currently Â£12.71 an hour. It is set to rise by 3.9% to Â£13.20, the Times said.

Andrea Egan, general secretary of the union Unison, said it was "deeply unfair" to keep paying different rates for the same job.

"Twenty year-old care workers, teaching assistants and security guards do the same work as their older colleagues," she said. "They don't pay less in the supermarket or at the petrol pump. They must be paid equally."

News.title: What does Israel's election mean for Gaza and the wider world?
News.content:
Israelis are voting in what many view as one of the most pivotal elections in the country's history.

Polling published on Friday suggests incumbent Benjamin Netanyahu is in a near neck-and-neck race with former military chief Gadi Eisenkot to become prime minister.

But where do the two rivals stand when it comes to foreign policy and how might their actions differ with regards to Gaza and the occupied West Bank?

The BBC's diplomatic correspondent James Landale reports from Jerusalem.

More on Israel's pivotal election.

News.title: Kane ends England’s 25-year wait to win men’s Ballon d’Or award
News.content:
Harry Kane has become the first English player to win the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001 after being crowned the world's best player at a ceremony in London.

The 33-year-old Bayern Munich striker is the fifth Englishman to win in total, with Stanley Matthews (1956), Bobby Charlton (1966) and Kevin Keegan (1978 and 1979) the others.

Denis Law of Scotland (1964) and Northern Ireland's George Best (1968) are the other winners from the United Kingdom.

Real Madrid and France forward Kylian Mbappe finished second, while Barcelona and Spain attacker Lamine Yamal completed the top three.

"Not many people would have thought it, and maybe even I wouldn't have thought I'd be this far," Kane told Dazn.

"I had to go through many ups and downs, especially early in my career. I was never the person that people thought was going to be the superstar like some of the guys now.

"I had to bide my time and work hard, a lot of times it was me against my own mind and I had to come through it, I had to show self-belief, determination.

"I think that grounded me even when I did make it at the highest level to keep improving and keep getting better."

England manager Thomas Tuchel said he was "delighted" to see Kane win the award as he hailed the forward's success as a "huge honour".

Prince William, meanwhile, said the former Tottenham Hotspur player was a "brilliant captain" and "remarkable player".

Kane scored 61 goals in 51 club matches last season, the most a Bayern player has ever struck in one campaign. Including England matches, it was 73 goals - plus eight assists - in 65 matches.

Only one player at a club in Europe's top five leagues has ever scored more goals in a season.

But he wins it despite not lifting either of football's biggest prizes last season, having lost in both the World Cup and Champions League semi-finals.

Remarkably the Three Lions captain becomes the first Bayern player to win the Ballon d'Or since Karl-Heinz Rummenigge in 1981.

To celebrate Kane's success, the Wembley arches were lit up in gold on Monday night.

BBC Sport looks at why Kane won it and how unusual it is to do so without securing one of those major trophies.

News.title: I'm a single mum and limit my weekly shop to £40 - here's what I want from the Budget
News.content:
Chloe Chin-Saad's husband passed away four years ago and her biggest worry is the cost of living.

She's very grateful that the rent she pays on her south London maisonette is set below the market rate as it is housing association accommodation, but says life was easier when she shared the bills. "Two incomes make a massive difference."

She lives with her 16-year-old son, and says her energy bill has risen sharply over the past year and she now pays about Â£200 a month on gas and electricity.

"We try to be more aware, we think more about how long we run the hot water when we do the dishes."

Chloe, 40, and her son have cut back on luxuries like going to M&S and the cinema, and she now tries to limit the weekly food shop to Â£40.

But she can't do anything to reduce her Â£200 council tax bill, the Â£250 a month she pays on car finance, or the amount she spends on medicines for her various health conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis.

Two mobile phone bills, and food and pet insurance for her dog also add to her costs. She says the amount she has left over at the end of each month varies, and sometimes she is left with as little as Â£50.

Chloe wants to see more help for single-parent families.

"I don't access benefits but I work full-time and it's hard. Can the government do anything else to help? Something on our tax bill perhaps."

News.title: Rise in sales of radios and tinned foods, say retailers, after call to stock up
News.content:
Some retailers have seen a dramatic increase in sales of essential goods after the government called for people to stock up in case of a crisis, according to figures obtained by Newsnight.

The Iceland supermarket chain said it was "clear" consumers had listened to warnings after it saw a 40% increase in sales of tinned products over the weekend.

The rise in sales came after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said that people should stockpile goods to prepare for an emergency such as a cyber attack or an extreme weather event.

Robert Dyas reported a 160% increase in sales of radios compared with last week, while Maplin said sales had increased by 92% in radios, 284% in torches and 106% in power banks.

The Maplin figures cover the period since the government's announcement last week compared with the same period last month.

"Within hours of the Be Ready announcement we saw people reach for the basics - a torch, a wind-up radio, a power bank. Torch sales nearly quadrupled and radio sales almost doubled in three days," said Ollie Marshall, managing director at Maplin.

"These are simple, affordable products that keep a household connected and informed when the power goes out, and it's encouraging to see people taking the advice seriously."

News.title: UK and EU officials to discuss freedom of movement
News.content:
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Reynolds said current discussions ahead of the summit are around food and drink, electricity and emissions trading.

He said: "What the prime minister has also said, quite rightly, is we face a series of policy changes on the European side that will affect us.

"We need to get as little uncertainty as possible, we need to have a way to resolve what our long-term relationship will be and he is going to set that out after the summit.

"He is going to be frank with the British people about what the trade-offs are but no assumptions have been made on that."

Pressed on whether UK officials are talking to the EU about freedom of movement Reynolds said: "They will be talking to them about what the future options for our relationship might be.

"But here and now, the focus should be on the summit and the tangible difference improvements we're going to make."

A government spokesperson stressed there were no current discussions on freedom of movement.

"We are working with the EU on the areas set out and agreed ahead of the UK-EU Summit and within the manifesto red lines," the spokesperson added.

Burnham is far more willing to have a public conversation around Brexit than his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer, whose government was nervous about reopening a debate that proved so contentious in the past.

Some people within the Labour Party had been urging Sir Keir to go further and there is a widely held view that Burnham's comments are likely to go down well with voters tempted by the Liberal Democrats and Greens.

But there is nervousness among Labour MPs with small majorities in Brexit-supporting, Reform-facing constituencies.

Labour MP Melanie Onn, whose constituency Great Grimsby and Cleethorpes backed leaving the EU, told the Today programme Burnham risked losing trust by talking about going beyond the 2024 manifesto at a future election.

"I don't think that the scars have healed for many people around the country so I do think this is an unnecessary conversation to be having at this time," she said.

Onn, who lost her seat in 2019 to the Conservatives but won it back in 2024, warned against re-opening the conversation, saying: "Trust is incredibly important, it's hard-earned and easily lost, and on this matter I think that we should tread incredibly carefully."

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage told BBC Breakfast that "Andy Burnham has no mandate to be in Brussels, to be negotiating any of this" and called for the prime minister to put his ideas to the public in a general election.

On Monday, Burnham left the door open to a potential referendum on freedom of movement with the EU.

The prime minister caused some confusion when he told broadcasters that he would not reintroduce free movement without a referendum, but Downing Street later said no decisions had been made on whether a public vote would be needed.

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told the BBC on Sunday that no options for the UK's future relationship could be taken off the table.

But Burnham did appear to draw some red lines of his own when he told the Sunday Times, external that he would not be in favour of the UK joining the euro or the border-free Schengen zone.

The fact the prime minister has not been willing to say the same thing about free movement is being seen in Westminster as evidence that he believes it is a genuine option.

News.title: 'Living next door to anti-social behaviour has been hell'
News.content:
For seven years James Daniel has been living next to successive "nightmare neighbours". Despite numerous complaints to various agencies, including his housing association, he said his situation had not improved.

It comes as new data from the Housing Ombudsman showed a rise over five years in the number of complaints upheld about social landlords' handling of anti-social behaviour.

While Devon and Cornwall Police has increased the number of closure orders placed on residential properties, housing associations report that dealing with anti-social behaviour can be a complex issue and requires working closely with other agencies.

Daniel said he had spent years reporting the alleged anti-social behaviour and collecting evidence, including security camera and mobile phone footage, which he passed on to the police, North Devon Homes and now the BBC.

The videos he shared with the BBC showed knives being thrown from a window, an altercation outside his house and a neighbour appearing to make gun gestures at his security camera.

Other footage showed a previous tenant shouting at Daniel and other residents, as well as throwing bags of rubbish and a dust pan brush.

"Living next door to anti-social behaviour has been hell to be honest, absolute hell, said Daniel.

News.title: More high winds hit parts of UK as Storm Boelo clean-up continues
News.content:
Strong winds are expected to continue across Scotland and parts of Northern Ireland on Tuesday, after Storm Boelo brought flooding and power cuts to thousands over the weekend.

While conditions are set to improve for much of the UK after a wet and windy morning, clean-up efforts could be hampered elsewhere - including in Scotland, where a third of a month's rain fell during the storm.

The Energy Networks Association (ENA) said almost 8,000 people were still without power after more than 800,000 experienced cuts.

Two men were killed by falling trees during the storm on Sunday - a man in his 20s whose car was hit in north London and a 60-year-old man in Dumfries and Galloway identified as Richard Baines, the long-serving curator of Logan Botanic Garden.

A deep area of low pressure, while not severe enough to be a named storm, still brought strong winds with gusts of 65-80mph to parts of western England and Wales in the early hours of Tuesday morning.

Through the rest of Tuesday, the strongest winds will be across Scotland and the northern coast of Northern Ireland, where a Met Office yellow warning is due to be in place until 21:00 GMT.

Gusts will continue to reach 50-60mph, possibly up to 70mph in the most exposed parts of northwest and northern Scotland.

That is is likely to bring further travel disruption and more power cuts in places.

Elsewhere across the UK, Tuesday will be a blustery day, but the wind is not likely to cause any major impacts.

Strong winds and heavy rain will ease off later on Tuesday, with the rest of the week looking much calmer across the UK.

Boelo is the second storm to have hit parts of the UK in recent days, following Storm Austen.

Leo Slade, CEO of the ENA said it had been "a tough weekend" and that efforts to reconnect some properties were being hampered by the weather, with sustained winds of 50-85mph across parts of Scotland and northern England.

"Until that weather system passes, we can't safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up, so today is going to be a hive of activity in getting engineers out into the field," he told the BBC.

He stressed that the UK's power network was very resilient and money was spent to prepare for these sorts of scenarios, but said a debate was needed over how much more investment was required to mitigate for further storms brought by climate change.

The Met Office has warned about the possibility of further power cuts and people should make sure they have essentials prepared, including torches and batteries.

News.title: Boy who stabbed girl at school was radicalised online, says father
News.content:
Warning: The following report contains details that some may find distressing

The father of a teenager who tried to kill a fellow pupil in a school knife attack has described his devastation and belief that his son was "radicalised" by extreme material online.

The boy, now 16, was found guilty of attempted murder last week after a trial heard how he harboured a hatred of women, had a fascination with serial killers and had planned to target others in the attack at Thorpe St Andrew School, near Norwich.

Speaking exclusively to the BBC and calling for tighter controls, the boy's father said he did not want to "absolve" his son but suggested online material and "a culture of violence and horror" had influenced him.

The government said it was committed to ensuring all children were safe from radicalisation and threats online, pointing to its Prevent anti-terrorism scheme and the Online Safety Act, which compels social media platforms to remove and prevent the spread of illegal content.

The boy cannot be identified due to his age, and nor can witnesses and the victim in the case.

His father, who we are calling John, apologised to the 15-year-old girl injured in the attack on 11 March, saying: "We're so very sorry for what happened."

John spoke of his fears that young men were being radicalised towards violence and hatred.

"You can think... it can never happen to my family or my son couldn't be involved, but that's what we thought and that wasn't the case," he said.

News.title: Boy, 14, denies murdering teenage girl whose body was found in park
News.content:
A 14-year-old boy has denied murdering a teenage girl whose body was found in woodland.

Lilly Jones, also 14, was discovered in Duffryn Park in Blaina, Blaenau Gwent, on 22 June, two days after her family reported her missing.

She died of multiple stab wounds to the neck and body.

At Newport Crown Court on Tuesday, the defendant from Blaenau Gwent, who cannot be named for legal reasons, pleaded not guilty to her murder.

A trial date was set for 23 November.

Dressed in a white shirt and a dark coloured tie, he sat in the dock flanked by four security officers.

When he was asked by the clerk if he pleaded guilty or not guilty to the charge of murder, he replied quietly, "not guilty".

The families of both Lilly and the defendant were in court for the hearing.

Lilly was previously described as "the most beautiful, kind and caring little girl", who was "completely and utterly herself".

News.title: MPs and MSP detained by Israel and barred from entering West Bank
News.content:
Two MPs and an MSP have said they were detained by Israeli authorities for eight hours while trying to enter the West Bank.

SNP MP Lara Bird, Labour MP Clive Lewis and Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens said they were prevented from entering the territory before being questioned and eventually turned away.

Bird said in a social media post that they had intended to "stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land".

They had travelled to the region as part of a Progressive International delegation that also included ex-Labour MP Sam Tarry and a former member of the Basque senate.

The Israeli military announced on Monday that all West Bank land crossings would be closed as part of increased security measures during Tuesday's national elections.

Posting on Instagram, Bird, the MP for Arbroath and Broughty Ferry, said the 23-strong group was "interrogated and ultimately prevented from crossing" the King Hussein Bridge between Jordan and the West Bank.

News.title: Busted's James Bourne says 'hero' brother saved his life with kidney donation
News.content:
Busted star James Bourne has said his brother "saved my life" by donating a kidney, after doctors had given him "a few years left to live".

The guitarist, 43, dropped out of an arena tour featuring his band and fellow punk-pop favourites McFly in September 2025, just a day before it began.

He blamed health problems and was replaced by his younger brother Chris.

James later said he needed major surgery to "extend my life", and has now thanked his "hero" Chris and said they are both recovering from their transplant operations.

News.title: Warrant for dad of A66 teen over funeral assault
News.content:
An arrest warrant has been issued for a man who attacked a celebrant at the funeral of his son, one of five men and two police officers killed in a head-on crash.

Gye Worthy, 40, admitted common assault and resisting arrest at his son's funeral at Teesside Crematorium in Middlesbrough after a disturbance during the service on 9 September.

His son Cole Worthy, 17, died when the Volkswagen Passat he and four others were in collided with a marked armed police car on the A66 in South Bank in the early hours of 22 August.

On Tuesday Worthy failed to turn up for sentencing at Teesside Crown Court, which heard he had not spoken to his solicitors or explained his absence to the court.

Worthy, of Ruskin Avenue, Middlesbrough, was also due to be sentenced for stealing four bottles of wine worth Â£30 from a shop on 8 October.

Deputy District Judge Julia Baggs agreed to an application by the prosecution for a warrant to be issued, "not backed by bail".

That meant he would have to be held in custody ahead of a future court date once he has been located.

The deputy district judge said: "In these circumstances, I do accept the application for a warrant not backed by bail."

Worthy previously admitted assaulting the celebrant Paul Maull during the funeral service for Cole Worthy.

Cole Worthy's funeral was held on the same day as that of PC Matthew Blades, 37, who was one of the officers killed in the crash.

News.title: Independent review announced into murder of student Henry Nowak
News.content:
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has announced an independent review into the murder of Henry Nowak.

The 18-year-old student was fatally stabbed in Southampton in December by Vickrum Digwa, who falsely claimed he had been racially abused and had acted in self-defence. Digwa was jailed for life on 1 June, with a minimum term of 21 years.

Following the teenager's murder, police bodycam footage of him being handcuffed as he lay dying led to intense scrutiny of the Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary and sparked wider debates around knife laws, race, policing and public trust.

The review, which was welcomed by Nowak's family, will be led by former Justice Secretary Alex Chalk KC.

"We must get to truth of what happened before, during and after that awful night and we must do everything in our power to ensure that no family suffers the same fate," Mahmood told the House of Commons on Monday.

Mahmood said the review will investigate what was known about Nowak's killer and if there were missed opportunities to intervene as well as the treatment of his family in the justice system and whether they received enough support.

In a statement published on Monday, the Home Office said the review will be carried out in two parts.

Phase one will cover the police, health services, local authorities educational institutions and faith organisations, including if any concerns were raised relating to weapon possession and violent behavior, the statement said.

It will also look to determine if there were missed opportunities to prevent Nowak's murder. Chalk told Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday that would include looking at whether any reports had been made but people or organisations had held back due to a "misplaced sense of cultural sensitivity".

Phase two will follow after the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) has concluded its investigation into the actions of police officers who attended the scene.

It will consider the actions of the IOPC and "if necessary" the police, the Home Office added.

The IOPC launched its own investigation into the response on the night of Nowak's death after bodycam footage showed the 18-year-old was handcuffed and left dying on the floor despite informing officers of his injuries.

The investigation was launched despite a sentencing judge ruling Nowak would not have survived his injuries, however quickly he received treatment.

The Nowak family described the announcement as a "significant moment in our fight for justice."

"We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for," they added in a statement.

"Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch welcomed the decision to launch the review.

"There must be proper accountability for those who failed Henry and his family," she said.

The review is due to report in five months.

News.title: No 10 appears to backtrack on PM's freedom of movement referendum suggestion
News.content:
Downing Street has appeared to backtrack on the prime minister's suggestion that he could call another referendum on whether to join the EU's freedom of movement.

Asked earlier by broadcasters if he could introduce freedom of movement without a referendum, Andy Burnham said "no".

But sources told the BBC no decision on that has been made and the prime minister's deputy spokesperson later said the government was not going to "get ahead" of how to consult the public.

Burnham has ruled out major changes to the UK's relationship with the EU before the next general election but says he wants start a conversation about potential options.

He told broadcasters that he would "never move ahead of the British public when it comes to Brexit".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about freedom of movement allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has said he is committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto, which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

And he has previously stressed any changes would require a mandate at a general election, which is due by 2029.

After lengthy questioning about the issue, Number 10 sought to clarify the prime minister's remarks, saying: "The prime minister isn't proposing a return to freedom of movement or any option."

"He is crucially not leaning either way and that will be for the British public to decide," the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said.

"What he wants to do first is have a conversation with the public. The process will follow."

She added: "The PM thinks the Brexit deal is not good enough."

Freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to travel, live, study and work in any member country, is a precondition of membership of the EU's single market.

The single market enables goods, services and people to move freely between member states, with countries also applying many common rules and standards.

News.title: Sunseeker shows robotic mowers and garden mapping plans at IFA
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Independent was not involved in the creation of this sponsored content.

At IFA 2026 in Berlin, Sunseeker presented its S5 and S7 robotic mowers alongside a plan to bring more information about the garden into the mowing experience. The company’s showcase centred on how the machines map a lawn, recognise objects in their path and let owners adjust the areas they maintain.

Mapping lawns without wires

The S5 and S7 use a system called AllSense 2.0, which combines 360-degree LiDAR with AI vision. LiDAR builds a spatial picture of the working area, while the vision system helps identify what is in it. Sunseeker says the software can recognise more than 360 types of obstacles. The machines are designed to map a lawn without a buried perimeter wire or an external RTK antenna.

MapOS, the company’s garden-management software, gives owners two- and three-dimensional views of the space. They can edit digital boundaries, create no-go areas and assign settings to separate mowing zones. Sunseeker also demonstrated a map intended to distinguish grass from other surfaces and planted areas. Those controls would allow a household to update the mowing area when a garden layout changes.

The S7 and the wider garden plan

An exploratory robotic-arm concept displayed on a Sunseeker mower at IFA 2026 ( Sunseeker )

The S7 LiDAR Ultra AWD 3000 is the larger of the two highlighted models. Sunseeker specifies it for lawns of up to 3,000 square metres and says its all-wheel-drive system can handle slopes of up to 80 per cent. It has a 35cm dual-disc cutting system and an Extension Hub that supports the optional EdgeZero trimmer head for work closer to lawn boundaries. The S5 LiDAR Ultra AWD 1800 is specified for up to 1,800 square metres and has a dedicated cut-to-edge disc.

Sunseeker also described a Smart Garden system that brings lawn-health and soil readings together with rainfall and weather information. The company says those inputs can inform recommendations about garden maintenance. Its longer-term plans include deeper connections with other outdoor-care equipment.

A robotic arm shown at IFA illustrated one possible direction for that work. Sunseeker has described the arm as a concept, with no announced consumer launch. The optional EdgeZero head is the attachment identified for the S7; further garden-care tools remain under exploration. The IFA presentation set out the current mower features and the company’s plans for using garden data alongside them.

News.title: Arise Sir Harry Kane? No 10 hints at knighthood for England striker after Ballon d’Or win
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Downing Street has hinted that Harry Kane could be in the running for a knighthood as the England Striker was congratulated by the prime minister for the “extraordinary achievement” of winning the Ballon d’Or.

The England captain and Bayern Munich striker secured the most prestigious individual prize in world football on Monday night, becoming the first Englishman in 25 years to win the award.

Asked if the prime minister wanted to congratulate Harry Kane on his triumph, a No 10 spokeswoman said: “The PM would like to congratulate Harry Kane on winning the Ballon d’Or.

“To be the first Englishman to win it in 25 years is an extraordinary achievement, and what a moment to do it here at home.

“Seventy years after Sir Stanley Matthews won the inaugural award, it caps a remarkable season, and Harry continues to set a brilliant example to young players across the country, and the PM knows the whole nation will be incredibly proud of him.

“And hopefully, there’s another trophy to celebrate with England before too long.

open image in gallery Harry Kane won the men’s Ballon d’Or (Kin Cheung/AP) ( AP )

Asked whether a knighthood could be on the cards for Mr Kane she said: “On your question about a knighthood, I think everyone would agree, Harry Kane has given enormous amount to English football, and this is a very special moment for him in the country, but as ever, I’m not going to pre-empt the honours process.”

Mr Kane was met with enormous cheers during a ceremony at London Palladium when former Brazil forward Ronaldo read out the name of England’s captain.

Following in the footsteps of Stanley Matthews, Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Owen in sealing Ballon d’Or glory, Mr Kane vowed to aim to retain the trophy in 12 months’ time.

“My heart was beating fast and I was just hoping he would say my name. I mean, what a legend, Ronaldo was one of my idols growing up, so for him to be the one to present me the award, it’s a dream come true,” Mr Kane said.

“Honestly just so many amazing feelings and to share these moments with my friends and with my family who are here. Yeah, I would say it’s a dream come true, but it’s beyond my wildest dreams.”

A stunning 2025-26 campaign where Mr Kane scored 73 goals for club and country, won two trophies with Bayern Munich and led England to third place at the World Cup, helped the 33-year-old beat Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal to the prestigious award.

open image in gallery Harry Kane was met with enormous cheers during a ceremony at London Palladium when former Brazil forward Ronaldo read out the name of England’s captain ( PA )

An emotional Mr Kane, 33, spoke for more than 10 minutes on stage after receiving the award before thanking his wife Katie Goodland.

“To my wife, Kate, my best friend,” Mr Kane said. “We've been through ups and downs for sure. You're my biggest supporter. I actually felt like you wanted this more than me myself.”

He added: “This is a trophy that we celebrate, not me. This is me and you, it's all the family, all our close-knit team, so I just want to say thank you, I love you.”

England manager Thomas Tuchel was among those to congratulate Mr Kane on his award.

He said: “I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I’m delighted to see that you have been formally recognised by the football world.

“To become the first Englishman to win this huge honour in 25 years makes it extra special and we are lucky to have you as our leader. I know you will enjoy this moment with your loved ones and then get back to doing what you do best – scoring goals and winning football matches.”

London City Lionesses and Spain midfielder Alexia Putellas, who won the women’s Ballon d’Or award for a record-equalling third time, said: “All the boys and girls around the world – if you love football and if you want to play football, play football. It doesn’t matter if you’re a boy or if you’re a girl.”

News.title: A huge explosion in space lasted for 27 days. Astronomers don’t know why
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Astronomers have been left puzzled after discovering a record-breaking cosmic explosion that lasted for 27 days.

Researchers at the University of Birmingham said the massive gamma-ray burst (GRB), designated GRB 220706A, remained active for 20 days longer than any previous GRB ever recorded.

GRBs are the most powerful explosions in the universe, releasing more energy in a few seconds than our Sun will emit it is entire lifespan.

They can be caused by a massive star running out of fuel and collapsing into a black hole, and are typically short-lived, lasting from a few milliseconds to several minutes.

The central power source usually exhausts itself quickly, however a rare type of ultra-long GRB can continue to churn out high-energy flares for longer.

“The fact that we see flaring at around 27 days in the GRB’s rest frame tells us that there’s an ongoing active process, and that’s unprecedented in the known population,” Benjamin Gompertz from the School of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Birmingham told Space.com.

“The previous record for delayed flaring was about six days after the GRB.”

open image in gallery Powerful gamma ray bursts can occur when a massive star collapses into a black hole

One possibility is that the star involved is much bigger than any previously observed in such events.

Dr Gompertz theorised that GRB 220706A may have required a type of star known as a blue supergiant, which is 1,000 times the radius of the Sun.

“We don’t know what the central engine driving this outburst is, and that’s what makes this such a compelling event," Dr Gompertz said.

“The fact that we see a supernova tells us that a star has collapsed, which is the standard power source for GRBs, but it doesn’t immediately account for the extremely late flaring or unusually bright supernova. We can interpret that through previous events to some degree."

open image in gallery Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are mostly associated with the explosion of stars that collapse into black holes. In the explosion, two jets of very fast-moving material are ejected, as depicted in this artist’s illustration ( ESO/A Roquette )

The researchers hope future observations of ultra-long GRBs will help further their understanding of the cosmic phenomena.

The Einstein Probe, launched in 2024, could be a crucial instrument in assisting these efforts, with the X-ray space telescope capable of tracking such events that were previously impossible to observe.

The latest findings were published in a study titled ‘An off-nuclear tidal disruption event discovered at late times: the case of TDE 2023mfm’.

News.title: Dollar General sued by FTC and 20 states for overcharging customers at the checkout
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Dollar General is being sued by the Federal Trade Commission and 20 states over allegations that it repeatedly charged customers more at checkout than the prices advertised on store shelves.

The lawsuit, filed Monday in federal court in Tennessee, claims the discount chain continued the practice for years despite receiving tens of thousands of complaints about incorrect prices.

Regulators say the overcharging particularly hurt low-income and fixed-income shoppers who rely on advertised prices to stretch their household budgets.

“Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement.

“The FTC’s action underscores the agency’s commitment to lowering costs for consumers by stopping deceptive pricing practices that harm Americans.”

open image in gallery The FTC and 20 states allege Dollar General overcharged customers for years despite receiving tens of thousands of complaints about incorrect prices on shelves, price tags and ads ( Getty )

The lawsuit follows an $8.5 million class-action settlement months ago over similar allegations, which Dollar General agreed to without admitting wrongdoing. Dollar General also paid more than $6 million in penalties under seven settlements with state authorities between 2019 and 2026 over inaccurate pricing, according to the FTC.

Dollar General operates more than 21,000 stores nationwide and markets itself as a low-priced alternative to larger discount and big-box retailers. The company sells thousands of everyday, essential household items.

According to the suit, the retailer received at least 29,265 complaints for failing to honor marked prices between January 2023 and March 2026. The complaints were made in all 48 states where Dollar General operates, the FTC alleged.

The lawsuit claims Dollar General failed to fix pricing problems despite repeated customer complaints and inspections revealing errors.

“Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and s,” the FTC and states alleged in the complaint. “This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country.”

open image in gallery Dollar General says the company tried to avoid litigation over the issue and cooperated with the FTC’s investigation ( AFP/Getty )

The lawsuit alleges violations of the FTC Act, the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and state consumer protection laws. The FTC and states seek a permanent injunction, monetary relief and other remedies.

The states joining the lawsuit are Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.

Dollar General told CBS News in a statement in response to the allegations: "Our goal is 100 percent accuracy between shelf and register prices in every store.”

"As with other retailers and despite our policies and procedures, occasional price discrepancies can occur. When that happens, our store teams are instructed, empowered, and expected to make things right for the customer. In recent years, we have enhanced our price-accuracy processes and remain committed to continuous improvement,” the company said.

The retailer said it cooperated with the FTC’s investigation, providing more than 200,000 documents and over 350 gigabytes of data, Newsweek reports. It also said it had attempted to negotiate a settlement before the lawsuit was filed.

“Although we respect the FTC’s role in protecting American consumers and the State representatives’ role in protecting the citizens of their respective states, we will defend this litigation vigorously,” the company said.

The Independent has contacted Dollar General for comment.

News.title: HSBC quarterly profit surge sparks fresh calls for bank tax hike in Budget
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A top HSBC executive has said the bank is not under pressure to relocate from the UK, despite a surge in its quarterly profit sparking fresh calls for the Chancellor to hike bank taxes in the Budget.

Pam Kaur, the banking group’s chief financial officer, said there was “no pressure” on the bank despite facing the prospect of higher costs.

It comes after HSBC reported a pre-tax profit of 9.6 billion US dollars (£7.2 billion) for the three months to September, which was 32% higher than the same period last year.

This was partly driven by an increase in net interest income, which is the difference between what banks make from loans and what they pay out in deposits, amid UK interest rates staying higher for longer.

Earnings were also bolstered by lower expected credit losses and a smaller provision for legal costs than the same period last year.

HSBC also announced it would be handing up to one billion dollars (£750 million) to shareholders as part of a new share buyback scheme.

The results announcement comes a day before John Healey is due to deliver his Budget, where reports have said he could increase the surcharge on bank profits from 3% to 8%, reversing a tax cut implemented by the former Conservative government.

Ms Kaur said she would not speculate on the Budget given it was a day away.

But asked about whether higher taxes could raise the pressure to shift its headquarters away from the UK, she said the bank was “very comfortable”, adding: “We are domiciled in the UK and we remain in the UK so that question is just not on the table.

“Irrespective of what happens on taxes, we are there to support our customers and that is what we will do.”

She added that there was “no pressure because we are doing well, we are meeting all our targets”.

Industry groups have warned that higher taxes on the financial services sector could divert investment, jobs and businesses away from the UK.

But HSBC’s financial results on Tuesday sparked fresh calls to the Chancellor to target banks in order to raise more money for the Treasury.

Paul Nowak, general secretary of Trades Union Congress (TUC), said the profits make it “blatantly obvious banks can afford to contribute more”, also referring to a Barclays reporting a 12% jump in its quarterly profit last week.

“Households and businesses are going to need more support – and it’s time for the Chancellor to make the banks pay a fairer share,” he said.

TUC said reversing the Tory tax cut and setting the surcharge at 8% would raise £9 billion over four years, while setting the surcharge at 16% could deliver £24 billion over the same period.

Sara Hall, the co-executive director of campaign group Positive Money, accused banks of “blowing billions of pounds” on bonuses and payouts to shareholders, adding: “The Chancellor should claw back some of these lost billions with a windfall tax on bank profits this week, to show the public that this Government will put the public interest ahead of corporate ones.”

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey will deliver his autumn Budget statement on Wednesday (Peter Byrne/PA) ( PA Wire )

Meanwhile, HSBC said it had made cost savings worth 1.9 billion dollars (£1.4 billion) under chief executive Georges Elhedery’s cost-cutting drive.

It expects this to reach two billion dollars (£1.5 billion) by the end of the year – exceeding the 1.5 billion dollar (£1.1 billion) target that was originally set.

Ms Kaur said the cost savings have come from “a range of places” including the “deduplication of roles” which particularly impacted more senior positions.

She also said the bank was encouraging its staff to build their AI skills and be “future ready”.

“And that’s so important for us because, in our judgment, what’s most important for an AI strategy to work is to keep the human accountability, judgment and decision-making very much at the core of what we do,” she said.

“So AI is there to help humans, not necessarily to replace humans.

“We know that AI will change how work is done across industries and of course it will impact some roles, it will transform other roles, while creating entirely new roles.”

It comes as reports said the bank was preparing to cut jobs in its UK wealth management business as part of efforts to ramp up the use of AI to serve wealthy customers more efficiently, according to the Financial Times.

Ms Kaur said she would not comment on the speculation about job losses but that the bank “absolutely focuses on the workforce we have, both in terms of skilling it and building on it”.

News.title: Christina Applegate issues message of resilience to MS community despite misdiagnosis
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Christina Applegate has shared a message with the multiple sclerosis community after revealing her misdiagnosis.

Applegate, 54, was diagnosed in 2021 with the incurable autoimmune disease that affects the brain and spinal cord, and has spoken openly about the debilitating pain of the condition. One week after revealing the health update on her MeSsy podcast — returning after a seven-month hiatus due to health issues — Applegate has shared a new message to the MS community.

Speaking on this week’s podcast episode, she said: “I’m still going to speak out on your behalf forever and ever. I still feel like part of this community and no matter what I love you.”

Applegate said she “feels OK” and that she’s been surrounded by support in the days following her misdiagnosis announcement, adding, “That’s all I can want.”

However, the Married... with Children actor said she continues to struggle with mobility issues. “I actually timed it today. It took me 10 minutes to be able to move off my pillow and get out of the bed and stand up. I don’t know what’s going on. This is what I am still living with,” she revealed.

open image in gallery Christina Applegate has issued a message to the MS community after her misdiagnosis ( Getty )

She shared that her next step in her health journey is to see a rheumatologist, “and then, you know, we’ll go from there. If that doesn’t come with any kind of results, then we’re going to go to a different specialist and then a different specialist,” she says. “That starts to overwhelm me...I think I just have to go, all right, one step at a time.”

Applegate’s co-host Jamie-Lynn Sigler — who was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2016 — addressed the future of their podcast, saying, “This is just about our lives and the messiness of life in general. It was never meant to be solely MS focused.”

Sigler added that Applegate’s openness about the misdiagnosis has “ignited and supported a conversation that’s been out there but maybe not getting the visibility or attention that some people felt that it should.”

“Not even just about a misdiagnosis, but about how difficult it is to get a correct diagnosis, and all of the different types of things, especially autoimmune and neurological that can mimic one of the other, and the frustration that comes along with that, and the heaviness that can come with a diagnosis, and all the feelings around it,” Sigler continued.

open image in gallery Applegate, pictured in 2022, has been open about her health struggles in recent years ( AFP/Getty )

In sharing the news of her misdiagnosis on her podcast, Applegate cited new technology that contributed to the finding, saying, “This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one.

“It’s hard to say that [my doctor] came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.’”

Applegate said she was “not happy at all” to hear the news.

“You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways,” she said. “So I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me.”

After announcing her diagnosis in 2021, Applegate retired from acting in 2022 following the finale of the hit Netflix drama series Dead to Me.

Now, she said, her illness is a mystery. “I have every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one,” she said. “Now, we both know that there are many things that mirror MS — many different things.”

Applegate added that “there’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS,” so this is not a rare occurrence.

“It’s clear now that they’re finding something different,” Applegate continued. “Something else is going on.”

News.title: Eurovision issue an apology as Netherlands withdraw from contest for second year
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Netherlands will not take part in the Eurovision Song Contest for a second year, having reversed a decision announced only last month that it would return.

The country's public broadcaster NPO has confirmed it will sit out the 2027 contest after discussions about its involvement failed to secure sufficient support.

The Eurovision Song Contest has said it is “deeply sorry” to hear of the Netherlands' decision.

In a statement, the NPO said it had taken a “step back” from Eurovision “due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play”.

The Netherlands was one of five countries to boycott this year's competition due to Israel's participation.

Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia also stayed away from 2026's event in Vienna, Austria, because of Israel's continued participation amid its actions in Gaza.

open image in gallery Pro-Palestinian and Iranian activists gather to demonstrate against Israel's participation in this year's Eurovision Song Contest on May 16, 2026 in Vienna ( Getty )

There were a number of protests in the Austrian capital during this year’s contest over Israel's inclusion amid its actions in Gaza.

In a statement issued to the BBC, Jet de Ranitz, the chairwoman of the NPO, said: "In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return.

"Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.

"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.

“Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being.”

Martin Green, director of the Eurovision Song Contest, said he was “deeply sorry” the country would not be taking part, adding: "We understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it in the Netherlands.

"The Netherlands is one of the founding countries of the contest and has been part of the Eurovision family since the very first edition in 1956. Dutch artists, fans and broadcasters have shaped the contest over seven decades, and the Netherlands has been a creative and valued voice in it.”

Mr Green also said organisers recognise that opinions about the contest “differ widely, both within countries and between them”, adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"Public service media exist to serve their audiences, and it is right that our members weigh these questions carefully, in dialogue with their own communities.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world.

"It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.

“That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it.”

open image in gallery Martin Green said he was ‘deeply sorry’ that the Netherlands had pulled out for a second year ( AFP/Getty )

Mr Green also said he was “very happy” the competition would continue to be broadcast in the Netherlands, adding that the organisation “looks forward” to welcoming a Dutch entry when “the time is right”.

The 71st edition will be held in the city of Burgas after Bulgarian entry Dara won this year's contest with her electro-pop song Bangaranga.

The semi-finals and grand final will be broadcast on BBC One, BBC iPlayer, BBC Radio 2 and BBC Sounds on May 11, 13 and 15.

News.title: Colorado's glaciers thinned dramatically due to record low snow and heat in 2026
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The most prominent glaciers in Colorado thinned dramatically over the past year due to record low mountain snow and record warm temperatures, according to new research.

Their shrinking is on par with recent observations of glacier loss across the planet as warmer temperatures accelerate melting and less snow falls to replenish their ice, threatening water sources, increasing mountain hazards and contributing to sea level rise.

While glaciologists typically measure changes over longer intervals, glaciologist Dan McGrath at Colorado State University sought to find out what happened over 2026 since it was such an exceptional year. The state’s worst snowpack on record, followed by record summer heat, left the year-round ice masses in the Rocky Mountains exposed.

The Andrews Glacier thinned by more than 12 feet (3.7 meters) in this single year, the Arapaho Glacier lost nearly 10 feet (3 meters), and the Isabelle Glacier lost about 6.5 feet (2 meters) — doubling their rate of thinning from the prior five years, McGrath said. In the decade before that, the thinning measured a foot or less per year.

St. Mary's Glacier, a perennial snowfield popular among hikers and skiers, melted completely in September.

“What we’re witnessing is the loss of that part of Colorado’s identity. And it’s not just Colorado,” said McGrath, who specializes in glacier dynamics. “Obviously we see it in the Alps and we’re seeing it in other mountain ranges in the western U.S., the European Alps and globally. There are very clear, consistent patterns across these ranges.”

Climate change is shrinking glaciers faster than ever

More than 7 trillion tons of ice (6.5 trillion metric tons) has been lost worldwide since 2000, according to research, a slow-motion disaster that sometimes provokes sudden devastation: More than 1,300 people were killed in August after a massive section of rock and overlying glacier collapsed near Nepal’s border with China.

Glaciers in Switzerland lost 5.5% of their ice volume this year, the second-biggest percentage drop on record, due to heat waves and low winter snowfall. The GLAMOS Swiss glacier monitoring service and Swiss Academy of Sciences said this month that alpine glaciers have no chance of surviving long-term under such conditions. Switzerland is home to the most glaciers in the Alps.

In Washington state, researchers with the North Cascade Glacier Climate Project have surveyed six glaciers on Mount Baker during an annual summer trip. Director Mauri Pelto said this year's survey shows the fastest average retreat since 1950 with the collapse of several large ice caves, which form as warm air circulates in retreating glaciers.

Mountain glaciers in the contiguous United States average just 0.16 square miles (0.41 square kilometers), or about 100 acres (about 40 hectares), and are widely distributed at high elevations. Since the mid-1900s, about one-quarter of them have disappeared and the remnants have lost a third of their area and volume, according to a new study co-authored by Brian Menounos, an earth sciences professor at the University of Northern British Columbia.

The runoff supplies water to high alpine and downstream ecosystems across the western United States, and eventually these areas may become more vulnerable to extreme drought as the glaciers disappear, he added.

And in a “one-two punch,” wildfires also are hastening the melting by darkening the surfaces of glaciers with soot and dust, Menounos said, making them more vulnerable to absorbing sunlight.

Glaciers could re-form if carbon pollution declines substantially and temperatures drop enough to enable snowfall to build year-round, eventually compressing again into glacial ice, but that may take several hundred years, Menounos added.

Colorado's glaciers may not have much time left

Looking at how much ice Colorado's remaining glaciers have lost, McGrath thinks they could soon disappear. The Andrews Glacier has already lost half of its ice since 2017, he said.

“This past decade has showed us that these glaciers are out of balance with the climate here in Colorado, in the western U.S., and they’re thinning at a rate that could lead to their demise in the next 20 years,” he said.

Harlan Ulmer, 20, is a student at Colorado State University who has photographed the glaciers annually since 2022 and volunteers with McGrath’s research project. He said it's sad to see their decline, but important to record.

“Being Gen Z, I came in too late to ever see the glaciers at their largest,” he said. “But I think we have the opportunity, I have the opportunity, to sort of document the changes that are taking place in my time to preserve them for future generations and for posterity.”

___

McDermott reported from Providence, Rhode Island.

News.title: The silent war: As Israel chooses a new leader Gazans wait for life to begin again
News.content:
One year after the ceasefire, Gaza’s health system is still on its knees. Of Gaza’s 228 primary care facilities, only just over half are functioning, according to the WHO.

Medicines are getting in, with almost 87 per cent of requests granted, says the WHO.

It means that someone with a fever or a minor injury can be treated but if it’s anything more complicated there are few options.

None of Gaza’s 36 hospitals are fully functioning, with just 19 partially working, according to the WHO.

There is no MRI scanner anywhere in the Strip, only about 30 per cent of facilities have basic X-rays, and only 12 to 17 per cent have dialysis capability, according to Physicians for Human Rights-Israel (PHRI), a medical NGO founded by Israeli doctors

Chronic illnesses are getting worse. Sally Saleh, head of health and emergency response at Medical Aid for Palestinians (MAP), says there is no capacity to monitor patients or guarantee consistent medical access, so preventable complications from cancer, kidney disease and diabetes will accumulate.

“We need to move beyond simply keeping services alive from one week to the next,” she told The Telegraph.

Power is the biggest hurdle, doctors say. Gaza’s electricity grid has been dead since Israel turned off the supply in October 2023, so hospitals rely on expensive and unreliable generators.

Dr Ahmed Muhanna of Al-Awda Hospital in central Gaza said that when his generators broke down, the hospital rented one for $1,200 a day, but it may only run for 10 hours.

Fuel and spare generator parts are in short supply – but Cogat blames Hamas for stealing fuel and it says that because “Hamas operates inside hospitals” it has to monitor where spare parts end up.

One major problem for those trying to get supplies into the Strip is Israel’s ban on “dual use” items, material it deems serves both a civilian and military purpose. Items that have been blacklisted include generators and metal tent poles.

Cogat says generators, X-ray machines and oxygen concentrators are allowed in under monitoring arrangement with aid groups. But aid agencies told The Telegraph that the rules on what is permitted change from day to day.

Israel allows 15 trucks of dual-use items to enter every week. But the WHO says repeated delays in bringing medical equipment, prosthetics and diagnostic tools into Gaza are delaying patients’ recovery.

In the last six months alone, a single shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices for amputees was rejected four times, the WHO added. It is particularly concerning as Gaza is now home to “the largest cohort of child amputees in modern history”, according to the UN.

“Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again,” said Dr Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, WHO Representative in the Occupied Palestinian Territory (OPT).

In July Cogat said over 10,300 pallets of health products had been approved since the start of the year, but only 3,238 had reached the crossing. It blamed “a delivery bottleneck” among the organisations that requested them rather than a “Cogat controlled supply bottleneck”.

Crumbling hospitals mean that around 20,000 patients, including 4,000 patients, need urgent medical evacuation. The WHO says about 5,700 patients have been evacuated since the ceasefire. Save the Children estimates that at the current rate the backlog would take four and a half years to clear.

Cogat disputes WHO and UN figures, and says that it has approved the majority of evacuation requests.

News.title: Harry Kane ends England’s 25-year wait for Ballon d’Or winner
News.content:
“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane said as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

In truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he said of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”

Kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”

News.title: Nurse accused of spreading Ebola murdered by mob
News.content:
A nurse was killed and a teacher badly injured in a mob attack after being accused of spreading Ebola in the water supply in Congo.

The unnamed victims were set upon in Bafwasende territory of Tshopo province after a group of young people accused them of being responsible for the outbreak of the haemorrhagic fever.

The nurse was killed outright and the teacher, who local media reported was close to the health worker, only survived after being rescued by police.

The World Health Organization (WHO) condemned the attack, which is only the latest incident of health workers being attacked by suspicious, scared or angry locals.

Medical workers have been forced to deal with widespread rumours that the outbreak – the world’s second largest – is spread by them.

Other conspiracy theories claim the outbreak is a money-making hoax for aid agencies, or that foreigners are using it as a pretext to grab the country’s minerals.

Strict rules imposed on how to conduct funerals in order to stop mourners becoming infected, have become another flashpoint.

Last month, a Congolese politician was beaten to death in North Kivu after publicly defending the government’s response.

He had been calling on the public to obey response measures, particularly social distancing and hand washing, on a radio show.

News.title: ‘Our world is yellow’: Fears for children as sickening smog blankets Indonesia
News.content:
For two months now, Natanael Undas has opened his curtains not to blue skies, but a sickening sepia haze that blocks out any sunlight. As the relentless fires smoulder nearby, his city looks “more like Mars” than Indonesian Borneo.

“We start our day in yellow, and we end our day in yellow,” the 32-year-old headteacher told the Telegraph. “When you inhale and take a breath, it feels like you’re choking. Your eyes hurt, your nose hurts… when you go outside, it feels like someone is burning dry leaves next to you.”

Palangkaraya, the capital of Central Kalimantan, is on the front lines of an environmental crisis that has cloaked much of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze for months.

According to Nusantara Atlas, an open-access platform that tracks deforestation, fires have torched roughly 1.9 million hectares across the archipelago so far this year – including one million hectares in September alone.

“I’ve seen burning in the city, burning in the forests, burning near the river, burning in the peatlands, burning near the street – it’s devastating,” said Mr Undas. “It’s the longest burning season I’ve seen. Usually the rainy season comes in October, but everything is still on fire.”

News.title: Britain sanctions warlords accused of rape in Sudan
News.content:
The British government is to sanction senior military and militia commanders accused of atrocities, including rape and sexual violence, during the fall of the city of El Fasher in Sudan.

At least 15 commanders from both the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) have been sanctioned after investigations found they used rape as a weapon of war during the brutal siege of the Sudanese city in October last year.

The siege, perpetrated by the RSF paramilitary group who have been battling SAF since 2023, resulted in the massacre of at least 60,000 people.

The fall of the city came after an 18-month blockade in which the city’s population were deliberately starved into submission, according to a report from the UK-government funded think tank the Centre for Information Resilience.

Reports from aid organisations, UN investigators, and eyewitness accounts have previously found that rape was used on a mass scale by both sides.

In one incident, aid workers said at least 54 children were raped or sexually assaulted by RSF fighters while fleeing the city to Tawila, a town 25 miles west of El Fasher.

News.title: Wolff puts ‘tequila on ice’ with Antonelli two points away from title
News.content:
Mercedes had chosen the medium tyres for the start, while Ferrari’s Leclerc and the Red Bulls of Verstappen and Isack Hadjar started on new softs. Antonelli was able to convert that choice into a one-stop race while almost everyone else did two, emphasising his superiority as he finished 16 seconds clear of Leclerc.

A late virtual safety car after Valtteri Bottas’s Cadillac ground to a halt by the side of the track made the final laps rather processional, denying the huge crowds at COTA the opportunity of seeing the fast-closing Hamilton take on Verstappen for the final podium spot.

That might have been fun, with Verstappen having lost his cool with his team midway through the race, furious that they didn’t order team-mate Hadjar out of the way when he came up behind him after stopping: “Thanks guys. Really good strategy there. Stuck in the dirty air.”

Incredibly, his third place finish in Austin means is the first time since the final race of 2020 that Verstappen has been out of title contention.

But it hardly mattered. The day belonged once again to Antonelli who should be champion by the end of next week. Not that he was getting carried away. “It was the result we needed,” he said. “The whole team deserved it so much, bringing this [upgrade] package. It was also the perfect execution with the strategy to do the one stop.”

Asked about the title, he added: “We’re very close, we try to finish on a high and hopefully we can finish it very soon. I mean, the perfect way will be to finish in style and then just enjoy the rest of the season. I’m very aware that it’s very close, but the mindset doesn’t change. I want to finish on a high to go into 2027 with momentum.”

“Yeah, what a boy, no?” Wolff said, admiringly. “I was just saying before, I got a question about whether he was nervous before the race, and I said, ‘Oh, he just sneaked into my office before getting ready and said, ‘I’m just going to enjoy this right now, and it’s weird, I’m not thinking about the championship at all. Isn’t that funny?’”

Wolff added that there would “definitely be a lot of tequila on ice” in Mexico. In hindsight it was always going to be a more appropriate venue to crown the sport’s youngest ever champion. Antonelli is not, after all, old enough to drink yet in the state of Texas.

News.title: Hapless and hopeless Man Utd bring curtain down on out-of-depth Carrick
News.content:
Hapless, hopeless and utterly humiliated. And that has to be that for Michael Carrick. It is surely inconceivable that he will continue any longer as Manchester United’s head coach. A proud club on its knees and a favoured son on his way out.

The former midfielder will carry the can. As managers always do. Even if the fault lines run so deep at United that it feels like they are almost irreparable. Owners – the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe – executives, players. A collective failing of monumental proportions. Although, again, it will be the manager who goes. Carrick knows it and it looked like it at the end. He knows the score, especially after this score.

More than four years ago Ralf Rangnick, the then interim manager, declared that United needed “open heart surgery”. Now there is barely a pulse.

An announcement must be imminent, with United turning to someone else in the fight against Premier League relegation. A joke? No, this abject performance against Bournemouth leaves United in 16th place, just a point above the bottom three, so the priority for the new man will be clear. Save them from the drop. They are 14 points off the top already, but forget that. It is irrelevant given their plight.

News.title: Trafford shows he has credentials to dislodge Pickford as England No 1
News.content:
Goalkeeping is defined by athleticism, physical strength and reflexes, but it is also about decision-making and mental fortitude. The two saves Trafford made to deny Sunderland’s Brian Brobbey in the first half were very different, but equally impressive.

The first was deceptively hard. Although the connection on Brobbey’s shot – back in the Sunderland side and causing chaos as usual – from the edge of the area was not the cleanest and that almost made it harder, as the flight of the ball was difficult to pick up. The bounce just in front of the goalkeeper meant he had to watch it closely, judge the trajectory in the air and spin off the grass and still keep a strong hand, at full stretch, to push it away from danger.

The second was, arguably, even better. Trafford had come off his line as Brobbey ran into the box. He was in a really vulnerable position, well outside his six-yard box in a one-on-one with the Netherlands international. The way he kept calm, stood up and timed when to move for the ball was superb, especially as an error could have led to a penalty.

Trafford may have saved with his feet, but he had cramped Brobbey for room, waited for the centre forward to make a move and timed the moment to dive at his feet perfectly. It was elite-level goalkeeping in a really tricky situation that favoured the striker.

Trafford made two more fine stops in the second half too, both from Nilson Angulo. The first was getting down low to tip another bouncing ball wide, which had flicked off a defender too. The second punching another deflected effort away after a block had taken some of the venom out of the shot.

Sunderland will feel like they shaded the battle, but Robin Roefs also made two decent stops from long-range shots in the second half while substitute Sean Longstaff saw an injury-time effort cleared off the line.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick keeps his job as Man Utd chiefs give under-fire boss another chance
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick keeps his job as Man Utd chiefs give under-fire boss another chance

Manchester United chiefs have decided to leave Michael Carrick in charge for Saturday's Premier League game against Chelsea after holding crisis talks

View 2 Images Michael Carrick arriving to Carrington this morning (Image: Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association)

Michael Carrick has been given a stay of execution by Manchester United.

‌



‌



Carrick had been widely expected to be sacked following the dreadful 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth at Old Trafford on Sunday. But he survived crisis talks at Carrington on Monday and took training as usual on Tuesday ahead of a crunch Premier League game against Chelsea this weekend.

‌



United have won just two of their 12 matches in all competitions season. They sit 16th in the Premier League, having taken just seven points from eight games - the club's worst start since 1986/87.

‌



The club have considered replacements, including Eddie Howe, Julian Nagelsmann and Antonio Conte, but have decided to stick rather than twist for now. Director of football Jason Wilcox and director of recruitment Christopher Vivell are reportedly split over Carrick's successor, with the former preferring Howe and the latter favouring Nagelsmann.

Carrick admitted that he was unsure over his position after overseeing the second heavy and embarrassing defeat on Sunday. "It's a tough situation, there's no hiding from it," he told Sky Sports when asked about his future.

‌



"But what it looks like and what's next, I really don't know. I will always do what's best for this football club, I've said it all along and I don't change that now. I love what I do, I love the position I'm in. I feel the responsibility but we'll have to wait and see."

Carrick was summoned to Carrington on Monday for talks with club chiefs and returned early on Tuesday morning. He is taking training as usual ahead of Saturday's early kick-off against Chelsea.

‌

Carrick appeared emotional as he left the Old Trafford pitch on Sunday, with the United supporters chanting his name in support. The former midfielder thanked the crowd in behaviour which some interpreted as a goodbye.

He was only appointed as permanent manager in the summer, having made a positive impact following his arrival in January in the wake of Ruben Amorim's sacking.

‌



Things have not gone to plan, however, with just two wins coming so far this season, against newly-promoted Ipswich and Champions League minnows Sabah. The past few weeks have also keen defender Lisandro Martinez and captain Bruno Fernandes publicly air their frustrations.

Having been given time to turn things around, Carrick faces a very tough test in the coming weeks. After facing Chelsea at Stamford Bridge this weekend, United play Roma, Aston Villa, Liverpool, Sporting Lisbon and Brentford in the Premier League and Champions League.
