World.title: Liberia: Justice Minister – Designate Blamo Vows No Witch-hunt of Opponents, No Shield for Friends
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s Justice Minister-designate, Cllr. Betty Lamin Blamo, has pledged that the state’s power to prosecute will not be turned into a weapon against political opponents or a shield for friends of those in power, whether in the public or the private sector.

By Obediah Johnson

Appearing before the Liberian Senate for her confirmation hearing on Monday, October 26, Blamo acknowledged that fear of selective prosecution is widely held among Liberians, and said no case would be prosecuted for reasons outside the law.



“I am not unaware of concerns expressed in the press, at the bar, and in ordinary homes that the prosecutorial power of the state can be sharpened against opponents and [used as a] shield for friends. I take this concern seriously. A case will be brought because the evidence supports it and for no other reason.”

She told senators that while she would advance President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s policy agenda and remain accountable to him and to the National Legislature, her first loyalty would be to the Constitution and laws of Liberia.

No case lacking evidence would go forward, she said, however loud the public demand for it, and none would be pursued on the basis of political affiliation or status.

“Where the law is applied evenly, disputes end in courtrooms instead of on the streets, and ordinary citizens can plan their lives; where the law bends to power, nothing else that the government does will hold. The decision to prosecute will rest on facts, the law, the standard of truth and the standard of proof, and never on political affiliation, county of origin, wealth or status.”

She vowed not to be a minister who prosecutes adversaries with zeal and friends with reluctance, and said she would recuse herself from any case involving a conflict of interest.

Drug cartels

Blamo said illicit drug trafficking continues to destroy the future of young Liberians, and vowed to go after the importers, traders, financiers and protectors of the trade.

She said her administration would settle for “nothing less” than dismantling drug cartels operating in Liberia, while ensuring rehabilitation for those struggling with addiction.

“Liberia will not be a transit country, a laundering point, or a soft place to do bad business. Our success will be measured not by the number of arrests, but by convictions.”

The test already on her desk

Blamo’s promises will be measured first against the biggest narcotics prosecution in Liberia’s history, a case she inherited and that has already drawn accusations of both political targeting and uneven justice.

In June, authorities seized about 237.6 kilograms of cocaine at Roberts International Airport. In July, about four tons, valued at an estimated US$317 million, were found at a warehouse in Duazon. West Africa has long been used as a transit route for South American cocaine bound for Europe.

On October 7, a Montserrado County grand jury indicted 20 people in the US$317 million case, including former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, who served under President George Weah from 2018 to 2024 and is standard bearer of the opposition National Patriotic Party. She faces eight counts, including drug trafficking, criminal conspiracy and money laundering. She denies the charges and is presumed innocent.

Howard-Taylor was arrested at Roberts International Airport on August 19 and held at the Monrovia Central Prison, the same facility Blamo cited for its overcrowding with pre-trial detainees, before being placed under house arrest on medical grounds.

Her arrest has fed exactly the concern Blamo addressed before the Senate. Weah has called the prosecution bogus and accused the Boakai administration of interfering with justice, and members of her party have warned of “growing public perceptions” that the case is politically motivated. The government insists its cases rest on evidence, not politics.

Critics, including

FrontPageAfrica, have raised the opposite concern: that the state moved quickly against an opposition figure but slowly against others named in the same investigation.

Among them is Mark Quiah, the former deputy director for operations at Roberts International Airport. He was named in a June writ of arrest and dismissed by President Boakai in late July, but he was left off the first charge sheet filed that month, even though it placed him in the alleged scheme, and was reportedly cooperating with investigators. He was among those indicted in October. The indictment also names a former National Security Agency deputy director, Gerald Foley Smith, and two senior police officers, Deputy Commissioner Anthony T. Blaye and Assistant Commissioner Wadell W. Kwarbo, along with Croatian, Ukrainian and other foreign nationals. Several defendants remain at large.

Police Inspector General Gregory Coleman said in July that the Duazon operation was “definitely sanctioned by state actors at the very, very senior level”, but he has named no one. Blamo’s vow to go after the “protectors” of the drug trade will be judged on whether those actors are ever identified and charged.

Her warning about poorly preserved evidence also bears directly on the case. The US$317 million seizure has already been destroyed, which raises chain-of-custody concerns similar to those in an earlier cocaine case under President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, when most of the drugs were destroyed before trial and the case ended in acquittal.

Blamo, who served as Solicitor General under Sirleaf, took over the ministry as acting minister on September 10. President Boakai had removed her predecessor, N. Oswald Tweh, and Solicitor General Augustine Fayiah a week earlier, while the prosecutions were under way.

The Executive Mansion described the move as an effort to strengthen institutions and did not link it to the drug probe. The October indictments were returned on her watch.

The weak link

Blamo identified the hand-over between police investigators and state prosecutors as one of the weakest links in Liberia’s criminal justice chain.

Too many cases collapse, she said, not because the accused are innocent, but because investigations are incomplete, evidence is poorly preserved and charges do not reflect the facts. The result: victims lose faith in the justice system, the guilty go free and the innocent languish in detention.

She promised to continue assessing the capacity of the ministry’s prosecution department and to draw up a clear roadmap to make it more effective. Cases, she said, must be evidence-based and professionally prepared, protecting the rights of the accused while assuring victims that serious crimes will be lawfully prosecuted.

Prosecutors quitting

None of this, Blamo admitted, can be achieved without well-trained staff. Many prosecutors have left the ministry since the government harmonized public-sector salaries, she said.

She urged lawmakers to provide budgetary support to recruit more prosecutors and to raise the pay of those still in service to reflect the risks and importance of their work.

Jailed but never tried

Blamo told senators that the conditions in which people are detained are a measure of the government’s commitment to human dignity.

Although Article 21 of the Liberian Constitution guarantees, among other things, that an accused person must be brought before a court within 48 hours, 2,848 of the 4,125 people held in prisons across the country – about 69 percent – had never been tried as of September 2026, she said. Some have not even been indicted.

At the Monrovia Central Prison alone, about 1,312 of the roughly 1,888 inmates – nearly 70 percent – are pre-trial detainees. Many, she said, are poor and cannot afford a lawyer or bail.

The ministry has begun reviewing the files of pre-trial detainees at the Monrovia Central Prison, an exercise she said would be extended nationwide once she is confirmed. She also called for additional correctional facilities to be built at Cheesemanburg in Montserrado County.

The government, she said, will either prosecute or release pre-trial detainees in accordance with the law. The ministry will also work with the judiciary to expand magisterial inspections, and with public defenders, the Liberia National Bar Association and legal aid providers to ensure that no one stays behind bars for long simply because they lack a lawyer.

“We must also state that the issue of pretrial detention and overcrowding of prisons is an issue that requires policy reform. If someone commits a crime, we can’t just let them go; we have to prosecute them. And so, the issue of pretrial detainees is a serious issue.”

She noted that specialized courts are overwhelmed with cases involving people accused or indicted for non-bailable offenses.

Corruption

Describing corruption as a menace in Liberia, Blamo said the ministry would work with the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission (LACC), the General Auditing Commission (GAC) and the Financial Intelligence Agency (FIA) to investigate and prosecute those accused of corruption and to recover stolen assets for the Liberian people.

“If we are confirmed, we will pursue matters strictly on the basis of the facts.”

She also promised a crackdown on human trafficking and sexual and gender-based violence, saying the interests of ordinary Liberians would come first in every decision the ministry makes.

World.title: Liberia’s official petrol price is among the lowest in West Africa, but rural consumers pay far more. The government says tighter monitoring is coming
World.content:
MONROVIA – On paper, Liberia has some of the cheapest petrol in West Africa. Away from the capital, it may have some of the most expensive in the region.

By Rodney D Sieh

The gap between those two facts is now a political problem for President Joseph Boakai’s economic team. Lawmakers are asking why better macroeconomic numbers have not lowered what ordinary Liberians pay for fuel, rice and building materials.



A regional bargain, on paper

Industry tracker GlobalPetrolPrices compiled data on 12 October covering 41 African countries. In that ranking, Liberia’s octane-95 petrol sold for $1.269 a litre, the 13th-cheapest of the 41. Every one of its neighbours pays more. Guinea’s price was $1.364 a litre and Côte d’Ivoire’s $1.55. Sierra Leone, at $2.03, was the third most expensive on the continent, behind only Zimbabwe and Malawi.

Liberia’s official ceiling price is also in a moderate range. The Ministry of Commerce and the Liberia Petroleum Refining Company (LPRC) set the retail pump price of gasoline at US$5.09 a gallon, or L$935, in a circular effective May 6. That works out to roughly $1.34 a litre.

Liberia gets no help from oil production. The country produces none of its own fuel, has no strategic petroleum reserves and has limited ability to cushion global price spikes. Prices therefore depend on Platts benchmarks, shipping costs and the exchange rate.

What Gbarpolu pays

The numbers look very different 100 kilometres inland.

Senator Amara Konneh chairs the Senate Committee on Public Accounts and Audit and represents Gbarpolu County. He told a Senate confirmation hearing that a gallon of fuel in his county sells for L$1,500. The Central Bank of Liberia’s rate was recently around L$174 to the dollar. At that rate, L$1,500 is roughly US$8.60 a gallon, or about $2.28 a litre.

That price is about 70% above the official ceiling. It is also higher than Sierra Leone’s national average, the third highest in Africa. For residents of rural western Liberia, fuel costs about as much as in Africa’s most expensive markets.

Fuel costs spread to other prices. Konneh said a 25kg bag of rice costs US$22 in parts of Gbarpolu, against US$17 in Monrovia. A bag of cement costs US$15, against US$8 in the capital. That is an 87% premium on the material Liberians need to move “from mud to brick houses,” as he put it. He linked the rising cost of petroleum products directly to the rising cost of basic goods.

Stability without relief

Konneh served as finance minister under former president Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, and he does not dispute the government’s numbers. He made his comments at the confirmation hearing of Euphemia Sweh Monmia, nominated as the Central Bank’s Deputy Governor for Economic Policy. He credited the economic management team with stabilising the economy.

“The economy is more stable now,” he said. Growth is expected to exceed 5% this year, and inflation stands at 4.6%. The Liberian dollar has also strengthened. The Central Bank has reported sharp appreciation, from about L$201 to the dollar at the end of August 2025 to around L$180 a week later. The currency has firmed further since then.

Normally a stronger currency would lower the local price of imported goods such as fuel, rice and cement. Konneh said that has not happened.

“Our money, the Liberian dollar, is stronger here today against the US dollar. With all of that, we should technically see some relief,” he said. “Even though inflation is 4.6% on paper, in Bopolu, Gbarpolu County, in Kinjor in Cape Mount, close to where the biggest mining company in our country is operating today, and in Tubmanburg, the prices are still high. The people are not feeling the impact of this impressive number.”

Where the money goes

Analysts point to three reasons why the official numbers and rural prices have moved apart.

The first is the last mile. Liberia’s price circular sets a national ceiling, but poor roads, few filling stations and informal resellers add large markups in the interior. Enforcement mostly happens in and around Monrovia.

The second is exchange-rate pass-through. Fuel prices are set in US dollars and converted at an official rate. A Senate committee report this year found that the exchange rate used in the price calculation, rather than the actual cost of fuel, had driven pump prices. It estimated that Liberians were overcharged by up to L$131 million. When the Liberian dollar strengthens but the price circular is not updated quickly, consumers lose the benefit.

The third is the mining economy. Konneh’s examples, Bopolu, Kinjor and Tubmanburg, lie along western Liberia’s mining corridor. Salaried mine workers and contractors there compete with subsistence households for the same goods, which can push local prices up.

The government’s response

The Ministry of Commerce and Industry says it is tightening controls. Stephen Marka Yekeson Jr. was appointed acting minister in September after President Boakai removed Magdalene Dagoseh. He said the ministry is focusing on the imports that matter most to household budgets.

“We are stepping up monitoring and enforcement and working closely with importers of socially and politically sensitive items—such as petroleum and rice—to help curb inflation,” Yekeson said.

The ministry’s challenge is reach. Its own price circulars warn that “hoarding, undercutting, or arbitrary price increases will not be tolerated.” But the gap between the official ceiling and what people pay in Gbarpolu suggests that warning carries less weight the further a filling station is from Monrovia.

The investor read-through

For investors, this shows the limits of Liberia’s improved macroeconomic picture. Low inflation, a firmer currency and a budget of more than US$1 billion matter for creditors and rating agencies. But Konneh warned that public anger rises when people cannot see those gains in their own costs, and he called that anger legitimate.

Fuel is the most visible example of that gap. Monrovia’s prices compare well with its neighbours’. In much of the interior, prices are among the highest in the region.

World.title: Liberia: No Specific Target- Speaker Koon Tells CSO Group As He Receives War and Economic Crimes Court Petition, Says Bills Still Under Committee Review
World.content:
Capitol Building, Capitol Hill, October 26, 2026 – As he received a petition on the War and Economic Crimes Court from a CSO group under the banner National Council of Chiefs Support Office and the Liberia Massacre Survivors Association (LIMASA), House Speaker Richard Nagbe Koon tells the petitioners that all is on course at the level of the Legislature for the actualization of the proposal.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

Receiving the document on Monday at his Capitol Building office in Monrovia, the Speaker of the 55th Legislature assured petitioners that the proposed War and Economic Crimes Court bills remain on the Legislature’s agenda.



LIMASA, the petitioners, was accompanied by a host of other civil society organizations and war victims, who are seeking justice, national healing, reconciliation and accountability for crimes committed during Liberia’s civil conflicts. The move signals the critical importance of the ensuring accountability from what many believe was a nonsensical civil war that ravaged the country for more than 14 years.

Speaker Koon acknowledged the concerns raised by victims and survivors across the country’s 15 counties and said the House leadership understands the importance of the proposed legislation.

Status Of The Proposal

He pointed out that the bills are currently before the relevant committees of both Houses and are undergoing thorough scrutiny.

According to him, the committees have already conducted public hearings and are seeking funding to conduct additional consultations to gather firsthand information from affected communities before submitting comprehensive reports to plenary.

He noted that the proposed legislation involves technical and complex issues that require careful review, adequate public consultation, and detailed explanations to enable lawmakers to make informed decisions.

No Specific Target

Speaker Koon clarified that the proposed bills are not intended to target any particular individual, tribe or religion, but is intended establish a legal framework for addressing war-related and economic crimes and to strengthen the rule of law.

“The committees are expected to continue consultations after the passage of the national budget, with further legislative discussions anticipated in the first session in January 2027. But what I can tell you is that the proposal is not targeted at any specific individual or group,” asserted the House Speaker.

The Montserrado County Electoral District #11 Representative and head of the Liberian Legislature among other things, assured the petitioners of the House’s commitment to responsible deliberation and encouraged them to continue engaging lawmakers throughout the process.

What The Petitioners Say?

Presenting the document, the petitioners emphasized the importance of establishing the proposed court to provide justice for victims and survivors, promote national reconciliation, and deter future atrocities.

They also highlighted concerns raised during public awareness engagements across Liberia’s 15 counties, noting that victims and survivors continue to seek accountability and closure for atrocities committed during the country’s civil wars.

The petitioners then appealed to the House leadership to prioritize the bills, arguing that their enactment would demonstrate Liberia’s commitment to addressing historical injustices and strengthening the rule of law.

World.title: Liberia: Dolphin Killed, Butchered Before NaFAA Rescue Team Arrived
World.content:
Monrovia — What began as a moment of hope for conservationists ended in frustration after a dolphin that washed ashore at Miami Beach in Monrovia was killed and butchered before a rescue team from the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority (NaFAA) arrived at the scene.

By Francis Boayue

Videos circulating on social media initially showed a group of men gathered around the stranded dolphin. The men appeared to be keeping watch over the animal and were heard saying they were waiting for fisheries authorities to arrive and take it to safety.



Following public attention to the incident, NaFAA announced that it had dispatched a team to the beach to respond to the situation.

In a Facebook post, the authority said it had sent a team to Miami Beach to address the reported incident involving a dolphin that had come ashore.

NaFAA also thanked Martin K. N. Kollie and his Verity Team for bringing the incident to public attention through social media. The authority commended community members for initially responding to the stranded animal.

“We extend our sincere appreciation to Martin K. N. Kollie and his Verity Team for bringing this matter to public attention through social media. We also commend the community members who took the initiative to act promptly in serving as first responders,” the authority said.

However, the initial optimism surrounding the rescue effort quickly faded.

In a subsequent Facebook update, NaFAA disclosed that the dolphin had not survived before its team reached the location. According to the authority, community members who had initially assisted the animal later killed it and shared the meat among themselves.

“It’s sad to report that the dolphin discovered on Miami Beach earlier 2day did not survive before our team arrived at the scene. The community helped but later killed and shared it,” NaFAA stated.

The circumstances surrounding the dolphin’s death, including whether any individuals will face legal consequences, were not immediately clear.

Conservation Concerns

The incident has renewed concerns about the protection of wildlife and marine species in Liberia, where conservation efforts continue to face challenges from the hunting and consumption of animals.

Dolphins play important roles in marine ecosystems, but stranded animals can be vulnerable to injury, stress, and human interference. Wildlife experts generally advise members of the public not to kill, handle unnecessarily or attempt to return stranded dolphins to the water without guidance from trained responders.

Instead, members of the public should notify the relevant authorities and keep a safe distance while awaiting assistance.

The Miami Beach incident also raises questions about public awareness of wildlife protection laws and the response mechanisms available when protected animals are found in distress.

Although the government has designated certain wildlife species for protection, animals continue to be hunted or killed for consumption and commercial purposes in some communities.

Another Wildlife Incident

The dolphin’s death comes less than a week after a crocodile was reportedly killed in a suburb of Monrovia.

In that incident, the Forestry Development Authority (FDA) reportedly intervened and burned the crocodile in an effort to discourage its continued consumption. It was not immediately clear whether anyone was arrested in connection with the incident.

The two cases have drawn attention to the challenges facing authorities responsible for protecting wildlife and enforcing conservation measures.

For conservationists, the death of the dolphin underscores the need for stronger public education, faster responses to reports of stranded animals and greater awareness of the importance of protecting vulnerable species.

While community members initially appeared willing to help the dolphin, its eventual killing before the arrival of trained responders turned a potential rescue into a loss for marine conservation.

The National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority had not announced any arrests or further enforcement measures in connection with the incident at the time of publication.

World.title: KEEP Liberia Opens Reading Room Stocked With Over 2,000 Books at Barnesville Public High School
World.content:
Monrovia – The Kids’ Educational Engagement Project (KEEP Liberia), through its Promoting Literacy Pillar, has dedicated a fully equipped reading room (mini library) at Barnesville Public High School, marking another significant milestone in its ongoing effort to strengthen literacy development among children and young people across Liberia.

The reading room was made possible through the generous support of Mount Pleasant Baptist Church in the United States of America, a longstanding partner committed to advancing educational opportunities and literacy initiatives for Liberian students.

Stocked with more than 2,000 books, the newly dedicated reading room provides students with a safe, inspiring, and conducive environment to read, learn, research, and expand their knowledge. The facility is expected to play a vital role in improving students’ reading fluency, comprehension, vocabulary development, and overall literacy skills while cultivating a lifelong love for reading.



In addition to supporting literacy efforts, Mount Pleasant Baptist Church donated five HP laptops to support KEEP Liberia’s Digital Literacy Program, further enhancing access to technology and digital learning opportunities for students.

Speaking during the dedication ceremony, KEEP Liberia’s Executive Director, Brenda Brewer Moore, expressed profound appreciation to Mount Pleasant Baptist Church for its unwavering commitment to education and literacy advancement in Liberia.

Before

“We are deeply grateful to Mount Pleasant Baptist Church for partnering with us to invest in the future of Liberia’s children. This reading room is more than just a space filled with books; it is a gateway to knowledge, imagination, opportunity, and lifelong learning (wealth),” Moore stated.

She encouraged school administrators, teachers, and students to make full use of the facility and to take collective responsibility for its upkeep and maintenance.

“The better this reading room is maintained and utilized, the stronger our commitment will be to continue supporting this institution through our Digital Literacy Program and the establishment of reading clubs that will host regular Saturday reading sessions,” she added.

Representatives of the education sector, including the District Education Officer, the Principal of Barnesville Public High School, and the Parent-Teacher Association Chairperson, praised both KEEP Liberia and Mount Pleasant Baptist Church for their vision and investment in education.

Before

According to school authorities, Barnesville Public High School, which was established in the early 1930s, had never previously benefited from a library facility. School leaders described the new reading room as a transformative development that opens new pathways for learning and academic achievement.

“This is a historic moment for our school. For decades, our students have gone without a library. Today, KEEP Liberia and Mount Pleasant Baptist Church have opened the doors of literacy and opportunity for our students,” one school representative remarked.

The Barnesville dedication adds to a growing number (53) of reading rooms established by KEEP Liberia in schools and communities throughout the country. Through its Promoting Literacy Pillar, the organization continues to expand access to books, create reader-friendly learning environments, support literacy instruction, and foster a culture of reading among children and youth.

The organization has also been integrating digital learning opportunities into its literacy programs, ensuring that young people are equipped with both foundational reading skills and the technological competencies needed to succeed in the modern world.

As KEEP Liberia continues its literacy drive, the organization remains committed to building partnerships that empower students, strengthen schools, and create sustainable opportunities for learning.

With every reading room dedicated, another door is opened to knowledge, imagination, and a brighter future for Liberia’s next generation. “Promoting a Reading Culture.”

World.title: Human Rights Groups Gather in Monrovia to Take Stock of Project Protecting Women Activists as Donor Support Winds Down
World.content:
KTK Two-day ENSURE reflection meeting hears that threats to human rights defenders are not ending even as project funding does

As the ENSURE Project closes this month, Liberian officials, donors and rights advocates gathered in Monrovia with a warning: the threats facing women human rights defenders are outlasting the funding meant to address them.

By Patience M. Jones, [email protected]

The Kvinna till Kvinna Foundation (KTK) is hosting a two-day reflection meeting at the Cape Hotel on October 22–23, under the theme “From Evidence to Action: Reflecting, Learning, Strengthening Collective Action.”



Opening the meeting, KTK Country Director Korto Williams said it should not be treated as routine. “This is not business as usual; this is not a workshop,” she said, explaining that while programs and donor support are ending, “the challenges that we face as human rights defenders are not ending.”

Williams said human rights defenders, women’s rights advocates and civil society groups face “increasing pressures and shrinking resources in a rapidly changing environment.” She described the work as, for many, “a personal commitment and a personal journey” rather than a nine-to-five job.

She said she had brought her niece to the meeting so the young woman could understand the realities of Liberian society. The measure of success, she told participants, is whether the project’s results continue to benefit people long after it has ended, and she urged partners to strengthen the systems, partnerships and leadership that will sustain them.

She thanked the International Development Research Centre (IDRC), the Embassy of Ireland, civil society partners and human rights defenders for making the work possible.

ENSURE was set up to address limited evidence on threats, backlash and rights violations against human rights defenders, particularly women activists, in Liberia and Sierra Leone. Project Lead Beatrice Newland said it ran from November 2024 to October 2026 and focused on research, advocacy, safety and security, and cross-border solidarity.

Working with local partners, and supported by Irish Aid and the Rights and Democracy Research Centre, the project produced two country-specific research reports, identified gaps in legal and institutional protection, and developed advocacy plans.

Its main achievements, Newland said, included sharing research findings across six Liberian counties, engaging stakeholders on the proposed Human Rights Act, and delivering physical and digital security training for defenders. Exchanges between activists in the two countries also strengthened collaboration.

She said the project’s lessons include the need for flexibility, coordination, context-specific approaches and follow-up training. Evidence-based advocacy and sustained partnerships, she added, are essential to protecting defenders and advancing policy reform.

Speaking for the Embassy of Ireland, a representative said Dublin’s partnership with Liberia rests on the conviction that democracy is strongest when every citizen can participate in public life and when rights defenders can work “with confidence and security.” That conviction, the representative said, guides Ireland’s Mission Strategy for 2024–2028.

The representative commended KTK and the Nunn-Lai Research and Consulting Firm for convening the meeting and recalled an August policy dialogue that examined risks to defenders, from physical violence to online harassment, along with gaps in legal protection and institutional capacity. This week’s question, the representative said, is “What has changed because of this work, and what must come next?”

The representative acknowledged that “the backlash against gender equality and women’s rights is real,” and said Liberia is not alone in facing it. Cross-border learning, including with partners in Sierra Leone, will continue, the representative said.

Deputy Minister for Research, Policy and Planning at the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection Curtis V. Dorley said protecting women and girls remains a national priority. He pointed to persistent violence and discrimination, including rape, child marriage, female genital mutilation, intimate partner violence and workplace sexual harassment, and said the government is working to address harmful social norms.

Dorley also flagged technology-facilitated violence as a growing threat, citing online bullying, internet scams and cyber fraud, which he said are damaging the mental health, financial security and dignity of women and girls. He called for public awareness, effective enforcement of relevant laws, accessible reporting mechanisms and support for survivors.

He said women and girls in domestic service, on plantations and at mining sites remain especially vulnerable to exploitation and abuse, and need better access to justice, support services and safe working conditions.

Dorley commended the Legislature for passing the Data Protection and Cybersecurity Act, but urged advocates to push for the Women and Girls Protection Bill, which remains pending. He said the bill is vital to strengthening legal safeguards and the national response to gender-based violence.

The Ministry, he said, remains committed to working with stakeholders to strengthen protection mechanisms, improve services for survivors and promote women’s leadership.

The meeting continues Friday, with participants expected to discuss how to sustain the project’s gains after its conclusion.

World.title: Liberian Environmental Expert Dorbor Wins Praise at UN Biodiversity Conference in Armenia Over Country’s 30×30 Conservation Efforts
World.content:
Sylvia Diamond Dorbor of the Society for the Conservation of Nature of Liberia Draws Positive Audience Reaction During Panel Discussion on Africa’s Biodiversity Future

YEREVAN, Armenia — Liberian environmental expert Sylvia Diamond Dorbor has drawn praise from participants at the ongoing United Nations Biodiversity Conference in Yerevan, Armenia, after outlining Liberia’s longstanding forest conservation commitments, national legal framework and emerging approaches to ensuring that communities benefit financially from protecting the country’s natural resources.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Dorbor, Technical Lead of the Guinean Forests Integrated Program Liberia Project and Sustainable Finance Coordinator at the Society for the Conservation of Nature of Liberia (SCNL), delivered her presentation during a panel discussion examining Africa’s progress toward achieving the global 30×30 biodiversity target by 2030.



Her intervention highlighted Liberia’s extensive forest resources, conservation legislation adopted before the international community agreed on the current global biodiversity framework, and efforts to develop a national action plan that translates international commitments into practical conservation measures.

She also drew attention to a fundamental question confronting countries seeking to protect their forests: how can governments ensure that communities receive predictable and equitable benefits from conservation, particularly when those same communities may already receive financial benefits from commercial activities involving their natural resources?

Participants at the panel discussion responded positively to Dorbor’s presentation, praising her explanation of Liberia’s conservation history and the importance of building on existing national laws to advance international environmental commitments. The reaction highlighted the relevance of Liberia’s experience to wider discussions about biodiversity protection, conservation financing and the role of local communities in safeguarding ecosystems.

The conference brings together government representatives, environmental experts, conservation organizations, researchers and development partners under the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, alongside meetings associated with the Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety and the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-sharing.

During her presentation, Dorbor challenged the perception that Liberia’s commitment to biodiversity conservation began with the adoption of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework in December 2022. She explained that the country had already established policies and legal instruments intended to protect its forests long before the international community adopted the current 30×30 target.

“Liberia’s conservation commitments did not begin with the global 30×30 target. We have a longstanding national policy and legal foundation for forest conservation,” Dorbor told participants.

Her remarks placed Liberia’s conservation ambitions within a historical context, emphasizing that the country’s existing laws and institutions provide an important foundation for meeting contemporary international biodiversity obligations.

According to Dorbor, Liberia’s National Forest Inventory, conducted between 2018 and 2019 and officially launched in 2021, estimated that the country possesses approximately 6.6 million hectares of forest, representing about 69 percent of its total land area.

The figures underscore Liberia’s importance in West Africa’s conservation landscape, particularly because the country contains a substantial portion of the remaining Upper Guinean forest ecosystem, one of the region’s most biologically diverse and environmentally significant landscapes.

Liberia’s forests provide habitats for numerous wildlife species, support the livelihoods of forest-dependent communities and contribute to climate regulation, carbon storage, watershed protection and the maintenance of ecological balance.

However, the continued existence of these forests does not automatically guarantee their long-term protection. Agricultural expansion, logging, mining, infrastructure development and other land-use pressures present continuing challenges for conservation authorities and communities seeking to maintain forest cover while pursuing economic opportunities.

Participants at the panel discussion responded positively to Dorbor’s presentation, praising her explanation of Liberia’s conservation history and the importance of building on existing national laws to advance international environmental commitments. The reaction highlighted the relevance of Liberia’s experience to wider discussions about biodiversity protection, conservation financing and the role of local communities in safeguarding ecosystems

Dorbor argued that addressing these competing demands requires more than the designation of protected areas. It also requires effective institutions, sustainable financing and mechanisms that demonstrate to communities that protecting their natural resources can generate tangible and lasting benefits.

She pointed to legislation adopted more than two decades ago, including the Act for the Establishment of a Protected Forest Areas Network in 2003 and the National Forestry Reform Law of 2006.

“Our national commitment is also reflected in the Act for the Establishment of a Protected Forest Areas Network, adopted in 2003, and the National Forestry Reform Law of 2006. Section 9.1 of the 2006 law provides for a Protected Forest Areas Network and conservation corridors covering at least 30% of existing forested areas,” she explained.

The provisions demonstrate that Liberia had established a national forest conservation objective before the international community adopted the current global biodiversity framework.

Dorbor’s presentation also highlighted the need to distinguish between Liberia’s longstanding legal commitment to protecting a proportion of its forested areas and the broader international 30×30 target.

Adopted in December 2022 at the 15th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework established a series of goals intended to address accelerating biodiversity loss, habitat destruction and ecosystem degradation.

Under Target 3, countries agreed to pursue the effective conservation and management of at least 30 percent of terrestrial and inland-water areas and at least 30 percent of marine and coastal areas by 2030.

The target requires more than simply designating land and water as protected. It calls for conservation systems that are ecologically representative, well-connected and effectively managed, while recognizing the rights and interests of Indigenous peoples and local communities.

For African countries, implementing the target presents significant challenges because conservation objectives must often be balanced against demands for agricultural land, mining, infrastructure development, settlement expansion and other economic activities.

Dorbor said Liberia began developing its national 30×30 Action Plan in 2024 as part of efforts to translate the international commitment into a practical framework suited to the country’s environmental circumstances.

“At the global level, the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework was adopted in December 2022. Its Target 3 calls for at least 30% of terrestrial and inland-water areas, and 30% of marine and coastal areas, to be effectively conserved and managed by 2030,” she said.

“Liberia subsequently embarked on developing its national 30×30 Action Plan in 2024, to translate that global commitment into a practical national pathway,” she added.

The development of the national action plan offers an opportunity to identify conservation priorities, strengthen protected-area management and establish mechanisms through which government institutions, conservation organizations, communities and international partners can coordinate their activities.

It also provides a framework for examining existing conservation arrangements and determining what additional measures may be necessary to achieve meaningful biodiversity protection by the 2030 deadline.

Conservation Benefits and Community Livelihoods

Beyond the legal framework and national action plan, Dorbor used her presentation to raise questions about the financial incentives available to communities that agree to conserve their forests rather than allow them to be used for commercial purposes.

She argued that Liberia must pay closer attention to the difference between the benefits communities receive from commercial resource extraction and the benefits available to them when they protect natural resources.

“I think one of the fundamental issues we need to address is the difference between how Liberia shares the benefits of commercial resource use and how it shares the benefits of conservation,” she said.

Dorbor explained that Liberia’s commercial forestry sector already has an established benefit-sharing framework through which communities receive a share of land rental fees paid by logging companies.

Under this arrangement, communities have used the proceeds to identify and pursue local priorities, including infrastructure and other social services.

However, she questioned whether communities that choose to preserve their forests have access to comparable, predictable benefits that can support their development needs.

“In the commercial forestry sector, we have an established benefit-sharing framework through which communities receive a share of land rental fees paid by logging companies. Communities have used this mechanism to identify priorities, including infrastructure and other social services. But this raises an important question: if communities can receive benefits from the commercial use of their forests, what predictable benefits do they receive when they choose to conserve those same forests instead?” Dorbor asked.

Her argument placed community participation at the center of the biodiversity discussion, suggesting that conservation strategies must address the economic realities facing people who live in and around forest landscapes.

Dorbor’s intervention therefore raised a question with direct implications for Liberia’s conservation policies: how can the country make forest protection economically meaningful to the people whose cooperation is essential to its success?

She linked that question to Liberia’s National Carbon Market Policy, which she said had recently been completed. The policy establishes different benefit-sharing arrangements based on ownership of the resource generating carbon credits.

World.title: ‘Toxic’ ref’s society forces veteran Mwamba to retire
World.content:
Veteran rugby referee Christopher Mwamba has quit Zambian rugby, citing toxic relations and gross insubordination in the Zambia Rugby Referees Society (ZRRS).

Mwamba, who has served the game for over 45 years, has resigned with immediate effect as Interim Vice Chairperson of the ZRRS Interim Committee and retired from all rugby activities in Zambia.

In his resignation letter to Zambia Rugby Union – ZRU – President Chileshe Bweupe, Mwamba said rugby refereeing in the country has become unbearable in the last seven months.

“This has been arrived at because relations in our rugby circles especially in the Zambia Rugby Referees Society have become toxic in the last seven months. In over 45 years involvement in the game of rugby in Zambia, it has never been this terrible and I cannot take it any further,” Mwamba said.

He accused some senior members of the Society of taking issues personally and turning the body into a personal to holder, while junior members have been duped into disrespecting senior officials and disregarding ZRU Game Regulations.

“Some junior members have been duped to behave in a manner where they have no respect for senior members like me – a lot of insubordination and no respect for ZRU Game Regulations,” he said.

Mwamba, a World Rugby accredited Match Official Educator, Citing Commissioner and Level 1 Coach of Match Officials, warned that if the situation remains unchecked, Zambia risks disaster in the development of match officials for Rugby Africa sanctioned competitions.

He said he will also formally inform World Rugby Regional Manager for Rugby Africa English, Mr. Denver Warnes, about his decision.

Mwamba has thanked the ZRU Executive Committee for the opportunity to serve on the interim committee.

The Zambia Rugby Union is yet to comment on this matter.

World.title: Where Is Jay Jay Banda? Mutumba Demands Proof of Life and a Formal Charge
World.content:
Political commentator Dennis Mutumba has called on the authorities to show the public that former Petauke Central MP Emmanuel ‘Jay Jay’ Banda is alive and in lawful custody. He said unverified claims on social media that Mr Banda has been shot dead are fuelling public anxiety and must be answered. Police have said Mr Banda is being held awaiting a formal charge, but no court appearance has yet confirmed his condition. Mr Mutumba said Zambians have a constitutional right to know the whereabouts of a man the State says it brought back from Mozambique.

Speaking in a televised interview, Mr Mutumba said he could not say with certainty whether Mr Banda had been arrested, because most of the available information was coming from social media. He said claims of tight security around a mortuary had added to the speculation. None of these claims has been confirmed by any official source. Mr Mutumba said the surest way to end the rumours was for the authorities to produce Mr Banda and charge him without further delay.

“As Zambians, it’s within our constitutional right to know the whereabouts of this man,” Mr Mutumba said.

The commentator linked the public’s suspicion to the handling of the death of Mutotwe Kafwaya, which he said was initially denied by those responsible for informing the public before it was later announced. That episode, he argued, has left many citizens unwilling to take official statements at face value. He said trust is earned through openness, particularly in politically sensitive cases. A clear and timely statement on Mr Banda’s status, he said, would close the space in which the rumours are spreading.

“Why not wait for the police to do their investigations and then give us a comprehensive statement to say JJ Banda is formally charged on such and such issues?” he asked.

Mr Mutumba questioned why charging Mr Banda was taking so long when he already faces an offence of escaping from lawful custody. He pointed to President Hakainde Hichilema’s own position that suspects should appear before a court within 48 hours of arrest. He said he was not defending Mr Banda’s alleged conduct and expected the former MP to face the full force of the law. His concern, he said, was the professionalism and speed with which the case is being handled.

“I’m not saying that what JJ Banda was doing is right, but I’m looking at professionalism, the quickness of taking these matters so seriously, so that people who have committed serious offences can be taken to court,” Mr Mutumba said.

The commentator did not criticise the operation itself. Asked whether the State had acted within domestic and international law in bringing Mr Banda back from Mozambique, he said it had. That places him at odds with Amnesty International and 24 local and international civil society organisations, which have raised human rights concerns about Mr Banda’s apprehension and transfer. It also puts him alongside a separate consortium of civil society groups, which argued this week that international law cannot shield a suspect from accountability.

Mr Banda has spent much of the past two years before the courts. He was charged in June 2024 with aggravated robbery over the alleged theft of property worth K12,000 in 2015, a non-bailable offence he denies. On the night of 4 August 2024, he escaped from Chipata General Hospital while under the guard of police and correctional officers. He was arrested in Harare three months later and is now reported to face allegations of attempted murder and aggravated robbery following his apprehension in Mozambique.

Police have not publicly responded to the claims circulating on social media. Until Mr Banda appears before a court, the questions raised by Mr Mutumba are likely to persist. A court appearance would settle the rumours about his condition and the debate about delay at the same time. For the authorities, it is also the simplest way to show that the process is being handled by the book.

World.title: Zambia Takes First SADC Regional Cybersecurity Chair
World.content:
ZAMBIA has assumed the first chairpersonship of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) Regional Computer Incident Response Team Steering Committee in a move aimed at strengthening cybersecurity across Southern Africa.

The Zambia Cyber Security Agency says its Director General, Dr Schmidt Chintu, took up the position on September 17, 2026, for the 2026 to 2027 period.

The Agency says the appointment will help Zambia strengthen cooperation with other SADC member states, improve the sharing of cyber threat information and enhance technical expertise to protect citizens, businesses and public institutions.

It says the regional team provides a platform for member states to share information on cyber threats and coordinate responses to cyber incidents that cross national borders.

The Agency says the regional cybersecurity framework was adopted in 2019 and is now being put into operation.

It says Dr Chintu will lead the Steering Committee in strengthening regional cooperation and building a safer digital environment to support public trust, business and economic development.

The Zambia Cyber Security Agency says it remains committed to working with regional partners to strengthen cyber defence and protect digital systems across the region.

World.title: Zambia, IFAW Join Forces to Boost Wildlife Conservation
World.content:
ZAMBIA and the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW) are working to attract more investment into wildlife conservation and tourism to improve the livelihoods of local communities.

This follows a meeting in Lusaka between IFAW President and Chief Executive Officer Azzedine Downes and Ministry of Tourism Permanent Secretary Evans Muhanga.

Mr Muhanga said conservation partnerships were important to Zambia’s target of attracting five million international tourists annually by 2031.

He said communities living alongside wildlife should benefit through job creation, improved livelihoods and tourism opportunities.

Mr Muhanga thanked IFAW for supporting wildlife conservation, infrastructure development, anti-poaching operations and efforts to reduce conflicts between people and wildlife, particularly in the Kasungu-Lukusuzi landscape.

He said IFAW had helped build 51 staff houses across five wildlife management sectors and supported ranger operations and community conservation programmes.

Mr Muhanga called for increased investment in protective fencing, early warning systems and support for communities affected by wildlife.

Meanwhile, Mr Downes said IFAW would continue working with Zambia to help people and wildlife coexist while creating tourism investment opportunities.

He said the organisation would support the country’s tourism growth through international partnerships, new conservation approaches and efforts to promote Zambia’s conservation work globally.

The meeting also welcomed plans by IFAW to open a country office in Zambia.

Both parties called for closer cooperation with traditional leaders to encourage communities to participate in wildlife conservation.

This is contained in a statement issued to the media by Ministry of Tourism Principal Public Relations Officer Nelly Chewe.

World.title: Lusaka Mayor Promotes Lusaka Tourism at Global Summit
World.content:
LUSAKA Mayor Chitambala Mwewa says the city is using local tourism to promote inclusive economic growth.

Speaking at the Global City Tourism Summit 2026 Mayors’ Roundtable in Busan, South Korea, Mr Mwewa said Lusaka, with a population of approximately 3.1 million, offers a rich mix of culture, heritage, local cuisine, commerce and community experiences.

He thanked the City of Busan for its hospitality and praised its transformation from a port city into a global centre for tourism, culture and innovation.

Mr Mwewa said this year’s summit theme, “Local Tourism: Connecting Urban Economies and Tourism Innovation,” aligns with Lusaka’s vision of using tourism to drive inclusive economic growth.

He said the city was linking its tourist attractions with local markets, restaurants, accommodation providers, creative industries and transport services to expand economic opportunities.

Mr Mwewa cited Kabwata Cultural Village, local markets, city food tours and township arts as some of the attractions that could help promote Lusaka’s tourism potential.

He also pointed to investments in waste management and green spaces under the Keep Lusaka Clean, Green and Healthy Campaign as part of efforts to improve the city’s environment.

World.title: Zambia Urged to Embrace Technology for Development
World.content:
TECHNOLOGY and Science Permanent Secretary Brilliant Habeenzu has called for sustained investment in knowledge, innovation, digital infrastructure and human capital to drive economic growth.

Speaking through Director of Technology and Science Dr Larry Mweetwa at the Africa Tech Expo in Lusaka, Dr Habeenzu said emerging technologies, particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI), were already transforming the global economy.

He said recent studies suggest that AI could contribute up to 4.9 percentage points to Africa’s economic growth, while generating productivity gains estimated at one trillion US dollars by 2035.

Dr Habeenzu said Africa could not afford to remain a passive consumer of technology but needed to play an active role in developing and adopting solutions that address the continent’s challenges.

Meanwhile, Acting United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Representative Laurent Rudasingwa said Zambia needed to develop technologies that support the country’s national development agenda.

And Tech Trends Zambia Chief Executive Officer Sandi Chimpala said the Africa Tech Expo had brought together key stakeholders to explore how innovation and emerging technologies could support infrastructure development and create opportunities across Africa.

The Africa Tech Expo is being held under the theme, “Innovation, Infrastructure and Africa’s Next Economy.”

World.title: ZAF Commander Hands Vehicle to Red Arrows Coach
World.content:
ZAMBIA Air Force (ZAF) Commander Lieutenant General Oscar Nyoni has handed over a Toyota Mark X vehicle to Red Arrows head coach Chisi Mbewe.

The vehicle is part of the ZAF fleet allocated to various sections, including the Red Arrows head coach and assistant coach.

Speaking during the handover ceremony, Lieutenant General Nyoni said more vehicles would be allocated to other personnel as funds became available.

He commended Mbewe for his patience and resilience in leading the team.

The handover comes after Red Arrows made history by qualifying for the group stage of the CAF Confederation Cup.

Lieutenant General Nyoni challenged the team to go beyond the group stage and secure a place in the knockout phase of the competition.

Receiving the vehicle, Warrant Officer Class Two Chisi Mbewe thanked the ZAF command for the gesture and pledged to continue working hard.

Mbewe said the technical bench had taken note of the command’s directive to advance beyond the group stage and would work towards achieving that objective.

He said the team’s target was to progress to the knockout stage of the CAF Confederation Cup.

World.title: Government urges guardians and parents to ensure children receive vaccines
World.content:
Kasenengwa District Commissioner (DC) Rachael Phiri has urged parents and guardians in the district to ensure that their children receive all the vaccines that will be administered during the child health week.

Speaking today during the launch of the child health week at Chiparamba Rural Health Centre, Ms Phiri said government spends a lot of money to procure the vaccines hence the need for the parents to take the exercise seriously by allowing their children to be vaccinated.

She said a number of health services will be provided during the week such as Vitamin A supplementation, deworming and routine immunization among others.

“Health workers will be following children in communities to ensure that eligible children receive the necessary care during this period,” the DC said.

Ms Phiri mentioned that the health services that will be provided are meant to protect children’s health and support their growth and development.

The child health week will run from October, 26 to 31st under the theme; “Strengthening Community System and Closing the Last Mile for Every Child.”
