World.title: Harry Kane becomes first Englishman in 25 years to win Ballon d'Or
World.content:
Harry Kane becomes first Englishman in 25 years to win Ballon d'Or

toggle caption i Kin Cheung/AP

LONDON — Harry Kane became the first Englishman in 25 years to win the Ballon d'Or on Monday thanks to his prolific scoring last season.

Kane scored 73 goals for club and country last campaign — he was Europe's top scorer — and smashed scoring records in Germany for Bayern Munich and at the World Cup, where he captained England to a third-place finish.

The 33-year-old Kane says winning the prestigious individual award was built on so much more.

"Anything is possible with hard work, when no one else is watching, to go through the ups and downs, to learn through resilience, determination and self-belief," an emotional Kane said in a message to young players, after reflecting on his early career struggles.

Sponsor Message

"My journey wasn't straightforward. I wasn't the kid who went straight to the top. I had to experience the downs," he added. "I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration as well."

Kane was followed in the voting by Kylian Mbappé, Lamine Yamal — voted best young talent for a third straight year — 2024 winner Rodri and record eight-time winner Lionel Messi.

Kane thanked his teammates, coaches, parents, children — "It's past your bedtime" — and wife Kate, " my best friend. We've been through ups and downs for sure. You're my biggest supporter. You always want the best for me."

Kane led Bayern to the Bundesliga and German Cup double, scoring a hat trick against Stuttgart in the cup final. Bayern also reached the Champions League semifinals.

At the World Cup, he scored six times to pass Gary Lineker as England's all-time leading World Cup scorer and placed himself among the all-time top five in tournament history. His lineup lost to Argentina in the semifinals but beat Mbappé's France for third place, England's best World Cup placing in 60 years.

An Englishman hadn't won the Ballon d'Or since Michael Owen in 2001.

"It's massive for England, for our country. (The ceremony) being here in London was a good omen for me," Kane said. "It's been too long. Certainly (there have been) incredible English players... To put us back on the map, to put us here with this trophy I'm extremely proud. Playing for England is my biggest honor, the thing I love to do the most."

Sponsor Message

England coach Thomas Tuchel told Kane the Three Lions are "lucky to have you as our leader."

"I ran out of superlatives to describe your performances a long time ago, but I'm delighted to see that you have now been formally recognized by the football world," Tuchel said.

Fans packed the streets and climbed light poles near the London Palladium, where the event was held, for a glimpse of the arriving athletes. Kane stopped to sign autographs on his way in.

They stayed through the ceremony and chanted Kane's name as he left the theater near Oxford Circus after midnight.

Kane planned to celebrate with family and friends, but just a little.

"We have a cup game on Wednesday so it can't get too messy," Kane said, noting he has an early Tuesday flight back to Munich in time for team training.

Monday's ceremony was held in London for the first time in recognition of the inaugural winner 70 years ago, England's Stanley Matthews in 1956.

toggle caption i Kin Cheung/AP

Putellas hat trick of awards

Earlier, Spain star Alexia Putellas won her record-equaling third women's Ballon d'Or after leading her former club Barcelona to multiple trophies last season including the Women's Champions League.

Putellas, who joined London City Lionesses in the offseason, also helped Spain win the Women's Nations League last December.

The 32-year-old midfielder ended Spain teammate Aitana Bonmati's three-year reign.

Putellas won the prestigious award in 2021 and 2022, tore her ACL and saw Bonmati rise to stardom. Bonmati, who completed her women's Ballon d'Or three-peat in 2025, was not on this year's shortlist after breaking her leg in December.

There wasn't a women's Ballon d'Or until 2018, when Ada Hegerberg won it.

Putellas urged young players to approach the sport with "love and passion."

"Believe in yourself, that's the most important thing," she said. "If you have a dream, go for it, even if at some point you have to start from zero."

Sponsor Message

Putellas had joined Barcelona in 2012 and called her time at the Catalan club "something special."

"I'm really grateful for having 14 seasons as a player (at Barcelona)," she said. "What I experienced last year was like a perfect story."

World.title: Olivia Chow races to victory as head of progressive new Toronto council
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

CBC News projects that Olivia Chow has been re-elected as mayor of Toronto, defeating former councillor Brad Bradford for the city's top job.

Olivia Chow is preparing to lead Toronto for another four years, after an emphatic victory over former councillor Brad Bradford Monday night.

Chow will oversee a progressive, new-look council with several of her key allies elected, putting her in a strong position to pursue her agenda.

The returning mayor started the year looking comfortably ahead, before it appeared Bradford could surge into the mayor's chair.

In the end, she won a massive victory — netting roughly 530,000 votes, according to the unofficial results (official results will come once they've been certified by the city clerk).

A close race and new messaging

While Bradford received just one per cent of the vote in the 2023 mayoral byelection, he gained on Chow through 2026.

As the race heated up after Labour Day, the gap between challenger and incumbent appeared to narrow significantly.

The timing of the surge seemed like it would be good for Bradford, coming toward the end of the race, when advance voting appeared to be more than 70 per cent higher than the 2023 mayoral byelection .

But as polling suggested the wind was in Bradford's sails, the Chow campaign settled on a clear message about the challenger and his platform, particularly his pledge to create a public utility company to handle the city's water and wastewater.

WATCH | The Toronto election race was frenetic. Here's how it looked at the end: Toronto mayoral candidates make final push ahead of election day | Duration closed caption 2:40 With just three days to go until election day, Toronto’s leading mayoral candidates were back on the campaign trail, making their final push Friday. With the finish line in sight, Olivia Chow and Brad Bradford took time to reflect on their humble beginnings. Dale Manucdoc reports.

Bradford said the plan would help raise funds for city hall and cut costs for residents, but Chow said it would mean the city losing control of an asset that is working well and opens the door to privatization.

That message may have struck a nerve with Torontonians, said political strategist Blue Knox, who served as former mayor John Tory's director of communications.

"Canadians like for their public institutions to stay public," she said.

"Her campaign was able — whether you agree with it or not — to very clearly distill their attack on one of Brad Bradford's promises."

Olivia Chow, left, and Brad Bradford were the two front-runners to be Toronto's mayor in a race polls suggested was close at the end. (CBC)

Erin Morrison, vice president of Texture Communications and a Chow supporter, said she thought the policy was a "serious mistake" from the Bradford campaign.

"That really started to play a role in the campaign with about 10 days to go," she said.

"Chow, to her credit, really knew that that was problematic to her voters … and made an issue out of it."

Strong get-out-the-vote operation

The Chow campaign was able to rely on a formidable team to help spread her campaign message and her criticism of her opponent.

She ran a "disciplined campaign," Knox said.

Even the Bradford campaign acknowledged on election night the combination of Progress Toronto, Ontario NDP supporters and unions backing Chow was a formidable force to reckon with.

WATCH | Olivia Chow celebrates victory with supporters: 'I will work every day to earn your trust,' says Chow during victory speech | Duration closed caption 1:48 Speaking to a crowd at The Great Hall, newly re-elected Mayor Olivia Chow made her promise to the city: "I will stand up for you and I will work every day to earn your trust."

"It's tough organizationally," Bradford's head of communications Laryssa Waler said shortly before polls closed.

"They know how to get them out to vote. They have union support, they're very, very organized."

Mandate to stay on the same path

While Bradford's camp had offered a slew of new ideas, particularly around the city's finances, Chow's camp stayed close to her record: renters, transit fares and a school nutrition program.

Knox said the Chow campaign's decision to stick to a few key promises building on the work of her first term in office will make for a smoother transition.

It means Chow's "hands aren't tied" to a series of rigid campaign pledges and she will get to "be flexible to different circumstances that come up."

Bradford conceded to Chow on election night. (Prasanjeet Chaudhary/CBC)

Chow pledged a 10-ride fare cap for riders on the TTC , enhanced protections for renters , a school lunch program and tax cuts for independent grocers. She also said she would continue work to build more affordable housing.

Delivering those promises will be made easier by a council still relatively aligned with Chow's core goals.

A number of high-profile progressive allies, including Nate Erskine-Smith and Mike Layton, Chow's own stepson, will join her at city hall.

WATCH | Why Olivia Chow thinks 'the cost of living is a problem': 'The cost of living is a problem': Olivia Chow's pitch to Toronto (in her own words) | Duration closed caption 18:37 Olivia Chow is making her pitch to stay in office, anchoring her platform on affordable housing and a city-wide lunch program. Speaking on CBC Radio's Metro Morning with Chris Glover, the incumbent detailed her vision for a second term — following our interview earlier this week with candidate Brad Bradford

Morrison said the 2026-2030 council should be one Chow can lead on most issues — getting her agenda through without needing to resort to strong mayor powers, which she has said she will not use.

"I think that tonight is good news for Chow in the sense that she's got even more progressive allies on council," she said.

"I think she's going to find it an easy council to work with."

World.title: N.S. woman refused to comply with phone scammer, so would-be fraudster swatted her house
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Truro-area woman says she is shaken and terrified after a would-be fraudster sent heavily armed police from two different departments to her home over the weekend.

The original call seemed like a routine phone scam. A woman claiming to be from the CIBC fraud department called Lynn Clark Colpitts and said someone had applied for a credit card in her name. In order to block it, she advised Clark Colpitts to download an app called CIBC Guard.

Colpitts said she didn’t feel comfortable doing that or sharing any information over the phone. While she was on the call she conferenced her IT expert from work into the call who told her to do nothing until she contacted her branch.

"I told her politely, I said I'm sorry I have to go by what my IT guy told me to do. And then she used some profanity toward me,” Clark Colpitts said.

“She called me a f-----g b---h, twice, and then hung up on me.”

Clark Colpitts figured she’d dodged a scam but 20 minutes later things escalated.

'She was threatening me the whole time'

“She calls me back and says, ‘I've got a surprise for you. Go to your front door. There's a surprise waiting for you there.’ And I'm like, ‘What are you talking about?’"

Sure enough, as she stepped onto her porch she saw heavily armed officers from the Colchester District RCMP and Truro Police in her yard and on the street.

“They holler at me and ask me who I am,” Clark Colpitts said. “And I tell them who I am and they tell me to get down to the end of the driveway.”

Several officers entered her home while Clark Colpitts tried to explain there was no such threat. While police checked on the property the fraudster kept up the phone calls to Clark Colpitts. She held it up so police could hear it.

“She was threatening me the whole time saying that she wasn't done with me and that this was gonna keep going on.”

RCMP explained to Clark Colpitts that they’d gotten a call about a hostage taking — and shooting — at her address.

Calls, emails and death threats

“It appears to be a level of retribution by the fraudsters in this case,” said Staff Sgt. Marc Rose, commander of the Colchester District RCMP.

“[It appears] they did this to cause her harm and pain and distress by having the police respond to her residence all because she didn’t follow the original instructions on the phone."

The calls from the female fraudster continued on Friday and into Saturday.

Staff Sgt. Marc Rose is the commander of the Colchester District RCMP. (Galen McRae/CBC)

“She just kept going on and on and on. It was relentless," Clark Colpitts said.

And there were emails too. Death threats.

Clark Colpitts is a realtor. She got a phone call from a coworker who said someone had hacked into their agency’s website, took down Clark Colpitts's photograph and replaced it with what Clark Colpitts says was a “deformed animal.” All of it has left her scared to be in her own home.

Swatting attack

David Shipley, CEO and co-founder of Beauceron Security, which is based in Fredericton, says Canadians have lost tens of millions of dollars to phone scams, but this is the first time he’s aware of it escalating into a “swatting” attack. That’s when a person calls police to someone’s property to report a crime or emergency that is entirely fiction.

“This seems like a criminal who was definitely not having a good day and decided to dramatically escalate the dangerousness and seriousness of this situation,” Shipley said.

“I would argue that this is a form of terrorism,” he said. “Canadians aren't used to having the SWAT team from the police department show up with assault rifles and body armour and riot shields to their front door. That's incredibly, incredibly traumatic.”

Rose said police have to take these calls at face value and deliver the appropriate response.

“We've offered victim support services to [Clark Colpitts] and we are working with our law enforcement partners in other countries — and in Canada — to determine if this connects to other offences and try to determine who's responsible for this.”

CIBC told CBC News in a statement that there is no app called "CIBC Guard" and that it would never contact customers requesting personal or financial information, or request you download an app. It urged people to be extremely cautious when dealing with unsolicited emails, texts or phone calls, and not to rely on caller ID.

The bank said it's actively working to educate clients about impersonation and other scams, and it urges people to contact 911 if there is an urgent threat to their safety or the safety of others.

Meanwhile Clark Colpitts says she's traumatized.

“There's so many things that could have gone badly wrong.”

MORE TOP STORIES

World.title: Cleveland-Cliffs says Stelco in 'full compliance' with commitments to Ottawa, wants to meet with Joly
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stelco’s American parent company said in a news release on Tuesday morning that after "an exhaustive review of its compliance with each of its 34 undertakings," it is in "full compliance" with the obligations it made under the Investment Canada Act when it bought Stelco in 2024.

This comes after Canada’s Industry Minister Mélanie Joly last week gave Cleveland Cliffs a 15-day deadline to reverse layoffs before turning to the courts.

Cleveland-Cliffs said late last month that it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers as it idles certain steel production at Hamilton-based Stelco.

In a demand letter sent to Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs on Thursday, Joly says the company is violating its commitments under the Investment Canada Act.

In Tuesday’s release, Cleveland Cliffs said "Stelco’s performance exceeds the commitments that were made at the time of the acquisition. This includes the employment undertakings."

The company also said that it asked for a meeting with Joly and Cleveland-Cliffs chairman and CEO Lourenco Goncalves "to discuss a path toward resuming full employment of the 175 workers in Hamilton who have been temporarily laid off." The release said "notwithstanding her publicly stated willingness to sit down, the Minister has not yet responded to this request."

Goncalves said the company wants "to find a solution for Hamilton and its workers as soon as possible and believes common sense trade policy will make this a reality."

Strong 3rd-quarter results

While the company has said the layoffs are required to ensure its survival, Cleveland-Cliffs said last week that Stelco's third quarter this year was its "strongest" since it acquired the Hamilton plant.

"Third quarter was Stelco's strongest ... since we acquired the company two years ago. The Canadian hot-rolled market has improved substantially," Goncalves said in a statement on Oct. 19.

The company said the planned layoffs are in order to "ensure the survival" of the company, as U.S. tariffs on steel squeeze its sales. But Joly has dismissed that reasoning.

"Let me be clear: no act of God or change in market conditions can relieve Cleveland-Cliffs of the commitments it made to Canada. Those commitments are not optional," she said in her statement.

World.title: Canadian 'tremendously sorry' after spending stolen crypto on Lamborghini, BMWs, jewelry
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 20-year-old who conned cryptocurrency holders out of millions of dollars — and lived large as a teenager in Florida with "extravagant" partying and access to a private jet and luxury cars — could soon be headed home to Canada.

A U.S. federal judge in Miami on Monday sentenced Trenton Richard David (Trent) Johnston to time served after he pleaded guilty to a money laundering conspiracy and handed over $3.8 million US worth of stolen crypto.

Johnston, then 19, was seated in the back of a Rolls-Royce Cullinan SUV that smelled of "freshly burned marijuana" when he was arrested in March , according to court documents. He's been in custody ever since.

U.S. Homeland Security Investigations found Johnston, a Canadian citizen, impersonated Google tech support staff and representatives of crypto firms to convince unwitting victims to share the codes to their cryptocurrency wallets.

The scheme made him a fortune.

Johnston was arrested after he was found with suspected amphetamine tablets in a Hermes bag while seated in the back of this Rolls-Royce Cullinan. (EpicVIN)

Prosecutors detailed 'extravagant' lifestyle

In one instance in March, Johnston and an unnamed co-conspirator swindled a victim in California out of his life savings — 185 bitcoin, or the equivalent of about $13 million US at the time, court documents say.

"We actually smacked a 185btc target today," Johnston wrote in a series of text messages to his accomplice, according to a criminal complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Miami. "Club feels mad good after today."

"And we ain't done," he added.

Prosecutors said Johston splurged on "an extravagant nightlife and entertainment lifestyle" while living in the Miami area, where he relocated in 2024.

Some of his big-ticket purchases are laid out in court documents: a high-powered Lamborghini Aventador SVJ, two BMWs, jewelry and a private jet rental.

He didn't hide the ruse. According to a witness interviewed by investigators, Johnston showed others how he carried out the thefts by sharing his screen over the social platform Discord.

Johnston's defence lawyer Brooke C. Watson said in a recent court filing that after his arrest, the Canadian "turned over all of the stolen cryptocurrency in his possession," approximately $3.8 million US in bitcoin and ether, another type of cryptocurrency.

"Mr. Johnston quickly admitted his conduct and is tremendously sorry for what he has done," Watson wrote.

Johnston had overstayed his 12-month U.S. tourist visa after crossing from Fort Erie, Ont., to Buffalo, N.Y., in October 2024 at age 18. But the lawyer revealed in a court filing last week that Johnston's scheme started months earlier — when he was just 17 — in January 2024.

In a court filing before sentencing, a defence lawyer for Johnston included pictures titled 'Trenton Johnston, growing up in Canada.' The name of his hometown is redacted in the court documents. (U.S. District Court, Southern District of Florida)

Hometown redacted in court documents

Watson did not respond to CBC News when asked where in Canada Johnston is from. His hometown and the names of his parents — a mechanic and a hair stylist — are redacted in court documents filed last week ahead of sentencing.

In a plea deal, federal prosecutors agreed to withdraw a wire fraud conspiracy charge in exchange for Johnston's guilty plea to one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. The U.S. Attorney's Office for the Southern District of Florida had previously announced that Johnston faced 20 years in prison if convicted on both counts.

Prosecutors later said Johnston provided "substantial assistance in the investigation and prosecution" of other unnamed individuals.

He still faces a drug possession charge from Florida state prosecutors stemming from amphetamine pills found in a Hermes bag at the time of his March arrest in the back of that Rolls-Royce Cullinan in North Miami.

It's unclear when Johnston will be released from custody.

He already agreed to a removal order issued in April by a U.S. immigration judge.

Eventually, Johnston is expected to be handed over to the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to be deported to Canada.

If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

World.title: Yukon photographer captures footage of caribou carrying dead rival in its antlers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains graphic images of wildlife.

Earlier this month, Yukon-based wildlife photographer Peter Mather was on assignment south of Whitehorse to film caribou when he noticed a bear acting unusually aggressive.

“It was huffing and puffing and making noises and we had to scare it off,” Mather said.

Then, another bear came through.

WATCH | Yukon photographer captures caribou carrying remains after antler entanglement: Yukon photographer captures caribou carrying remains after antler entanglement | Duration closed caption 1:33 A Yukon photographer caught sight of a caribou carrying the remains of another caribou entangled in its horns. Peter Mather captured the unique images in early October in the high mountains south of Whitehorse. He spent 10 days filming caribou rutting on the traditional territory of the Kwanlin Dün First Nation as part of a project with the Southern Lakes Caribou Recovery Plan.

“When I saw that second bear there, I’m like ‘Oh, there’s probably some sort of dead caribou up there’,” Mather said.

He sent a drone up to see what was happening.

“I was just shocked to see … there’s two caribou with their antlers locked together, and one of them is dead,” he said.

He said he watched a bear nearby try to attack the caribou, but the surviving bull would scare the bear off.

Mather captured a variety of wildlife as they fed on the carcass of the dead bull caribou. Here, a bear and a conspiracy of ravens are seen. (Submitted by Peter Mather)

Mather said he watched this bull caribou for days.

“Over the four days that [dead] caribou disappeared,” Mather said.

“There were foxes … ravens, golden eagles were eating it for four days."

He said on the last day, a pack of wolves arrived at the scene. He believes they got much of the last of the carcass.

“In some ways, [they] kind of freed up this other caribou who could kind of walk away at the end, with two heads,” Mather said.

At one point, a fox stopped by for a meal from the dead caribou. (Submitted by Peter Mather)

Locking antlers not unheard of

Mather said after the wolves arrived and feasted, the living caribou disappeared, and he couldn’t find it.

His work was to record the rut, mating season for caribou that often involve the males fighting one another, with the Southern Lakes Caribou Recovery Team and the Kwanlin Dün First Nation.

Lars Jessup, a biologist with the Southern Lakes Caribou Recovery Project, said this incident happened in a season where bull caribou are especially vulnerable.

“The rut season is the most dangerous time of year for bull caribou … they work really hard in the rut and the predators are usually around during the rut.”

He said bulls locking antlers is somewhat common, describing finding skulls and skeletons of caribou with locked antlers in the past.

“It’s probably more common that when that happens that they both die, not that one of them would live,” Jessup said, calling the living caribou “lucky.”

His time with the extra weight is also coming to an end, Jessup said.

“If he makes it another month or so, he’s likely to drop those antlers and lose the extra weight, and should be fine through winter,” Jessup said.

“By the time people usually see them down the mountains in and around Christmas time … the bulls are usually bald.”

Eventually, other animals managed to free the surviving caribou from having to carry the extra weight of another bull. (Submitted by Peter Mather)

A metaphor for the herd's resiliency

This particular caribou is part of the Ibex herd, Jessup said, one of four caribou herds that make up the southern lakes caribou herds.

It is protected by the southern lakes caribou recovery project, which has continued for more than 30 years.

“The herds have done really well to recover over the last three decades, through all kinds of hard work and effort,” Jessup said.

However, he said there were concerns the natural ebb and flow of the caribou population was in an ebb, as they haven’t seen many calves in the last five years.

For Mather, the photographer, the footage he captured of that one caribou surviving, gives him some hope.

“For me, it’s like a metaphor for the whole herd, that he’s just resilient, just a really, really resilient caribou.”

World.title: Why a spate of gun-for-hire shootings in Toronto were likely paid for by Iran
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A CBC News investigation has pinpointed a dozen politically-motivated gun-for-hire shootings in Toronto that appear to have been financed by the Iranian government.

The attacks targeted synagogues, a school and businesses in the Greater Toronto Area, as well as the U.S. Consulate in the city's downtown.

With many of the shootings coming in the hours and days after the United States and Israel began bombing Iran on Feb. 28 and assassinated the country's Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

No one was injured in the Toronto shootings, all of which bore the hallmarks of gun-for-hire incidents: early morning attacks where suspects arrived via stolen cars and emptied handguns into building entranceways, while they — or their accomplices — filmed the acts on a phone.

WATCH | The full CBC News investigation into gun-for-hire crimes in Toronto: There’s a gig economy for gunmen in Toronto. Is Iran hiring them? | Duration closed caption 9:47 A CBC News investigation has obtained exclusive new footage of a high-profile shooting outside the U.S. consulate in Toronto and uncovered some of the answers about who might be behind a surge in politically motivated gun-for-hire crimes in the city.

Toronto Police, the RCMP and CSIS have been investigating whether a foreign power instigated the politically-motivated attacks. But while some of the alleged trigger men have been arrested and charged, it has been harder to determine just who was paying them.

The gun-for-hire model, where shootings are arranged via encrypted apps and intermediaries, provides several layers of separation between the client and the criminal.

"We have heard information that there may be foreign actors that are involved. We are investigating every angle," said Chief Superintendent Joe Matthews, who is overseeing the Toronto Police Service investigation.

"At this point, I'm not willing to confirm or deny that piece of it, but what I will say is that we don't think there's a very direct connection between the financier and the perpetrator on the street."

CBC News spent weeks researching a slew of shootings in Toronto, obtaining court files where arrests have been made, and building profiles of the accused. Most of the suspects face charges for multiple attacks. Many are young — ranging in age from 15 to their early 20s.

What emerged was a pattern — shootings concentrated in the same corners of the city, over the same night — directed at both political and non-political targets. In several incidents, synagogues and Jewish-owned businesses were hit shortly before, or after, attacks on nearby business and residential addresses associated with waste management giant, Green For Life (GFL).

Toronto Police say ballistic tests confirm that link.

“We're seeing firearms that are being used in multiple shootings that aren't just geopolitical targeted, they are crossing over with GFL,” Matthews told CBC News.

All of which points to the same people — hired guns — having carried out both types of attacks.

In recent years, the Iranian government and its intelligence service have been linked to plots and attacks in Germany, the Netherlands, the U.K., Australia and the United States.

Last May, the FBI arrested Mohammad Baqer al-Saadi, whom they claim is a senior member of Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), a militia group controlled by Iran's Revolutionary Guard. He now faces six terrorism related charges.

The indictment filed in New York State , alleges he helped plan and co-ordinate at least 18 attacks in Europe, as well as two more in Canada — the March 2026 shooting at the U.S. Consulate in Toronto and an assault on an unnamed synagogue.

Police cordoned off the street in front of the U.S. Consulate in Toronto on July 27. They said a firearm was discharged at the building in the early morning hours. (Paul Smith/CBC)

In June, Canada issued a joint statement with 20 other nations , condemning Iran's "lethal plotting and other malign actions" in Europe, North America and Australia.

"The relationship between Iranian security services and international and local criminal groups is long standing," the statement read. "Their use of these groups is deplorable."

Still, allegations of Iranian subterfuge continue, most recently in the U.K., following a foiled plot to attack a Royal Air Force base in England.

The Iranian-linked attacks follow the same blueprint that Russia has been using to sow havoc in Europe since its invasion of Ukraine, said Keir Giles, a security analyst at Chatham House, an independent policy institute in London.

"Certainly the Russian use of this kind of approach, they pushed the boundaries further and faster," said Giles. "But inevitably, once a technique or a method of achieving these nefarious aims has been demonstrated, other people will latch on."

Gun-for-hire attacks, or Violence as a Service (VAAS) as it is also known, have been supercharged by the internet and the spread of encrypted communication apps, Giles said.

"It's always been the case that you could recruit willing, or unwilling, or even unknowing dupes to carry out your attacks for you," he said. "But it's become vastly easier to spread your network, to actually reach and recruit them at really, very little cost."

CBC News reached out to Iran’s Foreign Ministry to ask about Tehran's alleged involvement in the Toronto attacks, but did not receive a response. The Iranian government has dismissed past claims that it has sponsored violence around the world.

Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto (BAYT), was one of the synagogues that was attacked in early March 2026. Its front doors and windows peppered with gunfire late on a Friday night.

A bullet hole in a glass door at Beth Avraham Yoseph of Toronto (BAYT) synagogue following a March 2026 gun-for-hire attack. (Submitted by BAYT)

Rabbi Daniel Korobkin says there was anger and frustration following the shooting, but that the congregation refuses to be intimidated.

"We recognize that there are many players that are making Israel and Jews as the pariah of the story. We're used to it," Korobkin said. "It's not going to deter us from being Jews. It's not going to deter us from coming to synagogue."

Korobkin is aware that the attack on his synagogue may have been ordered and paid for by someone living thousands of miles away. But to him, it hardly matters.

"I don't think it really makes a difference whether the person who hates us is pulling the trigger, or paying a person to pull the trigger," he said. "The end result is the same and we just want it to stop and we need to figure out how we can control it in the future."

Jonathon Gatehouse can be contacted via email at jonathon.gatehouse@cbc.ca, or reached via the CBC's digitally encrypted Securedrop system at https://www.cbc.ca/securedrop/

World.title: Nopes to the nine? Blue walls? Five takeaways from Alberta's referendum results
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The “strong mandates” that Premier Danielle Smith requested on her nine referendum questions never materialized.

But aside from soft support, there might be another reason Smith is expressing reluctance to act quickly, even on the immigration questions where she won a majority.

Consider that Smith’s own government mandate isn’t derived from the popular vote — it’s based on prevailing in a majority of Alberta’s 87 seats.

And sifting through the riding results from all the referendum questions, some apparent political signals emerge.

Here are some takeaways:

Ridings say no to seven of nine

Smith has signalled she’ll act most quickly on the ballot measure that got the most support — Question 5, to require proof of Canadian citizenship when voting in provincial elections (58 per cent support).

She’s also intent to continue wresting from Ottawa more provincial control over immigration to Alberta, as Question 1 suggested (55 per cent support).

The victory margins were tighter on Questions 2, 3 and 4, to variously restrict social services and financial supports for temporary residents. But on each of those questions, a slight majority of ridings went no — meaning that while four of Smith’s questions failed in terms of total vote, seven of nine would have lost if this was a riding-by-riding contest.

Edmonton was almost uniformly opposed to those temporary resident questions, and only six Calgary ridings were supportive of them.

Twelve Calgary ridings had gone UCP in the last election, which suggests that several parts of Calgary that supported Smith in the 2023 election weren’t on board with her ideas on who should or shouldn’t get fully covered health and education .

Constitutionally blocked

The per-riding results on Question 1 (48 yes, 39 no) roughly tracked the seat math after the last provincial election (48 UCP, 39 NDP).

But on Questions 6 to 9, Smith would have been on the wrong end of the sort of landslides that former premiers Ralph Klein and Jason Kenney enjoyed, had this referendum been settled riding by riding.

More than two-thirds of ridings voted no to Question 8 on opting out of federal social service programs, the most lopsided of the constitutional ballot measures. But in all of them, no was the popular choice in more than 50 constituencies.

Not a single riding in Edmonton or Calgary said yes to a single one of the constitutional questions.

Rural Alberta, however, stayed loyal to Smith’s push for more provincial powers and to tilt Canada’s Constitution in favour of Alberta.

Blue wall, orange wall

Premier Smith asked voters to vote yes on all nine questions that didn’t threaten national unity; NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was effectively part of the “no to the nine” campaign.

According to Elections Alberta, 24 ridings voted no down the line, while 27 voted yes to all of them.

What went all the UCP government’s way? Ridings that solidly backed the party in 2023, including all predominantly rural or small-town seats, as well as the seats that include Grande Prairie, Medicine Hat and Fort McMurray.

The all-no seats? Most of them were in Edmonton, some in inner-city Calgary and its northeast, as well as St. Albert — a seat which has gone NDP in the last three elections — and Banff-Kananaskis, which has swung back and forth between UCP and NDP.

Swing ridings?

While a majority of ridings in Alberta went either solidly yes or solidly no, that still leaves 36 provincial constituencies where voters were choosier about how they marked their referendum ballots.

Which seats were running hot and cold on Smith’s plea for referendum support, and might wind up being hotly contested in next year’s election?

Of Calgary’s 26 ridings, 18 of them delivered a mixed yes-and-no verdict on the referendum questions. That includes a handful of NDP-held seats — as well as all the UCP-held seats in the province's largest city.

Calgary has become swing city in Alberta provincial politics, and offered the greatest mix of yes and no verdicts on the premier's referendum questions, compared to the solidly no-leaning Edmonton and yes-leaning other areas of the province. (CBC)

A few suburban Edmonton constituencies broke up the capital’s preference for no with yes majorities on Question 5.

Most of the ridings that surround Edmonton — known politically as the doughnut — swung between yes and no, including NDP-held Sherwood Park, as well as UCP-controlled Spruce Grove-Stony Plain, Strathcona-Sherwood Park, Morinville-St. Albert and Leduc-Beaumont.

Lethbridge’s two seats were a mixed bag too, as they have been politically in the last few elections.

Voters in Alberta’s other two cities of around 100,000 people — Red Deer and rapidly growing Airdrie — have been more consistently UCP in recent votes. But in all four of those cities’ ridings, voters defied Smith’s bid for a clean sweep by voting against Question 8 (and Question 9, in Airdrie-Cochrane).

Calgary-Shaw went orange, but…

Nenshi’s NDP managed to take away a formerly deep-blue suburban seat in September, in the Calgary-Shaw byelection.

The much-watched riding voted yes to all immigration questions last week, but no to all constitutional questions.

Newly elected Calgary-Shaw MLA Kyle Campbell, left, celebrates his byelection victory with NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi. (CBC News)

That more closely resembles voting patterns in other UCP ridings like Calgary-Peigan, Calgary-South East and Calgary-Hays.

However, it’s striking which seat featured a voting result more similar to NDP-held districts: Calgary-West, which voted yes to Question 5 on citizenship markers, but no to the rest. That seat has been held by Deputy Premier Mike Ellis since 2015.

World.title: Fresh faces take the reins as mayoral incumbents fall short across Waterloo, Ont., region
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

There were some major upsets during Monday night's municipal election with incumbent mayors in Cambridge, Waterloo, Wellesley and Wilmot losing their races.

Scott Hamilton in Cambridge, who is the city's Ward 7 councillor, beat incumbent Jan Liggett with over 56 per cent of the vote. Liggett placed third, capturing only 11 per cent of the vote.

In Waterloo, a rematch between sitting mayor Dorothy McCabe and Shannon Weber took place. Weber lost to McCabe in 2022 by 331 votes, but came back much stronger this time, beating McCabe by 6,379 votes.

Wilmot's Natasha Salonen also saw a major upset Monday night, placing third after second place Stephanie Goertz. Township Ward 2 councillor Kris Wilkinson ended up winning the mayoral race.

There was also a shake up in Wellesley as Chris Martin ousted incumbent Joe Nowak, who served three terms as mayor in that township. Martin was the only other candidate running for mayor in Wellesley.

Shannon Weber walks onto the stage at her watch party. She won the mayoral race in Waterloo, beating incumbent Dorothy McCabe. (Aastha Shetty/CBC)

Historically, incumbents are favoured to win since they have the advantage of name recognition on the ballot, especially in municipal elections.

Retired political professor from the University of Waterloo, Robert Williams, said it may be the case of residents seeing the situation as the "glass empty or half full."

"I think for a lot of people, those who think about it a lot or do the research, it's really a question of, 'Am I satisfied with the performance of the mayor leaving aside that I know that name' or are they saying maybe there's a better way to do this?" he told CBC News.

Williams said change in municipal politics is normally fueled by conflict during a mayor's term and residents doing their homework for a new candidate.

"That takes a fair bit of preparation, thinking and research and for a lot of people, it's probably a lot more than they would be putting into it," he said.

"It's often just as easy to look for a name you recognize and go for that."

Wave of fresh faces leading council

Local councils across the region will also look very different , as a wave of fresh faces will take charge of the region's municipalities over the next four years.

With the exception of the City of Kitchener, the municipalities of Cambridge, Waterloo, Woolwich, North Dumfries, Wellesley and Wilmot will have new mayors.

It will also mean that regional council will look a little different since elected mayors sit on regional council, making decisions around the regional budget and other big ticket items like homelessness and transit.

North Dumfries and Woolwich will also have new mayors leading the townships for the next four years after Sue Foxton and Sandy Shantz also announced they would not seek reelection.

Elmira councillor Evan Burgess was elected as Woolwich's new mayor and Rodney Rollerman was elected in North Dumfries.

Leanne Caron speaks to supporters at her watch party Monday night. (Diego Pizarro/CBC)

Guelph also has a brand new mayor after Cam Guthrie announced he would not seek re-election after serving three terms.

Leanne Caron won the mayoral race in that city with 54 per cent of the vote. Caron will be a familiar face in a different role, as someone who has been in council since 2006.

Mayors can capture identity of community

In Kitchener, Berry Vrbanovic will enter his fourth term as mayor. he won the vote by a landslide, earning 55 per cent of the vote. Runner up Cindy Ward only managed to capture 15 per cent of the vote.

Andrea Perrella, an associate professor of political science at Wilfrid Laurier University said a mayor can capture the identity of a community.

"Vrbanovic very much reflects that, so when you think of Vrbanovic, you think of Kitchener," he told CBC News.

"It's not just an administrator when you think of Kitchener. So he he's part of that brand, part of the Kitchener community brand."
