RIO DE JANEIRO — There is a great deal to do in Rio in November, and very little of it is written down anywhere in English. This guide is the monthly selection for people who live here rather than visit: what is on, where, when, what it costs, and why it might be worth crossing the city for.

The month opens with a long weekend, because Finados falls on Monday the 2nd, and closes with two nights of Brazilian classics at the Marina da Glória. In between come Turandot at the Theatro Municipal, Gilberto Gil with the Gilsons on the 13th, Black Consciousness Day on Friday the 20th and the Pride parade in Copacabana two days later.

Many of the exhibitions in Rio in November are free.

The First Week of Rio in November: Finados and a Food Festival

Sunday 1, Saturday 7 and Sunday 8 November Festival Gastronomia Sem Fronteiras on the Fashion Mall rooftop Rooftop of the Fashion Mall, Estrada da Gávea 899, São Conrado · Price from the ticket page; food and drink not included A food festival curated by chef Elia Schramm, with kitchens from several countries, a market and live music. It also runs on Saturday 31 October. Food needs no translation, which makes this one of the easiest outings in Rio in November. Tickets on Ingresse, a Brazilian ticketing site.

Until Sunday 8 November, Tuesday to Sunday, noon to 8pm CASACOR Rio marks 35 years in Centro Edifício Aliança da Bahia, Rua Araújo Porto Alegre 36, Centro · R$120 (about US$22) half-price R$60 (about US$11) children under 10 free Brazil’s best-known interior design and architecture show fills a downtown building with rooms created by local architects and designers. It is a visual show from start to finish, and its final days fall on the Finados long weekend.

Until Sunday 8 November · Thursdays and Fridays 8.30pm, weekends 7pm “Filho da Margem”, a wordless dance piece at Sesc Copacabana Sesc Copacabana, Rua Domingos Ferreira 160, Copacabana (Sesc is a cultural network of the retail trade) · Price from the venue Cia Boca do Mundo’s new dance work about Logunedé, an orixá (a deity of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé).

Monday 2 November, 7pm The Sitkovetsky Trio on the Finados holiday Theatro Municipal, Praça Floriano, Cinelândia (the square in central Rio) · Price from the venue Beethoven, Schumann and Dvořák, with a 1679 Stradivarius in the violinist’s hands. A holiday evening in the city’s grandest hall.

Tuesday 3 November, 8pm MARO at Circo Voador Circo Voador, Rua dos Arcos, Lapa · Half-price R$100 (about US$18) to R$150 (about US$28) full price R$200 (about US$37) to R$300 (about US$55) in three batches; 18 and over, or 14 with a parent The Portuguese singer-songwriter, who represented Portugal at Eurovision in 2022, brings her “So Much Has Changed” show to Lapa’s open-sided arena. Much of her repertoire is in English, which makes this an easy night for a newcomer. Our preview.

Thursday 5 November Ocean Alley’s first Rio date Circo Voador, Rua dos Arcos, Lapa · Price from the venue The Australian surf-rock band plays Lapa for the first time.

Friday 6 November, 9pm Festival Fado: Sara Correia and Camané Vivo Rio, Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · Price from the venue Two of Lisbon’s leading fado voices on one bill, as part of the touring Festival Fado. A rare chance in Rio to hear the genre live.

Sunday 8 November, 6pm Ivan Lins with the MPBJazz Orquestra Theatro Municipal, Praça Floriano, Cinelândia · From R$90 (about US$17) Ivan Lins, one of Brazil’s best-loved songwriters, revisits his best-known songs in big-band jazz arrangements with the MPBJazz Orquestra, a two-hour concert in the Theatro Municipal.

Sunday 8 November, 7.30pm Bossa Sempre Nova: Roberto Menescal and Danilo Caymmi Vivo Rio, Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · Price from the venue Roberto Menescal, one of the founders of bossa nova, plays “O Barquinho” and “Chega de Saudade” with Danilo Caymmi.

Mid-November: Turandot and Gilberto Gil

Monday 9 November, doors 6pm Hayley Williams at Qualistage Qualistage, Via Parque Shopping, Av. Ayrton Senna 3000, Barra da Tijuca · Floor from R$282.50 (about US$52) half-price, R$565 (about US$104) full price; boxes up to R$980 (about US$181) (prices at the start of sales) The Paramore singer brings her solo show to Barra. The date moved forward from 10 November, so check that your ticket shows the 9th.

Monday 9 and Tuesday 10 November, again Wednesday 25 and Thursday 26 November, midday Free lunchtime opera: Verdi’s Rigoletto Theatro Municipal, Praça Floriano, Cinelândia · Free The theatre’s Ópera do Meio-Dia series moves to Rigoletto, staged inside the building at lunchtime. Free opera in the middle of Centro; confirm the time on the theatre’s site on the day.

Tuesday 10 and Wednesday 11 November, 8pm City of God, with its score played live Teatro Riachuelo, Rua do Passeio 38/40, Centro · Price from the venue The Petrobras Sinfônica orchestra plays the soundtrack of Fernando Meirelles and Kátia Lund’s 2002 film, shot in Rio, while the full film is screened, with the original composers on stage. The film is in Portuguese.

Friday 13 November, 9pm The Gilsons with Gilberto Gil at Vivo Rio Vivo Rio, Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · Price from the venue; last tickets The family trio plays with Gilberto Gil himself, a night that marks Vivo Rio’s twentieth anniversary — Gil opened the venue. Probably the hardest ticket to find in Rio in November. Tickets on the Vivo Rio site.

Friday 13 November Tom Zé at 90: an extra night at Circo Voador Circo Voador, Rua dos Arcos, Lapa · Price from the venue One of the founding figures of Tropicália adds a night at Circo Voador, the open-sided arena in Lapa. Inventive, funny and unlike anything else in Brazilian music.

From Friday 13 November, seven performances Turandot in its centenary year at the Theatro Municipal Theatro Municipal, Praça Floriano, Cinelândia · Price from the venue Puccini’s last opera, first staged at La Scala in 1926, in André Heller-Lopes’s production, with soprano Eiko Senda among the soloists. The big opera of the season, sung in Italian. Sources differ on the last performance, so check the dates on the Theatro Municipal site.

Black Consciousness Day and Pride: 16 to 22 November

Friday 20 November, 9pm CA7RIEL & Paco Amoroso at Vivo Rio Vivo Rio, Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · From R$260 (about US$48) half-price, R$520 (about US$96) full price Argentina’s most talked-about live act brings its Free Spirits world tour to Rio on the Black Consciousness Day holiday.

Saturday 21 November, doors 4pm Mariah Carey’s Christmas Time in Barra Outdoor area of the Farmasi Arena, Av. Embaixador Abelardo Bueno 3401, Barra da Tijuca · Floor R$247.50 (about US$46) half-price, R$495 (about US$91) full price; premium floor R$447.50 (about US$83) / R$895 (about US$165) Her Christmas show comes to Brazil for the first time; Rio follows two nights in São Paulo. Our report on the tour.

Sunday 22 November The 31st Rio Pride parade in Copacabana Copacabana seafront The Parada do Orgulho LGBTI+ returns to the beach under the motto “Reconhecemos justa toda forma de amor e de existência”. The start time had not been published at the time of writing.

Late November: Seal, Bethânia and the Gipsy Kings

Wednesday 25 to Sunday 29 November Arpoarte, a new festival of folk art and craft Píer Mauá, Centro · Price from the venue The first edition of a festival of Brazilian popular art and handicraft on the old port pier beside the Museu do Amanhã. A good place to look for presents before the holidays.

Wednesday 25 November, 8pm “Beatles Abbey Road” at the Teatro Riachuelo Rio Teatro Riachuelo Rio, Rua do Passeio 38, Centro · R$160 (about US$30) to R$280 (about US$52), depending on the section A theatre tribute to the band that follows its career from the early hits to the late albums. It lasts about two hours and is open to all ages; the two cheapest sections, the balconies, are reached by stairs only.

Thursday 26 November Seal celebrates his first two albums, with Seu Jorge opening Qualistage, Via Parque Shopping, Av. Ayrton Senna 3000, Barra da Tijuca · Seats from R$197.50 (about US$36) half-price, R$395 (about US$73) full price; floor R$297.50 (about US$55) / R$595 (about US$110); boxes up to R$1,295 (about US$239) (prices at the start of sales) A tour built around his first two albums, Seal I and Seal II, with Seu Jorge, known abroad from City of God and The Life Aquatic, as the opening act. Our preview.

Friday 27 November, 8pm Groundation at Circo Voador Circo Voador, Rua dos Arcos, Lapa · Price from the venue The American roots-reggae band in Lapa’s open-air arena.

Saturday 28 November, 5pm, and Sunday 29 November, 3pm Festival Clássicos do Brasil on the bay at Glória Marina da Glória, Av. Infante Dom Henrique s/n, Glória · From R$120 (about US$22) Saturday brings Maria Bethânia and Alceu Valença, who both turn eighty this year, with Vanessa da Mata; Sunday is samba and pagode with Alexandre Pires, Péricles and Ferrugem. It is the big Brazilian music weekend of Rio in November, and the festival continues on 5 and 6 December. Details on the Riotur page.

Saturday 28 November, doors 9pm Fresno with an orchestra at the Fundição Progresso Fundição Progresso, Rua dos Arcos 24, Lapa · Price from the venue The Brazilian rock band’s first symphonic show, Sinfonia’26, with the Nova Orquestra, in the old foundry in Lapa.

Sunday 29 November, 9.30pm Gipsy Kings by Diego Baliardo, with Sidney Magal Qualistage, Via Parque Shopping, Av. Ayrton Senna 3000, Barra da Tijuca · From R$110 (about US$20) “Bamboleo” and the flamenco “Hotel California”, from the line-up led by Diego Baliardo — not the one led by Nicolas Reyes — with the Brazilian showman Sidney Magal as guest. Our preview.

Exhibitions in Rio in November

Until Monday 16 November · Wednesday to Monday, 9am to 8pm Amazônicas — Poéticas Femininas Centro Cultural Banco do Brasil, Rua Primeiro de Março 66, Centro · Free Eighty works by twenty-one women artists from the Amazon, on the CCBB’s second floor. Collect a free ticket at the box office or online.

Until Sunday 22 November The Prêmio PIPA 2026 winners at the Paço Imperial Paço Imperial, Praça XV de Novembro 48, Centro · Price from the venue The winners of the Prêmio PIPA, Brazil’s leading prize for young contemporary artists, with a selection from the PIPA collection, in the former royal palace on Praça XV.

Until Saturday 28 November · Tuesday to Saturday, noon to 7pm Five exhibitions at the Centro Cultural Correios Centro Cultural Correios, Rua Visconde de Itaboraí 20, Centro · Price from the venue Five exhibitions in the Correios (postal service) cultural centre, which sits beside the CCBB, so the two make one afternoon.

Until Sunday 29 November Zanele Muholi, “Beleza valente”, at the MAR Museu de Arte do Rio, Praça Mauá, Centro · Price from the venue More than a hundred works by the South African photographer, portraits that need no caption in any language.

Throughout November · Wednesday to Saturday 10am to 6pm, Sunday 11am to 6pm “Carnaval como método” at MAM Rio Museu de Arte Moderna, Av. Infante Dom Henrique 85, Parque do Flamengo · Price from the venue Carnival designers’ work shown as art, in the modernist Museu de Arte Moderna on the Aterro do Flamengo. The long-running collection show “Entre o moderno e o contemporâneo” runs alongside.

Running Through November

Saturday 7 to Sunday 22 November Bluey live on stage in Barra Teatro Multiplan, Shopping VillageMall, Av. das Américas 3900, Barra da Tijuca · From R$25 (about US$5) The official stage show of the Australian children’s series. The safest family outing in Rio in November, with characters most children already know.

Until 4 December The Jazz Room: a Sinatra and Armstrong tribute Teatro Rival Petrobras, Rua Álvaro Alvim 33, Cinelândia · From R$100 (about US$18) A tribute evening to Frank Sinatra and Louis Armstrong: the American songbook with a live band, in the Teatro Rival Petrobras off Cinelândia. The reliable option when nothing else on this list fits the night.

Football in Rio in November

Wednesday 4 November, 7.30pm and 9.30pm Flamengo against Grêmio, Botafogo against Atlético-MG Maracanã (Flamengo) and Estádio Nilton Santos (Botafogo) · Tickets from the clubs The first football of Rio in November: two home games on the same night in round 34 of the Brazilian championship (the top-flight league), Flamengo–Grêmio at 7.30pm at the Maracanã, Botafogo–Atlético-MG at 9.30pm at the Nilton Santos. Buy only through the clubs’ own sites.

Sunday 8 November, 5pm Vasco against Palmeiras in the Copa do Brasil semi-final São Januário, Vasco da Gama · Tickets from the club The second leg, after the first in São Paulo on 1 November, with a place in the cup final on 6 December at stake.

18 to 28 November, dates to be set The last home games of the league season Maracanã, Nilton Santos or São Januário · Tickets from the clubs Rounds 35 to 37 bring Flamengo–Athletico-PR, Vasco–Internacional, Fluminense–Mirassol, Botafogo–São Paulo, Fluminense–Cruzeiro and Botafogo–Bahia. The Brazilian football confederation (CBF) had not fixed the days, times or stadiums at the time of writing; the final round follows on 2 December.

Planning Your Rio in November

Three holidays fall in Rio in November. Monday 2 November is Finados, All Souls’ Day, when banks and public offices close.

Sunday 15 November, Proclamation of the Republic Day, falls on a weekend and brings no extra day off. Friday 20 November is Black Consciousness Day, a national holiday since 2024, and banks close again.

The LatAm Brief One email, every weekday morning. What moved in Latin American markets, politics and expat life. Yesterday’s subject line: “Brazil stocks plunge 13.9% in one day after Lula win” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

With Mariah Carey on the 21st and Pride on the 22nd, that holiday opens the busiest weekend of the month. Check the city traffic operator, CET-Rio, for road closures before you set out on holidays and on parade day.

Prices are in reais, and the real has moved sharply since the runoff election on 25 October (see our market report). Dollar values use the RT market rate of R$5.42 to US$1 at the close on 26 October 2026, so figures in dollars may shift by the time you buy.

Runners: foreign entries for the 2027 Rio half-marathon open on 16 November — dates and prices here. From 18 November the SSL Gold Cup, a sailing competition with crews from more than 65 countries, is based at the Marina da Glória until 13 December.

Where we have not printed a ticket price, the organisers had not published one at the time of writing. Programmes at the CCBB and the theatres change during the month, so check with the venue on the day.

“Half-price” means the legal meia-entrada discount for students, people over 60 and others. This guide to Rio in November runs monthly.

It returns in December.If you run a venue, a gallery or a production in Rio and would like to be considered, write to the newsroom with the date, the time, the address and the ticket price.

Those four things are what get an event into the list.

More on living here: our Rio de Janeiro coverage and Expats in Brazil.

Frequently Asked Questions

What are the holidays in Rio in November 2026?

Monday 2 November (Finados, All Souls’ Day), Sunday 15 November (Proclamation of the Republic) and Friday 20 November (Black Consciousness Day). Banks and public offices close on the two weekday holidays.

What is free in Rio in November?

The CCBB’s Amazônicas exhibition until 16 November, and the midday opera series at the Theatro Municipal on 9, 10, 25 and 26 November, which is free.

What are the biggest concerts in Rio in November?

The Gilsons with Gilberto Gil at Vivo Rio on 13 November, Mariah Carey at the Farmasi Arena on 21 November, Seal at Qualistage on 26 November and the Festival Clássicos do Brasil with Maria Bethânia at the Marina da Glória on 28 and 29 November.

When is the Rio Pride parade in 2026?

Sunday 22 November, on the Copacabana seafront. The start time had not been published at the time of writing.

World.title: Brazil Renews Diesel Aid for 30 More Days
World.content:
BRAZIL · ENERGY

Published Tuesday, 27 October, 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time (ET) · Source: Ministry of Planning and Budget

Key Facts — What happened Brazil will keep its diesel subsidy at R$2.12 a liter (about US$0.39) for one more month, the government said on Tuesday.

— The bill Brazil’s Planning and Budget Ministry puts the cost near R$10.5 billion (about US$1.9 billion) a month, paid from extra oil income.

— Why it matters Diesel is a core cost for trucking, which carries much of Brazil’s freight.

— What to watch Whether the aid is extended again after a month, and whether Petrobras, the state oil company, raises its own diesel price.

— Power Index Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in Brazil ranks 1st of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 75.0 points (October 2026 edition).

— Prediction markets Polymarket, a prediction-market platform, gives 39.0% to US crude (the WTI benchmark) touching US$105 in October and 10.5% to US$110 (27 October, 7:46 a.m. ET).

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro – · Lula – (US$249 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 0.4% · Lula 99.6% As of 25 October, 11:40 pm ET (03:40 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Want prediction market reports on Brazil? Get yours free, right after you confirm →

Brazil has decided to keep paying for cheaper diesel, and an oil windfall is footing the bill. On Tuesday, 27 October, the Ministry of Planning and Budget, the federal department that sets the budget, said the government will renew its diesel subsidy of R$2.12 per liter (about US$0.39) for one more month.

The ministry says the cost, about R$10.5 billion (about US$1.9 billion) a month, will be covered by extra income the state earns when oil prices are high. That keeps a major Brazil economy cost-of-living tool in place, two days after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won re-election.

What Brazil Just Decided

A subsidy, or subvenção in Portuguese, is a state payment that keeps a fuel cheaper than the market would set. The R$2.12 a liter is the level already in force, and the ministry says the expected fiscal impact of the renewal is the same as today.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Brazil ranks 1st of 14 with 75.0 points. Strongest pillar: military means (100); weakest: state capacity & security (56). Alignment group: Hedging. WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The extension runs for one month. Press reports of the announcement do not name the legal order that carries it, so we cannot yet say the exact end date.

File photo: a fuel station in Brazil with diesel, gasoline and ethanol pumps.

This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Why the Aid Survived the Election

Fuel is the price every Brazilian sees. Early this month, right after the first round of the presidential election, the government widened the diesel and ethanol subsidies and kept tax relief on pure ethanol.

The government also zeroed federal taxes on gasoline, worth R$0.89 per liter (about US$0.16). Officials said these measures were paid for with extra federal income from high oil prices.

The Bill and the Oil Windfall

The arithmetic is simple. Oil above budget assumptions swells state revenue, and the government spends part of it holding down fuel.

The risk is the reverse: if oil falls, the windfall shrinks while the subsidy bill stays. Prediction traders still see a meaningful chance of US crude touching US$105 this month.

What It Means for US Readers

For holders of Petrobras, Brazil’s state-controlled oil company, whose shares trade in New York as ADRs (American depositary receipts, shares of a foreign company), the renewal keeps the fuel-support policy unchanged for another month.

The real is also under strain. The dollar closed at about 5.40 reais on Monday, 26 October, from just under 5.00 on Friday, and a weaker real raises the cost of anything priced in dollars, including imported fuel (rates from RT market data, a market-data provider).

A later end to the aid would be the moment to watch.

In Plain English

Subsidy (subvenção): a payment from the state that holds a price below the market level.

a payment from the state that holds a price below the market level. Ministry of Planning and Budget: the federal department that sets the budget and announced the renewal.

What Is Not Known

The ministry has not said what happens to the other fuel measures announced earlier this month. We will update when the official text appears.

What did Brazil decide on diesel?

The government will renew its R$2.12 per liter (about US$0.39) diesel subsidy for one more month. The Ministry of Planning and Budget announced it on 27 October.

How much will it cost?

The ministry estimates about R$10.5 billion (about US$1.9 billion) a month. It says extra oil income will cover it.

World.title: Trump Calls Brazil’s Election Rigged
World.content:
BRAZIL · ELECTION

Published Tuesday, 27 October, 7:48 a.m. ET · Source: White House press remarks, Superior Electoral Court (TSE), Vice Presidency of Brazil, Liberal Party (PL)

Key Facts The claim On Monday Trump said Brazil’s runoff “looked like another rigged election” and offered no evidence.

The result Lula won 51.79% to 48.21%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes.

The extension Fewer than 35,000 votes were cast in two extra hours ordered by Justice Cristiano Zanin.

The answer Vice President Geraldo Alckmin called the claim “totally wrong”; Bolsonaro’s party accepts the result.

Prediction markets · who wins the runoff Implied chance of winning Brazil’s presidency on 25 October, from traders’ prices. Polymarket Flávio Bolsonaro – · Lula – (US$249 million traded) Kalshi (regulated in the US by the CFTC) Flávio Bolsonaro 0.4% · Lula 99.6% As of 25 October, 11:40 pm ET (03:40 Lisbon), updated every 20 minutes. Prices are bets, not polls, and can move fast. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them. Want prediction market reports on Brazil? Get yours free, right after you confirm →

What Trump Said

President Donald Trump said on Monday that Brazil’s presidential runoff “looked like another rigged election,” speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland before leaving for a campaign rally in Mississippi. He offered no evidence of fraud and said the vote “looked very bad” and that the two-hour voting extension was “very strange.”

Trump said he had not taken sides and added, “I like Lula,” referring to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Brazil’s left-wing president, who won a fourth non-consecutive term on Sunday. As of Tuesday morning we found no formal statement from the White House or the State Department recognising the result.

Download the PDF checklist

Why He Says It

Trump’s words echo Flávio Bolsonaro, the defeated conservative senator and son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, who has refused to concede and, as of Monday, wanted the result annulled. He objects to an order by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin that kept polling stations open for two extra hours because of transport problems and bad weather.

WatchRating below investment grade (BB); public debt at 93% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

An analysis by Pedro Burgos, a professor at the Insper business school in São Paulo, found that fewer than 35,000 votes were cast during the extra hours, far below Lula’s lead of about 4.4 million. Both campaigns had asked for more time in some places, Lula’s side because of a shortage of buses and Flávio’s because of rain.

What It Means for Americans

Brazil is Latin America’s largest economy and a major US trading partner, and a 25 percent US tariff already hits many Brazilian goods, although about 44 percent of exports, including coffee, beef, orange juice, crude oil and aircraft, are exempt. Washington also wants access to Brazil’s rare earths, the minerals used in phones and electric cars.

Markets took the result hard: the real lost about 8 percent against the dollar on Monday, and the São Paulo stock index fell 13.88 percent, its steepest one-day fall since March 2020. Americans who hold Brazilian shares listed in New York, known as ADRs, face more swings until Washington makes its position clear.

How Brazil and Its Neighbours Answer

Brazil’s vice president, Geraldo Alckmin, rejected Trump’s claim as “totally wrong” and “unfounded” and defended the country’s electronic voting system. Valdemar Costa Neto, head of Flávio Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party (PL), said in a statement that “we recognize the presidential election results”, while adding that the questions raised need to be clarified.

Chile’s government under José Antonio Kast and Uruguay’s government recognised Lula’s win, and the European Union congratulated him. Senator Bernie Sanders also congratulated Lula, while Donald Trump Jr. criticised the voting extension on X.

What Comes Next

For American investors, the immediate question is whether the White House will work with Lula or wait out the Bolsonaro challenge. A quick, friendly statement would calm tariff talks, while silence keeps nerves high over the real, Brazilian stocks and rare-earth supply.

The dispute echoes Trump’s rejection of his own 2020 defeat and Jair Bolsonaro’s refusal to clearly accept his loss in 2022. It also tests whether Washington puts trade and minerals ahead of its political ties to the Bolsonaro family; our companion piece asks whether Flávio can overturn the election.

What Is Not Known

Trump has not identified any fraudulent ballots, manipulated machines or falsified tallies, and he has not named anyone he believes rigged the election. No formal US government decision on diplomatic or economic consequences has been announced.

Flávio Bolsonaro has said he will seek an annulment, but it is unclear what has been filed, which court would decide it and what remedy he wants. We also do not know where the extra-hour votes were cast or for whom.

Frequently Asked Questions

Did Trump provide evidence of election fraud in Brazil?

No, he cited no specific evidence of fraud. An analysis found fewer than 35,000 votes in the two extra hours, against Lula’s lead of about 4.4 million.

Has Flávio Bolsonaro conceded the election?

No, as of Monday he refused to concede and wanted the result annulled over the voting extension. His Liberal Party, however, said it recognises the result.

What does this mean for US-Brazil trade?

A 25 percent US tariff already hits many Brazilian goods, though about 44 percent of exports are exempt. The dispute could complicate any deal to ease it, depending on whether the White House recognises Lula’s win.

Sources: White House press remarks, 26 October · Superior Electoral Court (TSE) · Vice Presidency of Brazil · Liberal Party (PL) statement · Office of the US Trade Representative · Insper.

World.title: France Sets November 5 Nationwide Strike
World.content:
Protesters hold up placards in Paris on 17 October 2026, the day the cost-of-living protests turned into riots. (Photo: FreCha, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Published Tuesday, 27 October, 7:25 a.m. ET (12:25 p.m. Paris) · Source: French Interior Ministry, union confederations

Key Facts Next protest: The Yellow Vests, a grassroots anti-tax movement, called rallies for Saturday, October 31, 2026.

Nationwide strike: Five union confederations called a strike for Thursday, November 5, 2026, over wages, pensions, public services and budget cuts.

Saturday turnout: France's Interior Ministry counted 410,000 marchers on October 24, 110,000 of them in Paris; the CGT, a major union federation, claimed about 800,000.

Arrests and injuries: Police made 1,314 arrests on October 24, half the previous weekend's total, and 53 officers were hurt.

Security deployment: France deployed 70,000 police and gendarmes for the October 24 demonstrations.

Prediction markets: Kalshi, a US prediction market, prices a 9% chance of a French state of emergency before Jan. 1, 2027 (Oct. 27, 7:22 a.m. ET).

This story is part of our coverage of the why France is in crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: French Ports Face a 24-Hour Strike on Oct 30

Unions Escalate Pressure

In our France protests coverage, the story is shifting: France's protest wave is moving from weekend marches to the workplace. Five union confederations (CFDT, CGT, FO, Unsa and FSU) have called a nationwide strike for Thursday, November 5, over wages, pensions, public services and planned budget cuts of about US$60 billion (€54 billion, at EUR/USD 1.115).

The strike could hit transport, energy and schools, but how many workers will join is not yet known. Before that, the Yellow Vests, a grassroots movement born in 2018 over fuel taxes, have called rallies on Saturday, October 31, in defence of public freedoms.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Saturday's Mobilisation

On Saturday, October 24, demonstrations took place across France after the previous weekend's riots and looting. France's Interior Ministry counted 410,000 participants nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris, while the CGT, one of the country's biggest union federations, put it near 800,000.

Authorities deployed 70,000 police and security personnel, and the Interior Ministry's provisional tally recorded 1,314 arrests, half the previous weekend's figure. Some 53 security officers were injured, compared with more than 1,100 a week earlier.

The demonstrations were largely peaceful during the day, but clashes later occurred in Paris, Marseille, Lyon and Bordeaux. Police used tear gas, water cannon and other crowd-control measures, while youths set rubbish bins on fire in Marseille.

File photo: CRS riot police on Boulevard Voltaire, Paris, during a student march on 6 October 2026.

Government Response

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said high-risk groups had broken away from the marches. President Emmanuel Macron had said only union-requested marches would be authorised on October 24, and Lyon, Nice and Montpellier banned wider gatherings.

The government's heavier security operation appears to have reduced the scale of disorder: turnout was lower by the official count, arrests fell from the previous weekend, and reported police injuries dropped sharply. The unions dispute the official turnout figures.

In Plain English

The CGT, CFDT, FO, Unsa and FSU are France's main union federations, and a joint call means they act together. A general strike means workers in many sectors stop work on the same day.

Background

The protests grew from anger over the cost of living and public services, drawing students, workers, unions and the Yellow Vests. The previous major day, October 17, drew 550,000 people by the Interior Ministry's count, with 2,628 arrests and more than 1,100 security officers injured.

The Yellow Vests plan sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly, France's lower house of parliament.

What It Means for US Readers

For US investors and policymakers, the escalation of France's protest movement into a nationwide strike on November 5 raises the risk of disruption to European supply chains, transport and energy markets. France is the eurozone's second-largest economy and prolonged industrial action could weigh on its growth.

Kalshi, a US exchange regulated by the CFTC (the federal derivatives regulator), prices a 9% chance that France declares a state of emergency before January 1, 2027, and 3% before November 1 (107,094 contracts traded, read 27 October 2026, 7:22 a.m. ET). These are bets, not polls.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What Is Not Known

It is not yet clear how many workers will strike on November 5, or how far transport, schools and energy supply will be disrupted. No charge or conviction totals have been published for the 1,314 arrests.

No market prices the strike itself, and the exact start times of the October 31 rallies are not confirmed.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the next nationwide strike in France?

Five union confederations have called a strike for Thursday, November 5, 2026. They cite wages, pensions, public services and planned budget cuts.

How many people participated in Saturday's protests?

France's Interior Ministry counted 410,000 on October 24, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT union federation put it near 800,000.

World.title: Spain’s Right Holds Poll Lead, Left Splits
World.content:
Santiago Abascal, leader of Vox, in the Congress of Deputies in March 2023. File photo: Vox Congreso, CC0.

Published Tuesday, 27 October, 6:58 a.m. ET (11:58 a.m. Madrid) · Source: Spanish polling institutes, CIS, Kalshi, Polymarket.

Spain’s right-wing parties are still heading for a majority, while the Socialist government wins back a little ground but finds no way to win. Sigma Dos, a leading Spanish polling firm, puts the People’s Party (PP) and the Vox party at 191 to 200 of the 350 seats in Congress, ahead of the Spain Election 2026 vote on 29 November.

A majority needs 176 seats. NC Report, another private pollster, goes further and puts the two parties above 200.

Key Facts What happened: Three new private polls keep the conservative PP and Vox above the 176 seats needed for a majority.

The numbers: Sigma Dos has PP and Vox at 191 to 200 of 350 seats; the left is split.

What next: Spain votes on Sunday, 29 November; the official campaign opens on 13 November.

Prediction markets: Kalshi, a US-regulated exchange, priced Feijóo at 83% to be prime minister (6:58 a.m. ET, 27 October).

This story is part of our coverage of the Spain Election 2026. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: Spain's Housing Costs Outrun Wages in 2026

In plain English Spain elects its parliament in two chambers, and the government must win a majority in the lower one, the Congress of Deputies. The PP is the main conservative party, Vox sits to its right, and the Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez governs.

Why the Right Keeps Its Majority

Every private poll we checked, including GESOP, 40dB, GAD3 and SocioMétrica, leaves the PP and Vox above 176 seats.

The PP, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, is projected at roughly 121 to 144 seats. That is level with or below the 137 it won in 2023, and NC Report shows it slipping from 146 to 148 seats in early October to about 141 to 144 now.

Vox is the real winner of the polls. It won 33 seats in 2023 and is now projected at 63 to 74, roughly double.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Socialists Recover, but the Left Splits

The PSOE is projected at about 100 to 117 seats, short of the 121 it won in 2023. It has gained a little since early October.

The reason is the split on the left. Frente Amplio, a left-wing alliance, and Podemos, a left-wing party, are running separately, so the bloc that won 31 seats as Sumar in 2023 now divides its votes.

One Poll Says the Opposite

The CIS, Spain’s state-run Centre for Sociological Research, published a survey on 14 October that put the PSOE at 34%, 11.8 points ahead of the PP. Private pollsters see a very different race, and we cannot say which will be closer on 29 November.

What Prediction Markets Say

On Kalshi’s market “Prime Minister of Spain after the next election?”, traders priced Alberto Núñez Feijóo at 83%, Pedro Sánchez at 15% and Vox leader Santiago Abascal at 7% on 27 October at 6:58 a.m. ET, with 27,891 contracts (bets) traded. Kalshi, a US exchange, is regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC).

On Polymarket, a crypto-based exchange, a contract on a PP and Vox majority traded at 80% (US$12,094 traded).

These prices are bets, not polls, and each is priced separately, so they need not add up to 100%.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for US Readers

Spain is a NATO ally and the euro area’s fourth-largest economy, so a PP and Vox government would shape its line on migration, energy and relations with Washington. US investors in Spanish assets will watch whether the right needs help from smaller parties to govern.

What Is Not Known

The polls we checked project only the Congress, not the Senate (Spain’s upper house). We also cannot say whether the PSOE’s recovery will last or fade.

See our Spain election polls page, our Alberto Núñez Feijóo profile and Pedro Sánchez explainer.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is ahead in Spain’s election polls?

Private polls put the conservative PP first and the PP and Vox above the 176 seats needed for a majority. The state-run CIS survey of 14 October is the exception and puts the Socialists 11.8 points ahead.

When does Spain vote?

Spain votes on Sunday, 29 November 2026, for both the Congress of Deputies and the Senate. The new parliament is due to meet on 23 December.

Sources: Sigma Dos, NC Report, SocioMétrica, GAD3, 40dB and GESOP polls; CIS barometer of 14 October; Boletín Oficial del Estado (Royal Decree 806/2026); Kalshi, Polymarket.

World.title: Can Latin America Be the New Middle East?
World.content:
LATIN AMERICA · ANALYSIS

Published Tuesday, 27 October, 6:13 a.m. ET · Source: EIA, IEA, UKMTO, ANP, ANH, Guyana’s Ministry of Finance, TotalEnergies, Campetrol, Wood Mackenzie

Key Facts — Gulf crisis Attacks on ships have cut traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, the world’s key oil chokepoint, by roughly 70 percent, and Brent trades near $110 a barrel.

— Guyana’s rise Guyana pumped about 902,000 barrels a day in the first half of 2026, and its December loading schedule could push exports past 1 million for the first time.

— Venezuela’s return Chevron plans to invest more than $7 billion over five years in Venezuela, aiming to lift its output to about 600,000 barrels a day.

— Argentina’s record Argentina’s crude output hit a record 973,700 barrels a day in September, and Wood Mackenzie expects it to pass Guyana by 2028 as South America’s third-largest liquids producer.

While the Gulf stays unstable, Latin America has a real chance to become the new Middle East of oil. It has giant reserves, ports on two oceans with no chokepoint, short routes to the United States and a wave of governments opening their doors to investors.

The proof is uneven. Guyana already makes more oil per resident than Kuwait, while Venezuela, Colombia and Ecuador are still mostly promises.

(A chokepoint is a narrow sea passage that can be blocked.)

Why the Gulf Is Losing Its Grip

The Strait of Hormuz normally carries about 20 percent of the world’s seaborne oil. The UKMTO maritime monitor counts about 254 ship transits a week, roughly 70 percent below pre-war levels, and more than 20 attacks on ships since 1 October.

October is the worst month of the war for attacks on commercial ships, and the Saudi-led coalition reports shooting down Houthi drones and missiles fired at Saudi Arabia almost every week. Iran says the strait stays shut without US concessions.

Kuwait has no route around the strait. It pumped about 2.5 million barrels a day before the war.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Latin America energy Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Guyana, the New Eldorado

Guyana is the most dramatic case. This small country on South America’s northern coast produced about 902,000 barrels a day in the first half of 2026, and Stabroek, the offshore block that supplies it, passed 1 billion barrels produced in September.

ExxonMobil operates Stabroek with a 45 percent stake. Chevron holds 30 percent, through its purchase of Hess, and China’s CNOOC holds 25 percent.

The Uaru production ship, which can produce 250,000 barrels a day, arrived in August, and its first cargo is scheduled for 11 to 12 December. By 2030, installed capacity on the block is expected to reach about 1.7 million barrels a day, though that measures capacity, not forecast output.

By our own arithmetic, Guyana pumps about 1.07 barrels a day for each resident. Kuwait managed about 0.51 before the war, so Guyana’s output per person is about twice Kuwait’s pre-war level.

Guyana’s income per person is about $33,000, almost the same as Kuwait’s, by IMF-based estimates, and the IMF projects growth of 16.2 percent for 2026 after 19.3 percent in 2025. The state’s Natural Resource Fund is paying about 32 percent of the 2026 budget.

But Guyana’s output is only about 36 percent of Kuwait’s pre-war output. Kuwait holds roughly 100 billion barrels of reserves against about 11 billion barrels of oil equivalent for Stabroek (a 2022 estimate), and Kuwait’s investment authority is estimated at $0.85 to $1.07 trillion against Guyana’s $4.1 billion fund.

Guyana is the Kuwait of per-person wealth, not yet of scale.

Suriname Is Next Door and Next in Line

Suriname, Guyana’s eastern neighbor, is following the same path. The GranMorgu project in Block 58 is operated by TotalEnergies with 40 percent; APA Corporation also holds 40 percent and the state company Staatsolie 20 percent.

The final investment decision came in October 2024, committing about $10.5 billion, and the floating production ship will handle 220,000 barrels a day. TotalEnergies’ chief executive said in July the project is 40 percent complete, with first oil expected in the first half of 2028.

In January the IMF said that fiscal slippages in 2025 had eroded earlier progress toward stability.

Venezuela Comes Back

Venezuela claims the world’s largest reserves, 303 billion barrels, though experts doubt that figure. US forces captured Maduro on 3 January 2026, and Delcy Rodríguez is now acting president; Washington recognised her on 5 March.

A hydrocarbons law reform passed on 29 January, and no election date has been set. US licenses allow established American companies to trade and invest, but they can be revoked at any time.

On Venezuela’s own figures, output rose from 924,000 barrels a day in January to 1.206 million in September, but it has been flat since July. Secondary sources put September at 1.15 million, and exports were 1.08 million, of which 629,000 went to the United States.

Chevron plans to invest more than $7 billion over five years, aiming to lift its output to about 600,000 barrels a day. Italy’s Eni signed a 25-year contract for the Junín 5 field, which holds about 35 billion barrels in place but produces only about 12,000 barrels a day today; GeoPark has committed about $1.2 billion.

State oil company PDVSA says 61 of 105 planned contracts are signed, with a 31 December deadline. Blackouts in July hit the plants that upgrade the thick crude, imports of the light fuel used to thin it more than doubled in August, and drilling rigs are scarce.

According to trading sources, buyers bid $18 to $20 under Brent for heavy Merey crude in September, as traders pushed discounts over freight costs and delays. Freight from Venezuela to the US Gulf Coast cost about $5 a barrel, up from $1.90 early in the year.

Colombia Opens the Door

Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, won the 21 June runoff with 49.65 percent of the vote against 48.70 percent, on the preliminary count. He took office on 7 August; his predecessor, Gustavo Petro, had halted new exploration contracts, and de la Espriella has pledged to reverse that.

On 7 August he pledged to revive oil and gas, expand exploration and allow fracking under strict technical and environmental standards. On 25 September, at the swearing-in of the new Ecopetrol president, Joaquín Gutiérrez, he said his government reopens the path of exploration fully.

No licensing round or fracking timetable has been announced. Output was about 733,000 barrels a day in August, down 2.3 percent from a year earlier, according to the industry group Campetrol.

Proved reserves stand at 2.02 billion barrels, about 7.4 years of supply at current rates, according to the National Hydrocarbons Agency (ANH). Imported gas now supplies about 41 percent of Colombia’s demand and costs about $25 per MMBtu, the standard gas price unit, against $10 to $12 for the domestic gas it replaces.

Risks remain. Attacks on the Caño Limón-Coveñas pipeline in October, suspected to be the work of the ELN guerrilla group, show the security challenge, and the president’s narrow mandate and community opposition to fracking limit his room to move.

Ecuador Wants to Turn Output Around

Ecuador, under President Daniel Noboa, produced about 460,000 barrels a day in the first eight months of 2026, and state company Petroecuador accounted for 365,704 in August. The ministry targets 500,000 barrels a day by December, but the central bank projects only about 463,000 for 2027.

A new hydrocarbons law is in final drafting, and a round of 14 fields, worth about $1 billion, is planned from December. A second round of 14 blocks on the Peru border, with potential of 300,000 barrels a day, is slated for late 2027.

Peru’s state company Petroperú awarded a 16.2 million barrel supply deal for Oriente, Ecuador’s main export crude, worth about $1.65 billion. It cuts freight per cargo from about $7 to $8 million to about $1.8 million.

A major risk is erosion of the Coca River, which shut the main pipelines in 2025; a bypass would take 18 to 24 months to build.

Argentina and Brazil Already Deliver

Argentina’s crude output hit a record 973,700 barrels a day in September, up 15.5 percent and 26,300 short of 1 million. Almost all of it comes from the Vaca Muerta shale in Neuquén province, which supplied 697,595 of the 714,089 barrels a day produced there in September.

Wood Mackenzie expects Argentina to pass Guyana by 2028 as South America’s third-largest liquids producer. The Vaca Muerta Sur export pipeline was about 80 percent complete in July, with first exports expected in early 2027.

Brazil remains the region’s giant. Its ANP oil agency reported August oil production of 4.615 million barrels a day, up 18.4 percent from a year earlier.

Oil and gas together reached 6.002 million barrels of oil equivalent a day (oil and gas counted in oil-barrel terms), the first time above 6 million. Petrobras produced 2.96 million barrels a day in September, and China bought 54 percent of Brazil’s crude exports in the first half of 2026.

The US Energy Information Administration’s October outlook, as reproduced by a secondary source, expects Brazil to produce 5.26 million barrels a day of liquids this year, Argentina 1.08 million and Guyana 0.92 million. The United States tops them all at 24.39 million.

The Honest Limits

The boom is real, but it is not a simple replacement for the Middle East. Shipping one barrel from the Americas to Asia now costs roughly $40, and the IEA put the Gulf-to-Asia rate at about $36 in early October.

That freight bill pushes down what Asian buyers will pay for heavy Latin American crude. Argus, a price-reporting agency, put Colombia’s Vasconia at about $84 and Ecuador’s Oriente at about $76 before freight on 8 October, each down more than $10 to a six-week low.

Venezuelan barrels compete directly with Colombian and Ecuadorian heavy grades. If the Strait of Hormuz reopens, part of the risk premium behind today’s prices could fall away.

Reserves are not barrels: contracts and pledges do not equal output. Venezuela’s claimed 303 billion barrels, Guyana’s roughly 11 billion barrels of oil equivalent and Argentina’s shale all need years of investment and stable politics.

What It Means for US Readers

For US buyers, the shipping route from Venezuela to the US Gulf Coast is short, at about $5 a barrel in freight. The United States took 629,000 barrels a day of Venezuela’s 1.08 million barrels of exports in September.

Chevron holds 30 percent of Guyana’s Stabroek Block and plans to invest more than $7 billion in Venezuela. Gas buyers should note that Colombia still imports about 41 percent of its own gas.

What to Watch

The US Federal Reserve decides on rates on 28 October, and US midterm elections follow on 3 November. Guyana expects Uaru’s first cargo on 11 to 12 December.

Guyana’s government expects the International Court of Justice to rule on Venezuela’s Essequibo claim from November 2026, and Venezuela rejects the court’s jurisdiction. PDVSA’s contract deadline falls on 31 December, and Argentina’s Vaca Muerta Sur pipeline is due to ship its first exports in early 2027.

What We Do Not Know

Ship transits counted by UKMTO are about 70 percent below pre-war, but barrel flows are harder to measure and trackers disagree. Kpler estimates about 14 million barrels a day including offshore transfers, about 82 percent of pre-war flows; another estimate puts the figure at 6 to 8 million, and Tankertrackers at 3.7 million.

Official Venezuelan figures show about 1.206 million barrels a day in September, while secondary sources show 1.15 million. Output has been flat since July, so the 1.4 million target for year-end looks hard to reach.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Latin America being compared to the Middle East for oil?

Guyana, Venezuela, Argentina and Brazil are all raising output, and their ports on the Atlantic and Pacific avoid chokepoints like Hormuz. Colombia’s new government and Ecuador’s planned bidding rounds are opening exploration.

How much oil does Guyana produce?

About 902,000 barrels a day in the first half of 2026. Its December loading schedule could push exports past 1 million barrels a day for the first time.

Is Venezuela really coming back as an oil producer?

Output is about 1.2 million barrels a day on Venezuela’s own figures, up from 924,000 in January. It has been flat since July, and the 1.4 million barrel target for year-end looks hard to reach.

What are the main risks to Latin America’s oil boom?

Freight costs hit heavy crude bound for Asia, and a reopened Hormuz could cut the risk premium. Reserves and pledges also do not become barrels without years of investment.

Which companies are involved?

ExxonMobil operates Guyana’s Stabroek block with Chevron and CNOOC as partners. TotalEnergies leads Suriname’s GranMorgu project, and Chevron plans to invest over $7 billion in Venezuela.

Sources: EIA, IEA, UKMTO, ANP, ANH, Guyana’s Ministry of Finance, TotalEnergies, Campetrol, Wood Mackenzie.

World.title: Drones Hit Power Grid in Sudan’s Capital
World.content:
File photo: the Omdurman Bridge lit at night, 2012. Hind Mekki ElMardi, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.

Published Tuesday, 27 October, 5:09 a.m. ET (11:09 a.m. Port Sudan) · Source: Sudan’s state electricity company, Sudan Electricity Holding Company

Khartoum woke up to another morning of darkness. A drone hit the Al-Markhiyat power substation, a local electricity site in Omdurman, the western half of Sudan’s capital region, early on Tuesday and cut electricity across large parts of the city.

It is the second day running that Sudan’s grid has been under attack in the war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group. Our Sudan war explainer covers how the conflict reached this point.

Key Facts What happened: A drone struck the Al-Markhiyat substation in northwestern Omdurman early Tuesday, cutting power in large parts of Khartoum.

A drone struck the Al-Markhiyat substation in northwestern Omdurman early Tuesday, cutting power in large parts of Khartoum. Who is blamed: A source at the state electricity company blamed the RSF; no official statement or RSF claim by 2:30 a.m. ET.

A source at the state electricity company blamed the RSF; no official statement or RSF claim by 2:30 a.m. ET. The day before: Sudan Electricity Holding Company, the state utility, said drones hit five power substations in four states on Monday.

Sudan Electricity Holding Company, the state utility, said drones hit five power substations in four states on Monday. Why it matters for US readers: Grid attacks hit hospitals, water and farms, deepening one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises.

In plain English Sudan’s army and the RSF have fought since April 2023. Both sides now use cheap armed drones, and power stations have become targets.

What Happened at Al-Markhiyat

Eyewitnesses said a drone hit the Al-Markhiyat substation early on Tuesday. Large parts of Khartoum lost power, and as of 6:30 a.m. GMT (2:30 a.m. ET, 8:30 a.m. Khartoum) no official damage report had been issued.

Videos on social media showed smoke over the site, but we could not verify them. No statement had given the extent of the damage, and no casualty figures had been published.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Sudan Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Is Blamed, and What Is Unproven

A source at Sudan’s state electricity company said RSF drones targeted the transformer station. Officials had issued no formal statement on responsibility by 2:30 a.m. ET, and the RSF had not claimed the attack.

The RSF rarely comments on such accusations and says it works to protect civilians.

A Second Day of Grid Attacks

On Monday, Sudan Electricity Holding Company, the state utility, accused the RSF of drone attacks on five power substations across four Sudanese states: Sennar, Gedaref, Al-Jazira and White Nile. Those strikes caused widespread blackouts.

We reported that wave in our coverage of the south-east blackout. Al-Markhiyat has been hit before, in drone attacks in May and September 2025.

Why Power Is a Lifeline

Hospitals, water pumps and farm irrigation all depend on the grid. Without electricity, pumps stop and food production suffers.

Each outage also strains hospitals that run on fuel-hungry generators. Repairs take time when the same sites are struck again.

What It Means for US Readers

Sudan gets little attention in the United States, yet the war has displaced millions and drives calls for more aid and pressure on both sides. Strikes on grids show how the fighting now reaches daily life far from the front line.

For aid groups and policymakers, a failing grid raises the risk of disease and hunger, which usually pushes more people to flee across borders.

What Is Not Known

The exact time of impact, the number of drones and the scale of the damage are not confirmed. Nor is how long the outage will last, or whether the RSF was responsible.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is blamed for the Khartoum power strike?

A source at Sudan’s state electricity company blamed the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group fighting Sudan’s army. No official statement or independent check confirmed that by 2:30 a.m. ET, and the RSF had not claimed the attack.

Why do attacks on power stations matter in Sudan?

Hospitals, water pumps and farm irrigation depend on the grid. When it fails, health care and food production suffer for millions of people.

Sources: statements of Sudan’s state electricity company and Sudan Electricity Holding Company; eyewitness accounts.

World.content:
SAN JOSÉ · Culture

Gorillaz are listed as sold out at Parque Viva on 14 November, and Karol G plays the Estadio Nacional on 27 and 28 November. The month, day by day.

The Teatro Nacional in central San José. Photo: Mariordo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
