y más de de uso habitual, y ofrece un informe con las a cada uno de estos medicamentos. En Europa ya se han hecho más de 1.000 perfiles farmacogenéticos con este sistema.

Hacia un pasaporte genético

En el futuro, coinciden los especialistas, se abre paso la idea de que todo ciudadano cuente con un carnet genético. Esta posibilidad existe gracias a la tecnología, explica Suela, que ha multiplicado el poder de las técnicas de genotipado: “Antes hacíamos un solo caso, un solo paciente, con cientos de marcadores. Ahora procesamos hasta 96 casos y en cada uno analizamos millones de marcadores. El salto es impresionante”.

0:00 JAVIER SUELA, director técnico del laboratorio de genética de Sanitas (Madrid)

El objetivo es que la farmacogenética sea útil, no un mero postulado teórico. Y ya lo es, pero todavía a pequeña escala. Mi Farmagen acumula ya mil análisis farmacogenéticos a pacientes con aplicación real. “Necesitamos que poco a poco todos tengamos un carnet farmacogenómico. En la actualidad esa información que tenemos ya nos salta a la historia clínica de forma automática como alerta a la hora de prescribir medicamentos con un programa propio, Farmacheck, y esta información también está a disposición del paciente en su app para poder ajustar e individualizar el tratamiento. En pocos años será un estándar”, señala Azcárate. Suela añade: “Nuestro sueño sería que en más del 90% de las prescripciones se tuviese en cuenta esa información genética de manera previa”.

Todo con un fin: obtener la mayor seguridad para el paciente, ya que, hasta hoy, “a la hora de prescribir algunos fármacos, operábamos con un método prueba-error: si no funcionaba uno, o si funcionaba mal, se probaba otro. Pero con la farmacogenética se abre otro camino, de máxima seguridad, basado en evidencias clínicas rigurosas”, afirma Suela.

World.title: PP y Vox, una alianza clarificadora
World.content:
El acuerdo alcanzado por Partido Popular y Vox para las listas del Senado surge en respuesta a los pactos alcanzados por las fuerzas progresistas para la Cámara alta. Vox renuncia a concurrir en 14 circunscripciones y en otras 14 presenta un solo candidato. El PP, por su parte, hará lo mismo en tres, Gipuzkoa, Girona y Tarragona, un alto precio para un partido de Estado que ha gobernado España más de 13 años y aspira a volver a hacerlo.

Esta alianza tiene sus hándicaps. Parece lógico pensar que los conservadores más templados serán reacios a marcar la equis en los nombres de Vox, de la misma forma que resultará complicado explicar a quienes surgen como una escisión del PP que deben votar por aquel partido del que han huido. Tampoco parece sensato pensar que quienes van a salir de la abstención para unirse al lado pretendidamente “antiestablishment” de Vox puedan apoyar a un partido tan sistémico como el PP. Veremos si el objetivo de acabar con “el sanchismo” es suficiente.

Más allá de cuestiones tácticas, desde el punto de vista estratégico, el acuerdo alcanzado por PP y Vox clarifica mucho más de lo que parece. En primer lugar, una alianza ya clara y firme entre la derecha conservadora, liberal y sistémica que representa el Partido Popular y la ultraderecha de Vox. Podrá pensarse que era previsible tras compartir gobierno en cuatro comunidades autónomas. Ciertamente. Pero ello no permite obviar la distancia que hay entre la estrategia actual de los populares y las declaraciones que tan solo tres años atrás, en la campaña de 2023, hacía Alberto Núñez Feijóo para diferenciarse de los ultras. En aquella ocasión, el líder popular manifestaba su objetivo de “gobernar en solitario” y buscaba conquistar el centro, para lo que necesitaba alejarse de Vox. Hoy todo esto ha cambiado. Así lo muestran los acuerdos PP-Vox en los gobiernos autonómicos, y la asunción cada vez más clara de los marcos de la ultraderecha en temas como la migración, las políticas ambientales, las cuestiones de género o el modelo fiscal. Esta alianza para el Senado es la puesta de largo, nada menos que en la Cámara alta, de esta connivencia previamente establecida.

Si todo esto es posible, no es solo por la necesidad de llegar a acuerdos para gobernar, dada la fragmentación del voto conservador. Si así fuera, se trataría de mera táctica. Una observación de las propuestas políticas y los marcos utilizados muestra algo más. El único leitmotiv conocido de la campaña del PP es acabar con el sanchismo. Poco se conoce de sus propuestas políticas, del modelo social, económico y político que plantea. Un vacío que guarda relación con la profunda crisis ideológica por la que atraviesan los conservadores en el conjunto de Occidente, y que explica, en buena medida, por qué están teniendo tanta facilidad para asumir los postulados ultras. Nostalgia de los conservadores, titulaba en una tribuna en este medio hace unos días el profesor Innerarity. Carecen de una oferta propia, de un programa elaborado desde ópticas conservadoras dentro de parámetros democráticos. Está por ver los resultados que esta alianza PP-Vox obtiene en la Cámara alta, pero el acuerdo es de lo más expresivo. Se trata de una alianza clarificadora.

World.title: Mi comunidad ha acordado suprimir la calefacción central. ¿Tenemos derecho a saber en qué plazo se cierra?
World.content:
Pregunta. Hemos aprobado en junta la supresión de servicios centrales de calefacción y agua caliente por las tres quintas partes de propietarios y de cuotas. ¿Es necesario establecer un plazo para la clausura? Si es así, ¿debe figurar en el acta de la reunión donde se aprobó la descentralización? M. A. Forcelledo

Respuesta. Sí, es necesario establecer un plazo para la clausura, y este debe figurar de manera explícita en el acta de la junta de propietarios donde se aprobó la descentralización. La supresión de la calefacción y el agua caliente central obliga a los copropietarios a instalar sistemas individuales en sus viviendas (por ejemplo, calderas de gas estancas o sistemas de aerotermia). Por lo tanto, los vecinos necesitan un margen de tiempo razonable para solicitar presupuestos, pedir licencias y acometer las obras en el interior de sus casas antes de que se proceda al apagado definitivo de la caldera comunitaria.

Por otro lado, el cese del servicio supone la eliminación del gasto comunitario de combustible y modifica la distribución de los gastos fijos de mantenimiento. El plazo establecido determina la fecha exacta a partir de la cual dejará de emitirse el recibo de la calefacción central.

En cuanto a si este extremo debe constar en el acta de la junta, la respuesta es sí: de manera obligatoria. Para que el acuerdo de supresión sea plenamente válido y ejecutable, el acta redactada por el administrador de fincas o el secretario debe recoger con total claridad los siguientes aspectos: la fecha exacta o el hito temporal en el que se producirá la clausura y el cómputo de los votos de los propietarios ausentes. Tras la votación en la junta, el acuerdo debe notificarse a los propietarios que no hayan asistido, quienes disponen de un plazo de 30 días naturales para manifestar su discrepancia. Si no se pronuncian dentro de ese periodo, su voto se entiende favorable al acuerdo. Por ello, el plazo efectivo para ejecutar materialmente el cierre debe contemplar siempre este mes de margen legal.

Si el acuerdo se limitara a aprobar la supresión de forma genérica, sin concretar cuándo ni cómo se llevará a cabo, carecería del grado de precisión necesario para ser considerado ejecutivo.

Si tiene dudas, sugerencias o simplemente quiere contarnos su caso, puede enviarnos un email a vivienda@elpais.es .

World.title: Mariana Enriquez, escritora: “El vampiro hoy come dátiles y la bruja está con el sérum”
World.content:
La escritora argentina reúne sus ideas y reflexiones sobre la literatura de terror en ‘Conversación con la oscuridad’

Cuando de niña leía La odisea, a Mariana Enriquez (Buenos Aires, 52 años) lo que le gustaba era la parte en que Odiseo bajaba al infierno, y quería saber más sobre los aterradores monstruos Escila y Caribdis. También en la Biblia tuvo claro que su episodio favorito era la matanza de los inocentes. Aunque era chica quería “rock”, recordaba afable y divertida el pasado viernes en Barcelona, en una de las paradas de su gira por España, adonde ha viajado desde Tasmania, donde reside desde hace un año con su esposo.

Figura indispensable de la narrativa actual, aclamada por crítica y público, la autora de Nuestra parte de noche o de las colecciones de cuentos Las cosas que perdimos en el fuego, Los peligros de fumar en la cama y Un lugar soleado para gente sombría (todos en Anagrama) reúne ahora en Conversación con la oscuridad (Páginas de Espuma) sus reflexiones, opiniones, humor, profundidad y vasto conocimiento sobre la literatura de terror y el gótico. Hilado a partir de clases, conferencias y entrevistas —con la ayuda de la académica Inti Soledad Bustos y el editor Juan Casamayor—, el volumen se estructura en cinco bloques sobre el espacio, el tiempo, la subjetividad, los cuerpos y el trauma, y propone una charla francamente ilustrada y divertida con el lector sobre el horror pasado y el presente y sobre cómo la literatura ha empleado y emplea ese miedo incontrolable como ”material de construcción”. La mente inquieta y la infatigable curiosidad de Enriquez, periodista además de escritora, guían esta Conversación con la oscuridad en la que la autora reivindica la presencia de lo macabro en lo cotidiano, y señala la marca indeleble que los horrores de las dictaduras han dejado en su literatura. Escribe: “El espacio gótico y el espacio del trauma político o del duelo impedido no son analogías, sino que son distintos lados de la misma herida”.

Pregunta. ¿El terror es una forma de reivindicar los márgenes?

Respuesta. Hay una sensibilidad, bastante inexplicable, que te acerca a eso. Luego, cuando lo entendés, un poco más y ves que a los demás eso les parece repulsivo. Una siente que tiene la capacidad y el disfrute de ir ahí y salir totalmente indemne. Eso es un superpoder y lo terminás reivindicando.

P. Como escritora, tardó en llegar a este género.

R. Siempre quise escribir terror, pero no sabía cómo y no me puse a estudiar cómo hacerlo. En Bajar es lo peor introduje elementos como el trío infernal, y esa relación entre los dos personajes principales un poco a lo Entrevista con el vampiro. Era 1995 y el libro está escrito en clave de realismo sucio. Después escribí una novela fantástica de terror que llevé a editoriales, pero no funcionó porque no sabía cómo hacerlo. Seguí con el realismo en Cómo desaparecer completamente. Y luego me dije ‘Por acá no puedo hacer nada más, vamos a hacer terror y a ver cómo lo hago’.

P. ¿Y entonces?

R. Me puse a leer de vuelta todo, por ejemplo, Stephen King. Y vi que yo no puedo escribir sobre Providence, ni fanatismo religioso baptista más masacre escolar, porque eso no existe en Argentina. Me puse a pensar qué existe en América Latina o en mi ambiente. Lo mismo con Edgar Allan Poe. Mi primer cuento de terror, El aljibe, es sobre una chica que tiene un ataque de pánico y no puede salir a la calle: es mi traslación de la ultraparanoia de Poe al trastorno de pánico. Además, empecé a escribir con un punto de vista de narradora femenina. Para hablar de ese tipo de terror muy cercano porque es muy íntimo, me sirvió.

P. ¿Cómo fue ese cambio?

R. Pensé, como todas las escritoras, que soy mujer, ergo puedo escribir una narradora, pero no. En mi vida lectora a esas alturas había leído muchos más narradores masculinos que femeninos. Ahora leemos más mujeres porque se descubren y publican más.

La escritora argentina Mariana Enriquez, durante la entrevista. Massimiliano Minocri

P. Después de una década escribiendo terror, ¿llegó el momento de ordenar sus ideas sobre el tema?

R. En todo este tiempo seguí investigando el terror, no solo la escritura técnicamente, porque eso más o menos te sale o no. El terror tiene que funcionar y, si no, ciao. En comedia, vos no podés estar cinco años tratando de hacer reír, y el terror es lo mismo. Pero en cuanto a qué conforma todo el campo, qué leo, qué me interesa, desde dónde lo pienso, seguí.

P. En el ensayo reflexiona sobre el lugar que el terror ocupa hoy en la narrativa latinoamericana. ¿Asume formar parte de una corriente?

R. No me gusta tomar la palabra por gente que no soy yo, decir que somos parte de este movimiento, ni esa noción de equipo, porque cada escritor escribe y hace lo que quiere. Pero llega un momento en que no podés no ver las conexiones: hay demasiadas escritoras y escritores de América Latina trabajando en terror, new weird, fantasía oscura, gótico, ciencia ficción muy extrema. Gente como Luis Barragán, colombiano lovecraftiano; Luciano Lamberti en Argentina, que ha ganado el premio Clarín con una novela sobre necromancia y dictadura; Maximiliano Barrientos, que es boliviano y escribe black metal andino; Mónica Ojeda con Nefando y los cuentos de Las voladoras; Fernanda Trías con esa cosa apocalíptica en un lugar tan gótico como Montevideo. Claramente es algo que está pasando, pero no está la idea de movimiento y me parece bien. Sí hay una sensibilidad compartida.

Mariana Enriquez, en Barcelona. Massimiliano Minocri

P. Y se da en un continente, según señala en el ensayo.

R. La experiencia como ciudadano y persona traumatizada por la migración, la violencia, la desigualdad, no puede no estar.

P. Apunta que se exige a los ciudadanos inmunizarse ante la desigualdad y la violencia. ¿Esa normalización es lo espeluznante?

R. No hay normalización de esto en nuestros países. Naciste con eso, históricamente conviviste con eso, es normal, es tu vida, es el mundo en el que vivís.

P. ¿Ahí encuentra la grieta para adentrarse en el terror?

R. Sí. Esa mala leche que tienen a veces mis personajes es resentimiento y supervivencia. No es una rabia gloriosa, es una pasión más baja, pero que te permite seguir y superadaptarte, y eso es lo que tienes que hacer. No son condiciones nuevas, son condiciones de tus padres, son probablemente condiciones de tus abuelos, de toda tu clase social. Esa clase media maltratada por muchas crisis económicas explica ciertos virajes políticos. Porque llega un momento en que vos tenés 60 años y decís: probemos esta locura a ver si ocurre algo.

P. ¿Y el terror?

R. Se filtra en eso, porque estás toda tu vida en un permanente estado de alarma. Y es esa condición pavorosa de pensar que estoy esperando el golpe, esperando cuándo va a pasar.

P. Señala el tiempo como un elemento clave. ¿Hoy se mira menos al futuro que al pasado?

R. La noción de políticas de la memoria que yo revindico al cien por cien en realidad es la memoria del horror, porque políticamente es lo que hay que recordar para no repetir y para la búsqueda de justicia y qué sé yo. Hay una insistencia diaria y política de la memoria que si lo atravesaste en tiempo real no se termina nunca, un loop, un tiempo detenido.

P. El trauma vuelve. Cuenta que a veces le dicen que deje de escribir de la dictadura.

R. Como escritor uno trata de ser lo más honesto posible con lo que tiene para contar y decir. Mientras siga supurando esto, es de lo que tengo o quiero o puedo escribir. Entiendo a la gente joven que no está en ese lugar. Mi generación pasó por millones de etapas con la dictadura. Tienes la infancia en dictadura, la revelación de todo lo que pasó, el encuentro con la gente de tu generación que es hija de desaparecidos. Muchos son artistas y están cambiando la mirada, hay una búsqueda de diferentes lenguajes para hablar de ese tiempo.

P. Muchas maneras de volver a leer aquello.

R. Es un tema que sigue latiendo, porque fue muy contemporáneo a nuestra vida en todo el proceso de lo que significó y de lo que significa ahora.

P. Describe el duelo como la experiencia más universal de lo fantástico.

R. En los primeros momentos es absolutamente liminal. Más allá de las personas, con una mascota la primera vez que vuelves a la casa la sientes. La producción de ese fantasma te dirán que es psicológica y, está bien, la tristeza también es psicológica y es real. Podemos vivir un poco en un mundo menos básico: no tengamos tanto miedo a imaginar. Lo que me gusta del terror es que permite articular los pensamientos jodidos.

P. Lo que no nos queremos decir.

R. Sí.

P. Habla de la desaparición de Miguel Bru y de cómo eso le marcó. ¿La identidad está marcada por cosas no solucionadas que vuelven?

R. En la muerte de Miguel hay algo muy significativo en cuanto a la formación de mi imaginación. Eran años en que estábamos en plena fiesta y a él lo secuestra la policía y lo matan dentro de sus dependencias y su cuerpo nunca aparece. Estábamos en democracia y se reproduce la narrativa de la represión del terrorismo de Estado, un secuestro, una negación de que eso ocurrió, el gaslighting. Los tipos habían reconstruido la comisaría para que cuando alguien declarara que había una ventana ahí ya no estuviera. Es lo siniestro, lo liminal y los back rooms. En medio de la primera juventud fue como decir “Chicos, la historia de ustedes vienen de esta matriz de mierda”. A todos nos cambió mucho.

P. Escribe sobre horrores que están en nuestra actualidad, temas como la inmortalidad o el transhumanismo.

R. Lo que me perturba es la enmierdización de dos conceptos que para mí durante mucho tiempo fueron tan románticos y atractivos: el vampiro y las brujas. El vampiro se convirtió en algo estéril, lleno de suero, que come dátiles, ultrasano. Es una tremenda decepción para alguien con una imaginación romántica. La bruja está hoy con el sérum. Cómo no estar deprimido cuando tus mitos atractivos y marginales y oscuros se convierten en esto plano y feo y caro.

P. ¿La vuelta del terror como género literario es un síntoma de la búsqueda de lo romántico y lo emocionante?

R. El terror es como un humanismo, aunque suene bestia. Está en busca de esas sensaciones humanas.

World.title: “Tienes el mismo carácter que tu abuelo”: cómo afectan a los niños las comparaciones familiares
World.content:
Cada persona tiene su propia personalidad y manera de actuar, y los niños, en muchas ocasiones, adoptan gestos o respuestas de sus adultos de referencia y los incorporan a su propia identidad. Puede ser una buena educación, una actitud concreta ante problemas e incluso acciones inconscientes de personas con las que se relacionan. Sin embargo, si estas características las adoptan de alguien con quien los padres no tienen una buena relación, ¿cómo afrontan sentir que ven a esa persona a través de su hijo?

“Cuando los padres reconocen en su hijo un gesto, tono de voz o forma de reaccionar que les recuerda a alguien con quien mantienen una relación dolorosa, lo primero que se activa no es un pensamiento razonado, sino una reacción emocional casi instantánea, como tensión, rechazo o alarma”, explica la psicóloga Irene López, responsable clínica terapéutica de los centros anda CONMiGO. En este momento, el adulto ve al menor como a otra persona cuya actitud quiere evitar. “Es un mecanismo humano y mucho más frecuente de lo que se admite en voz alta”, indica López, y apunta a la falta de distancia para cuestionar ese pensamiento y no a este en sí.

Más información Retirada una polémica campaña en Irlanda que pide el consentimiento de los nietos a los abrazos de sus abuelos

Comparar al hijo por actitudes espontáneas similares a las de la otra persona adulta puede suponer un problema si los padres no piensan en el contexto: “Si este tipo de proyecciones no las pasamos por un criterio reflexivo, puede darse un deterioro en el vínculo con el hijo porque interpretamos respuestas que pueden ser naturales y adecuadas a su edad con características propias de conflictos del mundo adulto”, sostiene Patricia Megías, psicóloga especializada en familias y codirectora de Neurohábilis. “Como, además, esto suele ocurrir en momentos de conflicto con nuestros hijos, podemos dejar de estar disponibles cuando más nos necesitan para calmarse y organizar sus sentimientos”, añade.

Cuando se dan estos momentos, puede afectar a ambas partes de manera distinta. El límite entre comentar un parecido familiar con naturalidad frente a trasladarle al niño los conflictos que tenemos con esa persona siempre está en “la emocionalidad desde la que nace ese comentario”, apunta Megías. Es decir, si el tono es para indicar algún aspecto positivo, que además genera un necesario sentido de pertenencia, o si se nombra a modo de crítica, porque además estos aspectos “se dan en momentos evolutivos tan diferentes que no son comparables”, desarrolla la psicóloga.

El menor no registra con precisión el porqué de la incomodidad de sus padres, sino algo “mucho más primario, es decir, una señal de que, siendo él mismo, provoca rechazo”, alerta López. Y esto supone algo fundamental por la alta sensibilidad infantil a las microseñales de desaprobación: “En las primeras etapas del desarrollo, el niño no es capaz de separar con claridad lo que hace frente a lo que es, porque la conducta puntual y la identidad todavía no están diferenciadas”, explica. Esto supone que el niño sufra un efecto acumulativo que provoque que se autorregule en presencia de esa figura y desarrolle una hipervigilancia relacional, avisa López: “Con el tiempo, esta anticipación del rechazo puede generalizarse a otras relaciones, no solo con ese progenitor, y condicionar cómo se vincula con iguales o figuras de autoridad”. Además, la psicóloga subraya que este proceso no requiere un mensaje verbal explícito, y que el rechazo silencioso puede tener un impacto tan significativo como la crítica directa por su dificultad de identificar y nombrar y, en consecuencia, de reparar.

Desde el punto de vista de los padres, sus propias experiencias pueden influir en la forma en que interpretan las conductas de sus hijos. skynesher (Getty Images)

Megías destaca también el papel de la autoestima infantil más allá del autoconcepto, dado el aspecto peyorativo de los comentarios que puede recibir un menor. Y avisa de que mantener estos reproches hacia el hijo empeorará su propia autoestima. “Si este tipo de comentarios se da de manera puntual y en un vínculo de apego seguro, un niño puede sentir enfado y tristeza, nombrarla y que el adulto repare este comentario dañino”, apunta. Pero cuando se alargan, en una situación vincular insegura donde el niño no expresa su molestia, normalmente se vive con culpa y autorreproche y se percibe a sí mismo como inadecuado o molesto, y esto lleva a conclusiones como las creencias nucleares, que son las convicciones más profundas que una persona tiene sobre sí misma, sobre los demás y sobre el mundo y que “pueden ser muy limitantes a lo largo de toda la vida”.

Desde el punto de vista de los padres, sus propias experiencias familiares pueden influir en la forma en que interpretan y responden a las conductas de sus hijos. El estudio Determinants of Child Emotion Regulation in the Context of Adversity: Examining the Effects of Parent’s Emotion Dysregulation and Hostile Attribution Biases, publicado en 2025 en International Journal of Early Childhood Education, encontró una relación entre las experiencias adversas de los progenitores, sus dificultades para regular las emociones y una mayor tendencia a atribuir intenciones negativas a los niños. Por su parte, el informe Parental Childhood Adversity and Emotional Functioning: Associations With Child’s Emotion Regulation, publicado en Family Relations en el mismo año, observó que determinadas experiencias difíciles durante la infancia de los padres se relacionaban con dificultades para comprender y regular las emociones, tanto propias como de sus hijos.

Hay varias señales que pueden indicar que los progenitores están reaccionando desde su propia historia emocional y no tanto desde lo que realmente ha hecho su hijo. Entre ellas, López destaca las reacciones desproporcionadas ante comportamientos leves, las respuestas automáticas de enfado o rechazo, sin apenas tiempo para valorar lo sucedido, y la aparición de frases recurrentes como “eres igual que” u “otra vez lo mismo”. Otros indicios son que la emoción intensa aparezca antes de interpretar lo ocurrido, que el adulto mantenga su enfado incluso cuando se le explica que el niño no tenía mala intención o que su comportamiento es propio de la edad, y lo que López denomina “desconexión selectiva”: cuando una misma conducta apenas provoca reacción si la protagoniza otro hijo, un sobrino o un niño ajeno.

Cuando ya se ha producido el comentario peyorativo o las comparaciones, López avisa de que “el error puntual no es lo que daña al niño, sino no repararlo”. Para ello, recomienda reconocer el fallo sin trasladar al hijo los conflictos del adulto, con frases como “me equivoqué al hablarte así, no fue justo”, y aprender a distinguir si el malestar procede de la conducta infantil o, por el contrario, de una experiencia familiar propia. También aconseja evitar expresiones como “eres igual que” y centrarse en comportamientos concretos: “La diferencia entre ‘eres un mentiroso’ y ‘esta vez no me has dicho la verdad’ no es cosmética, porque la primera etiqueta a la persona, pero la segunda señala un hecho puntual y reparable”, apunta. Para Megías, reparar el daño también es lo más importante: “La forma más simple siempre es la más acertada: reparar. Y abrirnos a poder escuchar con humildad lo que nuestros hijos necesitan nombrarnos de vuelta”.

World.title: Netherlands to stay away from Eurovision Song Contest after all
World.content:
The Netherlands will not take part in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest after public broadcaster NPO said there was “not enough support” for sending an act.

The decision reverses a previous U-turn after AVROTROS, the broadcasting company that is usually responsible for the Dutch entry, said it would boycott the contest for a second year in 2027 because of Israel’s continued participation.

NPO said last month it would make alternative arrangements to participate in the contest in the Bulgarian coastal city of Burgas next May.

But on Tuesday Jet de Ranitz, chair of NPO’s board of directors, said after holding talks with networks and staff that there was “not enough support” for a Dutch entry.

AVROTROS said in September it would be staying away until “transparent rules” were drawn up on countries involved in military conflicts to restore the “neutrality” of the event.

The Netherlands was one of five countries not to send an entry last year, but news broadcaster NOS still sent a team to cover the event and will do so again next year. Ireland has also said it will continue its boycott in 2027 and is not broadcasting the contest.

Staff critical

Around 500 NPO employees signed a letter a week ago criticising the broadcaster’s decision to look for a replacement for AVROTROS, saying that “the desire to take part in an entertainment programme is considered more important than the countless lives of people who are being murdered.”

De Ranitz did not directly mention Israel’s participation, but said NPO had concluded after consulting broadcasting license holders that “it is too early at the moment to take part in the Eurovision Song Contest”.

“Because of the sensitivities around the issues that are taking place now, we have decided to step aside for now,” she said.

NPO is in charge of the Dutch broadcasting infrastructure, but programmes are made by autonomous licensed companies.

The European Broadcasting Union, which organises the song contest, said it regretted NPO’s decision. It said it recognised the “deep-rooted and genuine opinions about the song contest and that they vary strongly”, but argued the event was an opportunity to bring unity to a “divided world”.

Culture minister Rianne Letschert said NPO had made an “editorial decision” and it was not her place to intervene.

“The song contest is an event that touches many people and understandably gives rise to widely differing opinions,” she said. “I understand that none of the broadcasters are prepared to take over the entry for the song festival for 2027.”

World.title: “Significant minority” feel disadvantaged in Dutch society – SCP
World.content:
A “significant minority” of people in the Netherlands believe other groups in society gain an unfair advantage at their expense, according to a survey for the Dutch government’s social research agency SCP.

Around 30% of people say they feel disadvantaged in the housing market, while 28% believe their views are not properly represented in politics. A smaller group of around 7% thought the justice system was biased against them.

The report found that people with minority ethnic backgrounds and white Dutch people with non-academic qualifications were most likely to feel they were being treated unfairly.

“Dutch people who feel they have drawn the short straw are often in a less favourable position in the housing or labour market,” the report’s authors said.

“They are also more likely to be dealing with other disadvantages such as a lower income, a smaller network or poorer health.”

The SCP tracks people’s perceptions of whether they are fairly treated on issues such as housing, justice and observation of traditions on a monthly basis, using focus groups and surveys.

Traditions

The agency said there was evidence that both people with recent migrant backgrounds and white Dutch people were disadvantaged, but both tended to perceive that the other group was better off.

Native Dutch people felt that traditions such as Sinterklaas were being diluted in favour of festivals such as Eid al-Fitr, while recent migrants said there was almost no recognition of their traditions outside a few major population centres.

The lack of trust in institutions also influenced people’s voting behaviour, with those who felt disadvantaged more likely to support far-right parties such as the PVV and FVD.

The report said the majority of people did not feel disadvantaged, while around one in five people perceived themselves to be privileged over others. They were more likely to be university educated and vote for progressive parties such as D66 and Pro.

“In contrast to many graduates, people with vocational educations are more likely to see society as a place where groups compete with each other for scarce resources, attention and recognition,” the report said.

“Moreover, they are more likely to feel that their own group systematically gets more than other groups and place the responsibility for this mainly with the political system and the government.”

World.title: Dutch bitcoin broker Bitonic hacked, funds stolen
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Dutch bitcoin broker Bitonic has been hacked and “small amounts” of cryptocurrency were stolen from customers, according to emails obtained by broadcaster NOS.

The hack took place on Sunday night, and all customers were immediately logged out of their accounts as a precaution. Bitonic says the vulnerability that led to the hack has since been fixed. Three customers lost money and have been fully compensated.

Other customer data could have been accessed during the attack, the company says, though there is no evidence of this yet.

Crypto stored offline on hard drive wallets, known as “cold storage”, remained unaffected.

Bitonic says it will closely monitor all transactions made online for the time being, potentially slowing down any trades.

The hack is the latest blow to the Dutch crypto market after a Rotterdam court declared Knaken, a Netherlands-based crypto platform, bankrupt in July. Prosecutors found that €7 million in customer funds had gone missing.

World.title: Number of millionaires in NL skyrockets as house prices rise
World.content:
Over 81,000 households achieved millionaire status last year without needing to do anything to earn it – the rise in house prices has quietly boosted their wealth.

The figures come from national statistics bureau CBS, which counted 547,000 households with net assets of at least €1 million at the start of 2025 – 6.6% of all Dutch households.

A year earlier the number stood at 466,000. In 2011 it was 170,000. The main driver is the rise in asset valuations – namely house prices.

Two-thirds of millionaire households have between €1 million and €2 million, and 3% have over €10 million.

Those who got rich this way tend to be older – the average millionaire is 61, and fewer than 3% are under 35. For younger people, entrepreneurship and ownership in company shares is the more common way to millionaire status. CBS does not say what role inheritance plays here.

Where you live, of course, makes a big difference. In Bloemendaal and Laren, close to two in five households are now millionaires. In Kerkrade, Zuid-Limburg, it’s closer to 1 in 100. Groningen, Flevoland and Friesland are all below 5%.

World.title: KLM cancels flights to Dubai until March as conflict goes on
World.content:
KLM has cancelled flights to Dubai until next March in the wake of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

The flag carrier also said it will not restart flights to the Saudi capital Riyadh until November 27 at the earliest, despite the reopening of King Khalid International Airport on Sunday. Scheduled flights to Dammam also remain suspended.

KLM had hoped to start flying to Dubai again at the end of October and to Saudi Arabia in early November, but the airline said the situation in the Middle East was too unstable.

It said it wanted to provide clarity to passengers and make the aircraft available to use on other routes.

King Khalid International Airport was closed following an attack two weeks ago that killed 13 people and left more than 300 injured. The Saudi government blamed Houthi rebels in Yemen, backed by Iran, for carrying out the strike.

A Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, warned airlines and travellers not to use the airport after it reopened at the weekend, calling it a “military target”.

World.title: Cabinet under pressure from both sides as budget talks resume
World.content:
The cabinet is resuming talks with seven opposition parties this week as it tries to secure the votes it needs to steer its budget for next year through parliament.

Prime minister Rob Jetten and finance minister Eelco Heinen still hope they can win support from both sides for a broad deal, despite warnings from party leaders that their demands are irreconcilable.

The largest opposition party, the left-wing Pro, is calling for the coalition parties to scrap plans to raise income tax to fill the gap created after it abandoned its welfare cuts, under pressure from Pro and the trade unions.

Pro and the pro-European party Volt say the money should be raised instead through higher taxes on savings and investments, but Heinen’s party, the liberal-conservative VVD, want to replace the wealth tax system with a capital gains tax.

The minority coalition of D66, VVD and CDA needs the support of at least two opposition parties to secure its legislation through parliament.

Pro and Volt have enough seats in the two houses of parliament to guarantee a majority, but the VVD fear that making too many concessions on the left will damage their already precarious standing in the opinion polls.

Asylum and nitrogen

Many VVD voters were dismayed by Heinen’s proposed reforms to the “box 3” wealth tax, which would have led to people with modest investment portfolios paying more, prompting the finance minister to go back to the drawing board.

Opposition parties on the right, such as JA21, are pressing the cabinet to tighten the rules on asylum further as the price for their support.

JA21 leader Joost Eerdmans wants the status of all 70,000 Syrian refugees in the Netherlands to be reviewed and asylum claims to be processed outside the EU. The party also wants to water down the so-called “spreading law” so that the government in The Hague cannot force municipalities to take in minimum numbers of asylum seekers.

Agriculture minister Jaimi van Essen is also expected to take part in the talks, suggesting the cabinet is prepared to compromise on its plans to cut nitrogen pollution, even though Pro has warned the reforms “must not be weakened”.

Another pivotal issue is likely to be the proposed surrogacy law, which the orthodox Protestant party SGP wants the cabinet to withdraw.

The bill was put in the spotlight last week when Jetten and his partner Nicolás Keenan announced they were having a baby next year with the help of a surrogate mother.

At the moment there is no law regulating surrogacy in the Netherlands. Couples who make their own arrangements must have the child adopted before they are legally recognised as parents.

The SGP have said they will not support the cabinet unless it withdraws a bill that would recognise the rights of parents who have children born through surrogacy immediately.

The party also wants the government to intervene to stop hospitals offering to perform abortions after 22 weeks without a compelling medical reason.

World.title: Indians in NL urge cabinet to speak out on “Cockroach” crackdown
World.content:
Indians living in the Netherlands are protesting for political solidarity and media attention to the ongoing “Cockroach” protests sweeping India, which are being met with a brutal crackdown by state forces.

The protests erupted in the summer over suspected corruption in the education system and have since turned to focus on changes in the voting system. Young Indians say they are being denied their democratic rights – something protesters say particularly affects minority groups and women.

Indians are a significant part of the Netherlands’ international community, with the statistics office CBS counting about 54,500 Indian nationals in the country – roughly 3.2% of all foreign nationals.

The Progressive Indians Europe group, based in Amsterdam, gathered in The Hague recently to call for recognition of the injustices they say Narendra Modi’s government is inflicting on its people.

A spokesperson for the group told Dutch News that it was asking the Dutch government to publicly stand up for the democratic principles and human rights commitments it recognises in its own foreign policy.

“These developments directly affect people in the Netherlands,” they said. “Our families, friends and communities remain connected to India. What happens there has real consequences for the people we care about, while the precedent set by the erosion of electoral safeguards matters to democracies everywhere.”

The suppression of the Cockroach movement, the group says, which has seen thousands arrested, journalists detained, and reports of widespread police brutality, means people in the Netherlands should “examine the reporting, listen to affected communities and recognise the importance of independent investigations, transparency and accountability.”

The group stressed that it was not asking people to accept every allegation without scrutiny.

“We hope it encourages the Dutch public, media and policymakers to engage seriously with these developments and recognise that defending democracy is a shared international responsibility.”

A spokesperson for the foreign affairs ministry told Dutch News: “The Netherlands follows the developments in India. As human rights and democracy are an important part of the Strategic Partnership between India and the Netherlands, the Netherlands and India discuss these topics regularly in diplomatic contacts and will continue to do so.”

Struck off

Some of the members said the situation abroad is significantly impacting their lives. Surabhi, from Amsterdam, said she takes her right to vote very seriously, both in India and in Dutch municipal elections.

“I am an Indian national and have always travelled back to India to vote,” she said. “Most recently, I voted in the national elections in 2024 and the municipality elections in Mumbai in January 2026.”

Her name, along with millions of others, has been removed during a revision of the electoral rolls by the Election Commission of India, which says it is improving the voting system by removing dead, duplicate and ineligible voters.

Another protester, Anubhav, described how he can only see the voting list on the Election Commission of India website by using a VPN. When he saw his name had been removed, he submitted a complaint, which was closed the very next day.

He says he is a “popular anti-BJP [the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party] guy on social media among my acquaintances. Is this just a coincidence? I don’t know.”

Cockroach movement

The Cockroach Janta Party, whose name plays on that of Modi’s BJP, started in May as an online satire account. It was a response to India’s chief justice, Surya Kant, describing some activists and unemployed young people as “cockroaches” and “parasites of society”. Kant later said his remarks had been misquoted and misrepresented.

In July, Modi’s education minister was forced to resign in the wake of street protests against leaked exam papers. Amnesty International found that police used pellet-firing shotguns, electric shock batons, tear gas and batons against demonstrators. Delhi police said more than 400 people, including officers, were injured.

The latest wave of protests that began on October 2 was a reaction to a nationwide revision of the voter rolls. According to reports, about 14% of the original names on the rolls – more than 133 million – have been removed since the process began last year. Protesters say eligible voters have been wrongly struck off in favour of the BJP.

The Indian electoral commission says voters removed in error can register again, and has said all its actions were lawful.

More than 2,000 protesters, including several opposition MPs, were detained in Delhi over the weekend of October 10 and 11. On October 13, Human Rights Watch said police had beaten protesters, dragged them through the streets, arbitrarily detained them and suspended mobile internet services.

Police have said protesters were uncooperative and that force was sometimes needed. The UN human rights office has called on the authorities to fully respect the right to peaceful assembly.

Dutch ties with India

Indians make up one of the largest groups of highly skilled migrants from outside the EU, according to statistics bureau CBS. Many work in IT, and more than 300 Indian companies now have a presence in the Netherlands.

The Netherlands is India’s third largest export destination worldwide, the largest in Europe, and the fourth largest investor in India. According to the Indian embassy, merchandise trade stood at $27.8 billion in 2024-2025.

In May this year, Modi visited the Netherlands and, at a roundtable with Dutch business leaders, spoke of a “new golden era in India–Europe relations”, following the conclusion of free trade talks with the bloc. The agreement “between the world’s two largest democratic and responsible powers will become a strong foundation for shared prosperity”, he said.

Before Modi arrived, prime minister Rob Jetten told reporters there were concerns in the Netherlands and other EU countries about developments in India. “It is not only about press freedom, but also about the rights of minorities, who are under severe pressure,” he said, according to de Volkskrant, adding that the concerns were “regularly raised” with India.

India’s foreign ministry later dismissed the remarks as showing a “lack of understanding”.

World.title: Protecting Frisian: trainee teacher numbers more than double
World.content:

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The number of students electing to train as Frisian language teachers has doubled this year, amid a historic drive to strengthen and revive the Netherlands’ only officially recognised second language.

More than 34 students signed up to take a Frisian teacher training course at Leeuwarden’s hbo college NHL Stenden, either as a minor or part-time element of their studies, according to Omroep Fryslân.

The change signals a growing revival trend as Friesland, often ranked the Netherlands’ culturally proudest province, fights to protect its linguistic identity. Only 10 years ago, experts warned the language was on the verge of extinction.

Geert Driessen, of Radboud University in Nijmegen, said in a 2016 study that it was the “eleventh hour” for the province’s mother tongue – especially in urban areas, where Dutch speaking newcomers increasingly mix with locals.

Between 1994 and 2014, he found, Frisian spoken outside family homes had halved. This led to the founding of Taalplan Frysk 2030, a government-backed scheme to protect the language through education and social initiatives.

The plan has received millions of euros in funding, much of which has gone to NHL Stenden. Recent studies show Frisian comprehension is rising, and since this school year all primary and secondary school pupils in Friesland are actively taught the language.

In September, the University of Groningen also launched the first standalone Frisian language degree in 15 years.

Polish far-right leader Grzegorz Braun has been charged with six alleged crimes, including inciting hatred against Jews and vandalising an LGBT+ exhibition. The other four allegations relate to an incident in which he confronted a doctor who performed a late-term abortion. The charges are the latest in a long line of legal cases against Braun, who is already on trial for attacking a Jewish ceremony in Poland’s parliament. However, his party continues to poll strongly, and may play a significant role in deciding what kind of government is formed after next year’s elections. Do sześciu razy sztuka. Grzegorz Braun dostał zarzuty, w tym za uwięzienie ginekolożki Gizeli Jagielskiej Wcześniej europoseł Grzegorz Braun pięć razy unikał przedstawienia zarzutów w Prokuraturze Okręgowej we Wrocławiu. Zainterweniował Prokurator Generalny Waldemar Żurek.… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 26, 2026 As a member of the European Parliament, Braun enjoys legal immunity from prosecution. However, in November 2025, the EP stripped him of immunity to face the six charges. Subsequently, prosecutors tried five times to present Braun with the charges. However, he evaded those attempts by filing motions to have prosecutors excluded from the case or simply by leaving the prosecutor’s office before the charges were read. In July, Poland’s justice minister and prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, filed a motion to the EP for permission to forcibly detain Braun and present him with the charges. That application has not yet been considered but, on Monday, Braun finally attended the prosecutor’s office and heard the charges. Afterwards, Braun told a small group of his followers and the media outside the office in Wrocław that he was the victim of a “state lynching” carried out by “the prosecutor’s office of the Hannukah cannibals, racists and genocide perpetrators”. Four of the charges against Braun relate to an incident in April 2025, when he entered a hospital and confronted a gynaecologist who had been involved in a late-term abortion that had drawn controversy and condemnation from right-wing groups. Braun claimed he was carrying out a citizen’s arrest, but is now charged with deprivation of liberty (for preventing the doctor from leaving her office), violating bodily integrity (by pushing her and holding her down), as well as insult and slander. The maximum sentence for those crimes is five years in prison. In separate proceedings, prosecutors later found that the doctor had not violated Poland’s strict abortion laws by terminating the pregnancy in the ninth month. The fifth charge Braun is now facing stems from an infamous incident in December 2023, when he attacked a Jewish Hanukkah celebration in parliament, putting out the candles with a fire extinguisher. Braun is already on trial over the incident itself. Now, however, prosecutors have charged him over a YouTube interview he gave shortly after the attack, in which they say he “described Hanukkah as a Satanic and racist celebration posing a threat to Polish Catholics, which should be counteracted”. For those remarks, he has been hit with a joint charge of inciting religious hatred and the obstruction of religious acts. The maximum penalty for those offences is a three-year jail term. Finally, Braun has been charged with destruction of property for an incident during his presidential campaign in March this year when he vandalised an exhibition about the local LGBT+ community in the city of Opole, spray-painting “stop the propaganda of perversion” on it. Police are investigating far-right presidential candidate and MEP Grzegorz Braun after he vandalised an LGBT+ exhibition. The city where it took place immediately cancelled a meeting he was due to hold there and is seeking compensation for the damage https://t.co/EbDpMzmpFw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 20, 2025 Braun has pleaded not guilty to all the charges against him, as he has done with a string of other charges for various offences relating to his antisemitic, anti-Ukrainian and anti-LGBT rhetoric and actions. In September, he was stripped of immunity by the EP for the sixth time in order to hear charges of Holocaust denial for his claims that the gas chambers in the Nazi-German death camp of Auschwitz are “fake”. Braun’s high-profile stunts have seen his popularity surge among a section of the electorate. He finished a surprise fourth in last year’s Polish presidential election, with over 6% of the vote, and his Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP) party is now polling around 9%. If it manages to secure that level of support at next autumn’s parliamentary elections, KKP could become a key player in deciding what kind of government can be formed after what looks likely to be a very close contest between the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, and the right-wing and far-right opposition. Poland and Vietnam have upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership, pledging to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, security and defence, as well as education, science, technology and cultural exchanges. “Vietnam and Poland share a success story in terms of development,” declared Prime Minister Donald Tusk at a joint press conference with his Vietnamese counterpart Lê Minh Hưng in Hanoi on Monday. “The time has come to turn our successes into joint actions that will open up more opportunities.” The announcement comes amid a broader flurry of Polish diplomacy in Asia, with Tusk arriving in Hanoi following a visit to India and President Karol Nawrocki visiting the Philippines earlier this month. Poland also recently signed new strategic agreements with South Korea and Japan. 🇵🇱🤝🇻🇳 Polska i Wietnam wchodzą na poziom partnerstwa strategicznego! ✅ Podczas wizyty w Hanoi premier @donaldtusk oraz szef wietnamskiego rządu Lê Minh Hưng podjęli decyzję o podniesieniu wzajemnych relacji do rangi partnerstwa strategicznego, otwierając nowy rozdział we… pic.twitter.com/CCvHmc3eva — Kancelaria Premiera (@PremierRP) October 26, 2026 Tusk, who was making the first visit by a Polish prime minister to Vietnam in 16 years, pointed to the two countries’ rapid recent economic development. “Within a single generation, Vietnam achieved middle-income status”, while “Poland recently joined the ranks of the world’s 20 largest economies”. In fact, while Poland was forecast to join the world’s 20 largest economies last year, it eventually fell narrowly short. However, it is expected to soon overtake Switzerland, the current holder of 20th place. Tusk said that, during his visit, he had often heard people say that “Poland is the Vietnam of Europe and Vietnam is the Poland of Asia”. Last year, Hưng’s predecessor, Phạm Minh Chính, became the first Vietnamese prime minister in 15 years to visit Poland. The two countries first established diplomatic relations in 1950, and both leaders emphasised Poland’s large Vietnamese community, which dates back to students arriving around that time. Speaking on Monday, Hưng noted the two countries’ strong traditional ties, adding that Vietnam always remembers and is grateful for Polish support and assistance during his country’s struggle for independence and national reunification, reports the Vietnamese News Agency (VNA). The Vietnamese are Poland's largest non-European migrant group. Photographer Zula Rabikowska, through her images and interviews, offers an insight into their experiences, identities and the challenges they face https://t.co/tsRwHINapQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 27, 2019 The new strategic partnership agreement signed by Tusk and Hưng pledges to “bring tangible benefits to both nations and contribute to peace, stability, cooperation and prosperity”. It contains commitments to “maintain regular high-level contacts”, reduce non-tariff barriers to trade, and strengthen cooperation on defence, including trade in military equipment. On Sunday, Poland’s deputy minister for state assets, Konrad Gołota, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that negotiations are already underway for Vietnam to buy Polish Krab howitzers and Rosomak armoured fighting vehicles, among other hardware. Polish arms firm Mesko has announced the best financial results in its 100-year history. Record revenues and profits were driven in large part by international demand for Mesko's flagship Piorun air-defence system, which has proved successful in Ukraine https://t.co/Dx1yY54qCP — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 16, 2026 Tusk, pointing to Poland’s current trade deficit with Vietnam, said that Warsaw’s “priority remains a better balance in trade”. “The sectors in which the Vietnamese side is most interested, and in which we really have something to offer, are the arms industry, satellite and space cooperation, pharmaceuticals and food, especially dairy products,” he added. Tusk also announced that the number of annual Polish-Vietnamese student exchanges would rise by 250% and noted that Poland’s national carrier, LOT, would resume direct Warsaw-Hanoi flights in the first quarter of 2027. Poland is taking steps to attract more foreign students as universities face lower enrollment due to demographic decline. Turkey, South Korea, Vietnam and Uzbekistan are among the countries with which the government is cultivating stronger academic ties https://t.co/r878KqS5OV — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 25, 2026 The Polish prime minister acknowledged differences between Poland and Vietnam’s approach to Russia’s war in Ukraine. Vietnam, which has long maintained close ties with Moscow, has avoided condemning the Russian invasion. But he emphasised his belief that, “because of their history, wartime experience and international relations, both Vietnam and Poland can contribute a great deal to the peace process”. Tusk’s trip to Vietnam follows a three-day visit to India, where he and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced a goal of doubling bilateral trade by 2030. Poland and India's PMs have, after meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies Polish-Indian relations are "gaining speed", said @narendramodi https://t.co/iIVIkCXnvr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 22, 2026 In April, Tusk visited South Korea, upgrading Poland’s relations with the country he described as Poland’s “most important ally after the United States”, and deepened Poland’s strategic partnership with Japan on the same tour. Earlier this month, Tusk also announced plans to visit China before the end of the year. Meanwhile, President Nawrocki visited the Philippines this month as part of a bid to secure backing from Asian nations for Poland’s hoped-for membership in the G20. World.title: Two thirds of Poles support liberalising abortion law, finds new poll
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Just over two thirds of Poles support liberalising the country’s abortion law, which is among the strictest in Europe, according to a new poll. However, most do not favour introducing abortion on demand, as protesters called for during demonstrations last week. The findings come shortly after parliament approved legislation intended to ease access to abortion. But the measures face a potential veto from right-wing, opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki. 🔴 Sondaż dla @rzeczpospolita: Niemal 7 na 10 Polaków chce liberalizacji przepisów ws. aborcjihttps://t.co/f7mxwygIxz — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) October 25, 2026 In 2020, Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means pregnancies can now only be legally terminated in two cases: where they result from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if they threaten the mother’s life or health. In a new poll by SW Research for Rzeczpospolita, a leading newspaper, a total of 67.2% of respondents said that they want to liberalise that law. However, only 37.7% favoured introducing abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. Meanwhile, 29.5% preferred the softer option of returning to the situation from before the 2020 TK ruling – often referred to the “abortion compromise” in Poland – in which terminations were only available in three cases. A further 16.2% supported maintaining the current abortion law; 6.0% wanted to make the rules even tougher (which would involve removing one or both justifications for abortion that currently exist); and 10.6% said they had no opinion. The poll found that support for liberalisation of abortion was stronger among women (73.8%) than men (60.3%). The latest findings are consistent with previous polling, which tends to show that a significant majority supports liberalising the abortion law but that there is not a majority in favour of abortion on demand (although some individual polls have narrowly found such a majority). One member of Poland's likely new ruling coalition, The Left, says polls show a majority in favour of abortion on demand. In fact, they do not. And this issue is likely to be one of the hardest for the incoming government to resolve, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4Nze9wwEC3 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2023 The issue has caused significant political disputes in Poland, not only between the right-wing opposition and the more liberal ruling coalition, but also within the coalition itself. Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) and one of its partners, The Left (Lewica), favour introducing abortion on demand. However, more conservative elements of the government, especially the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), prefer a return to the pre-2020 “compromise”. Much of the right-wing opposition, meanwhile, favours maintaining the status quo. However, some more moderate elements of the opposition have suggested it would be best to reverse the TK ruling and return to the “compromise”. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws https://t.co/q7eK7mV9zr — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 23, 2026 In 2024, due to disputes within his coalition, Tusk declared that it was unlikely there would be any abortion reform during the current parliamentary term due to differences within his coalition. However, last week the issue was revived, with the government’s majority in the Sejm, the lower house of parliament, approving a bill that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling (but not introduce abortion on demand). It also passed another bill decriminalising providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. After both bills go through the upper-house Senate, which can suggest amendments but not block them, they will pass to President Nawrocki, who can sign them, veto them, or send them to the TK for assessment. Given that Nawrocki is aligned with the right-wing opposition, has declared his opposition to abortion, and has vetoed a record number of government bills, it is widely expected that he will seek to block efforts to liberalise the abortion law. World.title: Time is running out for Germany to pay Polish WWII victims the compensation they deserve [Opinion]
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Philipp Fritz, Warsaw correspondent for Die Welt (which first published this article in German here) Negotiations on compensation for the still-living victims of the German occupation of Poland have been going on for years. There are some 30,000 to 50,000 such survivors, but their number dwindles every week. Berlin should act now. No “humanitarian gesture” has emerged. “The draft budget currently reflects the fact that no decision has been made,” said Josef Hinterseher, a German foreign office spokesman, at a press conference in late September. He thereby confirmed what many observers had suspected: survivors of concentration camps, ghettos and death marches, former forced workers and participants in the Warsaw Uprising who are still living in Poland will not receive any compensation, one-off payment or monthly pension from the German government. The German chancellor has announced that his country will offer support to surviving Polish victims of WW2 and will help strengthen Poland’s eastern border. However, in both cases he did not provide details of what these measures will involve in practice https://t.co/gKX6142Alo — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2024 Just a few sentences later, Hinterseher moved onto the next subject – the fact that two Russian oligarchs were to be removed from the EU’s sanctions list. Or at least, that Berlin had not been successful in opposing this decision. The fact that these two issues were dealt with publicly one after the other shows that the German government is quicker to reach a decision that makes Putin’s supporters’ lives easier than it is with victims of the Nazi terror. It is a declaration of moral bankruptcy. Warsaw and Berlin have been negotiating compensation for the last remaining victims of the German occupation of Poland for years. There are between 30,000 and 50,000 of them – aged over 90, often living alone and in poor health. Their numbers are dwindling every week. The fact that talks are taking place in Berlin ministries but without any decision being taken is met with sadness and fury in Poland. Increasingly, Poles are getting the impression that, even if the Germans manage to put up memorials, they cannot offer survivors tangible help when it is asked for. It is a common view that in Berlin the descendants of the perpetrators are simply waiting for the victims to die so that this pesky issue will sort itself out. Should that happen, those left behind will not forget, and the Germans will hardly be able to forgive themselves. Warsaw is no longer demanding war reparations from Berlin. In December 2023, Donald Tusk’s government switched to talking about “making amends”. Polish foreign minister @sikorskiradek has called on Germany to “think creatively” about compensating Poland for WWII. On a visit to Berlin, he also said that the new government would "end the cold war" waged by the former ruling PiS party against Germany https://t.co/kZ62nUuqqO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 31, 2024 This is not just splitting hairs. In so doing, Tusk put the ball in the German government’s court, giving it the chance to take action and, through a gesture recognising suffering and providing a relatively small sum of money, to offer people tangible help and do a service to the German-Polish relationship. Former German Chancellor Olaf Scholz is reported to have offered Tusk a one-off payment in 2024, but Poland’s prime minister turned the sum down as insufficient. Instead, Polish diplomats are demanding monthly pensions. In any case, we are talking about a few hundred million euro: a relatively small amount compared to the equivalent of €1.3 trillion that Poland’s former ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party once demanded from Germany, and also in comparison to many other budget items – and yet still there is nothing about compensation in the budget planning. Poland is seeking $1.3 trillion in war reparations from Germany, but Berlin says the issue was legally settled long ago. Legal scholar @MPiatkowski1 examines the arguments of both sides, explains the legal context, and looks at what could come next https://t.co/xsKAY2TukS — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2022 Rumour has it that, in return for compensation, German foreign ministry officials are asking for a kind of Polish guarantee that in future there will be no more demands for reparations, or at least that at least the German gesture will receive good press in Poland. If that is true, it would be thoroughly indecent, bringing to mind an image of a perpetrator trying to buy his victim’s silence. This reflects a belief in objectification, an ugly bureaucratic mentality stemming from a system in which “work” in a ghetto counts towards statutory pension contributions, but no one can bring themselves to pay compensation. This issue can be resolved at the very top. Chancellor Friedrich Merz would have to work with the relevant ministries – the foreign office and finance ministry – to provide for compensation for the victims in the budget. This would be a belated but major and morally right gesture. If politics is too slow – time really is of the essence – then civil society should take it upon itself to show where it stands. Donations for the still living victims of the German tyranny or a fund from which survivors would receive monthly payments can be created from within society. Business can also get involved. German corporations which were guilty of, for instance, exploiting forced labourers in occupied Poland, or those that emerged from them, such as BASF, Siemens, Volkswagen, BMW and Deutsche Bank, could contribute. Poland covers almost all the costs of maintaining former Nazi-German camps on its territory. It has spent more on this than Germany has paid in compensation to Polish war victims It's time for Germany to fund preservation of the sites, argues @W_Kononczuk https://t.co/08nf4c2jMz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 25, 2026 Right now, since its state elections in September, Germany gives the impression of a country whose compass for right and wrong is broken. As of 6 October, the state parliament of Sachsen-Anhalt has as its vice-president Hans-Thomas Tillschneider of the AfD, a man who wrote on X that “the Poles have been getting on my nerves for a long time now”. In Berlin, not only did the left-wing Die Linke celebrate their electoral success with Israel haters and antisemites, they even tolerate them in their ranks. It is shameful. But now Germany, and particularly its government, has the opportunity to show that the rhetoric of responsibility for the victims is not merely empty words. That, contrary to a mood that does not support it, they are doing what is morally right. Time is running out, Germany – it’s your last chance. World.title: Leader of junior coalition partner quits Polish government
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk. World.title: Protesters return to Poland’s streets demanding liberalisation of abortion law
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws. However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020. Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS — Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026 In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections. When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition. Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear. Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose. “It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.” In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”. Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw — Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026 The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023. Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition.
