World.title: Poland charges second Georgian man over murder of Russian dissident
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year. The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. Warto przypomnieć: ▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości. ▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026 Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states. World.title: Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies. Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades. During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”. Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies. Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20. “The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said. Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.” Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market. Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”. “Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.” However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals. The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible". "Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility. To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations. Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people. The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations. Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War. “In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”. The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year. World.title: Where to Celebrate Halloween in Prague: 6 Events for Children and Adults
World.content:
Prague will mark Halloween 2026 with events for children and adults, ranging from pumpkin carving and lantern parades to costume competitions and late-night club parties.

Here are some of the events planned across Prague, including admission prices where available.

Blackout Halloween Rave at SaSaZu

Blackout Events will hold its first Halloween rave on Tuesday, October 27, at SaSaZu, bringing hard techno, Halloween costumes and stage productions to the Prague club.

The lineup includes WYNTER at 9 p.m., HOOOR at 10:30 p.m., A.N.I. at midnight, NOTMYTYPE at 1:30 a.m. and KLAR at 3 a.m. The event is scheduled to finish at 4 a.m.

An afterparty will follow at Club Mecca in Holešovice from 3 a.m. The event is restricted to visitors aged 18 and over. Organizers say further program details will be published on Blackout Events’ Instagram account.

Halloween at Hybernia Theatre

Hybernia Theatre, near Náměstí Republiky, is also listed as a venue for a Halloween electronic music event. The program is set to combine electronic music, Halloween decorations and the historic theatre’s interior.

Italian DJ SPADA is announced as a special guest. Admission is listed at CZK 499, although the event date should be confirmed with the organizer before publication.

Spooks at Žluté lázně

Žluté lázně in Podolí will host a Halloween afternoon on Saturday, October 31, from 1 p.m. to 7 p.m.

Children can follow a spooky trail featuring a spiderweb tunnel, a mysterious castle and a series of challenges. The program will also include pumpkin carving, face painting and dancing.

The organizers will announce the winner of the best-costume competition at 6:10 p.m. Admission costs CZK 150, while children wearing costumes can enter for free. Pumpkins for carving will be available for CZK 100.

Halloween Among Dinosaurs at DinoPark Harfa

DinoPark on the rooftop of Galerie Harfa will offer Halloween activities on Saturday, October 31, including a trail where children can complete tasks among the dinosaurs.

The afternoon program will feature Stegoušek Kvído, a walking dinosaur character who will lead two lantern parades, at 4 p.m. and 5 p.m. Visitors should bring their own lanterns.

DinoPark will be open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. Children in Halloween costumes can enter for CZK 50.

Pumpkin Carving at the Public Transport Museum

The Public Transport Museum in Střešovice will combine Halloween activities with a look at Prague’s historic trams and buses on Saturday, October 31.

Visitors can carve pumpkins and explore the museum’s collection of historic vehicles. Those arriving in costume will receive a gift.

At 4:45 p.m., the carved pumpkins will be lit in the museum courtyard. The museum will be open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.

Bloody Sexy Halloween Returns to SaSaZu

Bloody Sexy Halloween will return to SaSaZu on Friday, October 30, and Saturday, October 31, for two nights of music, performances and themed productions.

Founded in 2009, the event has become one of the region’s established Halloween parties, attracting more than 4,000 visitors in previous editions, according to the organizers.

One of the weekend’s main attractions is the Bloody Sexy Costume Contest. Participants can register at SaSaZu between 9 p.m. and midnight. Costumes are judged on creativity, originality and presentation, with the winner selected by audience applause at midnight and awarded CZK 40,000.

World.title: Prague Tram Disruptions Will Affect Six Lines During Autumn School Break
World.content:
Prague tram passengers will face several service changes during the autumn school break, including a five-day suspension between I. P. Pavlova and Otakarova.

The changes come as Prague Public Transit Company adjusts services for the school holidays and carries out track repairs. Passengers travelling through Nusle, Vršovice and Žižkov should check their routes before setting off.

Six Tram Lines Affected by Track Repairs

Tram services between I. P. Pavlova and Otakarova will be suspended in both directions from approximately 4:30 a.m. on Wednesday, October 28, until midnight on Sunday, November 1.



Tram line 13 will be suspended entirely during this period. Lines 2 and 21 will be combined into one route, with trams running from Petřiny to Karlovo náměstí before continuing as line 21 to Slivenec. The same arrangement will apply in the opposite direction.

Other services will follow diverted routes. Tram line 6, travelling from Nádraží Holešovice, will run from Karlovo náměstí via Albertov, Ostrčilovo náměstí and Divadlo Na Fidlovačce to Otakarova, where it will rejoin its regular route.

Line 11 will be diverted from I. P. Pavlova via Náměstí Míru, Čechovo náměstí, Nádraží Vršovice and Otakarova. It will return to its usual route at Náměstí Bratří Synků and continue towards Spořilov.

Night tram line 96, which connects Petřiny with Spořilov, will also be diverted. It will run via Náměstí Míru, Čechovo náměstí, Nádraží Vršovice, Otakarova and Náměstí Bratří Synků.

A replacement bus service, X11, will operate during the day between Nádraží Vršovice and Sarajevská. It will also stop at Fričova, Divadlo Na Fidlovačce and Otakarova.

Žižkov Tram Restrictions to Last Until December 18

Separate restrictions in Žižkov have been in effect since October 11, with tram services suspended in both directions between Nákladové nádraží Žižkov and Ohrada. The disruption is scheduled to continue until December 18.

Tram lines 9 and 10 currently terminate at Nákladové nádraží Žižkov and are linked to each other. Lines 16 and 34 have been cancelled, while lines 5, 7, 11, 95 and 98 are operating on modified routes.

Three additional tram services have been introduced to help passengers travel through the affected area. Line 30 connects Sídliště Ďáblice with Spojovací via Palmovka and Ohrada. Line 37 runs from Lehovec to Spojovací, also serving Palmovka and Ohrada. Night line 90 connects Vozovna Kobylisy with Spojovací via the same two stops.

Replacement buses are running along the suspended section. Daytime services X9 and X95 connect Nákladové nádraží Žižkov, Biskupcova, Ohrada and Vozovna Žižkov. Night bus X98 serves Olšanské hřbitovy, Želivského, Nákladové nádraží Žižkov, Biskupcova, Ohrada and Vozovna Žižkov.

World.title: The Piano Bar Prague Combines Dining and Live Music at Savarin Palace
World.content:
Located inside Savarin Palace on Na Příkopě, The Piano Bar Prague brings together a restaurant, cocktail bar and live music venue under one roof.

The concept offers an alternative to an evening spent moving between different venues in the city centre.



The venue combines dinner, drinks and live performances, with separate spaces for dining, socialising and dancing.

Dining and Cocktails in One Venue

The restaurant is led by Executive Chef Ari Munandar, whose previous experience includes working at Mandarin Oriental, Hilton and SaSaZu. The menu focuses on contemporary cuisine, with an emphasis on ingredients, flavour and presentation.

Cocktails are also a central part of the offering, with the bar serving guests throughout the evening. The layout allows visitors to move from the dining room to the bar or lounge without leaving the venue.

Live Music and Dancing

Live music is another key element of The Piano Bar Prague. The program ranges from piano performances to live bands, depending on the evening.

While some guests may visit for dinner or drinks, the venue also caters to those looking for a later night out. The main bar and dance floor provide space for music and dancing, while the lounge offers a quieter setting for conversation.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by The Piano Bar Prague (@thepianobar_prague)

The different areas are designed to accommodate a range of occasions, from dinners for two and gatherings with friends to private celebrations and corporate events.

A Historic Setting in Prague 1

The Piano Bar Prague is located in Savarin Palace, a historic complex on Na Příkopě, one of Prague’s main shopping streets. Its central location makes it accessible to both residents and visitors staying in the city centre.

World.title: Smartwings Launches Direct Flights Between Prague and Lisbon
World.content:
Smartwings has launched a new direct route between Prague and Lisbon, with flights operating three times a week.

The first service departed on Friday, October 23, with every seat occupied, according to airline spokeswoman Vladimíra Dufková.

The new connection links Prague with the Portuguese capital on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays.



The route adds Lisbon to Smartwings’ existing scheduled services to Portugal, which already include Porto, Funchal on the island of Madeira, and Ponta Delgada in the Azores.

Flights are operated by Boeing 737 aircraft with a capacity of 189 passengers. The journey from Prague to Lisbon takes approximately three hours and 40 minutes, while the return flight takes three hours and 25 minutes.

One-way tickets start at CZK 2,940. The fare includes one piece of cabin baggage measuring up to 55 × 40 × 23 centimetres and weighing no more than eight kilograms.

Smartwings to Resume Prague–Bucharest Flights

Smartwings will also resume scheduled flights between Prague and Bucharest on November 26. The service will operate four times a week, on Tuesdays, Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays.

One-way fares for the Romanian capital start at CZK 2,470, including cabin baggage, Dufková said.

The two routes form part of Smartwings’ winter 2026–2027 flight schedule, which includes direct services from Czech airports to 39 destinations. The Smartwings Group will also operate flights from Poland, Slovakia and Hungary during the winter season.

World.title: Grand Jour de Champagne Returns to Prague With 30 French Producers
World.content:
Prague will host the 19th edition of Grand Jour de Champagne from November 5, bringing together French champagne producers, exclusive tastings and a gala dinner prepared by a two-Michelin-starred chef.

The festival’s main event, the Champagne Exhibition, will take place at Kaiserštejn Palace in Malá Strana, featuring around 50 cuvées from more than 18 champagne houses.

Visitors can sample different styles, meet producers and discover brands including Louis Roederer, Piper-Heidsieck, Philipponnat, Telmont and G. H. Mumm. Selected bottles will also be available to purchase at special festival prices.



The exhibition will run in two sessions, from 14:00 to 17:00 and 17:00 to 20:00. Tickets cost CZK 2,180.

Two-Michelin-Star Chef to Prepare Gala Dinner

Another highlight will be the Champagne Gala Banquet at Prague’s Municipal House, where French chef Valentin Loison will prepare a five-course tasting menu paired with champagnes from selected producers.

Loison, 32, earned two Michelin stars at his restaurant Bulle d’Osier in Langres, France, within approximately 18 months. The evening will also feature a musical performance by Czech violist Jitka Hosprová.

The gala begins at 20:00, with individual tickets priced at CZK 9,400.

Exclusive Tastings and Masterclasses

The festival programme also includes specialist tastings and masterclasses for champagne enthusiasts.

One session will focus on Louis Roederer’s Cristal, featuring vintages including 2006 and 2016, at the Zlatá Praha restaurant. Other events will explore the Meunier grape variety and pair foie gras with a rare 1996 de Venoge Blanc de Blancs Magnum.

Some masterclasses are limited to just 12 participants.

Tickets

Tickets and the full programme are available here. For additional information, contact [email protected].

Readers registering through Prague Morning can enter the code PM2026 in the designated field after their surname to help organisers identify their registration. Priority consideration is subject to ticket availability.

World.title: Beyond Tacos: Meet the Founders of La Casa Azteca in Prague
World.content:
La Casa Azteca brings traditional Mexican food and cultural celebrations to Prague.

Run by Miguel, originally from Mexico, and Modar, who comes from Syria, the restaurant draws on their experience in the city’s Mexican food scene while introducing customers to dishes and traditions from beyond the familiar.

Two routes to Prague

Modar arrived for work as a structural engineer. While learning Czech, he found himself working in a Mexican restaurant, where he became interested in the food and the business.

“I fell in love with the Mexican concept and the Mexican food, so I had to stay,” he says.



Miguel, meanwhile, had already spent years living abroad, including five years in Montreal and time in the United States. He had always wanted to experience different countries, and Prague was another step in that direction.

Still, the city felt unlike anywhere he had been before. He remembers seeing a tram when he first arrived and feeling as though he had landed in a fairy-tale country.

The two eventually met through Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, around nine years ago. What started as a shared connection to Mexican food eventually grew into a business partnership.

Keeping Mexican food authentic — and introducing it to Prague

At La Casa Azteca, Miguel and Modar want to keep the food close to what customers would find in Mexico, combining street food with dishes more commonly associated with traditional restaurants. The menu includes mole, chiles, flautas and tacos, with each dish bringing its own flavours and character.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Azteca Cocina & Bar (@azteca_prague)

Keeping those flavours in Prague, however, sometimes means working with ingredients that are harder to find locally. Herbs commonly used in Mexico can be difficult to source, while ingredients such as tortillas and chillies can also be more expensive. Some elements therefore have to be substituted without losing the character of the dish.

They have also had to navigate some of the expectations Czech customers bring with them. Part of that process has been showing customers that Mexican cuisine goes well beyond the familiar image of tacos, enchiladas and very spicy dishes.

“People think that in Mexico we are always eating spicy food,” Miguel says. “It’s true, but not all our food is tacos and enchiladas. We eat normal food too — pasta, a piece of meat with rice.”

The same approach extends to drinks. Mezcal is still relatively unfamiliar to many Czech customers, so the team uses the restaurant as a place to explain where it comes from, how it is produced and how different varieties can taste.

“It’s something that people can explore,” Miguel says. “They appreciate the taste. They appreciate the liquor. It’s not just a party drink.”

Building a business abroad

Although Miguel and Modar have around nine years of experience in Prague’s Mexican restaurant scene, La Casa Azteca is a newer chapter. The current project, which combines a restaurant with a neighbouring service window, has been running for around six months.

Starting their own business required learning how to navigate the Czech system from scratch. “We had to learn so much about running a business in the Czech Republic,” Modar says. “Everything is very well organized and very well thought out, so you really need to be prepared. You have to pay attention to every detail and every small thing.”

There was also the risk that came with building something abroad, without the same safety net they might have had at home. “I think it’s harder to take risks when you’re living abroad because, if you fall, there’s no one to pick you up. The stress is greater. But at the same time, you know there’s no way back, so you have to make it work,” Modar says.

Celebrating Mexican culture in Prague

Beyond the menu, Miguel and Modar celebrate Mexican traditions through events at the restaurant. After marking Mexican Independence Day in September, they are now preparing for the Day of the Dead, with Mexican dancers, live mariachi music, decorations and special dishes planned for the end of October.

World.title: Turn a Sleepover Into a Special Memory With atelier stories
World.content:
A sleepover with friends can be one of those childhood moments that children remember for years.

But for parents, organising one often means buying decorations, preparing bedding, rearranging furniture and dealing with the cleanup afterwards.

Prague-based atelier stories takes care of everything, bringing a fully styled teepee sleepover directly to the family home. Parents choose the theme, date and number of children, while the company handles the delivery, setup, styling and collection.

Founded by Jana Hrochová, who has a background in event production, organisation and guest services, atelier stories was created around a simple idea: making special moments for children without turning them into another project for parents.



The concept works for birthdays, but it doesn’t have to be a special occasion. A weekend with friends, a school holiday or simply an evening when children want to do something different can become a small adventure at home.

Families can choose from three themes: Mermaid World, Wizard Academy and SPA Night. Each setup features coordinated colours, soft textiles, fairy lights and themed accessories. The result is a playful sleeping space designed to appeal to children while remaining stylish enough to fit comfortably into the family home.

Every booking includes the equipment and styling, with teepees assembled and individual sleeping spaces prepared with mattresses, bedding, pillows, blankets, decorative cushions and other details suited to the chosen theme. Optional extras include creative kits, themed activities, photography and Instax memories.

The service is designed to make the experience as easy as possible for parents. There is no need to buy decorations, assemble teepees, wash bedding or find storage space for the equipment afterwards. Once the sleepover is over, atelier stories returns to dismantle the setup, pack everything away and collect it.

Quality, comfort and hygiene are central to the service. The equipment and textiles are cleaned and prepared between bookings, and each sleeping space is carefully arranged to ensure children have a comfortable place to settle in for the night.

Families can book a sleepover for one night or an entire weekend. Prices start at CZK 3,490 for two children for one night, or CZK 4,900 for two children for a full weekend, from Friday to Monday. Both options include the equipment, styling, setup and collection, with delivery within Prague included free of charge.

The service can also make a thoughtful gift from grandparents. Instead of another toy or physical present, a gift voucher gives grandchildren an experience to look forward to.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by atelier stories | tématické přespávačky pro děti (@atelierstories.cz)

Vouchers can cover a complete sleepover or contribute towards one, allowing the family to choose the theme and date later. They are valid for one year and delivered by email within 24 hours of payment.

While at-home sleepovers remain the main focus, atelier stories also creates children’s lounges and play areas for weddings and other events, giving younger guests a dedicated space to play and relax while adults enjoy the occasion.

World.title: Czechia Has the EU’s Lowest Poverty Risk Rate, Eurostat Finds
World.content:
Czechia has the lowest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion in the European Union, with 12% of its population affected, according to 2025 data from Eurostat.

The figure is well below the EU average of 21%, meaning that around one in five people across the bloc face the risk of poverty or social exclusion. Among children, the proportion rises to one in four.



The EU measure covers people whose incomes fall below the poverty-risk threshold, those experiencing severe material and social deprivation, and those living in households with very low work intensity.

Poland also records a relatively low rate, at 15%, followed by the Netherlands and Slovenia at 16%. Slovakia, Belgium, Finland and Cyprus each report 17%, while Austria stands at 19%.

At the other end of the scale, Bulgaria has the highest share of people at risk of poverty or social exclusion, at 29%. Greece follows at 28%, and Romania at 27%. Lithuania and Spain each report 26%, while Latvia stands at 25%. Italy records 23%, Estonia 22%, and Germany, France and Croatia each match the EU average of 21%.

EU Moves to Strengthen Anti-Poverty Measures

The figures come as European institutions seek to strengthen measures to reduce poverty and social exclusion across the bloc.

Earlier this year, the European Parliament called for more decisive action, stressing that poverty undermines human dignity and that everyone should have access to basic necessities.

In May, the European Commission adopted the EU’s first-ever anti-poverty strategy, setting out measures intended to prevent and reduce poverty across member states.

The strategy addresses several areas, including access to affordable housing, employment opportunities and support for families raising children. It also seeks to remove barriers to employment and tackle in-work poverty, which affects people who have jobs but still struggle to make ends meet.

Housing exclusion and the availability of social and affordable housing are among its priorities. The strategy also focuses on child poverty, support for older people through adequate pensions and opportunities to remain in employment, and efforts to combat discrimination and stigma.

World.title: Nursery workers in Hungary charged for verbally abusing and taping mouth of 3-year-old
World.content:
Two nursery workers in southern Hungary have been charged with endangering a minor after allegedly verbally abusing a three-year-old boy, repeatedly pulling him around and, in one incident, taping his mouth shut. Prosecutors are seeking suspended prison sentences and a permanent ban on both women working in professions involving children.

Child allegedly insulted and physically mistreated

The charges were announced by the Kaposvár District Prosecutor’s Office, which said the alleged incidents took place at a nursery in a village near Kaposvár, in Somogy County. According to the indictment, the two women, employed as a nursery educator and a childcare assistant, repeatedly mistreated the boy from November 2024 onwards.

They allegedly called him derogatory names, including terms equivalent to “disgusting”, “hateful” and even the f-slur, and repeatedly pulled him around as a means of disciplining him.

The most serious incident reportedly occurred during lunch, when the child crawled under a table. The childcare assistant allegedly became angry, led him to a bed and covered his mouth with a wide strip of adhesive tape. A few seconds later, she tore the tape off while the boy was crying.

Prosecutors said the child did not suffer physical injuries. However, they argued that both employees had seriously breached their professional duties and endangered the boy’s physical and emotional development.

Workers dismissed after incident came to light

The case reportedly took place at a nursery in Zselicszentpál, which opened in 2023. The incident came to light after a parent entering the building and another childcare worker allegedly witnessed the child’s mouth being taped.

The municipality subsequently filed a complaint, prompting a police investigation on suspicion of endangering a minor. The employer immediately terminated both women’s public-sector employment once the allegations emerged.

At the time, the village’s mayor, Katalin Szabó, told local news outlet Sonline that the employees had been hired with strong recommendations and that she had never imagined the nursery would face such a situation.

Prosecutors seek permanent ban from working with children

The Kaposvár District Prosecutor’s Office has submitted the indictment to the Kaposvár District Court. It is seeking suspended prison sentences for both defendants and asking the court to permanently prohibit them from any profession involving the education, supervision, care or medical treatment of anyone under 18.

The charges have not yet resulted in a court verdict. The proposed professional ban would prevent the women from returning to a broad range of roles involving children if imposed by the court.

World.title: Hungary’s refusal to join Ukraine loan could cost valuable EU funds
World.content:
Hungary could face a fresh dispute with major European Union member states over its decision to stay out of a proposed EUR 45 billion loan for Ukraine, as disagreements over Kyiv’s financing threaten to spill into negotiations on the bloc’s next long-term budget.

EUR 45 billion loan puts Hungary at odds with Kyiv’s supporters

The EU is considering raising the money on financial markets, backed by its common budget, to help cover Ukraine’s funding needs in 2027. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic are expected to remain outside the proposed arrangement, continuing their opposition to participating in joint EU borrowing for Ukraine.

According to Politico, diplomats say some of Kyiv’s strongest supporters could take a tougher line towards countries declining to contribute when negotiations begin over the EU’s 2028–2034 budget. The talks will determine the scale and distribution of future cohesion and agricultural funding, making the dispute potentially significant for Budapest.

German diplomat questions increased EU support

A German diplomat quoted by Politico questioned why German taxpayers should finance increased cohesion payments for countries that do not participate in common efforts to support Ukraine’s security. The remarks suggest that Hungary’s stance could become a point of contention in broader budget negotiations, although Berlin has not formally announced that participation in the loan would be a condition for receiving additional EU funding.

The issue could complicate Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s stated ambition to secure an additional EUR 2 billion in EU funding in the next budget period, partly to compensate for support Hungary has previously lost. Cohesion funding helps finance infrastructure, regional development, business support and energy projects.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

PM Magyar’s position remains unclear

Hungary’s position may also extend beyond the previous government of Viktor Orbán. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico has said he discussed the issue with Magyar and that they agreed their countries would not participate in joint borrowing for Ukraine. Magyar has not publicly confirmed that account or outlined his position in detail.

Stay up-to-date: The UN was no friend of Orbán – So why is he now linked to its top job?

Loan and budget arrangements remain undecided

The proposed EUR 45 billion package is itself still under discussion. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has previously indicated that Ukraine could need around EUR 70 billion in additional support, while Brussels is also seeking greater contributions from partners including the United Kingdom and Canada. The possible use of frozen Russian assets remains controversial, with Belgium among the countries expressing serious reservations.

EU leaders are expected to revisit Ukraine’s financing at a special summit scheduled for 26–27 November. By then, the debate may clarify both the structure of the loan and whether opposition to it will influence negotiations over future EU spending.

For now, neither the final loan arrangements nor the next EU budget has been agreed. Any direct link between Hungary’s refusal to participate and reductions in, or restrictions on, its future funding remains a possibility rather than an established policy.

World.title: Serbia’s shock election result echoes Hungary’s political earthquake – But there is one big difference
World.content:
Serbia’s student-led opposition has scored a decisive victory in the country’s snap parliamentary election, drawing striking comparisons with Hungary’s political transformation in April 2026. Both countries have seen voters rally behind new political forces promising change after years of dominance by established leaders. However, the movements behind the two victories differ significantly in their leadership, political outlook and challenges ahead.

According to preliminary results announced by Serbia’s Republic Electoral Commission (RIK) on 26 October, the Student List secured 52.71% of the vote, translating into 140 seats in the 250-member National Assembly. The electoral list led by President Aleksandar Vučić received 39.17%, equivalent to 104 seats.

The results, based on votes processed from 8,187 polling stations, give the student-backed movement an absolute parliamentary majority. Vučić conceded defeat on election night.

Hungary and Serbia: voters demand change

The similarities with Hungary are hard to ignore. On 12 April 2026, Péter Magyar’s Tisza Party won Hungary’s parliamentary election with 141 of the 199 seats, ending Viktor Orbán’s 16 years as prime minister. Tisza secured more than 70% of parliamentary seats, while the Fidesz–KDNP alliance was reduced to 52.

In both countries, political newcomers capitalised on widespread dissatisfaction with the established political order. Anti-corruption promises, demands for accountability and calls to improve public institutions became central themes in their campaigns.

The two elections also took place against a backdrop of criticism over unequal campaign conditions, including concerns about media coverage and the use of state resources. These issues were particularly prominent in Serbia, where election observers have documented concerns about the fairness of the electoral environment.

Both countries also have complicated relationships with Russia. Orbán maintained close ties with Moscow during his time in office, while Vučić has pursued relations with Russia alongside Serbia’s stated ambition to join the European Union. Political change in either country therefore carries implications beyond its borders.

A student movement versus a single political leader

Perhaps the biggest difference lies in how the two challengers organised themselves. Hungary’s political transformation centred on Magyar, a former Fidesz insider who built Tisza into a major electoral force in a relatively short period. The party offered a recognisable political programme, combining a pro-European orientation with promises to tackle corruption and restore public trust.

Serbia’s Student List, by contrast, emerged from a grassroots protest movement and has no single, established leader. Its candidates include academics, professionals and public figures, while its supporters come from diverse political backgrounds. The movement’s decentralised structure helped it unite people around demands for accountability, but governing as a cohesive administration could prove considerably more difficult.

The Serbian protests began after a concrete canopy collapsed at Novi Sad railway station on 1 November 2024, killing 16 people. The disaster triggered demonstrations over alleged corruption, government accountability and the handling of major infrastructure projects.

The movement’s success at the ballot box now presents a new challenge: translating its broad anti-corruption message into a detailed programme and selecting leaders capable of implementing it.

Why Serbia’s future matters to the EU

The two countries also occupy very different positions in Europe. Hungary is an EU member, meaning its government directly influences decisions within the bloc. Magyar’s victory created expectations of a change in Budapest’s relationship with Brussels, particularly over the rule of law and European funding.

Serbia, meanwhile, remains an EU candidate country, with accession negotiations facing significant obstacles. The Student List has emphasised domestic reforms, but its foreign policy direction remains less clearly defined than Tisza’s. Its candidates have also expressed support for maintaining ties with Russia, while the question of EU membership remains politically sensitive.

International observers have already highlighted the scale of the challenge facing Serbia’s incoming political leadership. In their preliminary assessment of the 25 October vote, the OSCE’s election observation mission reported serious inequalities in campaign opportunities, including the misuse of state resources, pressure on voters and pronounced bias in media coverage favouring the incumbent camp.

The Student List must now demonstrate that it can improve the institutions it campaigned against.

Two victories, one message

Hungary and Serbia have not followed identical political paths. One elected a leader-centred, pro-European party in a regularly scheduled parliamentary election; the other backed a decentralised student-led movement in a snap poll following prolonged street protests.

Yet both results demonstrate how dissatisfaction with long-established political power can create opportunities for relatively new challengers.

For Hungary, the decisive question is how Magyar’s government delivers on its promises. For Serbia, it is whether a movement built around protest can transform its electoral mandate into stable, accountable government. The victories may look similar from a distance, but what happens next will determine whether they lead to equally lasting political change.

World.title: Erasmus+ is finally back at all Hungarian universities – When can students go abroad again?
World.content:
Hungarian university students can once again access the full Erasmus+ exchange programme after all the necessary funding agreements were signed, ending years of restrictions on institutions run by public-interest asset management foundations.

The Erasmus+ student exchange programme has fully returned to all Hungarian universities, European Commission Executive Vice-President Roxana Mînzatu announced on Monday. The Tempus Public Foundation, which coordinates the programme in Hungary, confirmed that all the necessary funding agreements have now been signed following the removal of the legal obstacles.

🇭🇺🇪🇺 @EUErasmusPlus is back for students at every Hungarian university! For almost four years, students at some Hungarian universities missed out on opportunities that their peers across Europe could enjoy. Today, that changes. And I am happy to welcome them back to the Erasmus+ family! Students from all Hungarian universities can now access these opportunities again, with applications possible as early as this autumn. This means more opportunities for young people. More connections across Europe. And more doors open for every Hungarian student. #erasmusasaright — Roxana Mînzatu (@RoxanaMinzatu) October 26, 2026

When will students be able to study abroad again?

Despite the agreements being signed, students should not expect regular exchanges to resume immediately. According to the Tempus Public Foundation, regular student mobility is expected to restart in the second semester of the 2026/2027 academic year.

Some other forms of mobility may begin earlier, including short-term exchanges, blended mobility combining online and physical activities, and opportunities for university staff.

The access will allow students to study at partner universities abroad and gain professional experience through international placements. University lecturers and other staff will also be able to participate in exchanges, international research cooperation and professional development.

The affected institutions can additionally rejoin Erasmus+ partnership projects and apply for centrally managed funding opportunities.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Why were Hungarian universities excluded?

The restrictions date back to December 2022, when the Council of the European Union introduced measures under its rule-of-law conditionality mechanism. The measures prohibited new EU funding commitments with public-interest asset management foundations, known by their Hungarian abbreviation, KEKVA, and the institutions they maintained.

The EU raised concerns about transparency, conflicts of interest and the involvement of political decision-makers in these foundations. As a result, 21 Hungarian universities operating under the foundation model were unable to renew their Erasmus+ funding agreements when the previous agreements expired.

Although these institutions were not formally expelled from Erasmus+, their students could no longer participate in the programme through the affected universities in the usual way. The previous government launched a separate Pannónia mobility programme to mitigate the consequences.

If you missed it: FM Anita Orbán: Hungarian students to regain access to Erasmus+

What changed in October 2026?

The breakthrough came after Hungary’s new government agreed on reforms with the European Commission. On 13 October, EU member states unanimously ended the conditionality procedure, clearing the way for the affected universities to sign new Erasmus+ agreements.

The Tempus Public Foundation said it had begun notifying institutions about the signing process immediately after the decision.

World.title: Hungary to double the increased family allowance: here are the amounts
World.content:
Hungary’s Tisza government will double enhanced family allowances from 2027, extending the previously announced increase to families raising children with long-term illnesses or severe disabilities. Around 1.7 million children and one million families will benefit from the wider package, backed by nearly HUF 300 billion in additional funding in the 2027 budget.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has confirmed that the planned doubling of family allowance payments will also cover recipients of enhanced benefits, including families caring for children with long-term illnesses or severe disabilities, adults entitled to support in their own right, and children living in foster care or residential institutions.

In a Facebook video, Magyar outlined the exact new monthly amounts, saying the measure would extend the increase across all categories of family allowance recipients.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Enhanced benefits for children with disabilities to double

The enhanced family allowance paid for approximately 134,000 children with long-term illnesses or severe disabilities will rise from HUF 23,300 to HUF 46,600 (EUR 127) per month from 2027.

For parents raising an affected child alone, the monthly payment will increase to HUF 51,800 (EUR 141).

The change will also benefit more than 28,000 adults who qualify for the allowance in their own right because of a long-term illness or severe disability. Their monthly support will rise to HUF 40,600 (EUR 110).

Children living with foster parents, in children’s homes or in other eligible institutions will also be covered. The standard monthly allowance in this category will double from HUF 14,800 to HUF 29,600 (EUR 80).

How much will families receive from 2027?

The government previously announced that ordinary family allowances would double, and Magyar has now confirmed that the increase will apply across the board.

The new monthly rates for families raising children in their own households will be as follows:

Families with one child: HUF 24,400 (EUR 66) per month, up from HUF 12,200.

HUF 24,400 (EUR 66) per month, up from HUF 12,200. Families with two children: HUF 26,600 (EUR 72) per child, or HUF 53,200 in total each month.

HUF 26,600 (EUR 72) per child, or HUF 53,200 in total each month. Families with three or more children: HUF 32,000 (EUR 87) per child per month.

Single-parent families will receive higher amounts:

One child: HUF 27,400 (EUR 75) per month.

HUF 27,400 (EUR 75) per month. Two children: HUF 29,600 (EUR 80) per child per month.

HUF 29,600 (EUR 80) per child per month. Three or more children: HUF 34,000 (EUR 93) per child per month.

The wider increase is expected to benefit around 1.7 million children and one million families across Hungary.

Family allowance has not increased since 2008

Magyar highlighted that Hungary’s family allowance rates had remained unchanged since 2008, meaning the benefit had lost more than half of its purchasing power over the intervening years due to inflation.

The doubling is intended to address that long-standing decline in the value of the support. The additional expenditure required for the measures is expected to reach nearly HUF 300 billion (approx. EUR 817 million) in the 2027 budget.

World.title: Hungarian amateur astronomer discovers new near-Earth asteroid
World.content:
A Hungarian amateur astronomer has discovered a previously unknown asteroid that comes close to Earth’s orbit, marking his eighth discovery. The find was officially recognised by the Minor Planet Center just one day after the object was observed.

Eighth asteroid discovery for Hungarian astronomer

According to the Hungarian astronomy news portal csillagaszat.hu, amateur astronomer Tamás Maróti spotted the asteroid during the night of 13 October 2026.

The Minor Planet Center (MPC) officially recognised the discovery the following day, publishing it in circular MPEC 2026-T244 and assigning the asteroid the provisional designation 2026 TM77.

Twelve observatories from the international astronomical community immediately joined efforts to validate the discovery. They submitted follow-up observations to the MPC, confirming that the object was real and followed a predictable orbit. Astronomer Tamás Elek also captured a confirming image of the asteroid.

What do we know about asteroid 2026 TM77?

At the time of its discovery, the asteroid had an apparent magnitude of around 19 and was moving across the sky at an apparent rate of 20 arcseconds per minute.

Its orbital plane is inclined at 7.77 degrees to the plane of Earth’s orbit. Based on the data available so far, 2026 TM77 takes approximately 2.86 years to complete one orbit around the Sun.

The asteroid reached its closest point to the Sun, known as perihelion, on 24 September 2026, at a distance of 0.995 astronomical units (AU). At its most distant point, or aphelion, it travels approximately 3.034 AU from the Sun.

One astronomical unit is the average distance between the Earth and the Sun, approximately 150 million kilometres.

The announcement also confirmed that 2026 TM77 belongs to the Apollo group of asteroids, one of the largest and most significant categories of near-Earth objects. These asteroids are characterised by orbits that cross Earth’s orbit.

Why the discovery is a remarkable achievement

The report highlights Maróti’s remarkable perseverance. Systematic asteroid searches require observers to spend every clear night collecting observations over many months, often without finding a single new object despite examining thousands upon thousands of images.

The challenge has become even greater as professional sky-survey programmes have covered almost the entire observable sky, leaving amateur astronomers with fewer opportunities to make new discoveries.

World.title: Hungary signs EEA and Norway Grants deal after missing out on previous funding cycle
World.content:
Hungary has officially secured approximately HUF 92 billion (EUR 250.4 million) in funding through the European Economic Area (EEA) and Norway Grants for 2021–2028, following an agreement signed in Budapest with Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein.

Hungary to secure a huge amount of funds

The deal makes funding available for projects ranging from environmental initiatives and healthcare to local development, culture and Roma integration. The agreement was signed by Hungarian, Norwegian, Icelandic and Liechtenstein representatives at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

Hungary’s Rural and Settlement Development Minister, Viktória Lőrincz, and Finance Minister András Kármán attended the signing alongside Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide, Icelandic Foreign Ministry state secretary Martin Eyjólfsson and Liechtenstein’s ambassador, Pascal Schafhauser. The agreement follows renewed negotiations initiated by Hungary’s new government. Foreign minister Anita Orbán helped restart discussions in September.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Where will the money go?

Of the EUR 254.1 million available, the largest allocation — EUR 80 million — is earmarked for the green transition. A further EUR 42 million will support local development, while EUR 25 million is allocated to healthcare. Culture and Roma integration programmes will each receive EUR 16 million.

Another EUR 20 million will fund institutional cooperation and capacity-building, while EUR 9.4 million is assigned to the Fund for Bilateral Relations. The Civil Fund will receive EUR 26 million, with EUR 19.7 million reserved for other tasks and administrative costs.

The Civil Fund will be administered, monitored and supervised under the responsibility of the donor countries. A consortium led by the Ökotárs Foundation, alongside the Autonómia Foundation and Carpathian Foundation–Hungary, was selected to manage the fund.

Finance Minister Kármán promised that spending procedures would be public and transparent, adding that not a single euro would be lost. He also said Hungary would contribute approximately HUF 12 billion (more than EUR 32.6 million) from its own budget to co-finance the programmes.

More on foreign affairs: Reuters report claims Hungary could drop Russia’s Rosatom from Paks nuclear project

Why Hungary missed out last time

The agreement is a significant step forward from the previous funding period, when Hungary received none of the nearly EUR 215 million allocated to it — approximately HUF 77 billion at the time. The dispute with the previous Fidesz government centred on the management of the Civil Fund.

The Hungarian authorities and donor countries failed to agree on an independent organisation to distribute grants to civil society groups, leaving the broader funding package unavailable. Kármán criticised the previous administration for allowing the funding to be lost rather than accepting independent oversight of the civil grants.

Norwegian Foreign Minister Eide welcomed the new agreement, saying cooperation, the rule of law and confidence in democracy were essential to Europe’s future. He said Norway had approached Hungary’s new government after the April election to restore relations and reach an agreement.

The funding is intended to support economic and social development across Hungary while strengthening cooperation between the participating countries. Its impact will now depend on transparent allocation and the effective delivery of projects over the coming years.
