That satisfying pop of a jar lid, the snap of a foil seal, or the smooth peel of a fresh film, weâve all experienced it. Itâs that reassuring moment that says,This food is fresh, untouched, and safe.âBut hereâs the catch: the moment you break that seal, the safety bubble vanishes. While modern food packaging uses clever barrier technology and vacuum sealing to keep food pristine on store shelves, it isnât bulletproof once opened. Opening a package starts the countdown, shifting the responsibility of keeping food safe straight into your hands.Improper post-opening handling isn't just a minor oversight. It's a major driver of global food waste and foodborne illness:Inside an unopened package, food lives in a controlled environment. Once the package is opened, that protection is broken, and three key changes can begin to occur:Keeping food fresh after opening doesn't require complex science. It only requires just a few quick habits:Packaging helps keep food safe and fresh until it reaches your kitchen, but proper handling after opening is just as important. Paying attention to storage instructions, resealing products carefully and maintaining good kitchen hygiene, ensures every bite stays as fresh and safe as it should.

World.title: A decade after liquor ban, Bihar faces a new drug question: What the numbers reveal
World.content:
NCB destroyed 1,170.15 kg of seized narcotics worth Rs 4.54 crore in Patna, Bihar, across four cases to prevent their recirculation in September (Credit: NCB's X)

Does Bihar have a new drug problem?

Where are the drugs coming from?

Cops suggest that drugs in Bihar enters from multiple states

Is the trade limited to transportation?

Is Bihar seeing a rise in consumption or a rise in detection?

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Does Bihar have a new drug problem?

Punjab is set to go to polls in 2027, and the BJP, seeking to form its first government in the state, has made the drug menace a major election issue. The party has been targeting the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) over its handling of the problem. Union home minister Amit Shah has even promised to make Punjab "drug-free" by December 2029 if the BJP comes to power.But AAP has hit back. Its national convener Arvind Kejriwal questioned the BJP over the drug problem in states where it is in power, including Bihar, Gujarat, Rajasthan and Goa, asking why the same deadline had not been set for them.The political exchange has also put the focus on Bihar, where alcohol has been banned for a decade but recent drug seizures have raised fresh concerns. More than 4.13 lakh intoxicating injections were seized in Patna in the first eight months of 2026, while investigations have uncovered heroin consignments, codeine-based cough syrup and networks involved in preparing and distributing narcotics.But what do these seizures actually reveal? Is Bihar witnessing a rise in drug consumption, or is the state increasingly becoming a transit route for narcotics headed elsewhere? And has a decade of prohibition had any bearing on the availability and use of other intoxicants? Here's what the data revealsMore than 4.13 lakh intoxicating injections seized in Patna in the first eight months of 2026.A sharp rise in smack seizures. Growing quantities of codeine-based cough syrup being intercepted. Across Bihar, recent drug seizures and investigations point to a changing narcotics landscape, raising questions about what is entering the state, where it is going and who is using it.But do these seizures signal a growing drug problem within Bihar, or are they exposing the scale of a trafficking network that uses the state as a transit route? Police have traced consignments from the Northeast and Nepal-linked routes, while investigations in Patna have uncovered alleged local networks involved in preparing and distributing narcotics.The answers are not straightforward. Five years of seizure data show sharp fluctuations rather than a consistent rise across substances. Meanwhile, a debate over Biharâs liquor prohibition has raised another question about whether the use of alternative intoxicants has changed since the ban came into force in 2016.What do the numbers reveal?Biharâs drug seizure data over five years shows that ganja accounted for the largest quantities seized among the major narcotics listed, while seizures of heroin fluctuated sharply. Ganja seizures rose from 16,607 kg in 2020 to 33,603 kg in 2021, before falling to 23,023 kg in 2022 and 13,129 kg in 2023. They increased again to 18,356 kg in 2024.Heroin seizures fell from 363.77 kg in 2020 to 9.62 kg in 2021, before rising to 31.13 kg in 2022, 27.37 kg in 2023 and 53.35 kg in 2024. Hashish seizures also varied, peaking at 395.12 kg in 2021 before declining to 195 kg in 2024.A person whose circle consumes drugs said, on the condition of anonymity, that marijuana remained the most widely consumed substance in their social circle and that they had not noticed a significant shift in preferences towards other drugs.âIn most circles, marijuana is most widely consumed, and I don't think synthetic drugs have made their way to Bihar,â the person said.The data records smaller seizures of other substances, including ATS, cocaine and LSD in certain years. While these figures show fluctuations in the quantities of narcotics seized, they do not establish a steady year-on-year rise in drug trafficking or consumption. Seizure figures reflect what enforcement agencies intercept and, on their own, cannot establish how many people use drugs or whether drug abuse is increasing in Bihar.Police say a significant share of narcotics reaching Patna comes from the Northeast. The routes and methods of transportation vary according to the size of a consignment.Investigations have also pointed to supply chains passing through multiple states. In September, four people were arrested near JP Setu in Patna with 274 gm of heroin. Police traced the consignment to Assam, from where it allegedly travelled to Tamkuhi in Kushinagar, Uttar Pradesh, before being sent towards Patna.Biharâs location along the Nepal border adds another dimension to the problem. On October 25, Motihari Police, in a joint operation with the Bihar Special Task Force, seized smack valued at Rs 4 crore near Raxaul, close to the India-Nepal border.In a separate operation, the Directorate of Revenue Intelligenceâs Muzaffarpur unit and the Bihar STF busted a suspected network involved in smuggling Nepal-origin charas into India. Two people were arrested and 5.14 kg of charas, valued by officials at Rs 5.14 crore, was seized. Investigators said the consignment was intended for onward transportation to Indore in Madhya Pradesh.The cases point to Biharâs role as a route for narcotics moving between regions. However, seizures along transport corridors do not establish how much of the intercepted supply is consumed within the state.Police investigations suggest that local networks are also involved in storage, preparation and distribution.In March, police found a rented room in Patnaâs Ramakrishna Nagar area allegedly being used to prepare smack. A flat in Alamganj was allegedly used for distribution. Police recovered 1.68 kg of brown sugar and cash, along with cheques worth around Rs 70 lakh issued in the name of a police officer.The trade is not confined to substances traditionally associated with narcotics smuggling. Pharmaceutical products have also featured in investigations. In May, the DRI seized 7,500 bottles of codeine-based cough syrup from a pickup van outside Patnaâs Rajendra Nagar Terminal. Investigators found that the consigneeâs drug licence had been cancelled and that the firm did not exist at its stated address.Such cases raise questions about how pharmaceutical products enter illicit supply chains, how they are distributed and whether existing monitoring systems are able to detect diversion from legitimate channels.A Patna high court order has raised questions about how narcotics can travel long distances before being intercepted.In an order dated September 15, the court expressed concern over two minor boys who had travelled from Assam to Bihar in a car without a registration certificate. The vehicle was intercepted near Patna, and the directorate of revenue intelligence recovered more than 60 kg of cannabis from a concealed compartment.The court questioned how the vehicle had travelled uninterrupted from Assam to Bihar while carrying a commercial quantity of cannabis.Has prohibition changed pattern of substance use?Bihar banned the sale and consumption of alcohol in April 2016 under a policy introduced by the Nitish Kumar government. The prohibition was intended, among other objectives, to reduce domestic violence and encourage households to spend money on more productive needs.A research paper by the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER), titled Macro Perspective of Bihar's Development Achievements, Unfinished Agenda, and the Way Forward, has questioned whether the ban achieved its intended outcomes.The paper said reported crimes against women had not declined following prohibition and that total reported crimes against women increased over the post-2016 period. It also pointed to concerns about the expansion of illicit liquor trade, enforcement challenges, corruption and the use of alternative intoxicants, including illicit drugs."In tandem, there was a significant rise in illegal liquor trade leading to higher alcohol consumption, increased crime and corruption, and an increase in the use of alternative additive substances, such as illicit drugs," the paper said.The authors argued that Bihar should reconsider prohibition and restore alcohol excise duty to historical levels. They estimated that doing so could increase the stateâs own revenues by 14-15%.Some residents also believe prohibition may be one factor behind the availability of other intoxicants, although personal accounts cannot establish a direct link between the ban and drug consumption.âI would argue that it is a byproduct of the prohibition in the state, but that isn't the full picture,â another person who spoke on condition of anonymity said, referring to the perceived increase in drug availability.The person said their observations were based on the experiences of people in their social circle who use drugs, adding that young people and those in their 30s appeared to be among the users they had noticed.âIn a state like Bihar, with a large chunk of youth population that haven't so far been backed with job opportunities, [this] has also contributed to the rise of drug consumption in the state,â the person said.They also flagged a lack of awareness about addiction and the support available to people who use drugs.âI feel like there is a lack of awareness against remedial methods, like what to do if someone you know has become addicted to drugs, what are you supposed to do then. I feel like there is a lack of rehabilitation system and awareness among the people needed to curb the drug menace,â the person said.The distinction matters because seizures measure what enforcement agencies intercept, not the total volume of drugs entering the market or being consumed.Biharâs prohibition and narcotics enforcement policies also form part of a wider debate over how the state measures the effectiveness of its policing. A rise in seizures can reflect an increase in trafficking, improved detection or a combination of both.Bihar minister Madan Sahni has rejected the charge that rising seizures indicate a failure of prohibition. He said the increase was not confined to Bihar but was a phenomenon seen in other states as well."I must say that due to the alertness of the officials concerned, the quantity of the seizure of substances prohibited under the NDPS Act has increased in the state, but at the same time, people should know that the majority of the prohibited substances seized in Bihar are meant for supply to other states," he said.Sahni added that intercepting consignments within Bihar could create the impression that the drugs were intended for local consumption, even when they were being transported elsewhere. He also defended prohibition, saying it had been successful.The ministerâs argument points to an important gap in the available figures. Without comparable data on drug use, treatment demand, drug-related health emergencies and the destinations of intercepted consignments, it is difficult to determine how much of the rise reflects local consumption.RJD MP Manoj Kumar Jha, meanwhile, cited a media report and said the situation was out of control."An entire generation has been ruined. This is what happens when the government has no control. The situation here is completely out of control..." he said.Biharâs recent seizure figures and investigations point to a changing narcotics landscape. Police have reported sharp increases in some categories, identified supply routes running through several states and uncovered alleged local networks involved in preparation and distribution. Seizures near the Nepal border have also highlighted the stateâs role in cross-border trafficking.But the central question remains unresolved. Is Bihar facing a growing drug-consumption problem, a trafficking problem that extends beyond its borders, or both?

World.title: ‘India has engineers, but needs more chip-ready ones’
World.content:
India is not short of engineers, but of engineers who are ready to build chips, panelists said on Tuesday, arguing that the talent gap facing the semiconductor mission is one of practical competence, exposure and experience across the whole value chain, rather than of numbers.

Speaking at the ‘Who Will Build India’s Chips? Bridging the Semiconductor Talent Gap’ panel at SRM Presents The Hindu Semiconductor Summit 2026 here, Ranjith Kumar T.C., Director, PRSsemicon Technologies, said the country had 10,000 to 15,000 engineering colleges and 15 lakh to 20 lakh engineers passing out every year. “The actual shortfall is not the number of graduates that we have. The actual shortfall would be the skilled or the industry ready engineers that we are looking at,” he said, describing the shift needed as one “from knowing to doing,” that is, from learning a concept to bringing out a chip, inculcated during college itself.

Sujhatha, Senior Manager, Guidance, Government of Tamil Nadu, agreed that India was not short of people. India was home to 20% of the world’s semiconductor design talent, she said, but manufacturing was still nascent, leaving a shortfall across outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT), wafer fabrication, materials and machines, which is a gap the India Semiconductor Mission, in its first phase and now its second, has been expanding beyond fabrication and OSAT to address across the ecosystem.

Vikas Makhija, Senior R&D Director, Synopsys Inc., said that the deeper gap was of mindset. Indian semiconductor start-ups had innovated mainly in services, he said, while the United States and China had the real designs. Schemes such as Design Linked Incentive (DLI), which made electronic design automation tools easier to access, and Chips to Startup, under which students could learn the basics and design chips, could change that, he added.

Basics first

Asked what he wished every graduate entering the industry already understood, Mr. Makhija said industry expectations had never changed. “We still look for the basics,” he said, pointing to core electronics. Tools and languages would keep changing, and artificial intelligence (AI) was now enhancing productivity “by, say, 10x or even 100x”, but only for those who could judge its output. “An average engineer using AI is still not seeing a gain in productivity, but a good engineer using the same AI is seeing 100x,” he said.

Shaik Ayman Hameed Baig, a third-year B.Tech. student in Electronics and Communication Engineering at SRM Institute of Science and Technology and the panel’s student voice, said students tended to become “the first customers for the chip, building projects on it, rather than the true designers”, with many projects in robotics and embedded systems but few in designing chips. With AI automation entering Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) design, students were also confused about what to learn — manufacturing, fabrication or design — he said.

On the mismatch between what companies need and what education produces, the panel pointed to curriculum and exposure. Mr. Makhija recalled that at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, where he did his master’s in 2006, laboratories were sponsored by companies and students worked on industry projects, and said industry and universities should together design and continuously evolve the syllabus. Mr. Ranjith said the All India Council for Technical Education had restructured the curriculum in 2023 based on industry needs and industry sat on the Boards of Studies of universities such as SRM and Anna University, but the real challenge was dedicated resources and sustained investment, including in centres of excellence. “It is not actually a shortage of talent; it is more a shortage of exposure,” he said.

Beyond classrooms

For Mr. Baig, the most meaningful learning came from a university programme with Sony, working on its Spresense microcontroller with an industry expert. It taught him to submit on a deadline and to take ownership of his work, he said, and, in a conversation with an application engineer who had built the chip, about implementing a programme in Rust, that “there are multiple roles required to get a chip to where it is today and give it purpose”.

Ms. Sujhatha said working life had taught her how painstaking the industry was. “It is all about the yield, end of the day,” she said, pointing to the attention to detail that went into processes starting with a pristine clean room. Mr. Makhija said professional life, unlike college, had no ideal scenario. As a verification engineer whose job was to find bugs, he had learnt to be ready to fail and to find software or hardware workarounds when something was missed. “Things may not be ideal, but you need to figure out a way to make them work,” he said.

A meaningful industry-academia partnership, the panel agreed, should be judged by what students could actually do at the end of it. Beyond just a memorandum of understanding, Mr. Ranjith said, it was about building capability that translated into employment and innovation. “One student whom we train and develop should be developing a chip as well,” he said. Mr. Baig asked for industry to bring real problem statements to faculty and students, and for long-term collaborations. For example, the Sony collaboration, he noted, produced two journal papers. Asked why companies should invest in making graduates employable for other companies, Mr. Makhija likened it to electrons and holes: when one electron left, another came in, and a trained pool benefited the whole ecosystem.

Beyond design

The overlooked roles, the panel suggested, were often the ones that held the chain together. Mr. Makhija traced a chip from product planning and architecture through modelling, design, verification, synthesis and physical design to tape-out, fabrication and lithography, and then post-silicon validation, software bring-up and deployment. “Just think of it like the string of lights that you put up on Diwali. If you just pull out one, it will not glow,” he said. Mr. Baig said design verification, which students assumed was merely checking a design, proved far more complex, since “finding bugs in what is supposedly already right is a really hard job”. Mr. Ranjith pointed to design and register-transfer level work and, in the analogue domain, to analogue design and layout as an even more niche area.

Ms. Sujhatha pointed beyond the chip itself to equipment. Several companies in Tamil Nadu were making semiconductor equipment, she said, and in the current geopolitical scenario, with countries banning imports of certain equipment, even the small components that went into that equipment would become critical in a blockade. The moderator, Nagaraj N, Vice President, Content Analytics and Data, The Hindu, noted that supply chain and logistics roles had proved similarly critical when the industry halted during COVID.

IP and products

Why a young engineer would choose a specialised career in India, over another engineering career or going abroad, divided the panel less than might be expected. Awareness had been minimal in Tamil Nadu, Mr. Ranjith said. His organisation had created awareness among 10,000 to 15,000 engineers in the last four to five years. But the chip was now “the heart and brain of the entire technology”, and the mission’s aim of making India a product nation offered scope across design, manufacturing and assembly. He added that the gap was not uniquely Indian: a student from the University of California, Los Angeles, trained by his organisation on a RISC-V project had gone on to an internship at Apple in the United States.

Mr. Baig said most students chose software because it paid well from day one, while semiconductors demanded intense dedication and often a master’s degree. What inspired him, he said, was seeing seniors build chips that were fabricated in his own college: “It shows me this is not something impossible.” Mr. Makhija said the next decade, with the investment flowing under the semiconductor mission, was the opportunity, noting that though 20% of the world’s design workforce was in India, less than 10% of that, or 2%, worked on Indian semiconductors, against 85% of China’s workforce working on Chinese semiconductors.

Asked how success should be measured, Ms. Sujhatha chose intellectual property (IP) creation over training numbers and certificates. Governments were funding India’s own designs and products, she said, through the Centre’s DLI and Tamil Nadu’s design promotion scheme. She also announced a School of Semiconductor: a small-scale production fab planned at Central Polytechnic College, Tharamani, with the Indian Institute of Technology Madras and industry partners, for prototyping and training on an actual production line, on land already allocated and expected to be running by next year. Mr. Makhija said the outcome had to be products and more start-ups, and Mr. Ranjith said skilling worked only when knowledge was transformed into capability, capability into employment, and employment into innovation. Mr. Baig, for his part, pointed to a simpler metric: the number of openings for freshers, which remained low compared with other fields.

In a closing round on the next 12 months, Mr. Baig asked for more industry problem statements and for student projects to end up fabricated in their own institutes, Ms. Sujhatha said exposure should begin in high school. “Five to 10 years back, robotics was the word. And now I think it’s time for semiconductors,” she said. Mr. Makhija called for feedback to be collected and course corrected, lest schemes existed only on paper.

Mr. Ranjith said capitalising on schemes such as ‘Chips to Startup’ and the centres of excellence already established could, in roughly three years, give India very good capability. “The course of learning VLSI itself will take about one year,” he said.

World.title: Israel holds polls amid uncertainty over Netanyahu’s future, coalition numbers
World.content:
Israel is holding parliamentary elections on Tuesday (October 27, 2026), with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seeking to retain power amid debate over the government’s handling of the Hamas attack of October 7, 2023, the subsequent wars, and its domestic and foreign policies.

The election is widely seen as a test of Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership, as Opposition leaders, including former military chief Gadi Eisenkot and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, seek to challenge his right-wing coalition. Opinion polls indicate neither bloc is assured of the parliamentary majority needed to form a government.

Israel, roughly the size of north-eastern India’s Mizoram State, uses a nationwide proportional representation system, with the entire country serving as a single electoral constituency to elect the 120 members of the Knesset, Israel’s parliament.

Voters do not elect individual members of parliament; instead, they vote for closed party lists, a system that allows numerous political parties to compete for seats. To enter the Knesset, a party must cross the 3.25% electoral threshold, a requirement that often prompts pre-election alliances and mergers.

The Knesset serves a four-year term, but elections can be held early if it votes to dissolve itself, fails to approve the State budget within the prescribed period, or a new government cannot be formed.

The party winning the most seats does not automatically form the government; after the election, the President consults political factions and appoints a lawmaker to form a government, who must secure the support of at least 61 lawmakers.

Mr. Netanyahu, leader of the right-wing Likud party, has served as Israel’s Prime Minister for nearly 19 years across three separate periods since 1996. He seeks to retain power after a period marked by the October 7 attack, which took place three years ago, and the multiple military campaigns that followed.

The Hamas-led assault of 2023 killed about 1,200 people in Israel and triggered the war in Gaza, which subsequently widened into a broader regional conflict involving Israel, Iran and other armed groups.

Following the attack, Israel launched a large-scale military campaign in the Gaza Strip, involving airstrikes, ground operations and restrictions that severely disrupted civilian life. According to Gaza’s health ministry, more than 74,000 Palestinians have been reported killed and over 175,000 injured since the start of the war.

Security and accountability for the October 7, 2023, attack are central issues in the campaign. Mr. Netanyahu also faces charges of fraud, breach of trust and bribery, which he denies. The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for him in 2024, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Mr. Eisenkot, a former Chief of Staff of the Israel Defence Forces, leads the centrist Yashar party and has emerged as a principal challenger to Mr. Netanyahu. He previously served as an observer in Mr. Netanyahu’s war cabinet, but resigned in June 2024, after criticising the government for lacking a clear war strategy.

He has positioned himself as an alternative on governance while maintaining a hard line on security; his party has performed strongly in some opinion polls, though the Opposition faces the challenge of assembling a viable coalition.

Mr. Bennett, a former Prime Minister, is leading the B’Yachad electoral alliance, which includes former Prime Minister Yair Lapid’s Yesh Atid party.

A right-wing politician who opposes Palestinian independence and supports Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, Mr. Bennett has also criticised Mr. Netanyahu’s handling of security and governance. He briefly served as Prime Minister in 2021, under a power-sharing arrangement with Mr. Lapid; their alliance is among the Opposition forces seeking to replace Mr. Netanyahu’s government.

Other important political players include Yair Golan’s left-leaning Democrats, Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu, and Arab-led parties such as Ra’am and the Joint List. On Mr. Netanyahu’s side, far-right parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, along with ultra-Orthodox parties, are key coalition partners.

The election campaign is being shaped by questions over the future of the war in Gaza, relations with the United States, the threat posed by Iran, and Israel’s international standing. While the leading contenders differ on Mr. Netanyahu’s leadership and domestic governance, most share broadly similar positions on security and oppose the establishment of a Palestinian state in the foreseeable future.

The election also comes amid disputes over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox men, the role of religious parties in government, and concerns over the independence of democratic institutions and the judiciary. Most Jewish Israeli men are subject to compulsory military service, but ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, men studying in religious seminaries have historically received broad exemptions or deferments.

The issue has intensified during wars, as the military faces manpower demands and reservists serve longer. Haredi leaders argue that full-time religious study should be protected, while opponents say the system places an unequal burden on those who serve.

Israel’s Supreme Court ruled in 2024 that blanket exemptions could not continue without legislation. Ultra-Orthodox parties such as Shas and United Torah Judaism have been influential coalition partners, seeking protection for religious education, public funding for their institutions, and exemptions from military service; their support can be crucial to forming a parliamentary majority.

United Torah Judaism broke with Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition amid the dispute over military-service exemptions, while Shas has said it will not support a future government without legislation regulating the status of religious seminary students.

Mr. Netanyahu’s government has also pursued controversial judicial changes that would increase elected politicians’ influence over judicial appointments and limit aspects of judicial review. These issues have strained his coalition and remain important in negotiations over a possible government.

Opinion polls indicate that neither Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Opposition has a clear path to the 61 seats needed for a majority. The outcome may therefore depend on smaller parties crossing the electoral threshold, and on coalition arrangements negotiated after the vote.

World.title: Rooftop solar vendors in Coimbatore urge Energy Minister to simplify procedures to boost installations
World.content:
Rooftop solar vendors on Tuesday (October 27, 2026) sought simplified approval procedures, clarity on subsidy calculations and the introduction of virtual net metering at a meeting with Energy and Law Minister C.T.R. Nirmal Kumar at the Government College of Technology in Coimbatore.

The Minister said only around 87,000 rooftop solar installations had been completed in Tamil Nadu until April, lower than other States. To encourage wider adoption, the State government had recently announced a combined subsidy of up to ₹1 lakh, including the Central government subsidy for residential rooftop solar systems of up to 3 kW. He said nearly 30,000 applications had been received under the scheme in the three weeks following its launch.

Among the issues raised by vendors was the continued insistence by local electricity board offices on physical copies of documents that applicants had already uploaded to the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy’s portal.

They also called for automating the estimation sanction process, arguing that approvals based on a checklist of around seven criteria could be generated through the portal once the requirements were met.

Vendors suggested printing promotional messages about rooftop solar on electricity bills for an effective reach rather than relying mainly on mass advertising. Another proposal was to make rooftop solar installations of 2–3 kW mandatory at the building plan approval stage for houses seeking higher electricity loads.

They also sought clarity on subsidy calculations for systems whose capacity fell marginally below the standard 3 kW category. They raised questions about the Central subsidy, cited as ₹78,000 for a 3 kW system, and the applicable State subsidy for a system with a capacity of about 2.9 kW.

The vendors further sought the introduction of virtual net metering, which could allow electricity generated at one location to be adjusted against consumption at another eligible location, subject to regulatory provisions.

Responding to the queries, the Minister said a single-window portal had been introduced to simplify the application process, enabling consumers to apply for the scheme and the Central government subsidy. Vendor allocation would also be facilitated through the portal.

The government had also streamlined the release of subsidies, with the State subsidy to be disbursed within two days of the release of the Central government subsidy, he said. Delays in installing meters, which had been a major impediment to commissioning rooftop solar systems, had also been addressed, he added.

The Minister said the government would consider the practical difficulties raised by vendors at the meeting and make further improvements to the implementation process.

Earlier, the Minister inspected the Minnagam electricity consumer service centre at Tatabad, the 230/110 kV sub-station at Tatabad and reviewed the functioning of power management, control and data acquisition systems.

Performance data from August 5 to October 26, 2026 showed that the seven electricity circles in the Coimbatore region — Coimbatore North, Coimbatore South, Coimbatore Metro, Udumalpet, Tiruppur, Palladam and the Nilgiris — had collectively effected 1,123 rooftop solar installations against a target of 11,017 (10.19%). The circles received 4,212 applications, accounting for 38% of the target, during the period. A total of 21 Seva Sethu camps had been conducted across the region.

Coimbatore North recorded the highest number of installations at 300, followed by Coimbatore Metro- 245, Tiruppur- 182, Coimbatore South- 130, Palladam- 128, Udumalpet- 121 and the Nilgiris- 17.

World.title: Nobel committee says Venezuela needs democratic change despite Maria Machado’s return
World.content:
The Norwegian Nobel Committee said Tuesday (October 27, 2026) that a democratic transition was "still" necessary in Venezuela, after opposition leader and 2025 Nobel peace laureate Maria Corina Machado recently returned to the country.

"Much has changed in recent months, but the task remains urgent: Venezuela still requires a democratic transition founded on fundamental rights, political participation and free elections," Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said in a statement.

The Norwegian committee awards the prestigious Nobel Peace Prize and last year gave the nod to Ms. Machado for her work promoting democratic rights and a "just and peaceful" transition in the South American nation.

Ms. Machado returned to her country on Sunday (October 25) after nearly a year in exile, drawing jubilant crowds in a direct challenge to interim president Delcy Rodriguez's U.S.-backed government.

She left Venezuela last December to receive the Nobel Peace Prize after nearly a year in hiding, and has since made at least seven unsuccessful attempts to return, according to sources in her party.

President Nicolas Maduro was captured in a spectacular U.S. military operation in January. Rodriguez, his deputy, took over as interim leader with Washington's blessing.

As U.S.-backed talks on a political transition took place, Machado had been forced to observe from exile in Panama.

"The committee expresses its hope that her return will strengthen the democratic opposition and its peaceful struggle for democracy," Mr. Frydnes said.

Ms. Machado was unable to stand in the 2024 presidential election after she was declared ineligible. Maduro was declared winner of the election amid opposition claims of massive fraud.

World.title: Guntur Collector directs officials to safeguard election materials
World.content:
District Collector and District Election Officer C.M. Saikanth Varma inspected the strong rooms and election material distribution centre in Guntur on Tuesday as part of preparations for the local body elections.

Andhra Muslim College in Guntur is being used as the distribution centre for the Guntur Municipal Corporation elections, while strong rooms and counting facilities are being arranged at the Engineering College of Acharya Nagarjuna University (ANU). Similar arrangements are being made at the university for the Zilla Parishad elections.

Accompanied by GMC Commissioner K. Mayur Ashok and Zilla Parishad Chief Executive Officer V. Jyothi Basu, the Collector directed officials to ensure comprehensive arrangements without any shortcomings.

He instructed officials to keep all election materials ready, arrange refreshments and lunch for election staff, and ensure the availability of vehicles according to designated routes. Attendance of presiding officers, assistant presiding officers and other personnel should be monitored, he said.

Mr. Varma stressed the need for smooth vehicle movement at the reception centre, adequate staff at counters and prompt submission of election materials without traffic congestion or delays. He also directed officials to ensure quality food, install CCTV cameras at strong rooms and counting halls, and establish a media centre.

He instructed officials to make advance arrangements for smooth counting of votes. Revenue Divisional Officer K. Srinivasa Rao and other departmental officials participated in the inspection.

World.title: Tata Power in MoU with BPCL to develop 110 kV power infra at Mumbai refinery project
World.content:
Tata Power Company Ltd. has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Bharat Petroleum Corporation Ltd. (BPCL) to develop 110 kV power infrastructure involving an investment of around ₹250 crore.

The project will meet the 90 MW power requirement of BPCL's Petro Resid Fluidised Catalytic Cracking Unit (PRFCCU) project at its Mumbai refinery, Tata Power said in a statement.

With a processing capacity of 3 million metric tonnes per annum (MMTPA) and a project outlay of approximately ₹14,203 crore, PRFCCU is BPCL's second-largest project currently under execution and the largest ever undertaken at Mumbai refinery.

Under the MoU, Tata Power said it will provide 110 kV connectivity and undertake the design and development of the associated power infrastructure to meet the project's power requirement.

This infrastructure development is envisaged to be completed over approximately 24 months with a combined estimated outlay of about ₹250 crore for Tata Power and BPCL, subject to applicable approvals and project milestones.

World.title: Karnataka’s Forest Department and Bird Count India launch first Rajyotsava Bird Count
World.content:
The first Karnataka Rajyotsava Bird Count (KRBC), an attempt to document the 550-odd species of birds found in the State’s wetlands, forests, fields, lakes, gardens and parks, will be held between October 30 and November 2.

The four-day event, which is being organised by Bird Count India (BCI) and the Karnataka Bird Monitoring Network (KBMN), with support from the State’s Forest Department and the State’s birdwatching community, seeks to celebrate Karnataka’s natural heritage while building scientific data on its avian inhabitants.

To further encourage this initiative, the department has conducted a State-level online workshop for its officers. According to Kumar Pushkar, Principal Chief Conservator of Forests (Wildlife) and Chief Wildlife Warden, Government of Karnataka, birds are part of Karnataka’s heritage, and Rajyotsava is the perfect time to celebrate it. “We invite everyone to step outdoors, watch birds, and join the Karnataka Rajyotsava Bird Count over these four days.”

Citizen science

Anyone can participate in the event simply by observing and recording birds for about 15 minutes. All you need is a smartphone and two free apps: eBird to record observations and Merlin Bird ID to help you identify birds.

Participants can choose the number of days and time period during which they want to participate, though certain basic ethical caveats need to be maintained while they do so. These include keeping a safe distance from nesting birds, avoiding playback recordings to attract birds, staying on paths, abstaining from chasing or disturbing birds, respecting local communities and their privacy and delaying sharing the locations of sensitive nesting sites.

Complete checklists of these observations should be submitted to eBird by November 10, which, in turn, could help generate useful scientific data.

Step out and enjoy

Ashwin Viswanathan of BCI said that he was excited about conducting the first KRBC with the support of the Forest Department. “This event presents the perfect opportunity to show our State’s pride by counting birds. All it takes is 15 minutes to step out, enjoy the fresh air, and listen to birdsong. Every bird you watch and report also adds to science,” he said.

World.title: JI to 'no longer' postpone Islamabad march against petrol levy, says will resume it in mid-November
World.content:
Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) emir Hafiz Naeemur Rehman on Tuesday said his party would hold its march to Islamabad against the petroleum levy in mid-November.

He made the announcement during a press conference in Islamabad, which came shortly after he met with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to discuss his demand to abolish the petroleum levy.

“We want to make it clear that we will not postpone our Islamabad march any longer. It will now take place in mid-November, and it certainly will take place,” the JI chief said.

He added, “Let them announce this package, provide this relief, and devise a mechanism to abolish this extortionate levy before that, [but] if they do not do so, we might have to sit on the road to talk.

“We are prepared for anything,” Rehman declared.

Asked about the outcome of his meeting with PM Shehbaz — offered by the latter when urging the party to postpone its Islamabad march — the JI emir refrained from terming it “inconclusive”.

He noted that two sides had consensus on expanding the scope of relief, but there were disagreements over the “modalities” and “procedure”.

“We say eliminate the levy; they say we can move towards it phase by phase,” Rehman elaborated.

At around 4pm, a post on JI’s account said Rehman had reached PM House, accompanied by a delegation including the party’s Deputy Emir Liaquat Baloch, Deputy Secretary General Syed Farasat Shah, and JI Islamabad Emir Nasrullah Randhawa.

Rehman told the media that JI was forming another committee on the matter, comprising Baloch, Shah and Randhawa.

“We cannot simply accept peanuts,” the JI chief said when asked about a reported government offer to reduce the levies by Rs20-30. He stressed that his party stood firm on its stance.

He maintained that JI would continue its preparations and would begin nationwide mobilisation for its planned march to the federal capital, while negotiations would also continue at the same time.

“Our preparations are already complete; we will prepare further [and] we will talk to them (the government) further. However, we will also hold the Islamabad march in mid-November,” Rehman said.

Asked whether JI had presented any alternative to abolishing the levy, he responded in the affirmative, asserting that his party had comprehensive preparations.

Rehman highlighted that all past governments vowed not to take loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) but then entered into programmes with it after coming into power.

He said his party pointed this out, adding, “Give relief to the people; do not take retribution for your incompetence from the nation.”

The JI has been demanding for over two months that the Centre abolish petroleum levies, as fuel prices have skyrocketed due to conflicts in the Middle East since March.

The Centre and JI had agreed to form committees in early September — when the latter had planned a nationwide strike — to recommend measures to reduce the levy.

Rehman on Monday warned that the party would march to Islamabad in mid-November if the premier did not abolish the petroleum levy.

On Aug 16, the JI announced sit-ins in all the provincial capitals of Pakistan against the petroleum levy and had called for a nationwide strike on Sept 3.

On Sept 20, the party launched a protest march towards Islamabad, warning that if the government failed to abolish the petroleum levy, the protest could turn into one to oust the government.

On Sept 22, the JI emir said his party, whose convoy had reached Multan, was postponing its long march at the request of PM Shehbaz, who had assured the other side of a meeting to discuss the matters.

World.title: Madushanka’s five-for powers Sri Lanka into tri-series final after Pakistan drubbing
World.content:
Sri Lanka stormed into the final of the One-day International tri-series after overwhelming Pakistan by eight wickets, chasing a modest target of 111 in just 18.1 overs at the Gaddafi Stadium on Tuesday.

Left-arm pacer Dilshan Madushanka delivered a career-best five for 34 to dismantle Pakistan for 110 in 25.3 overs before Kamindu Mendis struck an unbeaten 62 to guide Sri Lanka to 114-2, sealing victory with 31.5 overs to spare.

The result confirmed Sri Lanka’s place in Saturday’s final alongside Pakistan, who had already qualified after winning their first three matches. England’s remaining league fixture against Sri Lanka on Thursday consequently became a dead rubber.

Pakistan’s batting collapsed against a disciplined Sri Lankan attack after captain Kusal Mendis won the toss and elected to field. The hosts struggled to cope with Madushanka’s short-pitched deliveries and never recovered from losing wickets at regular intervals.

Babar Azam top-scored with 29 off 33 balls, including five boundaries, while Hasan Nawaz made 17. Captain Shaheen Shah Afridi contributed 15 off 13 deliveries, striking two sixes in a late attempt to lift the total.

Pakistan lost Fakhar Zaman for five in the fourth over when he mistimed a short delivery from Madushanka and was caught at point. Maaz Sadaqat, making his first appearance in the tri-series after being added to the squad a day earlier, managed eight before Asitha Fernando trapped him leg-before with a yorker.

Saad Baig fell for five, caught at short cover off Madushanka, while Salman Ali Agha made nine before edging Sahan Arachchige behind. Pakistan were 61-4 when Babar was trapped leg-before by Eshan Malinga for 29, having already lost their two reviews.

The collapse gathered pace as Arachchige dismissed Shadab Khan for two and Dunith Wellalage removed Hasan Nawaz, who was caught by Arachchige for 17. Pakistan slumped to 91-8, leaving the lower order with too much to do.

Madushanka returned to claim the remaining wickets, dismissing Arafat Minhas for 10 and Haris Rauf for one before ending the innings with Shaheen’s wicket. The Pakistan captain’s brief counterattack included two sixes, but he was caught by Wellalage as Madushanka completed his five-wicket haul. Arachchige took two wickets, while Asitha, Malinga and Wellalage claimed one apiece.

Sri Lanka’s reply began aggressively, with Kamindu and Avishka Fernando putting on 50 for the opening wicket in 6.5 overs. Avishka struck two fours in his 17-ball 16 before pulling Shaheen to Fakhar at short midwicket.

Kamindu, however, continued to score freely, reaching his half-century off 43 balls. He survived a dropped catch in Shaheen’s opening over and successfully reviewed an lbw decision before going on to finish unbeaten on 62 from 60 deliveries, with eight fours and two sixes.

Pakistan briefly found another breakthrough when Kusal, who had struck two boundaries in his six-ball eight, was bowled by Arafat for 8. The dismissal came in unusual fashion, as the ball ricocheted off the batter’s bat and into the stumps.

But the hosts could not build on the wicket. Pavan Rathnayake joined Kamindu and remained unbeaten on 23 off 26 balls, striking two fours as the pair guided Sri Lanka home without further loss.

Kamindu’s fluent innings ensured the chase remained firmly under control, while Rathnayake finished the contest by driving Maaz’s spin through cover-point for four.

Shaheen and Arafat took one wicket each, but Pakistan’s total left their bowlers with little margin for error.

Sri Lanka completed a comprehensive victory that capped a strong turnaround in the tournament, with their batters having also impressed in their earlier win over England.

For Pakistan, the defeat exposed familiar top-order weaknesses after their dramatic one-wicket victory over England on Sunday. Shadab’s unbeaten century had rescued that match, but this time the batting line-up failed to provide a competitive total.

Madushanka’s outstanding spell proved decisive, giving Sri Lanka the momentum to secure qualification and setting up a final against Pakistan on Saturday.

World.title: Pakistan, China launch information corridor 'CPIC' to counter misleading narratives, promote cultural exchange
World.content:
Pakistan and China have launched the China-Pakistan Information Corridor (CPIC), with Information Minister Ataullah Tarar saying that the initiative will focus on countering misleading narratives, cultural exchanges and cooperation between think tanks.

The corridor was launched at a ceremony in Islamabad, which was televised on Tuesday. Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning and Chinese Ambassador Jiang Zaidong attended the launch.

In his televised remarks, Tarar expressed his “long-standing“ desire to collaborate with China in the fields of media, information sharing and digital platforms.

Hailing Pakistan and China’s bilateral relations, Tarar recalled the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC), noting that it had “turned decades of goodwill into steel, concrete and current”.

“It lit homes, laid motorways across our provinces and gave Pakistan at Gwadar a gateway to the world.”

Tarar said that while the first phase of CPEC connected lands, the next phase will “connect our minds and this information corridor will act as a bridge for connecting the minds of the people of the two countries”.

The information minister said the collaboration under the newly launched corridor will stand on four pillars — media, business and enterprises, think tanks, and culture/tourism.

“First, media. A news exchange working group of 18 Pakistani and Chinese media organisations. From our state broadcasters and private channels to Xinhua, CMG, and People’s Daily now share verified news on our cooperation.”

He added that it will also include a dedicated fact-check mechanism to track misleading narratives and counter them with “concrete facts”.

The second pillar, which includes businesses and enterprise, Tarar said, will draw on leading Pakistani and Chinese commercial groups.

“This pillar has opened its first regional office in Karachi,” Tarar said, adding that under the initiative, a trade portal to track trade, investment, and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) was being built, along with a podcast series about the stories of Chinese entrepreneurs in Pakistan and vice versa.

He said the third pillar will involve collaboration between think tanks from the two countries.

“Led by the Pakistan-China Institute and joined by our foremost research institutions, this pillar will bring evidence and depth to the bilateral conversation through joint dialogue, research, and publications with Chinese counterparts,” Tarar said.

The fourth pillar, which Tarar described as the “heart of the corridor”, will focus on tourism, with work already underway on the Xinjiang-Gilgit-Baltistan tourism corridor, “extending the journeys of Chinese travellers into the valleys of our north”.

Tarar also shared that the first cohort of CPEC Youth Ambassadors had been nominated from 13 universities across Pakistan.

“Before a community of shared future can be built in steel and stone, it must find its place in the minds of the people,” Tarar said, stressing that the principle was at the core of CPIC.

“If CPEC is its body and the shared future, CPIC will be its voice. If CPEC connects our economies, CPIC will connect our understanding. Through it, a student in Lahore will know the China of today, and not the caricatures of yesterday. A family in Chengdu will see Pakistan as it truly is: warm, resilient, and full of potential.”

He added that the corridor will counter “falsehoods with fact, isolation with exchange, and suspicion with trust,” lauding Chinese President Xi Jinping’s vision.

“President Xi gave us the vision of a shared future, and Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has given Pakistan the means to reach it,” Tarar said.

For PM Shehbaz, Tarar said the digital revolution was about people and “above all Pakistan’s young people”.

“More than 68 per cent of our nation is under 30 in their hands. A laptop is a passport and a smartphone is a marketplace. Through their talent, Pakistan is taking its place in the global digital economy.”

Tarar further stated that CPIC was at its core a “digital corridor”.

“Its news exchanges, fact-check mechanisms, trade portals, podcasts, social media channels, and youth ambassadors are tools of a digital age put to work for an old and trusted friendship. And here too, Pakistan walks with China,” Tarar said.

The information minister, in his address, also invited Chinese media houses, think tanks, universities, enterprises, and youth ambassadors to join each pillar of CPIC.

Concluding his address, Tarar said that while the Karakoram Highway was carved through the mountains, today Pakistan and China were building a “different highway [..] it is not made of rocks, but it is made of truth, and it will be carried not on trucks, but on voices.

Meanwhile, China’s Ning also addressed the ceremony, noting that China and Pakistan continue to face misinformation and fake news, according to state broadcaster Pakistan TV.

Ning stressed the need for the CPIC, saying that its four pillars can play a key role in highlighting bilateral cooperation.

Pakistan and China share a longstanding strategic partnership rooted in mutual trust, economic cooperation and regional connectivity. Over the decades, ties have expanded across different sectors — including trade, energy, defence and infrastructure — with the CPEC symbolising a shared vision for development.

A day earlier, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar met Ambassador Zaidong to review progress on CPEC.

During the meeting in Islamabad, Dar praised the ongoing expansion of the “all-weather strategic cooperative partnership” between the two nations. Discussions focused on advancing trade, investment, regional connectivity, agricultural modernisation and people-to-people exchanges.

World.title: Lahore ATC denies police further remand of PTI's Hammad Azhar, sends him on judicial remand
World.content:
LAHORE: An anti-terrorism court (ATC) on Tuesday rejected a police request for further physical remand of PTI leader Hammad Azhar in the Jinnah House attack case and sent him to jail on judicial remand.

Sarwar Road police had booked several PTI leaders and workers on charges of attacking and vandalising Jinnah House during the May 9, 2023 protests against the arrest of former prime minister Imran Khan.

According to his family , Azhar was arrested on Sept 5. However, police said the next day they were unaware of his arrest, and he was produced before an ATC on Sept 7. His initial 21-day physical remand was extended at least twice.

Subsequently, upon the completion of the latest 12-day remand, the PTI leader was presented before ATC Judge Sardar Muhammad Akram Khan on Tuesday.

The investigating officer sought further physical remand of the former finance minister, stating that the police wanted to conduct a polygraph test, also known as a lie detector test.

However, Azhar’s counsel, Barrister Abuzar Salman Niazi, argued that a polygraph test required the suspect’s consent.

He argued that according to a Lahore High Court judgment, the procedure was to be conducted during judicial remand.

The lawyer said the suspect was also required to make a statement before a magistrate indicating whether he wished to undergo the test.

Azhar told the court that he did not want to undergo the test if the law allowed him to refuse it. He said a suspect should not be punished for the prosecution’s alleged lack of knowledge about the legal requirements.

After hearing arguments from the prosecution and the defence over the proposed polygraph test, Judge Akram dismissed the police request for further physical remand and sent Azhar to jail under judicial custody.

Barrister Niazi hailed the verdict, writing on X that his client’s “50-day physical remand finally ends” and that he was sent to Kot Lakhpat jail.

Azhar served as a federal minister for multiple portfolios during the PTI government, including finance, industries and energy.

In the aftermath of the May 2023 riots, when the state launched a crackdown against the party leadership, he had gone into hiding and reappeared in public a year later, on May 22, 2024.

World.title: At least 1 killed, 6 injured as roof of under-construction building collapses in Multan
World.content:
LAHORE: At least one individual was killed, while six others were injured on Tuesday when the roof of an under-construction building collapsed near Multan’s Northern Bypass, Rescue 1122 said.

In a statement, the rescue service said the roof of an under-construction plaza had collapsed near the National College of Business Administration and Economics on Northern Bypass.

The agency said that so far, six injured individuals had been rescued and shifted to Nishtar Hospital, adding that one person was killed in the collapse.

Rescue officials launch a search and rescue operation after building collapse in Multan on October 27, 2026. — Photo via Rescue 1122

A rescue operation was underway to rescue trapped individuals, Rescue 1122 said, adding that at least 10 to 15 labourers were working at the site at the time of the incident.

Upon receiving the information, Rescue 1122 relief teams were immediately dispatched to the incident site, the statement said. “Rescue 1122 teams reached the incident site within three minutes and initiated the search and rescue operation,” it said.

The statement said 10 vehicles were actively engaged in the relief operations. The relief operations include five ambulances, three rescue motorbikes, one rescue vehicle, and one fire vehicle, it added.

Rescue officials launch a search and rescue operation after building collapse in Multan on October 27, 2026. — Photo via Rescue 1122

In a statement, a spokesperson for Nishtar Hospital said that six injured were shifted to the hospital, adding that the hospital record showed that another individual was brought dead.

As per the records, three injured received head injuries — whose nature and criticality are unknown — while the other three received minor injuries.

The spokesperson said doctors and paramedical staff were on high alert in the emergency room, and the best medical facilities were being provided to the injured.

Building and roof collapses are common in Pakistan, often attributed to poor safety standards and the use of substandard construction materials.

A teacher and 30 students were killed when a school’s roof collapsed in Peshawar earlier this month.

In September, two men died in Pakpattan after the roof of their house collapsed during heavy rain and a windstorm.

World.title: Pakistan reaffirms solidarity with Kashmiris on Black Day, calls for end to rights violations
World.content:
The country’s top leadership on Tuesday reaffirmed Pakistan’s support for the people of Indian Illegally Occupied Jammu and Kashmir (IIOJK) as the country observed Kashmir Black Day to mark the anniversary of the arrival of Indian forces in Srinagar on Oct 27, 1947.

In a statement issued on the occasion, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the arrival of Indian forces in Srinagar 79 years ago marked the beginning of a “tragic chapter” in the history of Jammu and Kashmir, which continued to cast a long shadow over the region.

He expressed deep concern over the prolonged incarceration of Kashmiri political leaders, activists and human rights defenders.

“Pakistan’s position on Jammu and Kashmir remains clear, consistent and principled,” he said, adding that lasting peace and stability in South Asia could not be achieved without a just and peaceful resolution of the dispute in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people.

Paying tribute to the sacrifices of the Kashmiri people, PM said countless men, women and children had made immense sacrifices in pursuit of their rights, adding that their memory would always be honoured.

He reaffirmed the government and people of Pakistan’s unwavering solidarity with the people of occupied Kashmir.

According to a statement issued by the Presidency, President Asif Ali Zardari said the people of IIOJK had endured decades of conflict, restrictions and denial of their fundamental rights since Oct 27, 1947.

He said, “continuing restrictions on fundamental freedoms, heightened militarisation, arrests and reports of human rights violations remained a matter of serious concern and underscored the need for sustained international attention”.

Dar calls for resolution in line with UN resolutions

In his message, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said the people of IIOJK continued to be deprived of their fundamental rights under Indian occupation, nearly eight decades after Indian forces entered Srinagar.

He said the Kashmiri people’s struggle for the right to self-determination, recognised by the United Nations, remained unfinished, adding that Pakistan stood firmly with them in their pursuit of freedom, dignity and the right to determine their own future.

Dar added that India’s unilateral measures of Aug 5, 2019, had further aggravated the situation in the disputed territory, intensified the suffering of its people and could not alter the occupied region’s disputed status.

He called on the international community to fulfil its responsibilities towards the Kashmiri people, take sustained notice of the human rights situation in IIOJK and urge India to end rights violations and allow them to exercise their right to self-determination.

He paid tribute to the sacrifices of the Kashmiri people and reaffirmed Pakistan’s commitment to extending them political, diplomatic and moral support.

Dar said a just, peaceful and lasting resolution of the dispute in accordance with relevant UN Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the Kashmiri people was essential for peace and stability in South Asia. He added that the dispute could not be resolved through unilateral actions or the use of force.

In his message, PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari said Kashmiris had been waiting for decades for their right to self-determination, as recognised in United Nations resolutions.

He said the international community must answer through its actions when Kashmiris would be granted their recognised right to self-determination.

Bilawal said the future of Kashmir’s children should be one of freedom, peace and a life free from fear, rather than another prolonged wait to decide their own future.

NA resolution urges sustained diplomatic efforts

The National Assembly also unanimously passed a resolution, reaffirming Pakistan’s “unwavering moral, political and diplomatic support” for the people of Jammu and Kashmir and their inalienable right to self-determination.

The resolution strongly condemned continuing human rights violations in occupied Kashmir, including extrajudicial killings, arbitrary arrests and detentions, enforced disappearances, custodial torture and restrictions on fundamental freedoms.

The House also expressed concern over the continued incarceration of Kashmiri political leaders and activists and rejected India’s unilateral actions of Aug 5, 2019, aimed at altering the disputed territory’s status and demographic character.

In August 2019, India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) had revoked occupied Kashmir’s special status by repealing Article 370 of the constitution. The law had limited the power of the Indian parliament to impose laws in the state, apart from matters of defence, foreign affairs and communications.

In its resolution, the NA reaffirmed that the final disposition of the dispute must be determined in accordance with relevant United Nations Security Council (UNSC) resolutions and the freely expressed will and aspirations of the Kashmiri people, and called for an end to human rights violations and measures aimed at changing the territory’s demographic character.

The House further urged the government to sustain diplomatic efforts at the United Nations, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and other relevant international forums to highlight the Jammu and Kashmir dispute in accordance with relevant UNSC resolutions.

The resolution said that “neither the passage of time, nor repression, nor unilateral actions could extinguish the legitimate aspirations of the Kashmiri people or diminish the international community’s responsibility to work towards a peaceful and just resolution of the Kashmir dispute”.

World.title: No pressure from US to cut Russian oil imports, says Indian oil minister
World.content:
India has faced no pressure from ​the US to reduce its Russian crude ‌imports, oil minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday at an industry event.

“I never felt anything,” Puri said when ​asked if there has been pressure to ​cut Russian oil imports.

Puri said Middle East oil ⁠supplies have been rising as the region is ​able to ship out more cargoes.

He said India ​was getting 0.2 per cent of its oil imports from Russia before the Ukraine war, while imports have surged since the war ​started due to discounts on Russian oil.

India’s imports ​of Middle Eastern crude oil surged in September, returning to pre-war ‌levels, ⁠while its refiners cut back purchases of Russian oil amid stiff competition from China, ship-tracking data showed.

The minister said that the purchase of Russian oil ​is linked ​to discounts ⁠and pricing when compared with other grades. Russian oil imports have been reduced ​as the refiners are buying more Gulf ​oil ⁠sold at a discount, he added.

“Whatever people say or do, ultimately it is anchored in their self-interest,” ⁠he ​said.

The minister also said India ​is expanding its refining capacity to help meet local demand and ​export commitments.

World.title: Israel to give verdict on Netanyahu in pivotal election
World.content:
A deeply divided Israel headed to the polls on Tuesday for the first time since Hamas’s Oct 7, 2023 attack, with voters delivering their verdict on veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and the country’s rightward drift.

Israelis are casting their ballots in the shadow of three years of multi-front regional wars, with the trauma of the Oct 7 attack still fresh and questions over accountability and security central to the campaign.

The close-fought vote comes as Israel looks increasingly isolated on the world stage, driven by a devastating military campaign in Gaza, soaring settlement construction and violence in the occupied West Bank, along with a move towards hard-right religious nationalism.

The last opinion polls to be published showed Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, running neck and neck with his main centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot, a political novice and former military chief whose mild manner is seen as the antithesis of the incumbent.

“I want change in our country. I want a good democratic centrist government,” Alexandra, 65, told AFP at a Jerusalem polling station, where a few dozen people waited to vote early in the morning.

Some 7.3 million people are eligible to vote, with hundreds of thousands of young people due to cast their ballot for the first time. Surveys show they overwhelmingly identify as centre-right or right-wing.

Tens of thousands of Israelis are estimated to have flown in from abroad to vote in an election seen as crucial to deciding the future character of their country.

“This is the most important election because half the country has rejected the basic values on which the state of Israel was created,” 78-year-old voter Noam told AFP, saying the government was threatening the separation of powers and equality for all citizens.

Netanyahu, 77, has served as Israel’s prime minister on and off for more than 19 years.

The wily political operator focused heavily on his security credentials during his campaign, playing on his relationship with US President Donald Trump and insisting he is the only one who can keep Israelis safe.

In the years since October 7, Netanyahu led multiple wars that have seen Israeli forces reduce Gaza to rubble, occupy southern Lebanon and pummel Iran with US help.

‘Not afraid to take action’

Zipporah Bennett, an 85-year-old retiree, said she was voting for Netanyahu “because he has had the experience of navigating the country through a lot of difficult seasons”, praising his support from the US and adding: “He’s a man who’s not afraid to take action.”

Netanyahu returned to power in December 2022, bringing into his coalition far-right ultra-nationalists who have since seen their political clout skyrocket.

Wearing his trademark noose-shaped lapel pin, far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir cast his ballot in the West Bank settlement of Kiryat Arba, where his supporters had set up banners and speakers.

The opposition has scorned Netanyahu for his backing of ultra-Orthodox parties fighting to keep exemptions for religious Jewish students from drafting into the military, which faces personnel shortages.

But one of the biggest criticisms levelled at the premier is his failure to take responsibility for the Oct 7 attack, the deadliest day in the country’s history.

Eisenkot, 66, has pledged to establish an independent state commission of inquiry into the security failures that led to the attack, something Netanyahu’s government has resisted.

Seeking to unseat the premier is an informal bloc of parties led by Eisenkot’s Yashar and spanning from the right to the centre-left.

Eisenkot has vowed to prevent the creation of a Palestinian state and expressed support for Israeli settlements, but has promised to crack down on violent settlers.

Neither Eisenkot nor Netanyahu has publicly said they would partner with the predominantly Arab lists, which represent some 21 per cent of Israel’s population and who could become kingmakers if the results are as close as expected.

Yousef Jabareen, who heads one of the Arab-majority lists, told AFP he hoped for a high turnout among his community to help topple Netanyahu’s coalition, after voting in the northern town of Umm al Fahm.

Most polling stations will close at 10 pm (2000 GMT).

Final results could take days to trickle in and it is highly unlikely that any single party will come close to the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-member parliament.

Cobbling together any coalition could take weeks or months, with possible new elections on the horizon if negotiations fail.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry.
