Such episodes highlight a central challenge for the region: agreements can establish rules for sharing water, but they cannot guarantee sufficient supply when river flows decline.

Planning for 2040

Nurzhigitov also shared Kazakhstan’s plans for all eight water basins over five-, 10-, and 15-year horizons, extending through 2040. The plans will assess three water-availability scenarios and estimate how much water different sectors could receive under each. The minister said drinking water supplies would take priority if water were scarce.

Separately, the ministry’s press service told Tengrinews that the basin plans would account for scenarios involving reductions in water availability of 50% and 75%.

The longer-term outlook is a key reason for moving from annual allocation decisions toward more detailed planning. Nurzhigitov said forecasts suggest that water availability across Central Asia could decline by 15 billion cubic meters by 2040. This is a forecast, not a certainty, but it underscores the need to prepare for several possible outcomes.

The plans aim to help the government determine where water infrastructure is needed, how to allocate available resources, and which economic activities can be sustained under different conditions.

The ministry is also working to reduce losses and improve water efficiency at home. Agriculture accounts for about 60% of Kazakhstan’s water use, according to Nurzhigitov. Water-saving technologies were being applied to more than 700,000 hectares in 2026, with estimated savings of about 1 billion cubic meters.

By 2030, Kazakhstan aims to expand the area using such technologies to 1.3 million hectares, potentially saving an additional 2 billion cubic meters. Industrial enterprises are also expected to increase water reuse and recirculation.

As part of a broader package of measures, Kazakhstan aims to save and accumulate about 10 billion cubic meters of water by 2030 through infrastructure upgrades, new reservoirs, digitalization and more efficient water use.

World.title: EU-Funded Study Finds Progress, Challenges in Kazakhstan’s Housing Support System
World.content:
ASTANA – A study of housing support in Kazakhstan has found that some recipients experienced greater housing stability and lower living expenses, while others faced challenges with information, registration and housing maintenance, according to findings presented at a conference in Astana on Oct. 23.

According to the European Union (EU) Delegation to Kazakhstan, the qualitative study was conducted under the European Union-funded Shanyraq project, which focuses on strengthening communities and promoting access to adequate housing.

The research drew on 99 interviews, 10 focus groups across 10 cities, inspections at 83 addresses and an analysis of relevant regulations. The findings reflect participants’ experiences and are not statistically representative of all housing-support recipients. Some participants reported fewer forced relocations and less dependence on private landlords. Others said lower regular housing expenses left them with more money for food, health care and education.

The findings were presented at the conference, which brought together representatives of the EU Delegation to Kazakhstan, the Ministry of Industry and Construction, Otbasy Bank, the construction sector and civil society organizations.

Juana Mera Cabello, deputy head of partnerships at the EU Delegation to Kazakhstan, said access to housing was closely linked to dignity, opportunity and social inclusion.

“Accessible housing is a matter of dignity, opportunity and social inclusion. Through the Shanyraq project, the EU supports evidence-based dialogue and action that promote human rights and inclusive social and economic development for all,” she said.

The study’s authors presented recommendations covering the housing-support process, from initial consultations to conditions after recipients move into their homes. The authors will next discuss the recommendations with government agencies, developers and experts to identify ways to improve access to housing support and address the challenges identified in the research.

World.title: Global Breast Cancer Awareness Drive Puts Early Detection in Focus in Kazakhstan
World.content:
ALMATY – Kazakhstan is holding free breast cancer consultations and diagnostic examinations throughout October as part of an annual Pink October awareness campaign, encouraging women to undergo regular screening and seek medical attention if they notice changes in their breasts.

Breast cancer remains the most common cancer among women in Kazakhstan. In 2025, the country registered 5,743 new cases, according to figures provided by the Ministry of Healthcare.

Breast cancer also remains a major global health challenge. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), an estimated 2.4 million women were diagnosed with breast cancer worldwide in 2024, and 694,000 died from the disease. Breast cancer occurs in every country and can affect women at any age after puberty, with rates increasing in later life.

Since Kazakhstan launched its national breast cancer screening program in 2008, 19,018 cases have been identified, including 17,186 detected at Stages 1 and 2, when treatment is generally more effective. The number of Stage 3 and 4 cases detected through screening fell from 66 in 2011 to 16 in 2025, according to the ministry.

The Pink October campaign includes open days at oncology centers, consultations with oncologists and mammologists, mammography and breast ultrasound examinations. Organizers aim to raise awareness of breast cancer prevention and the importance of early diagnosis.

Breast cancer statistics in Kazakhstan

National figures highlight the importance of early detection. Since the launch of the screening program, thousands of cases have been identified at earlier stages, giving patients a better opportunity to receive timely treatment.

In Almaty, breast cancer is also the most common cancer among women. According to the Almaty Oncology Center, 659 new cases were identified in the city during the first eight months of 2026. A total of 9,520 patients are registered with the disease at the center.

Speaking at a briefing organized by the Regional Communications Service in Almaty, oncologists said the growing number of recorded cases is partly associated with expanded screening and greater attention to women’s health. However, specialists stressed that the disease can also affect younger people.

“Unfortunately, breast cancer is getting younger every year. The youngest patient we registered at the Almaty Oncology Center this year is 21 years old. She is currently receiving comprehensive treatment, and we are seeing a good response to therapy,” said Akerke Orazbayeva, an oncologist and head of the center’s specialized consultation and diagnostic department.

The oldest breast cancer patient observed at the center was 93, Orazbayeva told The Astana Times.

“The disease can develop not only in women – around 20 men are registered with this diagnosis at the Almaty Oncology Center. Of course, it occurs much less frequently in men, but the risk cannot be ruled out,” said Akbota Adilova, head of the center’s consultation and diagnostic department.

During the first eight months of 2026, doctors in Almaty detected breast cancer at Stage 0 in five women, Stage 1 in 305, Stage 2 in 312, Stage 3 in 20 and Stage 4 in 70.

Who can receive free screening?

The Ministry of Healthcare encourages women to undergo regular cancer screening at their local polyclinics. Kazakhstan currently offers three types of screening: breast cancer screening for women aged 40 to 76 once every two years, cervical cancer screening for women aged 30 to 70 once every four years, and colorectal cancer screening for men and women aged 50 to 70 once every two years.

Mammography can identify suspicious changes before symptoms appear. Specialists emphasize that ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can be used as additional diagnostic methods when medically indicated but do not replace screening mammography.

The WHO also stresses that awareness of symptoms, timely diagnosis and access to treatment are essential to improving breast cancer outcomes. In places where mammography screening is not practical or widely available, public education can still encourage women to seek medical attention when they first notice symptoms.

Risk factors and common misconceptions

Most women diagnosed with breast cancer have no known family history of the disease, and the absence of other obvious risk factors does not necessarily mean they are at low risk.

According to the World Health Organization, approximately 80% of breast cancers occur in women with no specific risk factors other than sex and age.

Risk increases with age, while other contributing factors include certain inherited genetic mutations, excess weight, particularly after menopause, alcohol consumption, hormonal and reproductive factors, dense breast tissue and previous exposure to high levels of radiation.

Having one or more risk factors does not mean a person will necessarily develop cancer. Specialists say the disease can develop through a combination of factors, and regular screening remains important.

Speaking at the briefing, doctors also sought to dispel common misconceptions that may discourage women from seeking medical care.

One widespread myth is that breast cancer can always be detected by feeling a lump. Adilova said small tumors may not be noticeable through self-examination, which is why regular screening and attention to changes in breast shape and skin are important.

Doctors also addressed concerns about deodorants, antiperspirants and biopsies. Research has not established a link between underarm deodorant or antiperspirant use and breast cancer.

Doctors also stress that ultrasound alone is not sufficient to replace mammography as a screening method. Women who notice unusual changes or have concerns about their breast health are advised to consult a medical professional.

Preventive surgery and genetic risk

Oncologists in Almaty also perform bilateral preventive mastectomy in selected cases involving women with a high hereditary risk of breast cancer. Kaisar Nakipbekov, an oncologist, mammologist and oncosurgeon at the Almaty Oncology Center, said the procedure may be considered when a patient has a genetic mutation associated with an increased risk of breast cancer. In some cases, it may also be performed at the patient’s request following medical consultation.

Certain inherited genetic mutations, including those affecting the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes, can substantially increase breast cancer risk. The WHO says women with high-risk genetic mutations may consider risk-reduction strategies, including medication or preventive surgery, in consultation with medical specialists.

Preventive mastectomy involves removing both breasts to substantially reduce the risk of developing breast cancer. The procedure became more widely known after actress Angelina Jolie disclosed in 2013 that she had undergone the surgery after learning she carried an inherited mutation associated with a high risk of the disease.

Pink October events across Kazakhstan

Oncology centers across Kazakhstan are offering free breast cancer consultations and examinations as part of Pink October, an annual campaign to raise awareness of the disease and encourage early detection.

A nationwide open day is scheduled for Oct. 31, including at the Kazakh Research Institute of Oncology and Radiology in Almaty, where women can consult an oncologist-mammologist free of charge. Visitors are advised to confirm appointment times, registration requirements and available examinations with their local medical facilities.

In 2025, more than 8,400 women took part in examinations organized as part of the campaign. Various breast conditions were identified in 3,337 women, including 144 cases of breast cancer.

The campaign also invites people to support awareness efforts by wearing a pink ribbon, scarf or another pink accessory, sharing information and using the hashtag Pink October Kazakhstan.

Breast cancer screening and treatment are also available through Kazakhstan’s state-guaranteed health care system. Treatment for malignant cancers is covered regardless of a patient’s mandatory social health insurance status.

Patients with suspected cancer can access consultations and initial diagnostic examinations through the Green Corridor, which provides expedited pathways within 18 working days.

Globally, the WHO is working to reduce breast cancer deaths through its Global Breast Cancer Initiative, established in 2021.

The initiative aims to reduce global breast cancer mortality by 2.5% annually and avert 2.5 million deaths by 2040. Its three pillars are health promotion for early detection, timely diagnosis and comprehensive breast cancer management. As organization reminds, improving outcomes requires not only awareness and early detection but also reliable referral pathways and access to effective treatment.

World.title: EDB to Provide Over $30 Million for Astana Data Center Project
World.content:
ASTANA – The Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) will provide $31.2 million in financing for the construction of a commercial data center in Astana, expanding Kazakhstan’s digital infrastructure and computing capacity, the bank announced on Oct. 19.

The agreement was signed with AKASHI Data Center PLC. The project marks the first data center construction project in the EDB’s investment portfolio.

The planned campus will have a total capacity of 100 megawatts (MW), with approximately 10 MW allocated to the first phase. The company estimates the project’s total investment at $354 million. The first phase is scheduled to begin commercial operations in 2027.

The facility is designed to provide data storage and processing services for financial institutions, technology companies and cloud service providers. The Uptime Institute has awarded Tier IV Certification of Design Documents for the first phase.

Sergey Ignatov, EDB senior managing director and head of the project block, said the investment supports Kazakhstan’s priorities in digitalization and artificial intelligence.

The project will expand opportunities for businesses to use modern data infrastructure and support the development of digital services, he said.

AKASHI Data Center Chairman of the Management Board Vladislav Minkevich said the project aims to position Kazakhstan as an exporter of digital infrastructure services, attracting international companies seeking to host computing workloads in the country.

He said such activity could generate export revenues and increase demand for local engineering, telecommunications and other services.

The campus will comprise four independent data center modules, supported by dedicated power and telecommunications infrastructure. One module is being designed for high-density artificial intelligence workloads and high-performance computing, using liquid cooling technology.

The facility will operate as a carrier-neutral data center, with four independent optical fiber entry points and connectivity options through Kazakh and international telecommunications operators.

The EDB is a multilateral development bank focused on investment and economic integration across Eurasia. As of the end of December 2025, the bank reported that its cumulative portfolio comprised 348 projects with total investments of $22.1 billion.

World.title: Alatau City Breaks Ground on First Skyscraper in $800 Million Project
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan’s Alatau City has broken ground on Iconic Complex, a multifunctional development set to become the city’s first skyscraper, with Deputy Prime Minister Kanat Bozumbayev attending the ceremony on Oct. 26, according to the Prime Minister’s press service.

The project, with investments exceeding $800 million, includes two towers measuring 272 and 78 meters. The complex will house offices, residences, a hotel, retail facilities and public spaces. Construction is scheduled for completion by the end of 2029.

The city is gradually introducing a special legal regime intended to attract investment and establish a modern governance system. According to the press release, investment in fixed capital in Alatau reached 70.3 billion tenge (US$133 million) in the first nine months of 2026, a 1.6-fold increase. The city’s investment portfolio includes 67 projects worth approximately $6.9 billion, with the potential to create around 55,000 jobs.

Infrastructure development is also underway. Work is progressing on 28 projects supported by 35.3 billion tenge (US$ 78.2 million) from the state reserve. These include the reconstruction of the Kokpa-1 substation, water supply facilities and road repairs.

Bozumbayev emphasized the need to meet construction deadlines and comply with seismic safety and energy-efficiency standards. He also called for the involvement of Kazakh companies and specialists.

Under its special legal regime, the city has introduced independent technical reviews of project documentation involving international experts, according to the statement.

“We expect Iconic Complex to set a new standard for design and construction quality and contribute to Alatau’s development as a modern city. The project must be completed on schedule and meet high standards of quality and safety,” Bozumbayev said.

China State Construction Engineering Corporation (CSCEC) is the general contractor, while the architectural concept was developed by the United States-based firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill (SOM).

Building a new economic center

Iconic Complex is part of a broader effort to develop Alatau into a regional economic hub combining manufacturing, logistics, technology and finance. In a September analysis, The Astana Times examined whether Kazakhstan could build such a center from scratch, noting that the project’s success would depend on turning investment plans into sustained economic activity and effective governance.

The city’s location between Almaty and Konayev, near Almaty International Airport and major transport routes connecting China with Central Asia, the Caucasus, Europe and the Middle East, is central to the government’s economic rationale.

Yernar Serik, a trading and investment analyst interviewed for the analysis, said a new economic center could help diversify an economy in which much of the business activity, capital and human resources are concentrated in Almaty and Astana.

Economist Anuar Nurtazin, however, cautioned that investment announcements and company registrations alone would not demonstrate success. He said key indicators should include exports, technological supply chains, local production and productivity growth.

The analysis also highlighted the importance of infrastructure, predictable regulation and a skilled workforce in determining whether Alatau can develop into an independent economic center rather than an extension of neighboring Almaty.

The city’s development plans extend to 2040, with a long-term vision through 2055 being prepared with international firms ARUP and Boston Consulting Group.

World.title: FlyArystan Launches Astana-Yining Route, Becomes Xinjiang’s Largest Foreign Airline
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s FlyArystan has launched direct flights between Astana and Yining on Oct. 26, becoming the largest foreign airline operating in China’s Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, Kazinform reported.

An Airbus A320 operated flight FS 7989, which departed Astana International Airport at 7:55 a.m. The flight took two hours and 25 minutes. Upon arrival in Yining, the aircraft received a traditional water cannon salute. Regular direct flights on the new route operate three times a week, on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays.

FlyArystan President Johan Eidhagen said demand for direct flights to Xinjiang was growing among business travelers, trading companies and tourists discovering the region.

“Today, the Kazakh airline has become the largest foreign carrier in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region of China, and we are proud of this,” he said, adding that the airline intends to expand its presence in the region and open new routes.

FlyArystan operates four direct routes between Kazakhstan and Xinjiang, connecting Almaty, Astana and Aktau with Urumqi and Yining.

The new route comes as Kazakhstan continues to expand its international air connectivity. Air Astana plans to launch seasonal direct flights between Almaty and Malaysia’s Langkawi on Dec. 25, as well as flights between Astana and Bangkok on Dec. 11. Both routes are expected to strengthen tourism and business links.

Kazakhstan is also preparing for a possible direct route between Astana and New York in 2027. The launch will depend on the completion of a U.S. aviation safety assessment, the readiness of Air Astana’s Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner aircraft and the required training hours for flight crews and technical staff.

World.title: Rybakina Defends Ningbo Open Title to Boost WTA Lead
World.content:
Kazakhstan’s Elena Rybakina strengthened her position at the top of the Women’s Tennis Association (WTA) rankings after winning the Ningbo Open in China on Oct.26, Tengri Sport reported.

Rybakina secured the title by defeating Canada’s Leylah Fernandez 6-2, 6-2 in the final, successfully defending her Ningbo Open championship.

Rybakina’s ranking points increased from 9,196 to 9,501 following her title win. She now leads Belarusian Aryna Sabalenka by 1,951 points, with Sabalenka holding 7,550 points.

According to the tournament organizers, the 2026 singles competition offered a total prize pool of $1.206 million, with the winner receiving $185,000.

The Kazakh player first officially reached the top of the WTA rankings on Sept. 14, after winning the US Open.

Since beginning her professional tennis career in 2016, Rybakina has won 15 WTA titles in 10 years. Her major achievements include a 2022 Wimbledon title, the 2025 WTA Finals title, and the 2026 Australian Open and US Open titles.

World.title: Chinese visitor numbers to Georgia rise by 23% in nine months, setting a record
Iran offers education to Azerbaijani girls in hijabs, Baku calls it interference
World.content:
Iran offers education to Azerbaijani girls

Azerbaijan and Iran have exchanged fresh accusations amid public discontent in parts of Azerbaijani society over new secular school uniform rules that have effectively banned the wearing of hijabs in schools.

Iran has offered to enrol Azerbaijani girls wearing hijabs in Iranian schools and universities. In response, Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Science and Education said the remarks were inappropriate and amounted to an attempt to interfere in the country’s education policy.

The ministry also pointed out that there were no schools or universities in Iran offering education in Azerbaijani, despite the fact that, according to the ministry, around 40 million ethnic Azerbaijanis live in Iran.

“For decades, they have been deprived of the opportunity to receive education in their native language,” Azerbaijan’s Education Ministry said.

Invitation to study extended to schoolchildren

On 22 October, Iran’s Minister of Science, Research and Technology, Hossein Simaei-Sarraf, published a video address inviting Azerbaijani girls to study at Iranian universities. He addressed his appeal to girls who, he said, were being forced to give up wearing hijabs in order to receive an education in Azerbaijan.

On 25 October, Iran’s First Vice-President Mohammad Reza Aref joined the initiative. He called on the ministers of health and education, as well as the head of Islamic Azad University, to make arrangements for admitting schoolchildren and university students from Azerbaijan. The offer, initially limited to higher education, was thus extended to schoolchildren.

However, the specific admission conditions remain unclear. It is not known which educational institutions would accept the students, what language classes would be taught in, who would cover the costs or how accommodation for underage students and their parents would be arranged.

Baku reminds Tehran of Azerbaijani-language education issue

On 26 October, Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Science and Education responded to the Iranian minister’s statement. The ministry described interference in Azerbaijan’s education policy as unacceptable and urged Iranian officials to “deal with their own country’s problems”.

Baku’s main criticism concerns the lack of opportunities to receive education in Azerbaijani in Iran. According to the ministry, there are no schools teaching in Azerbaijani in the country, nor is the language used as a medium of instruction at universities. Baku maintains that ethnic Azerbaijanis living in Iran have been deprived of the opportunity to receive education in their native language for decades.

In response to the neighbouring country’s statements about protecting Azerbaijani girls’ right to education, Baku has raised the issue of the language rights of ethnic Azerbaijanis living in Iran.

A separate practical question concerns the language in which the invited schoolchildren would be taught. While studying abroad in a foreign language is possible, it may require language training and support with adaptation. The Iranian proposal does not specify how the necessary arrangements would be made.

How did dispute over wearing hijabs in Azerbaijan begin?

A new wave of controversy began after Azerbaijan’s Cabinet of Ministers amended school uniform regulations on 21 September. Under the decree, the use of “additional items of clothing that undermine the uniformity of school uniforms and contradict the principle of secular education” is prohibited. Although the hijab is not explicitly mentioned in the document, complaints subsequently emerged that schoolgirls wearing headscarves were being barred from attending classes.

Protests took place at several schools in Baku and other parts of Azerbaijan, involving students and parents. Some students refused to attend classes in solidarity with their classmates who wear hijabs.

Police intervened during the protests. On 12 October, the Interior Ministry reported that 37 people had been detained in connection with incidents following the introduction of the new school uniform rules. According to the ministry, those detained were suspected of disturbing public order. A criminal case was also reportedly opened.

Reports later emerged that another 200 people had been detained after taking part in a protest near the 28 May metro station in Baku. Criminal cases were also reportedly opened against some of them.

Education dispute turns into political row

Iranian officials have presented their initiative as an attempt to help girls wearing hijabs continue their education. However, the link between the offer and restrictions in Azerbaijan gives it a political dimension. Tehran is openly criticising Baku’s education policy and appealing to families dissatisfied with the restrictions.

Azerbaijan’s response also focuses primarily on the political aspect of the issue rather than the conditions for admitting students. Instead of discussing arrangements for their enrolment in Iranian educational institutions, the ministry has accused Tehran of interfering in the country’s internal affairs and highlighted the lack of opportunities for ethnic Azerbaijanis living in Iran to receive education in their native language.

However, the mutual accusations do not resolve either problem. Limited opportunities to receive education in Azerbaijani in Iran do not address complaints about schoolgirls wearing hijabs being barred from attending classes in Azerbaijan. In turn, Iran’s offer does not resolve the issue preventing these girls from continuing their education at their own schools.

World.title: ‘Foreign-controlled spy forces have been eliminated’: Pashinyan on local elections
World.content:
Pashinyan on Armenia’s 2026 local elections

“The ruling Civil Contract party, along with candidates and teams affiliated with it, secured a convincing victory in the local elections,” Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said during a live broadcast on his Facebook page.

On 25 October, Armenia held local elections in 21 communities. Voters used a proportional representation system in 19 communities and a majoritarian system in the other two.

In five communities — Armavir, Vardenis, Garni, Akhuryan and Vayk — the ruling Civil Contract party ran unopposed.

In other words, no other political forces chose to contest the elections or take part in governing these communities.

According to preliminary results from the Central Electoral Commission, Civil Contract won in 16 communities. The Amerashkhut’yun (Solidarity) bloc secured the most votes in two others. In Stepanavan, the Gortsarar (Entrepreneur) party took the lead. Its list was headed by incumbent community leader Armen Grigoryan, who won the post in 2021 on the Civil Contract party list.

Pashinyan congratulated the candidates for community leadership positions and the ruling party’s teams as a whole on their victory. He stressed that Armenian citizens had helped deliver election results that led to the “destruction of spy opposition forces”. At the same time, he expressed concern about the outcome.

“As someone who became prime minister after the Velvet Revolution, I am far from pleased when a party wins more than 90%, 80% or 70% of the vote in some communities. However appealing such figures may seem at first glance, they evoke certain associations. They also raise questions about the opposition in Armenia. We need to assess this situation correctly. On the one hand, we must completely eradicate the spy opposition in Armenia that takes orders from abroad. On the other hand, Armenia needs an opposition that puts the interests of the state first,” the prime minister said.

Stepanavan records the highest voter turnout

Armenia’s Central Electoral Commission has released the final voter turnout figures. The Lori region community of Stepanavan recorded the highest turnout, at 68.83%.

Other communities also reported high turnout:

Yeghegnadzor (Vayots Dzor region) — 62.56%,

Tsaghkadzor (Kotayk region) — 61.78%,

Meghri (Syunik region) — 57.97%.

The lowest turnout among the 21 communities came in Fioletovo, in the Lori region, at 25.39%.

54 reports of possible violations

During the elections, the Interior Ministry’s 112 Operations Management Centre received 54 reports of possible violations. Investigators have received evidence relating to 10 incidents for preliminary investigation. These include:

one case of breaching ballot secrecy;

one case of obstructing people involved in the elections from exercising their rights or performing their duties;

seven cases of repeat voting or voting on behalf of another person;

one case of voter bribery.

Election observers also reported irregularities. The Akanates (Eyewitness) observation mission recorded 217 potential violations of the electoral process at 137 of the 407 polling stations it visited.

The observers noted crowds gathering at polling stations, risks to ballot secrecy and cases of “family voting”, in which several people enter a voting booth at the same time.

On 24 October, the day before the elections, Armenian media reported the arrests of opposition candidates and their supporters in three of the 21 communities. The Anti-Corruption Committee confirmed the arrests but did not disclose the identities of those detained, citing the interests of the preliminary investigation.

“As part of criminal proceedings launched by the Anti-Corruption Committee over alleged corruption offences linked to the electoral process, investigators are carrying out investigative and other procedural measures in several communities across Armenia,” the committee said.

“We solved one problem, but two or three new ones emerged” — prime minister’s assessment

Continuing his argument that Armenia must “eradicate” an opposition network he describes as a foreign-controlled spy network, the prime minister said: “These local elections have resolved the issue to some extent, but three new challenges have now emerged.”

He was referring in particular to the following questions:

“How can we prevent election results from creating the impression of authoritarianism or dictatorship?

How can we introduce an objective mechanism for public oversight in communities where we have secured a high level of trust?

How can we build an opposition in Armenia that puts the interests of the state first — young, intellectually capable, objective and honest — and answers solely to the will of its voters and citizens?”

Pashinyan stressed that the government must not take part in creating a new opposition, as this would lead to the emergence of a “controlled, fake opposition”.

The prime minister said independent political forces needed to become more active. He added that the government would neither help nor hinder their emergence.

“We want to see a genuine opposition emerge in Armenia — one that acts in the interests of Armenia and its people and is guided by democratic values and principles. We do not want an opposition that bribes voters or channels stolen and misappropriated funds into politics to turn the political sphere into a tool for protecting assets acquired dishonestly.”

In his view, an opposition that puts the interests of the state first could also provide “genuine and constructive oversight” of the government’s actions.

“I want to point out that in communities where the elections did not produce a strong opposition, public oversight remains an open question. I hope that civic groups and representatives of civil society will take on this role.”

Pashinyan on Armenia’s 2026 local elections

World.title: Billionaire Ivanishvili won’t testify in Georgia opposition ban case. Constitutional Court, day four
World.content:
Georgia opposition ban trial

On 26 October, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began substantive hearings on a lawsuit seeking to ban opposition parties.

The lawsuit, signed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party, calls for five opposition parties to be declared unconstitutional and banned: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists.

Georgian Dream argues that the parties have violated Article 23 of the constitution, which prohibits political parties whose objectives include overthrowing or forcibly changing the country’s constitutional order. One of the arguments cited in the lawsuit is the parties’ refusal to recognise the legitimacy of the current authorities. The lawsuit also accuses them of organising attempts to overthrow the government. The National Movement faces additional accusations of undermining the country’s independence and violating its territorial integrity. The party is held responsible for the August 2008 war with Russia, when it was in power. All five opposition parties reject the allegations.

The hearing began at 14:00 and continued until 19:00, with a break. The court was due to hear explanations from both sides.

On the first day, the court heard arguments from Georgian Dream and Zaza Bibilashvili, a member of Unity – National Movement.

Bibilashvili presented his party’s position for two and a half hours, and the presiding judge interrupted him several times.

The hearing will resume on 27 October at 12:00 and continue until 30 October. The court must issue its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Below is a brief account of the main developments at the 26 October hearing.

Bidzina Ivanishvili will not be called as a witness

Shortly after the substantive hearing began, the full bench of Georgia’s Constitutional Court announced its decision on a motion filed by the Gakharia for Georgia party.

The motion was partially granted. Constitutional Court judge Revaz Nadaraya said the court had agreed to admit certain types of materials as evidence in the case.



However, the party was denied the right to question politicians as witnesses, including billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling party, as well as other current and former Georgian Dream leaders.

The court also refused to question Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze, former State Security Service chief Mamuka Mdinaradze, MP Archil Talakvadze and others.

This was the 14th and final motion submitted by the opposition parties. The court had rejected the previous 13 motions concerning the questioning of witnesses.

Political statements prohibited

Judge-rapporteur Vasil Roinishvili then presented a brief overview of the lawsuit and its contents.

After his presentation, Judge Revaz Nadaraya once again reminded the parties to refrain from political statements.

Although the case concerns the assessment of political activities and parties, he said, the parties should avoid political statements and speak “with the utmost restraint and propriety, without any insults, so as not to offend the other side”.

After the introductory part, the court began hearing arguments from the parties. The claimant, Georgian Dream, was represented by MP Archil Gorduladze. The defendants are the five opposition parties. On this day, only Zaza Bibilashvili, a member of Unity – National Movement, addressed the court.

What exactly are the opposition parties accused of?

The accusations were presented by Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze, who outlined the allegations against the five opposition parties. According to him:

● Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change and the Federalists are accused of supporting attempts to overthrow the constitutional order by force.

Gorduladze argued that, during the National Movement’s rule in 2004–2012, they turned a blind eye to systematic human rights violations and acted against Georgia’s independence and territorial integrity by attempting to start a war with Russia in August 2008.

He also accused the party of denying the legitimacy of parliament and government after losing power.

● Lelo – Strong Georgia, led by Mamuka Khazaradze and Badri Japaridze, is accused of denying the legitimacy of the current elected parliament and government. Gorduladze said the party supported the idea of a parallel “technical government” in 2022 and backed attempts to overthrow the government and forcibly change the constitutional order between 2019 and 2025.

The party’s leaders are also accused of refusing to distance themselves from opposition politician Aleksandre Elisashvili, who was convicted over an attempted arson attack on a court building.

● For Georgia, led by former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia, is accused of refusing to distance itself from the events of 20 June 2019, when a protest was dispersed, and from the circumstances surrounding the 2021 arrest of Nika Melia, then leader of Unity – National Movement. Gorduladze also alleged that Gakharia denied the legitimacy of the elected government, supported the idea of a “technical government” and attempts to overthrow the constitutional order during protests, and backed foreign forces.

Gakharia is further accused of undermining Georgia’s territorial integrity by unilaterally ordering the establishment of a police checkpoint near the village of Chorchana in the Georgian-Ossetian conflict zone in 2019. A criminal case has been brought against him over the decision, alleging that it sharply escalated tensions in the region and resulted in Georgia losing control over additional territory.

“We have no right to turn a blind eye to these facts and leave future generations a state whose constitutional foundations remain unprotected. That is why the actions of the National Movement and its offshoots [referring to the other four parties named in the lawsuit] must be declared unconstitutional and the parties banned,” Gorduladze said.

“Are you responding to the lawsuit or criticising us?”

Zaza Bibilashvili spoke on behalf of Unity – National Movement. Shortly after he began his statement, Constitutional Court President Revaz Nadaraya interrupted him.

The judge objected to Bibilashvili’s remark that the parties had “no illusions about the outcome of the proceedings”.

Nadaraya interpreted the remark as an insult to the court.

“Are you responding to the lawsuit or criticising us? Are you challenging us, or what? To some extent, indirectly, you insulted the court by questioning our impartiality. You are showing disrespect, and there are limits to that too. Bear that in mind!” he said.

Bibilashvili: “The result will be the legitimisation of Russia’s military aggression in a Constitutional Court ruling”

Zaza Bibilashvili spoke for almost two and a half hours about Unity – National Movement after his opening remarks.

He recalled the difficult socio-economic situation in Georgia in the early 2000s, when the party came to power, and described how developed the country had become by the time Georgian Dream took office in 2012.

Bibilashvili criticised Georgian Dream’s policies and several of its decisions, which he said had harmed the country as a whole.

He also argued that “the actual aim of these proceedings is to give Russia confirmation that its military aggression against Georgia in 2008 was justified, because Georgia’s own Constitutional Court would be arguing that Georgia itself supposedly created the grounds for Russia’s aggression”.

“Some may object that this is not the court’s aim. But it is impossible to dispute that, if the claims in the lawsuit are upheld, the result will be the legitimisation of Russia’s military aggression through a ruling by Georgia’s Constitutional Court,” Bibilashvili said.

He stressed that the claimant, Georgian Dream, was deliberately conflating political and legal responsibility and failing to distinguish between the state and a political party.

Bibilashvili: “The fox brought its own tail as a witness”

Zaza Bibilashvili said the only evidence cited in the lawsuit to prove the opposition parties’ guilt was a report by a temporary parliamentary investigative commission.

According to him, the report contains so many factual and legal errors that it cannot be made public.

Bibilashvili noted that the opposition had effectively been found guilty even before the commission was established, in the explanatory note prepared for its creation.

“This means the outcome was known even before the commission was set up. It’s as if the fox brought its own tail as a witness — that is the essence of these proceedings,” Bibilashvili said.

Bibilashvili: “If the opposition is annulled, it can no longer pose an immediate threat to the state”

Zaza Bibilashvili used a football analogy to question how a championship could ban every team except one from competing.

He said that in a democratic country, banning political parties should not be a form of punishment but a means of protecting the state from an immediate threat posed by those parties. The state must demonstrate that a ban is urgently necessary.

In this case, Bibilashvili argued, the claimant had failed to prove any such necessity.

Moreover, he said, “Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze himself has stated that there is no immediate threat from the opposition and no need to ban it”.

Bibilashvili also urged the court to consider a statement Kobakhidze had made earlier: “Why ban the opposition? It has already been annulled.”

Bibilashvili to judges: “Act in a way you want to be remembered by history”

At the end of his lengthy statement, Zaza Bibilashvili said his closing remarks would be anything but conventional.

“I am not asking you to reject the lawsuit. But act in a way that you want to be remembered by history, in a way you would want your children to see you. Apply the same standards you would want those who come after you to apply to you.

“Servants of authoritarianism often hope that democratic forces will treat them according to democratic standards, rather than the standards they themselves have established. However, after 14 years of Georgian Dream rule, more and more people in Georgian society are rejecting this approach.

“They support the idea that, in future, everyone should be judged by the standards they themselves have established, both politically and legally. This would allow us to break once and for all the so-called vicious circle into which our enemy, Russia, has pushed us.”

Bibilashvili’s remarks once again angered the Constitutional Court judge.

“I told you to behave with dignity! How are we supposed to interpret your statement — as an attempt to put pressure on us?”

“What kind of pressure could I possibly exert on you?” Bibilashvili asked rhetorically.

“Stop lecturing us,” the judge replied.

Zaza Bibilashvili finished his statement at 18:30, with only 30 minutes remaining before the end of the court session. Ana Tsitlidze, another member of Unity – National Movement, was due to speak next, but said she needed more time. The court therefore decided to adjourn.

Hearings on the constitutional lawsuit will resume tomorrow, 27 October, with Tsitlidze’s statement. Proceedings will begin at 12:00, and the court has agreed to sit until 19:00. According to the presiding judge, 20 representatives of the defendant parties are due to speak.

Reactions after the hearing

● After the hearing, Georgian Dream MP Archil Gorduladze said that the National Movement had no evidence to refute the facts presented in the lawsuit:

“The National Movement representative talked about everything and nothing. He claimed that Georgia experienced a triumph of democracy in 2004–2012, and that there was no torture or inhuman treatment.”

● “We heard truly unique accusations against Lelo – Strong Georgia. Apparently, signing the charter proposed by Ex-President Salome Zourabichvili and agreeing to cooperate with Giorgi Gakharia’s party during the municipal elections constitute violations of the Constitution,” said Badri Japaridze, one of the leaders of Lelo – Strong Georgia.

📌 Maia Kopaleishvili, a member of Coalition for Change, said: “We will fully refute all of Georgian Dream’s arguments and unfounded claims. An objective observer will see that Georgian Dream’s lawsuit is political in nature. Its aim is not to uphold the constitutional order in the country, but to eliminate political parties and establish one-party rule. This, of course, contributes to the establishment of a dictatorship in the country.”

News in Georgia

World.title: Opinion: If Georgia’s Constitutional Court bans opposition parties, Russia will use it against Georgia
World.content:
The banning of opposition parties in Georgia

Davit Usupashvili, chairman of the political council of the Lelo party, said the state itself faced the greatest risk from a ban on opposition parties.

On 21 October 2026, Georgia’s Constitutional Court in Batumi began hearing a petition filed by 88 MPs from the ruling Georgian Dream party. The petition seeks to ban five opposition parties: Unity – National Movement, Coalition for Change, Lelo – Strong Georgia, Gakharia for Georgia and the Federalists. The hearings will continue from 26 to 30 October. The court must deliver its ruling by 24 June 2027.

Usupashvili said that if the Constitutional Court accepted the arguments set out in Georgian Dream’s petition, Russia would use the ruling to bolster its own demands concerning Georgia’s occupied territories.

Georgia’s Constitutional Court is considering a constitutional petition filed by 88 MPs in the Georgian parliament, seeking to ban five opposition parties.

Politician Davit Usupashvili discussed the possible consequences of the ruling in detail in an interview with Sopho Zurabiani on Formula TV.

“Irreparable harm to the country”

The petition holds the United National Movement responsible for the August 2008 war, which took place while the party was in power.

Usupashvili said Georgian Dream’s political statements effectively give Russia a narrative similar to the one it uses against Ukraine: that Georgia acted as the provocateur in 2008. He warned that if the Constitutional Court’s ruling endorsed this narrative, “it would cause enormous, irreparable harm to the country”.

Usupashvili believes Russia would then press even harder for the legal recognition of borders and guarantees of “independence” for the occupied regions. In effect, he said, Moscow would tell Georgia: “Your own Constitutional Court has ruled this way.”

Usupashvili noted that until now, firm opposition from the European Union, the United States, Japan and other partners had helped prevent attempts to secure recognition of the occupied territories. But what position would the international community find itself in if the Constitutional Court declared that the occupied territories were victims and Russia had acted only to protect them? After all, as a rule, “the international community sides with the oppressed and seeks to restrain the aggressor, punish it and so on”.

Davit Usupashvili draws attention to the appointment of Giorgi Zurabashvili as special representative for relations with Russia, a move that coincided with the start of the Constitutional Court proceedings.

On the very day the court began hearing the petition, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze appointed Zurabashvili, the first deputy foreign minister, as special representative for Russia. The position had remained vacant since December 2025. Kobakhidze said the appointment did not signal the start of a new phase in relations with Russia.

Usupashvili believes Georgian Dream has given the role a new purpose by appointing Zurabashvili:

“It was a highly symbolic gesture. On the one hand, we hear claims that ‘Western lackeys’ — or their ‘masters’ — are manipulating political parties and citizens who have taken to the streets. On the other hand, the message is: ‘Now we will sort out our relations with you ourselves.’ Clearly, this creates a serious problem.”

He notes that when Zurab Abashidze held the position, Georgia managed its engagement with Russia with Western support. Now, however, the country has effectively been left without allies.

Gathering evidence for future legal disputes

Four of the five parties facing a ban are taking part in the hearings. The fifth, the Federalists, has refused to participate in the proceedings. Over the past three hearings, the judges have rejected every motion submitted by the opposition parties.

Nevertheless, Davit Usupashvili believes the opposition should take part in the proceedings, focusing above all on gathering evidence.

He argues that this is necessary both for disputes on the international stage and for legal proceedings within Georgia, which he believes will inevitably follow.

“What is happening there is essentially preparation for a future lawsuit over Georgian Dream’s unconstitutional actions. In effect, they are preparing a future legal case.”

Usupashvili is convinced that once power changes hands, the evidence gathered during these proceedings will be used to seek a ban on Georgian Dream itself.

“The case will be heard in the same courtroom, but by different judges — perhaps even by some of those currently in office. They have a habit of switching sides whenever power changes hands. And these are the very people who will have to ban a party that resorts to such actions,” Usupashvili said.

“Healthy opposition” and a one-party system

Usupashvili says the demand to ban five opposition parties has no legal basis and amounts to purely political persecution. He calls it “an attempt by Georgian Dream to pave the way for a constitutional coup”.

In his assessment, the ruling party aims to eliminate its opponents, secure a constitutional majority and reshape the Constitution to suit its own interests.

Usupashvili recalls Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s statement that Georgian Dream would hold a constitutional majority in parliament once the opposition parties were banned.

Responding to the government’s argument that a ban would pave the way for a “healthy opposition”, Usupashvili said: “They want to appoint the opposition themselves.”

He says that over the past 12–14 years, the government has failed to name a single opposition party it considers healthy, apart from its own offshoots.

Usupashvili compares the logic behind the petition to Article 6 of the Soviet Constitution, which established the Communist Party as the sole legitimate political force. He argues that if the court rules that only the ruling party represents the interests of the state, Georgia will return to a constitutionally enshrined one-party system, placing it among the enemies of the free world.

What lies ahead for the opposition parties, and what should they do now?

Usupashvili believes that a ban on political parties would pose a less serious threat to the parties themselves than to the country as a whole.

“A political party is a tool for conducting political activity. Elections took place in 1990 even though not a single political party had been registered. Nevertheless, a way forward was found — we managed to register directly for the elections. There are mechanisms available.”

He says the parties should already be discussing what they will do if a ban comes into force.

“We need to talk about this because the situation will change fundamentally. Under these circumstances, we must not fall into their trap or start playing by their rules. Their ‘game’ is to drive the active part of society — ordinary citizens — into a state of utter despair.”

Usupashvili says political leaders need to reassess and analyse current events and find a way forward.

“We must understand what is really happening — why is all this happening to us? The political front needs renewal. Fifteen to 20 years ago, I was a party chairman. We set up local branches and held meetings. Yes, we faced interference and persecution, but we still managed to achieve something. The situation is different now. However, examples from Hungary and Guatemala show that change is possible even under such circumstances.”

Usupashvili stresses that it is crucial for active citizens — those who believe in their country’s independence, freedom and progress — not to give in to despair.

The banning of opposition parties in Georgia

World.title: Opinion: Why agreement between Abkhazia’s interior ministry and Russia conflicts with Abkhaz law
World.content:
The opposition in Abkhazia is demanding the immediate resignation of Interior Minister Robert Kiut. The call follows an agreement he signed with Russia’s Interior Ministry. The opposition argues that the deal violates Abkhazia’s constitution and undermines its national interests.

One provision has provoked particular outrage. It envisages sharing with the Russian side data on individuals who could “destabilise the situation in the border region”. Many suspect that the agreement would legitimise a growing trend in which Russian authorities punish Abkhaz public figures and politicians who oppose arrangements with Russia that they consider detrimental to Abkhazia.

Prominent Abkhaz public figure Akhra Bzhania has examined whether the agreement complies with Abkhaz law. He concludes that it does not.

Akhra Bzhania: “Most supporters of the agreement between Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry and Russia cite legal continuity with the provisions of the 2014 Treaty of Alliance between Russia and Abkhazia as their main argument. But can these references really be considered made in good faith?

Here is what Article 10 of the 2014 treaty says in its main provisions on cooperation between the two sides’ interior ministries:

1. Within one year of the treaty’s entry into force, the parties must establish a Joint Information and Coordination Centre for their interior affairs agencies.

2. The Joint Information and Coordination Centre for Interior Affairs Agencies is responsible for:

organising the exchange of operationally significant information between the law enforcement agencies of the Russian Federation and the Republic of Abkhazia, as well as maintaining the necessary operational and forensic records;

compiling and maintaining a specialised database on organised criminal groups whose illegal activities affect the interests of the contracting parties;

collecting, consolidating and analysing information on efforts to combat organised crime and other serious offences;

assisting with the international search for and extradition of people who have evaded criminal prosecution or the enforcement of a sentence;

facilitating the implementation of necessary coordinated measures to combat serious crimes that threaten the security of the contracting parties;

developing and submitting proposals to the contracting parties on improving the effectiveness of their cooperation.

None of these provisions, nor the treaty as a whole, states or implies that the Joint Information and Coordination Centre (JICC) may be used to “monitor and analyse the crime situation and operational environment in the Republic of Abkhazia, as well as the activities of Abkhazia’s interior affairs agencies”, as stated in Article 1 of the new agreement.

That last point is particularly absurd. Why have an entire ministry if it needs to rely on an external organisation to monitor its activities? Not to mention that Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry may have internal matters that the JICC should know nothing about.

The 2014 treaty also says nothing about the JICC, let alone specialised units of Russia’s Interior Ministry, tackling “economic crime and corruption” in Abkhazia.

Nor does it mention any Russian Interior Ministry units directly engaging in “countering the spread of criminal ideas on social media and messaging platforms”. Yet Article 4 of the new agreement between the two interior ministries explicitly includes this provision.

Incidentally, many have interpreted this clause as an attempt to monitor online spaces for dissenting views.

There is also the fact that the very definition of what constitutes “criminal” content online may differ significantly between our two countries. In Russia, for example, even this text, published on Facebook, a platform owned by Meta, is illegal.

And, of course, the 2014 treaty nowhere states that the Russian and Abkhaz interior ministries will “conduct joint operational and preventive measures in border areas” — activities that infringe on our sovereign jurisdiction. Yet Article 6 of the new agreement explicitly provides for them.

And so it goes with many other provisions…

International treaties are not folk songs from which you can create a new work by developing the main theme. They are complete legal documents, and their provisions cannot be freely reinterpreted.

For this reason, and because the two instruments differ substantially in their content, the new agreement cannot be said to “derive” from the 2014 treaty, as some “experts” are trying to argue. If anyone really wants to establish a new legal framework for the work of Abkhazia’s Interior Ministry, they should try doing so openly and through the lawful procedure. Then we can see how that works out.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Serbia protests timeline: how students brought Vucic’s 12-year rule to end
World.content:
The end of Vučić’s rule

Aleksandar Vučić, Serbia’s former president and the ruling party’s candidate for prime minister, conceded defeat in the snap parliamentary election held on 25 October. He said the “Student List” had won.

“Judging by the preliminary results, it is clear that we have lost this election. The Student List has won — they will get between 135 and 140 seats, while we will have around 105,” Vučić said.

The snap election, which Vučić called before stepping down as president, followed a wave of student-led protests that had lasted for almost two years.

The demonstrations began after a disaster at the railway station in Novi Sad in 2024 that killed 16 people. Protesters blamed corruption and negligence for the tragedy and demanded that those responsible face justice.

Vučić’s party had been in power in Serbia for 12 years.

Here is a chronological account of how the protests began, grew into a student movement, challenged Aleksandar Vučić’s government and brought Serbia to the 25 October 2026 election, in which Vučić conceded defeat.

From a spark to a change of government

Aleksandar Vučić and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) have dominated Serbian politics since 2012. Vučić became prime minister in 2014 and was elected president in 2017.

Government supporters portrayed him as a guarantor of stability, economic development and a foreign policy that balanced relations with the West and Russia. Critics, however, pointed to the concentration of power, the ruling party’s influence over the media, corruption and concerns about the independence of state institutions.

Public discontent periodically spilled onto the streets. Protests included demonstrations over electoral fairness and rallies against a proposed lithium mining project. Until 2024, however, the government had largely managed to prevent the emergence of large-scale, sustained protest movements.

1 November 2024: the tragedy that changed everything

On 1 November 2024, a concrete canopy collapsed at the railway station in Novi Sad, a city in northern Serbia, killing 16 people.

The station had undergone renovation shortly before the disaster, prompting immediate questions. How could recently refurbished infrastructure collapse? Who was responsible for the quality of the work? How transparent were the public procurement procedures and the renovation project itself?

Authorities opened an investigation, but for many people, the fact that an investigation had begun was not enough. Suspicions grew that the collapse might not have been merely a technical failure, but could also involve corruption and attempts to evade accountability. Further concerns over access to project documents only deepened those suspicions. Protesters demanded that those responsible be identified.

The tragedy, which claimed 16 lives, became more than a moment of mourning. It turned into a test of accountability for state institutions. People wanted to know not only what caused the canopy to collapse, but also who had allowed potential wrongdoing to take place and why the oversight system had failed.

November 2024: students take to the streets

On 22 November, students at the Faculty of Dramatic Arts in Belgrade were attacked during a silent protest in memory of those killed in the disaster. The incident gave the protests a new focus: students demanded that authorities identify the attackers and hold them accountable.

University students soon began disrupting classes. The movement spread from Novi Sad and Belgrade to other cities across the country.

The way the protests were organised was also significant. Students made decisions at general assemblies known as “plenums”. From the outset, the movement had no single central leader whose removal would have allowed the authorities to bring the entire campaign to a halt.

What were the students demanding?

Make all documents related to the station’s reconstruction publicly available;

Identify those responsible for the disaster and hold them accountable under the law;

Punish those involved in the attacks on students and drop charges against detained protesters;

Increase funding for higher education by 20%.

In other words, the movement was never solely about calling for the government to resign. Its main goals were transparency, justice and accountability from state institutions.

By December, the protests had evolved beyond a reaction to the Novi Sad tragedy. University blockades, daily demonstrations and public support for the students had turned the movement into a nationwide campaign.

One of its most powerful symbols was the minute of silence. Every day at 11:52 — the exact time the canopy collapsed — protesters stopped to honour the victims. They also held 16-minute silences in memory of the 16 people who died.

The movement drew its strength from the fact that it differed from a typical political opposition campaign. Students stressed that political parties should not dictate their demands. This helped bring a wide range of social groups into the protests.

January 2025: the first major political outcome

On 28 January 2025, Prime Minister Miloš Vučević announced his resignation. Around the same time, the mayor of Novi Sad also stepped down.

This marked a significant political concession. The authorities could no longer maintain that street protests were failing to achieve any tangible results.

However, the students continued their protests. In their view, the resignation of individual officials did not answer the key questions: who was responsible for the disaster, how independent was the judicial system, and how should the system of government be reformed?

This marked an important turning point. The protests showed that a sustained, organised mass movement could impose significant political costs on the authorities.

The students adopted a new strategy. Rather than limiting their demonstrations to the capital, they began organising marches, cycle rides and meetings with local residents across the country.

This strategy was important for several reasons:

The protests spread beyond the capital. The movement built ties with residents of smaller towns and regional communities;

Students positioned themselves as representatives of society as a whole. They won support from university staff, teachers, ordinary citizens and people from a wide range of professions;

The movement built its own communications network. Citizens critical of the government ensured that the flow of information no longer depended solely on traditional media.

By this stage, the student protests had become one of the largest popular movements in Serbia’s recent history.

Miloš Vučević

15 March 2025: the historic rally in Belgrade

The rally on 15 March 2025 marked a pivotal moment for the movement. Hundreds of thousands of people gathered in Belgrade.

The independent organisation Archive of Public Gatherings estimated that between 275,000 and 325,000 people took part. Serbia’s Interior Ministry gave a significantly lower figure. The discrepancy itself became a subject of debate.

Why was this event important?

First, it showed that the students enjoyed support well beyond university campuses;

Second, the government faced a challenge not only from the traditional opposition, but also from a broad coalition of citizens united by a common demand for justice and state accountability;

Third, the movement had grown so powerful that the question of Serbia’s political future could no longer be ignored.

Once again, the protest showed that calls for a change of government were coming from beyond political parties. A sense emerged across society that the existing system could be changed.

Spring and summer 2025: when the demands turned into a political struggle

On 5 May 2025, the student movement called for snap parliamentary elections. This broadened the scope of the protests. Vučić’s government, meanwhile, said the demonstrations aimed to destabilise the state and alleged that foreign powers were involved. The student movement rejected these accusations, identifying its main goals as fighting corruption, establishing independent institutions and holding fair elections.

Tensions continued to rise throughout this period. Reports emerged of arrests, clashes and acts of violence against protesters. Government opponents accused the authorities of controlling the media and weakening democratic institutions — allegations the government denied.

One of the movement’s most significant decisions was to create a political alternative from within the protest movement.

Students began selecting candidates to represent them in the parliamentary election. They formed an electoral list called “Student List — Students Win”. The aim was to broaden the movement’s representation by including people from different professions and social groups.

On 9 September 2026, Vučić called a snap parliamentary election for 25 October. He made the announcement amid a prolonged political standoff, as the student movement was already preparing to contest the election.

22 октября 2026 года: сотни тысяч сторонников движутся к предвыборной финишной прямой

За несколько дней до выборов, назначенных на 25 октября, студенческое движение провело в Белграде масштабный заключительный митинг. Сторонники из разных городов страны направились в столицу.

Согласно данным, опубликованным накануне выборов, между студенческим списком и правящей партией развернулась упорная борьба. Вучич предрекал победу, хотя и признавал, что она достанется нелегко.

Это стало кульминацией движения, которое продолжалось почти два года: протест, начавшийся с требований справедливости после гибели 16 человек, теперь стремился обеспечить себе большинство в парламенте.

25 October 2026: Vučić concedes defeat

On election night, something that many in Serbian political circles had long considered unthinkable happened.

Vučić announced that his political camp had lost the election and that the Student List had won. He estimated that the Student List would secure between 135 and 140 seats in parliament, while his own camp would get around 105.

According to Reuters, preliminary projections gave the Student List 138 seats in the 250-member parliament, compared with 104 for Vučić’s Serbian Progressive Party. The Student List had therefore secured a parliamentary majority. Voter turnout stood at around 70%, one of the highest levels since 1992.

According to Serbian political sociologist Gazela Pudar Draško, writing in The Washington Post, the student movement had taken the protests to a new level: citizens had moved beyond simply expressing discontent and begun taking direct part in political change. Students across the country had created an alternative model of political mobilisation by building relationships with local communities and making decisions collectively.

Radomir Šajčić, a professor at the University of Belgrade, commented on the victory at the students’ campaign headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate our victory, and tomorrow we will start building the future!” he said, Reuters reported.

The end of Vučić’s rule

World.title: Two teenagers arrested in Tbilisi over alleged plot to attack school: what we know
World.content:
School attack plot in Georgia

Two 14-year-olds have been arrested in Tbilisi on suspicion of planning an attack on a school and acts of violence against pupils. They attend different schools and communicated with each other through social media.

According to the prosecutor’s office, the teenagers had already chosen a specific school and planned their actions.

One of the teenagers has already been remanded in custody. The court is due to hold a hearing on the second suspect today.

What we know about the case

The Georgian outlet Sando Tskaro was the first to report the teenagers’ arrests. According to its report, police detained 14-year-old S.T. on the afternoon of Thursday, 22 October.

The following day, 23 October, police arrested the second teenager at his home. The first suspect exercised his right to remain silent, while the second denies the charges against him.

Police searched both teenagers’ homes. They seized a number of items, including a starter pistol, ammunition, pepper spray, gloves, a helmet and a knife.

The father of the first suspect, S.T., told Sando Tskaro that he did not know who the teenager was with whom his son had allegedly planned to commit the crime.

According to the father, the teenagers communicated through video calls on Telegram and TikTok.

He said they had discussed the 2011 terrorist attacks in Oslo. They had also talked about films based on real events that depicted acts of violence.

The prosecutor’s office has largely confirmed this account. It issued an official statement only after the information had already appeared in the media.

According to the statement, the teenagers met in April and May 2026. They chose a specific school in Tbilisi, studied its layout and began preparing an attack.

The prosecutor’s office says the teenagers planned to place a dummy explosive device outside the school. This would have allowed them to enter the building undetected, cause a disturbance and use weapons to injure people inside.

“They acquired various items and created all the necessary conditions to commit the crime. However, they failed to carry out their plan because law enforcement officers uncovered their activities,” the prosecutor’s office said.

Defence lawyer’s position

Gia Darchia, the lawyer representing one of the teenagers, told Radio Liberty that the prosecution had no evidence in the case.

According to Darchia, the case file contains only two days’ worth of messages from October, none of which mentions organising anything.

According to the defence, the items seized from the suspects’ homes as evidence were intended for personal use. They included souvenirs given to them by their parents and ordinary household objects. The lawyers argue that any claims that the teenagers were “preparing to commit a crime” are therefore entirely “unserious”.

“These people did not know each other. They had never even seen each other and had made no attempt to meet. What is more, they had never been to the school they allegedly planned to attack.”

The lawyer says his client would not even recognise the second suspect if someone showed him to him. He notes that his client had never seen a photograph of the other teenager, who used an avatar on social media. He also stresses that the teenagers never communicated via video calls.

The defence lawyer says the investigation began after the second suspect published a social media post calling for violence. However, the case file contains neither a screenshot nor any other visual evidence that the post existed. The lawyer argues that neither the investigative materials nor interviews with the suspects indicate any links between the teenagers and radical groups. Nor had anyone observed any suspicious behaviour on their part.

“They had no intention of blowing anything up or harming anyone. There is no basis for talking about any kind of organised activity,” he says.

The lawyer representing the second suspect has declined to comment to the media at this stage.

Authorities have opened a criminal case under Article 225, parts 1 and 2, of the Criminal Code. The article covers organising group actions involving violence, looting, damage to or destruction of other people’s property, and the use of weapons. It also covers preparing to take part in such actions.

The article provides for a prison sentence of six to nine years.

School attack plot in Georgia

World.title: Azerbaijan bolsters human-centered approach in CICA – deputy Sec-Gen
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Azerbaijan, which has held the chairmanship of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA) since 2024, has strengthened a human-centered approach within the organization, CICA Deputy Secretary General Zhang Ling said during a panel session titled "Culture at the center: secure paths to a shared future," held as part of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku on Tuesday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

According to her, within the framework of the 7th CICA Summit held in Baku, member states demonstrated a strong commitment to strengthening trust, cooperation, and stability in Asia.

"The Baku Declaration was adopted at the conclusion of the Summit, and the states reaffirmed their commitments in this regard. The organization's security strategy is based on the premise that peace and stability can be achieved not merely through military agreements, but through a comprehensive approach and mutual understanding among peoples. In this context, cultural dialogue and the human dimension play a central role in CICA's activities," she noted.

Ling added that long-term peace and sustainable security are rooted in mutual understanding among peoples.

"Therefore, cultural dialogue can play a vital role in this process and make a significant contribution to strengthening understanding and trust among nations," she emphasized.

The 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue is taking place in Baku from October 27 through October 29, under the theme "Dialogue for a Shared Future: Building Bridges in a Fragmented World."

The forum is the primary international event of the 'Baku Process,' an initiative launched in 2008 at the proposal of the President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev. First organized in 2011, the forum brings together countries, international organizations, experts, and representatives of civil society to engage in intercultural dialogue and cooperation.

The forum’s program includes discussions on topics such as peace and security, intercultural and interreligious dialogue, the role of youth, artificial intelligence, the creative economy, media, cultural heritage, and tourism.

World.title: Uzbekistan highlights nuclear power's role in energy independence in Minsk
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Uzbekistan is emphasizing international cooperation, workforce development, and domestic technological capabilities as it advances its nuclear energy program, Uzbek Atomic Energy Agency Director Azim Akhmedkhadjaev said at the EnergyExpo 2026 forum in Minsk on October 27.

According to Uzatom, Akhmedkhadjaev spoke during a high-level international roundtable titled “The Formula for Energy Independence: Economy, Integration and Development,” held as part of the 30th Belarusian Energy and Environmental Forum, EnergyExpo 2026.

The event brought together senior officials from energy agencies and major organizations across the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), as well as representatives of regional integration groups. Discussions focused on energy independence, electricity system management, financial instruments, infrastructure investment, and regional energy security.

“Energy independence is a comprehensive concept. It involves not only the ability to generate the required amount of electricity, but also having our own specialists, engineering expertise, industrial base and technological capabilities,” Akhmedkhadjaev said.

He added that energy independence did not mean isolation, but could be strengthened through effective international cooperation and integration.

Moreover, the Uzbek official highlighted the country’s expanding power system and the practical implementation of an integrated nuclear power plant project in the Jizzakh region. The planned facility combines large-capacity and small modular reactors, an approach intended to support baseload electricity generation while providing greater flexibility to the power system.

According to Akhmedkhadjaev, the project is also expected to support the development of a high-technology industry, with an emphasis on workforce training, localization and nuclear safety.

He highlighted Belarus’ experience in building and operating the Belarusian Nuclear Power Plant, as well as developing infrastructure around the facility, as potentially relevant to Uzbekistan. Regional cooperation could support specialist training, scientific and technical exchanges, industrial partnerships and the sharing of operational expertise.
