The roundtable also addressed how regional integration could help countries improve energy system resilience, strengthen industrial cooperation and attract investment amid changes in the global energy landscape.

EnergyExpo 2026 is being held in Minsk through October 30. Its business program includes conferences, seminars, and roundtables on energy security, electric transport, energy efficiency, digitalization, artificial intelligence in the energy sector, engineering education, environmental protection, and modern technologies.

World.title: Iran raises gas capacity to 300 bcm despite sanctions – president
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Despite years of sanctions against Iran, the country has increased its natural gas production capacity to 300 billion cubic meters, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said.

According to the Iranian president’s news portal, the President made the announcement on Tuesday (October 27) at the 8th summit of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum (GECF) in Moscow.

"By increasing its natural gas production capacity, Iran has been able to maintain its position as the world’s third-largest natural gas producer," he said.

The Iranian president added that Iran is one of the leading countries in terms of natural gas consumption, accounting for 70% of its energy mix. Currently, 95% of Iran’s population uses natural gas.

Pezeshkian noted that Iran can significantly enhance its energy stability on a global scale, given its strategic location at the center of the world’s most important energy corridors. In addition to Iran’s existing gas sector potential, there are favorable opportunities for cooperation between the private sectors of the member countries of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum.

The president emphasized that foreign investors can confidently take advantage of the incentives offered in the oil, gas, and petrochemical sectors and benefit from Iran’s opportunities on a mutually beneficial basis.

“Developments in the global energy market are prompting gas-exporting countries to strengthen cooperation in the areas of strategic management and technical and engineering operations. In strategic management, greater attention should be paid to increasing the volume of natural gas trade at the regional and global levels and to market stability. In the technical and engineering sphere, the main task for member countries of the Gas Exporting Countries Forum is to develop joint investments in gas processing and distribution, from production through processing, transportation, and consumption,” he added.

Pezeshkian noted that, at the same time, cooperation should focus on improving technological capabilities to increase efficiency and reduce the negative environmental impact of production and consumption. In this regard, the existing potential of member countries can be transformed into projects of mutual interest, creating conditions for the effective implementation of the forum’s long-term strategy in line with long-term supply and demand trends.

“The U.S. imposition of sanctions and a naval and air blockade against Iran, as well as pressure on other countries to enforce this blockade, are considered illegal actions by Iran. This is because these actions seriously threaten the stability of energy markets,” he added.

World.title: Uzbekistan Airports holds talks with 12 airlines to expand routes
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. Uzbekistan Airports held talks with 12 international airlines and aviation industry representatives at Routes World 2026 in Frankfurt on October 21-23 to explore new flight routes, expand existing services, and strengthen the country’s international air connectivity.

According to Uzbekistan Airports, the Uzbek delegation participated in the international aviation forum with discussions focused on attracting new carriers to Uzbekistan and expanding the geographical reach of its flight network.

During the event, the company’s representatives met with executives from All Nippon Airways, Japan Airlines, Aegean Airlines, Edelweiss Air, Bangkok Airways, FlyOne Armenia, ITA Airways, SunExpress, Transavia France, Delta Air Lines, Qantas and Vietjet Air.

Additionally, the delegation held meetings with representatives of logistics company UPS and Japan’s Chubu Centrair International Airport.

The discussions covered opportunities to launch new routes, increase flight services on existing connections and strengthen cooperation with international carriers. Particular attention was given to expanding international air services through Uzbekistan’s regional airports and improving their accessibility.

Uzbekistan Airports said direct engagement with airlines at Routes World provides an opportunity to present the country’s aviation market, assess carriers’ interest in new destinations, and identify potential areas for further cooperation.

Expanding the route network is intended to increase travel options for passengers and improve connectivity between Uzbekistan and international markets. Developing services through regional airports could also help broaden access to air travel beyond the country’s main aviation hubs.

Routes World brings together airport operators, airlines and other aviation industry stakeholders to discuss route development, market opportunities and partnerships in international air transport.

World.title: Turkmenistan exchange concludes three trade deals worth over $1.4M
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. During the October 20 trading session on SCRMET, foreign and domestic deals in the agricultural and textile sectors were concluded.

This was reflected in a press release published by the State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET).

According to the report, entrepreneurs from Azerbaijan purchased cotton yarn, while entrepreneurs from the UAE reached agreements with local business representatives for the purchase of first-grade wheat flour.

On the domestic market, local entrepreneurs reached agreements with the State Association of Food Industry of Turkmenistan for the purchase of crude fatty acids derived from cotton soapstock.

SCRMET reported that a total of three transactions were finalized during the session, amounting to 1.5 million Turkmen manat ($428.521) and $1 million.

The State Commodity and Raw Materials Exchange of Turkmenistan (SCRMET), established in 1994, is the country’s main organized marketplace for trading commodities and one of the key institutions through which Turkmenistan conducts and facilitates foreign trade. The exchange brings together domestic producers, exporters, and foreign buyers through regular trading sessions, where a range of export-oriented goods are offered, and transactions are concluded. Its trading portfolio covers petrochemicals, polymers, textiles, cotton products, construction materials, machinery, and chemical goods, among other commodities.

SCRMET also plays an administrative and information role in Turkmenistan’s trade system. In addition to organizing trading sessions and registering export-import contracts, the exchange publishes official quotations based on transactions conducted on the platform. These quotations provide information on the commodities traded, their values, and the markets involved, making SCRMET data a useful indicator of the composition and direction of exchange-based trade.

Through these quotations, SCRMET provides a snapshot of the value and sectoral composition of goods offered to international buyers during each trading session, reflecting shifts in the country’s export offering and highlighting which industries dominate Turkmenistan’s exchange-based trade.

World.title: Fuzuli largely cleared of mines - Azerbaijani presidential representative
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. A large part of Fuzuli has already been cleared of mines, Emin Huseynov, the Special Representative of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan in the Aghdam, Fuzuli, and Khojavend districts, said during a panel session titled "Culture at the center: secure paths to a shared future," held as part of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue in Baku on Tuesday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

According to him, Fuzuli is considered the gateway to Karabakh and the infrastructure and transport hub for the entire region.

"In accordance with the new urban planning principles being implemented in the liberated territories, significant steps are being taken to preserve historical heritage and pass it on to future generations.

Certain ruins located in the historic city center will be preserved in their current state and incorporated into open-air memorial complexes. This approach is being applied not only in Aghdam and Fuzuli but also in other major liberated cities," he noted.

The 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue is taking place in Baku from October 27 through October 29, under the theme "Dialogue for a Shared Future: Building Bridges in a Fragmented World."

The forum is the primary international event of the 'Baku Process,' an initiative launched in 2008 at the proposal of the President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev. First organized in 2011, the forum brings together countries, international organizations, experts, and representatives of civil society to engage in intercultural dialogue and cooperation.

The forum’s program includes discussions on topics such as peace and security, intercultural and interreligious dialogue, the role of youth, artificial intelligence, the creative economy, media, cultural heritage, and tourism.

World.title: Tourism boosts Azerbaijani women’s role in Khinalig’s economy – agency
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 27. The development of tourism in Azerbaijan’s Khinalig has increased local women's participation in handicrafts and other tourism-related activities, Head of the Cultural Heritage Development Division of the Cultural Heritage Department of the State Tourism Agency, Leyla Musayeva, said during a discussion titled "Tourism for a shared future: how inclusivity, equality, and community leadership contribute meaningfully to peacebuilding" held as part of the 7th World Forum on Intercultural Dialogue, in Baku on Tuesday, Trend’s correspondent reports from the event.

She noted that Khinalig, one of the villages located in the highest mountainous areas of Azerbaijan, was declared a state reserve in 2007 by the order of President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev. This was an important step towards protecting the village from population decline and gradual erosion.

According to Musayeva, the cultural heritage of Khinalig is part of a wider landscape that connects different regions of Azerbaijan both physically and culturally. The Migratory Road connecting the seasonal summer and winter pastures is also included in that landscape.

"In 2023, after extensive research and the efforts of the State Tourism Agency, the cultural landscape of Khinalig and Koch Road was included in the UNESCO World Heritage List," she remarked.

The agency’s representative added that restoration and conservation works were carried out in Khinalig from 2021 through 2024. These works and the recognition of the area as a UNESCO World Heritage Site have strengthened efforts to preserve the village's architectural heritage and traditional settlement structure.

Furthermore, Musayeva emphasized the importance of preserving local traditions and language, promoting the younger generation's commitment to heritage. According to her, tourism can create new economic opportunities, increase awareness of local heritage, and encourage greater community participation in the preservation and development of the countryside.

World.title: Fighting paused in Ukrainian city under deal announced by Melania Trump
World.content:
A ceasefire brokered with the assistance of Melania Trump has come into effect in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky.

Both sides said they would observe the truce, which began on Tuesday at 3am, local time, to allow for the establishment of a humanitarian corridor.

In a Telegram post, the Russian defence ministry said it had halted shelling in the direction of the city of Kherson, which faces Oleshky across the Dnipro River.

Ukrainian negotiator and parliamentary human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said on social media that his country was "honouring its commitments".

He said the deal was reached with the help of the US first lady and the cooperation of Russian human rights commissioner Yana Lantratova.

The city, on the southern bank of the Dnipro River, was seized by Russian troops in 2022.

The population of Oleshky has dropped from about 24,000 before the Russian invasion in 2022 to about 2,000 today, including as many as 50 children, according to Ukrainian and US estimates.

Earlier this year former residents told AFP that those still in the city were hunting pigeons or subsisting on whatever they had in their garden.

The city was heavily damaged by the 2023 destruction of the Kakhovka dam, which unleashed major flooding along the Dnipro River.

A destroyed building in Oleshky. (Reuters)

The ceasefire comes as the Ukraine war grinds through its fifth year and ahead of the resumption of peace talks between Washington, Moscow and Kyiv next month.

None of the parties have said who will monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia and some to Ukraine," she said.

US cable network Newsmax says it has been granted "exclusive television access" to accompany observers entering the city later this week.

Ukraine receives 'no early warning' as missile barrage pounds Kyiv US Secretary of State Marco Rubio denies intelligence-sharing with Ukraine is suspended as Vladimir Putin proposes a summit with Xi Jinping and Donald Trump to discuss the war.

Neither Russia nor Ukraine have said how long the truce would last.

In the meantime, Russian strikes have continued on Kyiv.

On Tuesday morning, the Ukrainian air force command issued nearly a dozen messages warning of ballistic missiles fired toward the capital.

Mayor Vitaly Klitschko said a strike hit the Southern Bridge -- one of Kyiv's main bridges -- and damaged its metro infrastructure.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Two charged with helping Iran over RAF Fairford incident
World.content:
Two men have been charged with national security offences over last month's incident at RAF Fairford, a US-run military base in England, prosecutors have said.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, were both charged on Tuesday under the National Security Act, the Crown Prosecution Service said.

Mr Abdulkarim has been charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service and Mr Essghir with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.

Armed police officers work on a road outside the perimeter of the RAF Fairford airbase, after police declared a major incident. (Reuters: Toby Shepheard)

The base has been used for strikes on Iran.

Surrounds evacuated

Scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts swarmed the rural area 148 kilometres west of London.

Police later said they had found a quantity of an accelerant, gasoline, in three vans at the site, but no explosives.

Two vans seen on a roadway in Whelford, near the RAF Fairford air base in Gloucestershire. (Reuters: Supplied/BBC News)

Five men who were arrested near the military base in England are all British citizens from London, authorities have confirmed, amid claims Iran's regime was attempting to attack the facility.

One of the suspects was first arrested on September 27. The second suspect was first arrested on October 1.

Both men were released on bail pending further investigation, and re-arrested on October 20.

Growing international threat

British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which led the US to pull its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the apparent plot was "almost certainly" directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard, or IRGC.

US President Donald Trump also claimed the arrested men had been under investigation "for a long time".

However, residents maintain they raised the alarm after spotting several suspicious vehicles in the area surrounding the base early on the day of the incident.

Iran has denied involvement, although it has previously said that it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

Fallout from RAF Fairford Mystery still surrounds what happened near UK RAF base Fairford but analysts warn US allies may face seeing their bases targeted.

The head of Britain's MI5 spy agency, Ken McCallum, has warned both Iran and Russia were expanding their attacks against the UK, and the RAF base incident was not unique.

Mr McCallum said Tehran is seeking to intensify its attacks in Britain beyond the traditional targets of Iranians opposed to the country's Islamic authorities.

More than 50 people have been arrested over Iran-linked plots in the past year, Mr McCallum said.

AP

World.title: AFP boss warns boys as young as 12 being radicalised at home
World.content:
Australia's top cop Krissy Barrett has warned teenage boys as young as 12 are being radicalised in their bedrooms, lured by a chaotic blend of violent jihadism, white supremacy and anti-government rage.

A statement from Commissioner Barrett tabled at Senate Estimates details an internal AFP analysis of 55 radicalised children aged 12 to 17, revealing a chilling evolution in modern extremism.

All of the subjects were male, and every single one was radicalised all or in part online.

While violent jihadism remained the most prevalent belief system, it was closely followed by anti-authority and white supremacist ideologies, with an increasing number of boys displaying no clear ideology at all.

"The ideological presentation in youths has shifted over the past two years, with fewer presenting with clearly defined ideologies, and an increasing number having mixed/hybrid ideologies, unclear/ incoherent ideologies, a superficial understanding of ideologies and ideological fluidity," she said.

Police warn of radicalisation Law enforcement agencies have told a parliamentary inquiry about an increasingly dangerous security environment.

The data shatters long-held intelligence assumptions that youth extremism is confined to broken homes, revealing that boys from stable families with secure parental bonds are increasingly being weaponised by digital algorithms.

While more than one-quarter did not have a stable male role model and about one-third had witnessed or experienced violence from their caregivers, Commissioner Barrett said there "were also youth cases where there was a secure bond to one or both caregivers."

"This shows kids who come from stable family environments and have few vulnerabilities are also becoming radicalised and manipulated," she said.

Commissioner Barrett did point to some clear warning signs among the cohort, including 13 per cent being suspended or expelled in primary school, with more than a third kicked-out from high school.

"In three out of five cases, the youths had received support, treatment or intervention for a mental health condition," she said.

She also warned presentations were not clear-cut and increasingly complex, with "no single profile of a radicalised young person and no one pathway to violent extremism."

She said she hoped the study would help the federal police and policy makers intervene earlier to prevent youth offending.

Parliamentarian security

In the wake of last week's attack on independent MP Helen Haines, Commissioner Barrett told Senate Estimates the AFP handled nearly 800 protective security reports targeting parliamentarians in the first six months of the year.

She warned basic policy debate is increasingly triggering direct threats against politicians.

"At times there is an almost immediate link from a policy announcement or comment, to a threat being sent," Commissioner Barrett said.

"It would be wrong to think only inflammatory comments are creating the flood of threats. In some cases, just the debate causes the hate."

Labor MPs deploy AI to tackle online abuse Labor MPs are turning to an AI tool to strip hundreds of thousands of abusive comments and threats from their pages but want social media companies to take responsibility.

Detailing the drivers behind the harassment, the commissioner said AFP caseloads showed hostility is typically triggered by four factors: policy, perceived performance, profile, and personality.

"In some cases, parliamentarians are being targeted because of their accent, what they look like, or their political party," she said.

The evidence presented to the committee exposed a stark gender divide in the abuse directed at elected officials with female parliamentarians three times more likely than their male colleagues to receive sexualised or gender-based threats.

That toll is highest for female MPs from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds, who report the most frequent and varied attacks.

Male parliamentarians are also subject to gender-based abuse, with Commissioner Barrett noting that threats directed at men frequently rely on "accusations of weakness, femininity or subordinate masculine traits."

Facing pressure from MPs and senators over the adequacy of current protection measures, Commissioner Barrett acknowledged the AFP needed to "do better" in demonstrating how seriously threats are managed.

She committed to implementing more consistent officer training and confirmed she would raise parliamentarian security at an upcoming meeting with state and territory police commissioners.

Social media and technology

The surge in threats against politicians is unfolding against a broader, more alarming shift across Australian society, one Commissioner Barrett warned is driven by an "instant pipeline" of digital hostility home-delivered into everyday lives.

"The threats are instant and voluminous. And they instantly shock and cause legitimate fear," she said.

" Perceived or real anonymity have given cowards courage. "

Pointing to a dangerous convergence between digital platforms, social hostility, and ideological obsession, the commissioner warned that online abuse is spilling into physical violence.

"The contagion of online hate has breached the digital compound and is spilling into the physical world. This is corroding our communities and has normalised violence — and it continues to impact on many, most notably, the Jewish community," she said.

Crucially, Commissioner Barrett warned that hyper-connectivity and artificial intelligence have erased the geographic isolation that historically shielded Australia from global threats.

"Across the world, we are witnessing a trend where violence emerges with little or no warning, particularly where individuals do not have a protection intelligence footprint," she said.

"Lone actors are being motivated by a convergence of personal grievance, mental health vulnerabilities and ideological concerns. What helped keep us safe in recent times, such as our geography, analogue systems and far away criminals, has been impacted by fully-integrated technology, social media and artificial intelligence."

World.title: Greens launch $21-a-week tax cut in bid to 'replace Labor'
World.content:
The Greens have called for a $21-a-week tax cut for all taxpayers and a welfare boost, in the party's first major policy launch since its new leader vowed to "replace Labor".

David Shoebridge, whose first weeks in the role have been derailed by allegations against Greens senator Jordon-Steele John, will front the National Press Club on Wednesday to launch a tax policy to "turn the tide" on inequality.

The new proposal would raise the tax-free threshold from $18,200 to $26,000 for all personal income taxpayers, a tax cut of up to $1,092 a year or $21 a week.

It would also add the same amount to all income support payments, including the JobSeeker unemployment benefit, student and carer payments, and the Age Pension.

"No matter who you are, whether you're working, studying, looking for work or on a pension, you'll get more," he will say, according to an extract of a speech seen by the ABC.

The policy would cost the budget $22 billion each year, according to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO). Senator Shoebridge will propose the cost be offset by collecting "rivers of gold" from gas and mining companies.

Greens search for burst of enthusiasm

Some Greens insiders have framed the new leadership as an opportunity to reinvigorate the minor party, with published opinion polls suggesting minimal gain on the 12 per cent primary vote it recorded in the 2025 election, when it lost three lower house seats.

Greens parliamentarians were divided on how to interpret that loss, with some advocating a more constructive relationship with Labor, and others urging sharper differentiation.

Richard Denniss, whose left-wing think tank The Australia Institute is influential in Greens circles, wrote that former leader Larissa Waters was not "shouty" enough and had too much "nuance and subtlety" to cut through.

Richard Denniss (pictured) was critical of David Shoebridge's predecessor, Larissa Waters. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Senator Shoebridge's claim he would "replace Labor" was seen as a decisive shift from his predecessor, and social media ads featuring deputy Steph Hodgins-May appear modelled on the approach of left-wing politicians in the United States and the United Kingdom.

But allegations of inappropriate behaviour towards women by Senator Steele-John, which he denies, have disrupted the reset, as have reports of a disagreement over Ukraine policy with leadership rival Sarah Hanson-Young.

'Rivers of gold' uncosted

The press club speech will focus on economic policy, although key details have not yet been fully fleshed out. The Greens's proposal for a 25 per cent gas export tax, adapted from The Australia Institute, has not been costed by the PBO.

Senator Shoebridge will use a figure by The Australia Institute, which suggested a gas tax could raise $17 billion a year.

A related proposal to apply a progressive royalties regime to mining has fewer details. Senator Shoebridge will claim the Greens "would raise" $28 billion from the tax, citing a report from the research organisation Prosper Australia.

WA Greens senator to miss parliament amid allegations WA Greens senator Jordon Steele-John won’t be attending parliament next week.

But that figure is a ballpark calculation of how much state governments could raise if they all taxed royalties as much as Queensland does. The only federal tax canvassed by the report is offshore petroleum.

Senator Shoebridge's speech extract refers to a "Commonwealth tax" but does not specify which resources it would cover or how it would interact with state royalties, details a Greens source said were still to be determined.

The PBO also noted that the proposed welfare boost "may discourage [some] recipients from working additional hours" because of the way it is structured.

The Greens do not propose to means-test the $1,092 stipend, but the welfare payments themselves would remain means-tested. That means recipients would lose the full $1,092 all at once when they cross over the eligibility threshold for their welfare payment.

World.title: Loyal back to reclaim Sydney to Hobart record
World.content:
A decade after his last appearance in the Sydney to Hobart Yacht Race, Anthony Bell has unveiled a new Loyal boat to challenge for line honours in this year's race.

But it's not a new boat — it's an old one.

Bell was first to Hobart in 2011 with Investec Loyal and in 2016 with Perpetual Loyal, setting a then-race record in the latter race of one day 13 hours, 31 minutes and 20 seconds.

On Tuesday in Sydney, Bell revealed his boat for this year's edition of the bluewater classic — the race record-holder and last year's winner, Comanche.

Comanche takes out line honours in Sydney to Hobart race Master Lock Comanche claims line honours in the 80th edition of the gruelling Sydney to Hobart yacht race, with a stunning daylight hours finish.

Bell spent up big to buy the five-time line honours-winning boat, which will race on Boxing Day as Tribeca Loyal.

Bell, the owner and skipper of the supermaxi, is aiming to lift the J.H. Illingworth Challenge Cup for a third time.

He has again recruited America's Cup and Olympic gold medallist Tom Slingsby to serve as the crew's sailing master.

The three-time world sailor of the year is delighted to be working on a yacht with the quality and power of Comanche.

"It's the most powerful supermaxi there is in the world," Slingsby said in Sydney.

"There's times there where we actually try to slow the boat down because it's got so much power and the waves could be too big that you're flying off the waves too fast.

"It averages really high speeds, it loves it when it's windy, so it's an exciting boat. You wouldn't want to choose any other boats to do the home run on.

"This boat already owns the Sydney Hobart race record, but … if we get the right conditions, we can break that record by a lot."

Master Lock Comanche took line honours in Hobart last year. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

Despite his past success with Loyal, the 2012 Olympic gold medallist admits sailing on the open seas is a long way from his comfort zone.

"I'm not an ocean racer," Slingsby declared.

"I'm more of the short-course stuff.

"It's not something that I'm good at and really want to do, but I love coming back."

A major motivation for Slingsby and the crew is the continuing partnership with the Humpty Dumpty Foundation, which raises money for life-saving infant medical equipment for Australian hospitals.

The worthy cause is why Loyal will once again take on some celebrity deckhands to boost its fundraising profile.

Former Wallaby turned Rugby Australia chief executive Phil Waugh and Sydney Roosters great Anthony Minichello are among the famous names heading south.

"I certainly don't miss the contact of playing rugby league, but the camaraderie, and everyone being laser-focused on achieving a goal, that's the stuff you do miss when you retire from professional sport," Minichello said.

This year's star-studded crew continues the tradition for Loyal to rely on some unconventional athletes taking up a new sport.

"We've had 21 people who represented Australia, won world surfing titles, gold medals, played for the Wallabies, played rugby league, and we have two TV Week Gold Logie winners as well," Bell said.

AAP

World.title: Chinese sponsors cut ties with Kylian Mbappé after Mao meme backlash
World.content:
French soccer star Kylian Mbappé has been cancelled by Chinese sponsors after the emergence of a video appearing to show him commenting about a meme depicting him as Mao Zedong.

In the clip, Mbappé says the meme that made him laugh the most featured his face on the body of "a guy — I think he's a Chinese dictator".

He added that he would "use it a lot with my friends online".

The clip includes a picture of Mbappé's head superimposed onto what appears to be the body of Mao Zedong, the founding leader of the People's Republic of China.

Kylian Mbappé says in the clip that he "uses it a lot with his friends online." (Supplied)

The ABC has been unable to verify the authenticity of the video and contacted the creator of the meme for comment.

The clip appears to be taken from a backstage interview conducted with French-language talk show The Bridge earlier this year.

Mbappé apologised on Tuesday evening to "everyone my words have upset".

"My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China and in Chinese communities around the world," he said in a statement.

"This was absolutely not my intention.

" I have deep respect for the Chinese people and their history, and I am sincerely sorry. "

It caused the furore around the same time as the prestigious Ballon d'Or international football awards on Monday.

The Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said Mbappé's "remarks and deeds … hurt Chinese people's feelings".

"[It] will naturally meet joint rejection from people across Chinese society," he said.

Today the Dongpeng Beverage Group announced it had terminated its relationship with Mbappé.

The company had named him a brand ambassador for its electrolyte drink in April, ahead of the World Cup.

"Dongpeng Beverage firmly opposes and has zero tolerance for any conduct that hurts national feelings. Effective immediately, we are terminating all cooperation with Kylian Mbappé," the company said in a statement.

Chinese dairy companies Mengniu and Milkground also announced they had terminated their partnerships with the French athlete.

'What did he actually say?'

Dongpeng Beverage's announcement topped Weibo's trending chart this afternoon and nearly 400 million views were recorded on the related topic page.

But some Chinese social media users appeared unclear about what had prompted the backlash.

"What did he actually say? The trending top list is full of posts about the contract termination, but I can't find a single one explaining what he said," one user wrote.

Dongpeng Beverage says it has terminated its partnership with Kylian Mbappé. (Weibo: Yi Cheng Feng Xu)

Others referred to the controversy in more oblique terms.

"He's talking about the person on the 100-yuan note," another user wrote.

Chinese sports platform Dongqiudi said it would not translate Mbappé's remarks.

"Recently, Kylian Mbappé, the French player who plays for Real Madrid, made inappropriate remarks concerning China in an interview. As his remarks involve causing offence to China and the Chinese people, we will not translate them," it said in a statement.

In China, making jokes about the country’s leaders is generally considered taboo. (Reuters: Tingshu Wang)

The original interview footage cannot be found on Chinese social media platforms examined by the ABC.

The Bridge has since removed the clip from its social media accounts, according to Spanish news outlet elDiario, though it can be found on Reddit and in other media reports.

YouTube, Instagram and Reddit are blocked in mainland China and users generally cannot access content on those platforms without VPNs.

At least three Chinese companies have terminated their partnerships with Kylian Mbappé. (Weibo: Mengniu)

In a September interview with France Football Mbappé acknowledged the humour behind AI-generated memes depicting him as a dictator, but said he disliked being compared to such figures.

"There's a part of it that's funny, because you can tell that for some people it's good-natured," he told the magazine.

"There's also a part that's a little less funny, because we know the damage that people like that have caused throughout history.

"Being compared to people who murder others, or who have made millions and millions of people miserable … I don't think I've done that in my life. So there's a mixture of things."

The ABC has contacted Real Madrid for comment.

World.title: Company director charged over alleged kickbacks in Pilbara corruption scandal
World.content:
A company director has faced court on corruption charges over alleged bribery of a council official in Western Australia's remote Pilbara.

Richard Carroll, a director of Victorian companies VicFlow and VicFlow Civil, faced court on Monday over his alleged involvement with embattled former Shire of East Pilbara manager Bevan Klein.

He was charged with with eight counts of a public officer acting corruptly in the performance or discharge of their functions after a joint investigation by the WA Police Financial Crimes Squad and the Corruption and Crime Commission (CCC).

Police said the two companies were the recipients of more than $5 million in contracts from the shire, for which Mr Carroll allegedly paid more than $50,000 in gratuities to Mr Klein.

A CCC report published earlier this month found Mr Klein, while employed as the Shire of East Pilbara's operations manager, had engaged in serious misconduct, favouring VicFlow and the company Dick Tracey when awarding contracts.

Dick Tracey has denied conferring any benefit.

The Newman-based Shire of East Pilbara encompasses an enormous part of inland Western Australia. (ABC News)

The Shire of East Pilbara awarded more than $11 million in contracts to the two companies, according to a CCC report.

Mr Klein and Mr Carroll had previously worked together on the other side of the country, when Mr Klein was employed by the Towong Shire Council and Mr Carroll performed contract work for the shire.

Mr Klein would later cite Mr Carroll as a referee when applying for the position at the Shire of East Pilbara.

The CCC delayed the finalising of its investigation while Mr Klein was holidaying in the Philippines in June last year.

'Community deserves accountability'

Shire of East Pilbara president Anthony Middleton said he welcomed progress in the investigation.

"Our community deserves accountability in how public money is managed. We support efforts to establish the facts and hold anyone found to have acted unlawfully to account," Mr Middleton said.

"The shire reported its concerns to the CCC as soon as there was a reasonable suspicion of misconduct.

"We cooperated fully with the investigation and have strengthened our procurement controls, contract oversight and governance arrangements to better protect public funds."

Anthony Middleton says the shire reported its concerns to the CCC. (ABC News: Kimberley Putland)

Mr Middleton said neither VicFlow nor Dick Tracey was currently engaged by the shire.

"With the matter now before the courts, we will respect that process and will not comment on the specific allegations," he said.

Mr Klein had not returned from the Philippines by the time the CCC report was published at the start of October.

His representation cited "significant health conditions and financial problems" preventing his return.

Mr Carroll is due back in court in February.

World.title: Man charged with murder over alleged fatal stabbing of partner
World.content:
A 39-year-old man has been charged with murder for allegedly fatally stabbing his female partner, who died in hospital last month.

On September 19, a Northern Territory Police spokesperson said the man dropped off his 47-year-old partner about 8pm at Palmerston Regional Hospital the previous evening, telling staff she was unwell.

"A medical assessment by staff identified that the [alleged] victim had suffered two stab wounds to her chest," they said in a statement at the time.

"The [alleged] victim has since been transferred to Royal Darwin Hospital in a critical condition."

The woman died from her injuries at Royal Darwin Hospital. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

The man was arrested that day and was initially charged with acts intended to cause serious harm.

On September 28, police said they had received confirmation of the woman's death and were liaising with prosecutors.

An NT Police spokesperson today said the man's charge had been upgraded to murder after he appeared in the Darwin Local Court.

The man remains remanded in custody, with his next court appearance scheduled for November 2.

World.title: Uber faces Australian class action over sexual assaults, harassment by drivers
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessConsumer affairsHarassment Uber faces Australian class action over sexual assaults, harassment by drivers Adam Hegarty Elias Visontay and October 28, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Uber is facing a class action from women who have experienced sexual assault, harassment or misconduct while using its services, amid criticism of the ride-share giant’s handling of complaints and questions about its responsibility when matching riders with potentially predatory drivers. On Wednesday, law firm Slater and Gordon announced it is investigating whether Uber’s systems, policies and practices adequately protected the safety of female passengers, and whether the company responded appropriately when complaints involving alleged driver sexual misconduct, assault and harassment were reported. Canberra woman Taylor Mostacci. She was 19 when she was indecently assaulted by an Uber driver on the way to her university ball. 60 Minutes Slater and Gordon’s public callout for women to register their experiences and potentially join a class action follows a flood of legal actions in Australia and abroad centring on Uber’s handling of driver misconduct claims. Cindy Bors, Slater and Gordon’s practice group leader, stressed the firm’s legal action concerned Uber’s broad role in passenger safety, as opposed to claims made against individual drivers. At its core would be the question of whether Uber has done enough to protect women.



“Women should be able to get home in an Uber safely, without being frightened or violated by the person behind the wheel, or left wondering whether anyone will listen and act,” Bors said. The law firm began investigating the class action in response to women coming forward with their experiences. Related Article Exclusive

Harassment How banned Uber drivers are reinstated, while passenger evidence goes unheard “The harm doesn’t end when the Uber trip ends,” Bors said. “Some people may have felt that their experience was not serious enough to report, or that reporting would not make a difference. We want to hear from women about what happened, and how Uber responded.” Uber has long insisted its drivers aren’t employees but contractors, and that it isn’t a transport provider but simply matches contractors with riders – an argument it has previously leant on in questions over minimum wages and potential discrimination complaints. Bors said she did not believe the argument was adequate when it came to sexual assault.



“Ultimately, Uber control and operate a tech platform and control who has access. I don’t think it’s a shield to say that [the drivers] are independent contractors.” Uber, which has a sharemarket value of $US135 billion ($192 billion), has faced sustained scrutiny of how it deals with driver complaints. While it has stepped up its efforts to ban problematic drivers, it has lost a stream of claims from sacked drivers under an unfair dismissal-style appeals avenue, which opened in February last year. Reporting from this masthead has revealed that repeated Fair Work Commission decisions have been scathing of Uber’s hands-off approach in response to drivers lodging “unfair deactivation cases”, including its policy of not gathering evidence from complainants – which it argues is best practice to avoid retraumatising victims. In the absence of any evidence from complainants, the commission has routinely ordered that drivers facing serious misconduct allegations be reinstated to drive on the platform.



Also central to Slater and Gordon’s investigation have been developments in the US, including the litigation of more than 4000 complainants’ cases. The first plaintiff victory occurred earlier this year, with Uber ordered to pay $US8.5 million in damages to a rider. The New York Times reported last year that Uber had underreported sexual assaults and misconduct in the US, publicly disclosing only 12,522 allegations over five years when court documents later revealed a total of 400,181. According to the Times, Uber has invested in a sophisticated algorithmic tool to determine the risk associated with pairing specific drivers and passengers. The predictive tool was based on 43 factors such as past complaints about “creepy” behaviour, a driver’s safety history and geographic information such as if a customer is being picked up in a nightlife area densely populated with bars. In US testing, the tool correctly anticipated 15 per cent of assaults. However, Uber conceded it continued to pair drivers and riders deemed high risk, in part because there were certain situations, such as pick-ups outside bars late at night, where blocking such pairings would leave riders stranded. Bors said the Times reports raised a key question: “When a platform connects users with service providers and has visibility of safety risks, what responsibility should it bear for identifying and reducing those risks?”



An Uber spokeswoman said that regardless of whether class action proceedings eventuated, “we remain committed to listening to feedback, pushing harder, and innovating more to make every trip better and safer, every single day”. Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Uber blasts laws as it’s forced to reinstate banned driver The spokeswoman said the unfair-deactivation laws continued to make it hard to respond swiftly to allegations and kick drivers off the platform, despite reforms from the Albanese government in June designed to lessen such obstacles. Uber is calling for further immediate reform. “Safety is a core value at Uber, and we have invested billions of dollars and countless hours to protect the safety of users during trips,” the company spokeswoman said. “One sexual assault is one too many, and we take every report seriously … We are committed to continually strengthening our technology, policies, and procedures to protect riders.” An upcoming 60 Minutes investigation has shed light on Uber’s processes locally, looking at the case of Canberra woman Taylor Mostacci, who was indecently assaulted by her Uber driver on the way to her university ball in 2021.



“He touched my breasts and I just froze,” Mostacci said, describing the moment when the driver was putting on her seatbelt. Her driver’s account was suspended after she complained to Uber but was later reactivated after he denied the assault. She reported the incident to police, and in 2025 an ACT court convicted the driver. Mostacci said five years on, the incident still affects her life. “I’ll never risk being in an Uber by myself. Uber has a responsibility to take care of its customers, and it has a responsibility to protect us, to look after us.” Taylor Mostacci’s full story will be shared in a 60 Minutes investigation airing this Sunday. Western Australia will become the first state in the country to legalise plug-in solar panels and batteries, Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson will reveal on Wednesday. The products are extremely popular in Germany, where plug-in solar panels are sold in large numbers from major outlets like Ikea. Portable solar panels on apartment balconies in Freiburg, Germany. Alamy Stock Photo Commonly known as balcony solar, the products can be plugged into a standard power socket, and Sanderson estimated households could save $240 a year on power bills, or $500 when paired with a battery. The products can be sold in Australia – but not legally plugged in.



Sanderson will unveil the development at a CEDA Energy Outlook lunch on Wednesday, touting the products’ benefit to renters and apartment owners who were constrained when it came to sourcing their household power from renewables. “For too long, the benefits of cheap solar have been out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their roof,” she said. “That isn’t fair, and the Cook Labor Government is doing something about it. “I’m proud that our state is leading the nation on this issue – millions of European households already use these systems every day, and WA families should be able to do the same. “Western Australians are already taking up solar and batteries in record numbers and this will ensure even more families can see the savings from the energy transition.”



Consultation will open on Wednesday on safety standards for the products with legislation to follow at an undetermined date. Related Article Updated

Gas Mystery client drives plans for WA’s biggest gas power station amid green push Last month, Sanderson discussed balcony solar at a meeting of state and federal energy ministers. Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowan said another benefit was that renters could take the kit with them wherever they move to. “It’s been legal for a long time and now United Kingdom and New Zealand are doing it, and we’re going to do it too,” he said.



About one in 10 German households have balcony or plug-in solar installed. Solar Citizens chief executive Heidi Lee Douglas last month welcomed the push for plug-in solar. “Renters, apartment dwellers and low-income homes will soon be able to plug-in, switch-on and save, save, save,” she said. “This commitment to make plug-in solar and plug-in batteries legal in Australia is great news for more than a third of Australians who rent or live in apartments, and also for low-income households so they can access some of the bill-busting benefits that cheap clean solar homeowners enjoy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot cast votes as Israel’s polls open in defining test
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastWorld elections Netanyahu, Eisenkot cast votes as Israel’s polls open in defining test Matthew Knott Updated October 27, 2026 — 10:55pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Tel Aviv: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, have cast their votes in an election widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s almost two decades in power, with the prospect of a return to war with Iran dominating the final days of the campaign. Netanyahu, who voted shortly after noon on Tuesday, local time, said: “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed. We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.” Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu casts his ballot in Jerusalem. Yonatan Sindel/Pool Flash90 via AP Gadi Eisenkot votes at a polling station in Herzliya, Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit After voting, standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of the “the worst government Israel has known”. He noted that victory wasn’t certain, adding that “we are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state”.



Voting began early on Tuesday in Israel (4pm AEDT) in the first national elections since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, a day that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil. Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but the polls have shown a close result between the two blocs, and it may take time before clear results are known. A television campaign  on a bridge featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, and his main rival, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the election. AP Photo/Oded Balilty Israeli media reports passed by the official military censor and published in the final days of the campaign have stated that Netanyahu pressured his military chief to provoke a confrontation with Iran ahead of the elections, suggesting high-level leaks from within the defence establishment. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz denied the reports. US President Donald Trump told Fox News on the weekend he was deciding whether to “make a deal” with Iran or “finish it off”, adding: “It’s getting to be decision time.”



Netanyahu posted an alarming AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv and spoke about using cryptocurrency to avoid international sanctions in the final days of the campaign. Some disunity broke out within the opposition bloc before polls closed over the question of whether anti-Netanyahu voters should vote for Eisenkot’s Yashar party or spread their votes among the four parties in the bloc. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict These voters could hold the key to Netanyahu’s demise. Why are they being shunned? Eisenkot has been pursuing a so-called “big party” strategy in recent days, designed to give him the upper-hand in post-election negotiations by scoring a lead over Netanyahu’s Likud in the final seat tally. “The ‘big party’ campaign is a mistake,” Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats party, said. “It’s a dangerous lie designed to weaken us. I urge people not to fall for the ‘big party’ narrative.”



What happens on election day? Benjamin Netanyahu took to social media to post an apocalyptic AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb being dropped in the middle of Tel Aviv. Voting in Israel is voluntary, not compulsory. Even so, turnout is usually high, reflecting the level of political engagement in society. In the last elections, 4.8 million of the country’s 6.8 million eligible voters showed up at the polls – a turnout rate of 71 per cent. Even more people are expected to vote this year, reflecting the heightened stakes. Unlike in Australia, where postal voting has become increasingly popular in recent elections, Israelis must vote in person on election day. (Only those serving their nation overseas, like diplomats and defence personnel, can vote in advance by mail.) When will we know who won?



It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear. The first strong indication of the results will come at 10pm (6am Wednesday AEDT), when Israeli TV channels begin airing exit polls. The official election results will then start coming in. A clear picture may emerge quickly, but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer. The final tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.



Why is it so complicated? Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be ​held every four years, but early elections have been frequent. Crucially, voters vote for party lists rather than individual candidates. The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25 per cent of the national vote to secure seats. About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.



The key number to aim for is the 61 seats required to form a government, though leaders prefer a more substantial buffer to create a more durable coalition. It is possible to govern in minority, but such a government would be even more fragile. What happens after the results are published? After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government. That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.

World.title: Knocked out and inked up: Why WA doctors are warning against Bali’s pain-free tattoo fad
World.content:
NationalWAHealth Knocked out and inked up: Why WA doctors are warning against Bali’s pain-free tattoo fad Indigo Lemay-Conway and Alastair Kirkby October 27, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Perth doctors are sounding the alarm over a new tattoo trend where people are opting to go under general anaesthesia for hours and wake up covered in ink. Thousands of people have flocked to Bali this year to receive the procedure which can have up to nine tattoo artists working on a person at a time. Loading While a full-body tattoo would typically take multiple sessions over a number of days, the Bali tattoo trend achieves the same result in 10 hours under anaesthesia. Kuta tattoo artist Madhe Ink says Australians have made up the majority of his clientele.



“From last year, talking about percentage, maybe 70 per cent is [from] Australia, and the rest is America, Singapore, Malaysia, Canada, like all over the world,” he said. The artist says that people have to go through two checkups before being allowed to go under general anaesthesia which include a form and a medical examination. A full-body tattoo under general anaesthesia in Bali can cost around $16,000. It’s becoming an increasingly popular trend on the holiday island. 9News Perth “The first checkup ... you need to fill all the forms first. You need to be honest with everything. Your symptoms, your sickness, everything,” he said. “And after this ... we need to take you to the hospital to do a medical checkup. That is the last checkup you need to do to make sure you are possible to do anaesthesia after that or not.”



Australian studios can charge tens of thousands of dollars for a full-body tattoo, but those travelling to Kuta for the art to be done under general anaesthesia can pay $16,000. The tattooist insisted that the procedures are done in a licensed hospital and not a standard tattoo parlour. Related Article Opinion

Workplace culture Is it OK to take an iced coffee into a job interview? “We need to do that in the proper hospital that has an operation room, doctor and everything there,” he said. Getting a tattoo under general anaesthesia is not available in Australia, with doctors fearing about the additional health risks for what should be a simple procedure.



But Australian Medical Association WA president Kyle Hoath said he had concerns over whether the procedures in Bali are being done in a safe environment with a trained anesthetist. “A general anesthetic is a serious procedure. We’re talking about being unconscious for multiple hours while somebody has to keep you breathing, keep you alive,” he told 9News Perth. “We never take a general anesthetic as a simple thing. This is quite a complicated part of the overall procedure and carries with it pretty extreme risks. AMA WA president Kyle Hoath. AMA “So I always kind of caution that if we go to that extreme of an anesthetic for something that can be done without, we should generally try and preference doing it without because otherwise we’re adding unnecessary risk into people’s lives.”



Hoath believes the procedure will likely never be done in Australia. “This is not done in Australia for a reason. It’s a completely unnecessary risk to add into having a tattoo,” he said. “Tattooing can be done safely and can be done in safe sterile environments, but there is no need to go through a general anesthetic, which adds considerable risk to the procedure, just for convenience’s sake. “That’s not convenient – that’s dangerous and that’s unsafe, and something that should be avoided. “We don’t see this happening in Australia, and I can’t imagine we ever will because it’s an unnecessary complication and risk to add into what should be something that’s pretty straightforward in getting a tattoo.”



Using general anaesthesia to get tattooed comes with the same medical risks as when it is used for surgery. “Surgery and anesthetic can carry with it a risk of death,” Hoath said. A full-body tattoo under general anaesthesia in Bali can cost around $16,000. 9News Perth “So doing that in an environment where you don’t know how the credentialing is done, where you don’t know the safety and the protocols and the rigor in which things are done safely is something you should be very cautious about. “An anesthetic, just for convenience, is a dangerous proposition, and not one I think you should entertain.”



One American man who was at Madhe Ink last week was turned away from getting both legs tattooed under anaesthesia due to health concerns. “I have an irregular heartbeat, so they did not allow me to do anaesthesia,” he said. As for why the New Yorker wanted to get the procedure done as opposed to sitting in the chair the old-fashioned way, the answer was simple – pain. “Because I don’t want to feel pain, but no pain, no gain, right? I was gonna do both legs in one shot, but now I gotta do three sessions, three days of pain,” he said. The artist behind the studio says he thinks people are opting to go under to save time and pain.



“Let’s just say a full arm on average, we finish that in two days. While under anaesthesia … let’s say arm and leg, we can finish that in 10 hours, that’s quick compared to without anaesthesia,” he said. But despite doing the procedures, he still advocates for people sitting in the chair to get a tattoo. “If you really don’t have time, but have money, go do it,” he said. “If you pass [the tests] you can do anaesthesia. If not, sorry, you can feel the pain like a man. “No pain, no gain.” with 9News Perth

World.title: AFP reveals nearly 800 threats against MPs in six months as Labor rushes to boost safety
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack AFP reveals nearly 800 threats against MPs in six months as Labor rushes to boost safety Natassia Chrysanthos, Paul Sakkal and Nick Newling Updated October 27, 2026 — 9:15pm ,first published 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Politicians will receive a safety boost that could include a wider use of emergency alarms, as the government fast-tracks a security review following last week’s attack on independent Helen Haines. The Australian Federal Police has received almost 800 security complaints from federal politicians in the first six months of the year, commissioner Krissy Barrett revealed at Senate hearing Tuesday night as she vowed to “do better” to inform MPs of the progress of investigations. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Addressing his MPs on Tuesday morning, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: “Last week was a turning point, and people have been putting up with this growing threat environment for too long”. “More can and should be done. I understand you want to feel safe when you’re in the community and have better security at your office and your home. There are a series of options you have raised including duress alarms, and we are looking at all of it.”



MPs of all stripes attended briefings with intelligence agencies following the attack on Haines. Many aired their ongoing frustrations about how long it took for their security requests to be actioned, and several MPs also made requests about duress alarms. This masthead revealed last week that the government was examining a major round of security upgrades for MPs’ homes, as well as swifter upgrades for offices and more proactive threat assessments from the AFP. Barrett told the Senate’s legal and constitutional affairs hearings the AFP had received 785 protective security reports about federal parliamentarians, with 50 per cent directed to men, and 47 per cent to women. Three per cent were generic threats against politicians. Albanese has asked for the parliament’s review of security to be fast-tracked, and requested Special Minister of State Don Farrell, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke work together on delivering a “swift government response”. Related Article Workplace culture ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud



“I know so many of you have experienced an increase in aggressive and threatening behaviour online and in person. There have been vile threats towards you and your family and damage to your electorate offices,” Albanese said. “This is particularly acute for women members of the caucus, who often receive vile and misogynistic threats to their safety and increased hatred online, often of a violent and sexual nature. “I know how hard every single one of you works each day to ensure that we are accessible to our community and that people can speak to us... We need to do more to combat these threats.” Last week’s four-wheel-drive attack on the independent MP has exposed long-running tensions between federal parliamentarians and the authorities responsible for protecting them. Elected officials claim security agencies are too reactive and need to improve their communication with MPs to ensure politicians and their staff feel safe. But authorities have also expressed frustration with MPs who fail to follow protocol when flagging high-risk events or reporting incidents.



Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett. Eamon Gallagher On Tuesday night, Barrett said the AFP needed to “do better in showing you how we take these threats seriously”, and that training and communication would be improved. Female politicians were three times more likely to report sexualised or gender-based security concerns, Barrett said. Those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds also copped offensive content more frequently. “It would be wrong to think only inflammatory comments are creating the flood of threats. In some

cases, just the debate causes the hate,” Barrett said. “In some cases, parliamentarians are being targeted because of their accent, what they look like, or

their political party. The fact is this: at times there is an almost immediate link from a policy announcement or comment, to a threat being sent.”



The commissioner will soon meet with her state and territory counterparts to discuss politicians’ safety. Opposition leader Angus Taylor also addressed the security concerns of MPs in a joint party room meeting of Coalition MPs on Tuesday morning, saying it was important to “get that right”. Speaking in the House on Tuesday night, Albanese described the impending Digital Duty of Care bill as “a much-needed but moderate and common-sense response to a problem that is becoming more serious with every passing day”. On Monday evening independent senator Fatima Payman stunned a parliamentary hearing by asking whether Albanese was waiting for a Haines-style attack against her to provide her with comparable staffing levels to other senators. Payman refused to withdraw her comments unless provided additional staff. Payman has long petitioned the prime minister for additional staffing, and was one of four independent and crossbench MPs to tell this masthead their staff were suffering under a deluge of vitriol coming into their offices.

The first plaintiff victory occurred earlier this year, with Uber ordered to pay $US8.5 million in damages to a rider. The New York Times reported last year that Uber had underreported sexual assaults and misconduct in the US, publicly disclosing only 12,522 allegations over five years when court documents later revealed a total of 400,181. According to the Times, Uber has invested in a sophisticated algorithmic tool to determine the risk associated with pairing specific drivers and passengers. The predictive tool was based on 43 factors such as past complaints about “creepy” behaviour, a driver’s safety history and geographic information such as if a customer is being picked up in a nightlife area densely populated with bars. In US testing, the tool correctly anticipated 15 per cent of assaults. However, Uber conceded it continued to pair drivers and riders deemed high risk, in part because there were certain situations, such as pick-ups outside bars late at night, where blocking such pairings would leave riders stranded. Bors said the Times reports raised a key question: “When a platform connects users with service providers and has visibility of safety risks, what responsibility should it bear for identifying and reducing those risks?”



An Uber spokeswoman said that regardless of whether class action proceedings eventuated, “we remain committed to listening to feedback, pushing harder, and innovating more to make every trip better and safer, every single day”. Related Article Exclusive

Unfair dismissal Uber blasts laws as it’s forced to reinstate banned driver The spokeswoman said the unfair-deactivation laws continued to make it hard to respond swiftly to allegations and kick drivers off the platform, despite reforms from the Albanese government in June designed to lessen such obstacles. Uber is calling for further immediate reform. “Safety is a core value at Uber, and we have invested billions of dollars and countless hours to protect the safety of users during trips,” the company spokeswoman said. “One sexual assault is one too many, and we take every report seriously … We are committed to continually strengthening our technology, policies, and procedures to protect riders.” An upcoming 60 Minutes investigation has shed light on Uber’s processes locally, looking at the case of Canberra woman Taylor Mostacci, who was indecently assaulted by her Uber driver on the way to her university ball in 2021.



“He touched my breasts and I just froze,” Mostacci said, describing the moment when the driver was putting on her seatbelt. Her driver’s account was suspended after she complained to Uber but was later reactivated after he denied the assault. She reported the incident to police, and in 2025 an ACT court convicted the driver. Mostacci said five years on, the incident still affects her life. “I’ll never risk being in an Uber by myself. Uber has a responsibility to take care of its customers, and it has a responsibility to protect us, to look after us.” Taylor Mostacci’s full story will be shared in a 60 Minutes investigation airing this Sunday. Western Australia will become the first state in the country to legalise plug-in solar panels and batteries, Energy Minister Amber-Jade Sanderson will reveal on Wednesday. The products are extremely popular in Germany, where plug-in solar panels are sold in large numbers from major outlets like Ikea. Portable solar panels on apartment balconies in Freiburg, Germany. Alamy Stock Photo Commonly known as balcony solar, the products can be plugged into a standard power socket, and Sanderson estimated households could save $240 a year on power bills, or $500 when paired with a battery. The products can be sold in Australia – but not legally plugged in.



Sanderson will unveil the development at a CEDA Energy Outlook lunch on Wednesday, touting the products’ benefit to renters and apartment owners who were constrained when it came to sourcing their household power from renewables. “For too long, the benefits of cheap solar have been out of reach for anyone who doesn’t own their roof,” she said. “That isn’t fair, and the Cook Labor Government is doing something about it. “I’m proud that our state is leading the nation on this issue – millions of European households already use these systems every day, and WA families should be able to do the same. “Western Australians are already taking up solar and batteries in record numbers and this will ensure even more families can see the savings from the energy transition.”



Consultation will open on Wednesday on safety standards for the products with legislation to follow at an undetermined date. Related Article Updated

Gas Mystery client drives plans for WA’s biggest gas power station amid green push Last month, Sanderson discussed balcony solar at a meeting of state and federal energy ministers. Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowan said another benefit was that renters could take the kit with them wherever they move to. “It’s been legal for a long time and now United Kingdom and New Zealand are doing it, and we’re going to do it too,” he said.



About one in 10 German households have balcony or plug-in solar installed. Solar Citizens chief executive Heidi Lee Douglas last month welcomed the push for plug-in solar. “Renters, apartment dwellers and low-income homes will soon be able to plug-in, switch-on and save, save, save,” she said. “This commitment to make plug-in solar and plug-in batteries legal in Australia is great news for more than a third of Australians who rent or live in apartments, and also for low-income households so they can access some of the bill-busting benefits that cheap clean solar homeowners enjoy.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Netanyahu, Eisenkot cast votes as Israel’s polls open in defining test
World.content:
WorldMiddle EastWorld elections Netanyahu, Eisenkot cast votes as Israel’s polls open in defining test Matthew Knott Updated October 27, 2026 — 10:55pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Tel Aviv: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, have cast their votes in an election widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu’s almost two decades in power, with the prospect of a return to war with Iran dominating the final days of the campaign. Netanyahu, who voted shortly after noon on Tuesday, local time, said: “This is a very moving and fateful moment. My wife and I are truly overwhelmed. We know what is at stake, and since I am not allowed to say things explicitly, I will say: Vote correctly.” Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu casts his ballot in Jerusalem. Yonatan Sindel/Pool Flash90 via AP Gadi Eisenkot votes at a polling station in Herzliya, Israel. AP Photo/Ariel Schalit After voting, standing in a cheering crowd, Eisenkot called on all Israelis to vote to get rid of the “the worst government Israel has known”. He noted that victory wasn’t certain, adding that “we are on perhaps the most critical day since the founding of the state”.



Voting began early on Tuesday in Israel (4pm AEDT) in the first national elections since the Hamas attack on October 7, 2023, a day that shook the country and plunged the Middle East into turmoil. Netanyahu’s hold on power is at stake, with centrist rivals promising to usher in a new era, but the polls have shown a close result between the two blocs, and it may take time before clear results are known. A television campaign  on a bridge featuring Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, right, and his main rival, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, ahead of the election. AP Photo/Oded Balilty Israeli media reports passed by the official military censor and published in the final days of the campaign have stated that Netanyahu pressured his military chief to provoke a confrontation with Iran ahead of the elections, suggesting high-level leaks from within the defence establishment. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz denied the reports. US President Donald Trump told Fox News on the weekend he was deciding whether to “make a deal” with Iran or “finish it off”, adding: “It’s getting to be decision time.”



Netanyahu posted an alarming AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv and spoke about using cryptocurrency to avoid international sanctions in the final days of the campaign. Some disunity broke out within the opposition bloc before polls closed over the question of whether anti-Netanyahu voters should vote for Eisenkot’s Yashar party or spread their votes among the four parties in the bloc. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict These voters could hold the key to Netanyahu’s demise. Why are they being shunned? Eisenkot has been pursuing a so-called “big party” strategy in recent days, designed to give him the upper-hand in post-election negotiations by scoring a lead over Netanyahu’s Likud in the final seat tally. “The ‘big party’ campaign is a mistake,” Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats party, said. “It’s a dangerous lie designed to weaken us. I urge people not to fall for the ‘big party’ narrative.”



What happens on election day? Benjamin Netanyahu took to social media to post an apocalyptic AI-generated image of a nuclear bomb being dropped in the middle of Tel Aviv. Voting in Israel is voluntary, not compulsory. Even so, turnout is usually high, reflecting the level of political engagement in society. In the last elections, 4.8 million of the country’s 6.8 million eligible voters showed up at the polls – a turnout rate of 71 per cent. Even more people are expected to vote this year, reflecting the heightened stakes. Unlike in Australia, where postal voting has become increasingly popular in recent elections, Israelis must vote in person on election day. (Only those serving their nation overseas, like diplomats and defence personnel, can vote in advance by mail.) When will we know who won?



It is likely this will be known within a few hours of polls closing, but it could take days or even weeks to become clear. The first strong indication of the results will come at 10pm (6am Wednesday AEDT), when Israeli TV channels begin airing exit polls. The official election results will then start coming in. A clear picture may emerge quickly, but if no party or group of parties has a clear parliamentary majority, it could take much longer. The final tally is expected by October 30 and official election results are formally published a week after the election, on November 4.



Why is it so complicated? Elections to the 120-seat Knesset are meant to be ​held every four years, but early elections have been frequent. Crucially, voters vote for party lists rather than individual candidates. The Knesset seats are allocated by proportional representation to national party lists, with parties needing to pass a threshold of 3.25 per cent of the national vote to secure seats. About a dozen parties are widely thought to have a chance of crossing the threshold, so the final tally and seat allocation will take time.



The key number to aim for is the 61 seats required to form a government, though leaders prefer a more substantial buffer to create a more durable coalition. It is possible to govern in minority, but such a government would be even more fragile. What happens after the results are published? After the final tally is in, President Isaac Herzog will consult party leaders on whom they want as prime minister and then tap the candidate he believes has the best chance of forming a government. That nominee has up to 42 days to form a government.
