World.title: Knocked out and inked up: Why WA doctors are warning against Bali’s pain-free tattoo fad
World.content:
NationalWAHealth Knocked out and inked up: Why WA doctors are warning against Bali’s pain-free tattoo fad Indigo Lemay-Conway and Alastair Kirkby October 27, 2026 — 9:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Perth doctors are sounding the alarm over a new tattoo trend where people are opting to go under general anaesthesia for hours and wake up covered in ink. Thousands of people have flocked to Bali this year to receive the procedure which can have up to nine tattoo artists working on a person at a time. Loading While a full-body tattoo would typically take multiple sessions over a number of days, the Bali tattoo trend achieves the same result in 10 hours under anaesthesia. Kuta tattoo artist Madhe Ink says Australians have made up the majority of his clientele.



“From last year, talking about percentage, maybe 70 per cent is [from] Australia, and the rest is America, Singapore, Malaysia, Canada, like all over the world,” he said. The artist says that people have to go through two checkups before being allowed to go under general anaesthesia which include a form and a medical examination. A full-body tattoo under general anaesthesia in Bali can cost around $16,000. It’s becoming an increasingly popular trend on the holiday island. 9News Perth “The first checkup ... you need to fill all the forms first. You need to be honest with everything. Your symptoms, your sickness, everything,” he said. “And after this ... we need to take you to the hospital to do a medical checkup. That is the last checkup you need to do to make sure you are possible to do anaesthesia after that or not.”



Australian studios can charge tens of thousands of dollars for a full-body tattoo, but those travelling to Kuta for the art to be done under general anaesthesia can pay $16,000. The tattooist insisted that the procedures are done in a licensed hospital and not a standard tattoo parlour. Related Article Opinion

Workplace culture Is it OK to take an iced coffee into a job interview? “We need to do that in the proper hospital that has an operation room, doctor and everything there,” he said. Getting a tattoo under general anaesthesia is not available in Australia, with doctors fearing about the additional health risks for what should be a simple procedure.



But Australian Medical Association WA president Kyle Hoath said he had concerns over whether the procedures in Bali are being done in a safe environment with a trained anesthetist. “A general anesthetic is a serious procedure. We’re talking about being unconscious for multiple hours while somebody has to keep you breathing, keep you alive,” he told 9News Perth. “We never take a general anesthetic as a simple thing. This is quite a complicated part of the overall procedure and carries with it pretty extreme risks. AMA WA president Kyle Hoath. AMA “So I always kind of caution that if we go to that extreme of an anesthetic for something that can be done without, we should generally try and preference doing it without because otherwise we’re adding unnecessary risk into people’s lives.”



Hoath believes the procedure will likely never be done in Australia. “This is not done in Australia for a reason. It’s a completely unnecessary risk to add into having a tattoo,” he said. “Tattooing can be done safely and can be done in safe sterile environments, but there is no need to go through a general anesthetic, which adds considerable risk to the procedure, just for convenience’s sake. “That’s not convenient – that’s dangerous and that’s unsafe, and something that should be avoided. “We don’t see this happening in Australia, and I can’t imagine we ever will because it’s an unnecessary complication and risk to add into what should be something that’s pretty straightforward in getting a tattoo.”



Using general anaesthesia to get tattooed comes with the same medical risks as when it is used for surgery. “Surgery and anesthetic can carry with it a risk of death,” Hoath said. A full-body tattoo under general anaesthesia in Bali can cost around $16,000. 9News Perth “So doing that in an environment where you don’t know how the credentialing is done, where you don’t know the safety and the protocols and the rigor in which things are done safely is something you should be very cautious about. “An anesthetic, just for convenience, is a dangerous proposition, and not one I think you should entertain.”



One American man who was at Madhe Ink last week was turned away from getting both legs tattooed under anaesthesia due to health concerns. “I have an irregular heartbeat, so they did not allow me to do anaesthesia,” he said. As for why the New Yorker wanted to get the procedure done as opposed to sitting in the chair the old-fashioned way, the answer was simple – pain. “Because I don’t want to feel pain, but no pain, no gain, right? I was gonna do both legs in one shot, but now I gotta do three sessions, three days of pain,” he said. The artist behind the studio says he thinks people are opting to go under to save time and pain.



“Let’s just say a full arm on average, we finish that in two days. While under anaesthesia … let’s say arm and leg, we can finish that in 10 hours, that’s quick compared to without anaesthesia,” he said. But despite doing the procedures, he still advocates for people sitting in the chair to get a tattoo. “If you really don’t have time, but have money, go do it,” he said. “If you pass [the tests] you can do anaesthesia. If not, sorry, you can feel the pain like a man. “No pain, no gain.” with 9News Perth

World.title: AFP reveals nearly 800 threats against MPs in six months as Labor rushes to boost safety
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack AFP reveals nearly 800 threats against MPs in six months as Labor rushes to boost safety Natassia Chrysanthos, Paul Sakkal and Nick Newling Updated October 27, 2026 — 9:15pm ,first published 12:10pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Politicians will receive a safety boost that could include a wider use of emergency alarms, as the government fast-tracks a security review following last week’s attack on independent Helen Haines. The Australian Federal Police has received almost 800 security complaints from federal politicians in the first six months of the year, commissioner Krissy Barrett revealed at Senate hearing Tuesday night as she vowed to “do better” to inform MPs of the progress of investigations. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese during question time at Parliament House in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Addressing his MPs on Tuesday morning, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: “Last week was a turning point, and people have been putting up with this growing threat environment for too long”. “More can and should be done. I understand you want to feel safe when you’re in the community and have better security at your office and your home. There are a series of options you have raised including duress alarms, and we are looking at all of it.”



MPs of all stripes attended briefings with intelligence agencies following the attack on Haines. Many aired their ongoing frustrations about how long it took for their security requests to be actioned, and several MPs also made requests about duress alarms. This masthead revealed last week that the government was examining a major round of security upgrades for MPs’ homes, as well as swifter upgrades for offices and more proactive threat assessments from the AFP. Barrett told the Senate’s legal and constitutional affairs hearings the AFP had received 785 protective security reports about federal parliamentarians, with 50 per cent directed to men, and 47 per cent to women. Three per cent were generic threats against politicians. Albanese has asked for the parliament’s review of security to be fast-tracked, and requested Special Minister of State Don Farrell, Finance Minister Katy Gallagher and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke work together on delivering a “swift government response”. Related Article Workplace culture ‘Outrageous’: Payman asks if PM is waiting for attack on her in bitter staff feud



“I know so many of you have experienced an increase in aggressive and threatening behaviour online and in person. There have been vile threats towards you and your family and damage to your electorate offices,” Albanese said. “This is particularly acute for women members of the caucus, who often receive vile and misogynistic threats to their safety and increased hatred online, often of a violent and sexual nature. “I know how hard every single one of you works each day to ensure that we are accessible to our community and that people can speak to us... We need to do more to combat these threats.” Last week’s four-wheel-drive attack on the independent MP has exposed long-running tensions between federal parliamentarians and the authorities responsible for protecting them. Elected officials claim security agencies are too reactive and need to improve their communication with MPs to ensure politicians and their staff feel safe. But authorities have also expressed frustration with MPs who fail to follow protocol when flagging high-risk events or reporting incidents.



Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett. Eamon Gallagher On Tuesday night, Barrett said the AFP needed to “do better in showing you how we take these threats seriously”, and that training and communication would be improved. Female politicians were three times more likely to report sexualised or gender-based security concerns, Barrett said. Those from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds also copped offensive content more frequently. “It would be wrong to think only inflammatory comments are creating the flood of threats. In some

cases, just the debate causes the hate,” Barrett said. “In some cases, parliamentarians are being targeted because of their accent, what they look like, or

their political party. The fact is this: at times there is an almost immediate link from a policy announcement or comment, to a threat being sent.”



The commissioner will soon meet with her state and territory counterparts to discuss politicians’ safety. Opposition leader Angus Taylor also addressed the security concerns of MPs in a joint party room meeting of Coalition MPs on Tuesday morning, saying it was important to “get that right”. Speaking in the House on Tuesday night, Albanese described the impending Digital Duty of Care bill as “a much-needed but moderate and common-sense response to a problem that is becoming more serious with every passing day”. On Monday evening independent senator Fatima Payman stunned a parliamentary hearing by asking whether Albanese was waiting for a Haines-style attack against her to provide her with comparable staffing levels to other senators. Payman refused to withdraw her comments unless provided additional staff. Payman has long petitioned the prime minister for additional staffing, and was one of four independent and crossbench MPs to tell this masthead their staff were suffering under a deluge of vitriol coming into their offices.

World.title: Waiouru fire spreads over 3800ha, South Island blaze contained
World.content:
Drone crews will work overnight to monitor an out-of-control scrub blaze in the Waiouru Defence Area.

The vegetation fire has ripped through almost 3840 hectares since it was sparked by gun fire during military training on Sunday.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ)'s incident controller District Commander Nigel Dravitzki said the fire died down on Tuedsay but flare-ups were expected overnight.

He said the steep terrain and weather conditions made containing the fire challenging.

Defence Force personnel and the fire brigade would be supported by aircraft on Wednesday, with heavy machinery on standby.

"Firefighters have worked to protect a repeater station, a pā site and other culturally significant areas," Dravitzki said.

He said smoke from the fire was affecting a wide area, with Health New Zealand advising that people sensitive to smoke could experience symtoms such as coughing and shortness of breah.

"Anyone with health concerns can call Healthline 24/7 on 0800 611 116 for free health advice, or their own family doctor."

Earlier, the wind in the central North Island eased, allowing firefighters tackling the blaze to resume ground and aerial operations.

FENZ said light rain was also helping crews as they worked to bring the blaze under control.

Dravitzki said it may take several days to fully contain and extinguish.

He said five ground crews were working on the western flank of the fire, and seven helicopters resumed the air attack on Tuesday afternoon to stop the fire's spread along the eastern perimetre.

Teams from FENZ, the NZ Defence Force and local volunteer brigades were all involved in fighting the fire.

Fire and Emergency's National Coordination Centre was also activated to support the fire as well as other large-scale fires across New Zealand.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407440740112

Winds forecast to ease, cold weather on the way

On Tuesday morning, MetService head of weather news Heather Keats told Morning Report the strong winds were making it difficult to fight wildfires, but rain was expected to help and the wind forecast to ease.

Audio player for " Heather Keats on what to expect from the strong winds " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/weather/2173538%2Fwaiouru-fire-spreads-over-3800ha-south-island-blaze-contained

Heather Keats on what to expect from the strong winds Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Keats said another front was expected to arrive over the South Island on Wednesday bringing a further change in wind direction and strength, but was not expected to be as severe.

The country was in for "yo-yo temperatures" as the strong north-west wind turned to a southerly before easing, she said. Dunedin reached 28C on Monday, but would have a high of 13C on Tuesday, then 20C on Wednesday, and Thursday it would be 13C maximum again.

Over the weekend, Wellington's Mt Kaukau recorded a maximum 148km/h and Mt Somers in Canterbury had gusts of 222 km/h.

Wellington airport had 113 km/hr winds at 4am on Tuesday and Dunedin had 87 km/h.

Keats said strong winds and rising temperatures could make for a challenging wildfire season as the country headed into summer.

Heavy rain warnings for the Grey and Buller districts and Tararua Ranges were lifted on Tuesday morning, as were strong wind warnings for Marlborough, Wellington and Wairarapa.

Smoke warning issued after Roxburgh fire

Firefighters - helped by rain - put out a blaze in the central Otago town of Roxburgh.

Crews were back at the site to dampen remaining hotspots on Tuesday and heavy machinery was being used to fell damaged trees.

Fire and Emergency advised locals to stay inside and close windows and doors as a significant amount of smoke was expected in the area.

At least seven fire crews had worked on the blaze - which was thought to have started in trees about 2.45pm Monday - with FENZ saying strong winds added to the problem.

A scrub fire on Monday afternoon in the Central Otago town of Roxburgh. Supplied / Carly McDowell

Six households east of Roxburgh township had been evacuated and hundreds were left without power. By Tuesday morning all but 35 properties had the power supply back.

Central Otago Mayor Tamah Alley told RNZ on Tuesday the last evacuees were on their way home. She said sustained rain overnight had helped put the blaze out.

Alley said the community had rallied together."It was really heartening to see the community come together yesterday and offers of assistance and places to stay and food and kennels for animals and the like were put out very quickly."

In Southland, crews were brought back on Monday to work on a scrub fire that burned through about 80 hectares. The fire started on Sunday afternoon on high-country land in the Centre Hill area.

Firefighters work to extinguish a scrub fire in the Central Otago town of Roxburgh. Supplied / Carly McDowell

Fire restriction

The Bay of Plenty issued fire restrictions from Tuesday following a spate of fires in the region.

Outdoor fires will need permission from Fire and Emergency New Zealand until further notice in Whakatāne, Waihau Bay, Ōpōtiki, Coastal Strip, Urewera, Galatea, Plateau North, and Plateau Central.

FENZ Bay of Plenty Community Risk Manager Luke Burgess said restrictions were coming in earlier because of forecast El Niño conditions that made fires easier to start.

He said more than 70 fires had started in the past month, many starting from unattended beach fires or burn piles.

"The Bay of Plenty has a lot of valuable conservation land, beaches, agriculture, and forestry, and we need the community to help us keep them safe from fire this summer."

World.title: Police hunt for duo following reports of Upper Hutt robbery and car-jacking
World.content:
A manhunt is underway for two people following reports of a robbery and car-jacking north of Wellington.

Police responded to a report of a robbery on Ararino Street in Upper Hutt around 5.30pm on Tuesday.

They say three offenders, reportedly carrying an axe and a hammer, took a cash till before fleeing in a stolen vehicle.

The trio abandoned the vehicle and stole another car, but attempts to stop it failed, police said.

The driver lost control and crashed on State Highway 1 between Porirua and Tawa.

Police said no serious injuries were reported and no other vehicles were involved.

The southbound lane near the Kenepuru off-ramp is currently closed.

World.title: Gap narrows between National and Labour in new poll
World.content:
The two major parties have narrowed the gap between them, with National dropping to 29 points and Labour remaining the same on 27 percent.

That's according to the latest 1News-Verian poll which has seen National topple from its result last week, 32 points.

The Green Party is down one point to 15 and Te Pāti Māori is down to 0.1 points - their lowest ever result on the poll. However, they are pursuing a candidate-only campaign.

The coalition partners are both up: ACT is up one point to 12 and New Zealand First is up two points to 10.

Opportunity has fallen slightly to six points, down one point.

On these numbers Labour would have 33 seats, the Greens 18, Te Pāti Māori would have four and Te Tai Tokerau Party would have one.

That's a total of 56.

Meanwhile National would have 34, ACT 15 and New Zealand First would pick up 12 seats - a total of 61.

Opportunity would have eight seats and remains the power broker between the right and left blocs.

Last week, the poll had National on 32, Labour on 27, the Greens on 16, ACT on 11, New Zealand First on eight percent and Te Pāti Māori on 0.7 percent - but they are running a candidate vote campaign.

An overhang on either side could add extra seats in Parliament and alter the results.

On the preferred prime minister rankings, Christopher Luxon is on 24 percent - up four points - while Chris Hipkins sits on 18, up one.

World.title: Sensible Sentencing Trust removes images of politicians from attack advertisement
World.content:
The Sensible Sentencing Trust says it has removed images of Chris Hipkins, Chlöe Swarbrick and Marama Davidson from an attack , but not the message.

The lobby group launched election attack ads featuring the party leaders alongside the text "BACKING THE GANGS", above the Greens' campaign slogan "for all of us".

Speaking to RNZ's Checkpoint programme, the trust's national director Louise Parsons said their images had been removed.

Audio player for " Greens lodge complaint over 'Backing the Gangs' billboard " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/politics_election-2026/2192780%2Fsensible-sentencing-trust-removes-images-of-politicians-from-attack-

Greens lodge complaint over 'Backing the Gangs' billboard Checkpoint Download MP3 12m

"Apparently that seems to be an issue for Chlöe, which I think is a bit of a double standard because their images are all over the place and associated with gang members," she said.

"Are they saying that they don't back the gangs? Because the way we see it, and the reason we've responded, is from their actions, not our actions."

Asked if the ad could potentially confuse people into thinking it was a legitimate party campaign ad, Parsons said it was "satire".

The Greens accused the SST of being a Taxpayers' Union "astroturf group" - a fake grassroots organisation supporting the same cause.

Parsons denied that, but told Checkpoint the two organisations worked together for media campaigns.

"We're not Taxpayers Union. We don't campaign for their things that they do, and they don't campaign for things that we do."

The billboard ads were created by the Campaign Company, owned by Taxpayers' Union boss Jordan Williams. The SST and the Taxpayers' Union also run a shared website called 'We can't afford Labour'.

Swarbrick said those behind the ads knew they were mis-representing the Green Party - and things crossed a serious line when it turned into impersonation the SST knew can confuse voters.

The party complained to the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA).

Swarbrick said they were pleased the digital billboard company had suspended their advertising for the time being.

Parsons said she still wanted to see the Green Party meet with victims of gang violence.

The ads follow the saga involving Labour, Greens and Te Pāti Māori candidates campaigning with gang members.

World.title: Stalled opening of Waitākere Hospital intensive care unit a 'smack in the face' for community, leader says
World.content:
The stalled opening of Waitākere Hospital's long awaited intensive care unit is a "smack in the face" for the community, a West Auckland leader says.

Waitākere Hospital's brand new six bed unit is fully equipped and had originally been due to open by the end of the year.

It was part of the new Manaaki Hōhonu building that opened last month, but the ICU was sitting empty with no operating budget, no staff and no opening date.

Audio player for " Waitakare Hospital's new ICU unit sitting empty with no staff " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2194530%2Fstalled-opening-of-waitakere-hospital-intensive-care-unit-a-smack-in-the-face-for-community-leader-says

Waitakare Hospital's new ICU unit sitting empty with no staff Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Waitākere Ranges local board chairperson Mark Allen said the current default ICU for the areas is North Shore Hospital which can take 90 minutes to get to for some people in the areas he represents.

It had long been acknowledged more health services - including the ICU - were needed in the west, he said.

"Then to find it's not being resourced is like a smack in the face," he said.

"It takes years, I know, to plan these things but I just don't understand how we couldn't have had the staffing and the operating system decided before [the building] was opened."

Auckland Council's Waitākere ward councillor Shane Henderson said the situation was a disgrace and a lot of people in the community were angry.

Councillor Shane Henderson. (File photo) Facebook / Shane Henderson

"We've been slammed for so long but now we're feeling let down and we feel like we're getting the raw end of the stick again and we're being sent half way across the city for treatment when we shouldn't be," he said.

West Auckland resident and former pro wakeboarder Brad Smeele was a regular user of the health system as someone with C4 quadraplegia.

Being close to a hospital could make a big difference to whether patients could easily get support from those who cared about them, he said.

"I spent five weeks in an ICU after my accident and I know the importance of not only quality care but also the added comforts that allow family members to be able to stay and to really be able to support someone in a tough situation," he said.

That support can help seriously ill people survive, he said.

Last year, Smeele advocated online for West Foundation's fundraising drive for the ICU, particularly for family services, and said he was disappointed its opening was delayed.

Brad Smeele on a hike with friends. (File photo) Brad Smeele

Health NZ's operations director for Waitematā Brad Healey said the plan had always been to open the new Waitākere development in stages.

"This includes the intensive care service, which requires a specialist workforce and clinical arrangements to be in place before it can safely open," he said.

Health NZ's infrastructure plan does note that the services will open in stages, with the intensive care unit last, however it has previously said the ICU would be open by the end of this year.

An earlier 2024 official document had estimated April 2026.

Healey said the details of how the unit would be run were still being worked out - until that happened an operating budget could not be set and all the staff needed could not be hired.

It was important to get it right for a service where safety was so important, he said.

Health NZ was recruiting only for a clinical lead for the ICU - a one year, part time contract.

World.title: Rightful homes for more than 200 stolen garden gnomes sought by police
World.content:
The owners of more than 200 stolen garden gnomes and other ornaments are being sought by police after being found during a search warrant.

Wairarapa police said the gnomes had been stolen from the Wairarapa region in the past six to 12 months.

The ornaments were discovered during a search warrant at a home in Masterton on 17 October.

The extensive collection was found at a Masterton home. NZ POLICE / SUPPLIED

The haul also included bird baths, outdoor furniture, a gazebo, trollies, windmills, solar lights, children's wheelbarrows, metal birds, pot plants, statues, sculptures, a concrete giraffe and even a few buddha, police said.

The ornaments were at the Masterton Police Station, Sergeant Nick Bunny said.

"We'd really like people to check their gardens and outdoor areas, and if they are missing anything, they should pop into the station with their identification, and we'll work with them to identify items.

"We're hoping the public can help us get them gnome sweet gnome."

World.title: Injured Kiwis left to 'fall off the cliff' as approval of ACC claims becomes harder
World.content:
Audio player for " Lawyer questions ACC's approach to investigating claims " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2193578%2Finjured-kiwis-left-to-fall-off-the-cliff-as-approval-of-acc-claims-becomes-harder

Lawyer questions ACC's approach to investigating claims Morning Report Download MP3 7m

A Wellington lawyer is worried it's becoming harder to get ACC claims approved.

Hazel Armstrong, who has represented ACC claimants for nearly 30 years, told Morning Report the requirements to get compensation and treatment costs paid were already tough.

She said GPs were facing increasing pressure and had less time to help their patients meet the increasingly rigourous requirements.

It follows comments by general practitioner Dr Rachelle Pound last week who said a recent request by ACC for decades worth of patient notes was taking up valuable appointment time.

"We've had a request come in for 40 years of mental health notes for a patient in their 40s. That means 40 years of notes will need to be read through, redacted, all the relevant information removed and then sent back through to ACC."

Audio player for " ACC requests for historic patient notes add to GP workload " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._f0.YIZs2-J2FpwgcBcJJb29s1vXmFAWHLh_p1oUyv-l-RA/health/2193578%2Finjured-kiwis-left-to-fall-off-the-cliff-as-approval-of-acc-claims-becomes-harder

ACC requests for historic patient notes add to GP workload Morning Report Download MP3 4m

Pound said it left more questions as to what was happening to their information at the other end.

Armstrong told Morning Report complex claims like those for mental injury and work-related gradual injury were particularly difficult to prove, especially without fulsome GP notes.

While she agreed with Pound's perspective on the problem, she said claimants were squeezed, too.

"ACC is a big machine and in my view, it's getting tougher and tougher for claimants to get claims accepted - particularly if they're complex claims, which is what the GP that you interviewed is suggesting - it would've been a sensitive claim, probably, or a mental injury claim that's complex and those claims and work-related graduate process claims are very difficult to prove and the GP doesn't have the time to back their patient now.

"In the past, you could form quite good relationships with your GP and they would back you, but now they're under pressure and they don't."

The exterior of the ACC Building in Auckland. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Armstrong claimed ACC was very political and used rejecting people's claims as a way to cost costs.

She claimed they "don't care" what happens to the injured person once they are out of the scheme and lets them "fall off the cliff".

The injured person is "up against it" and most don't have representation and don't know what to do, she said.

ACC declined to speak on Morning Report on Tuesday. However, in a statement, ACC head of service operations Phil Riley said ACC's focus is on helping injured New Zealanders get the right support at the right time so they can return to work and independence.

"We are strengthening how we commission services and work with the health sector so people can access effective rehabilitation sooner," he said.

Riley said ACC is an entitlement-based scheme established in law and that they "do not delay individual entitlement decisions to manage budgets, and entitlements are not subject to funding caps, targets or annual quotas".

Decisions are based on a client's covered injury, individual circumstances and the Accident Compensation Act 2001, he said.

"Ninety-nine percent of new claims were accepted, with 65 percent accepted within one minute and 88 percent accepted within 24 hours."

In a statement on Friday, the Royal NZ College of GPs said it had raised concerns on multiple occasions about the time demands being placed on GPs.

"ACC has given assurance that they are working to improve the process with regards to requests such as these. GPs are encouraged to advise ACC and get sign-off for payment to be authorised beforehand for work that will take the GP more than an hour to complete."

On Friday, ACC also said in a statement: "Access to relevant medical information is an important part of making timely and appropriate decisions about a client's cover and entitlements.

"We know the GP workforce is under pressure, and we acknowledge it can take time to collate these notes, especially when a client has a complex injury or is seeking backdated support. We are conscious of only asking for information that is required to make these decisions and the level of information required will depend on an individual client's circumstances, including the nature and complexity of their claim. ACC does fund GPs for the time it takes them to provide us with medical notes."

ACC said it has been working to improve its processes to ensure it only requests the information it needs.

World.title: NZ First announces $4b 'Commonsense Express' plan for rail
World.content:
New Zealand First has announced a 10-point rail policy, building on its commitment to trial commuter rail in Canterbury and bring back the Southerner Train as well as commitments from the coalition already underway.

Making the announcement at a public meeting in Levin, Winston Peters says his party is the "Commonsense Express" and had always backed rail.

"Unlike the other parties that sold it off, ran it down, or talked about it without delivering, we have the track record to prove it."

He said New Zealand First would continue to deliver the goods for rail by maintaining and improving the national network, removing bottlenecks, strengthening regional connections, and putting existing rail assets to better use.

The party outlined 10 points, including some commitments that have already been announced or are underway, with a cost for each. The total cost would be nearly $4 billion, but some of that has already been allocated.

The policy commits New Zealand First to delivering the $1.35 billion Rail Network Investment Programme announced earlier this year, building the Marsden Point Rail Link, and introducing the two new Cook Strait ferries, Kupe and Cook, in 2029.

The 10 points are to:

Deliver the $1.135 billion Rail Network Investment Programme. Cost: already fully funded and reflected in the PREFU.

Build the Marsden Point Rail Link.Cost: The $410 million already allocated will support delivery and is already reflected in the PREFU, with the remaining funding determined following the current KiwiRail competitive design and tender process involving Acciona, Downer/HEB, and Martinus Rail which will result in a firm construction price substantially below KiwiRail's previous $1.1 billion estimate.

Unlock capacity through the Kaimai Tunnel. Cost: Less than $100 million, primarily for additional passing loops.

Establish Auckland Rail and Wellington Rail as companies co-owned by taxpayers and ratepayers, bringing metropolitan rail infrastructure and passenger trains under clear, accountable ownership that responds to taxpayers and ratepayers. Cost: $5 million establishment and transition costs.

Make Te Huia permanent. Cost: $130 million from capital allowance to purchase new trains, Government's operating co-funding from the National Land Transport Fund.

Back permanent passenger rail in Christchurch. Cost: $4 million per annum for Government's operating co-funding for commuter rail, low millions in commercial finance deal to procure new locomotives for Mainlander.

Continue removing dangerous level crossings. Cost: national level crossing upgrades included in the Rail Network Investment Programme, $300 million fund from the capital allowance to progress the next three-year stage of level crossing removals in Auckland and Kapiti.

Deliver the new Cook Strait ferries. Cost: $1.7 billion upper limit already fully funded and reflected in the PREFU.

Plan Auckland's third and fourth main lines and protect the Avondale-Southdown rail corridor. Cost: $50 million to progress engineering planning, with bulk of funding allocated to land acquisitions.

Protect heritage rail. Cost: $500,000 per annum already allocated and reflected in the PREFU.

World.title: Live: Connolly claims maiden Test wicket as Aussies fight back in Cape Town
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Is this arguably the most beautiful cricket ground in the world?

Members of the South Australian Cricket Association will likely disagree, as will those of the Himachal Pradesh Cricket Association.

But why quibble? Nobody can with Newlands' awe-inspiring vista, the 1,000-metre majesty of Table Mountain a towering symbol of nature's awesome scale and grace.

Test cricket has been played at Newlands since March 1889 - this is the 62nd time South Africa will play a red-ball match at the home of Western Province.

(Getty Images)

No man has scored more runs here than Jacques Kallis, whose 2,181 Test runs includes a 224 effort against Sri Lanka in 2012.

Graeme Pollock's 209 in 1966 is the highest score against Australia at the ground, with Neil Harvey's 178 in 1949 the best by an Aussie here.

Dale Steyn is the most prolific wicket taker at the ground with 74, but Kagiso Rabada has 52 in the nine matches he's played, with a best of 6/55. His average of 21.55 and a strike rate of 34.25.

Australia has played 14 times at Newlands since first visiting in 1902. They've won 10 of them.

Five of those victories came in the seven Tests held before 1970 and South Africa's international exclusion.

Since then, the ledger has flipped, with the Proteas winning five of seven.

Australia last won here in 2014, by 245 runs, but that is their only victory in their last four Tests here.

World.title: Walsh back at fullback in Kangaroos team to face Cook Islands
World.content:
Reece Walsh appears to be the frontrunner to wear the number one jersey for the Rugby League World Cup knockout stages after being named to start against the Cook Islands.

The Brisbane game-breaker opened Australia's campaign against New Zealand before veteran James Tedesco had his turn in their win over Fiji.

Both were among their team's best players, giving Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters a selection headache.

Despite his impressive showing that included three try assists, it appears Sydney Roosters premiership captain Tedesco may have paid the price for the Kangaroos' below-par showing in their 36-22 win over Fiji last Sunday.

He has been named on the bench, with Walters turning back to Walsh for his side's final pool game.

With the unbeaten hosts needing to stiffen their defence across the park, Tom Dearden has won the race to partner Cameron Munster in a third halves pairing, with Sam Walker relegated to the reserves.

Walker has been in the headlines since the Fiji match, with his Roosters outfit withdrawing their contract offer.

Walters has recalled rested forwards including skipper Isaah Yeo and his battle-hardened Penrith teammate Liam Martin, who will line up in the second row alongside Jacob Preston, who came off the bench against Fiji.

After coming off the bench against Fiji, who made easy metres through the middle in a gallant defeat, Pat Carrigan and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui are back in the starting pack.

David Fifita and Keaon Koloamatangi have been demoted for the clash in Townsville.

Centre Bradman Best did enough in his first Kangaroos match to keep his spot ahead of Latrell Mitchell.

Ethan Strange, who replaced the injured Mitchell Moses in the squad, is set to make his Test debut after being named on the six-man bench in the number 14 jumper.

Julia Robinson scored one of Australia's 15 tries against England, but the Jillaroo will miss the rest of the tournament with a dislocated wrist. (Getty Images: Janelle St Pierre)

Robinson dislocated her wrist in Saturday's 78-0 win over England. Scans ruled out a fracture, but confirmed ligament damage.

World.title: Tasmania Devils' inaugural VFL captain axed after pub incident
World.content:
The Tasmania Devils have axed VFL captain Robbie Fox, following an incident at a Hobart pub, the ABC understands.

Fox, 33, is understood to have been removed from the Granada Tavern, in Hobart's northern suburbs, after becoming drunk and disorderly at the venue two weeks ago.

It's understood Fox was abusive toward some staff at the venue, and at one point a bottle was thrown.

The Granada Tavern was contacted but declined to comment.

The ABC understands Fox was removed from the Granada Tavern following an incident two weeks ago. (ABC News: Owain Stia-James)

The incident has contributed to the Devils parting ways with their inaugural skipper, opting not to offer him a fresh contract for the 2027 season.

In a statement, Devils VFL boss Aaron Pidgeon said "the club's expectations regarding player behaviour, and adherence to our standards" were part of the decision not to offer him a new deal.

Fox is also employed by the Devils as the club's strategic projects and impact lead, and it's understood he will remain in the role.

Robbie Fox is a former Sydney Swans AFL player. (Facebook: Tasmania Football Club)

The veteran defender, who hails from Burnie, was recruited to the Devils after playing 105 games with the Sydney Swans, including the 2022 and 2024 AFL Grand Finals.

In an injury-affected season, he played 13 games this year for Tasmania in the VFL, leading the club to a top four finish and a home semi-final.

World.title: Music mogul Jay-Z picks himself to perform at next Super Bowl
World.content:
Jay-Z, the American music mogul behind Empire State of Mind, 99 Problems and entertainment company Roc Nation, that helps produce Super Bowl half-time shows, will himself be next year's featured performer at the NFL showpiece in California.

The NFL, Apple Music and Roc Nation announced Jay-Z will headline the 2027 Super Bowl half-time festivities on February 14 at SoFi Stadium in Inglewood, California.

Jay-Z attending a NFL game between Washington Commanders and the Dallas Cowboys at Northwest Stadium. (Reuters: Peter Casey-Imagn Images)

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said he had one request when the league first reached an agreement with Roc Nation: that Jay-Z take the stage himself "whenever the moment felt right to him".

"From Reasonable Doubt to standing on the Super Bowl half-time stage, this has been a journey," Jay-Z said in a statement.

"Thirty years of music, work, and culture on the world's biggest stage.

"This run continues to be a dream come true."

After days of speculation, Jay-Z is set to return to the stadium where he closed his celebration of the 30th anniversary of Reasonable Doubt, the mogul's 1996 debut album.

The concerts included three sold-out shows at Yankee Stadium and sold-out performances in London and Paris ahead of a stop at SoFi Stadium over the weekend.

Jay-Z's Roc Nation has partnered with the NFL since 2019 to advise on and help produce the league's entertainment presentations, including the Super Bowl half-time show.

At the time, Jay-Z said he told Mr Goodell: "If this is about me performing at the Super Bowl, then we can just end this conversation now."

Inside SoFi Stadium at Inglewood, California, ahead of the Super Bowl 2022. (Getty Images: Gregory Shamus)

Seven years later, Jay-Z is ready to perform after all.

Jay-Z, born Shawn Carter, has won 25 Grammy Awards and received 89 nominations, the second-most in history behind his wife, Beyoncé — who has performed at two Super Bowls.

His catalogue also includes the albums The Blueprint and The Black Album, and hit songs such as Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem), 99 Problems and Empire State of Mind, his collaboration with Alicia Keys.

NFL half-time entertainment The NFL announces the Jonas Brothers will be the half-time entertainment when Melbourne hosts the Rams and 49ers to launch the season in September.

Last year, Reasonable Doubt was inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame.

His recent concerts brought out a rotating cast of guests.

At SoFi Stadium, his daughter Blue Ivy played piano on The Story of O.J. and Dead Presidents, while Scarface, John Legend and DJ Khaled joined him on opening night. Dr. Dre, Snoop Dogg and Too $hort appeared during Saturday's finale.

Earlier in the run, Beyoncé, Rihanna, Eminem and Nas were among the guests at Yankee Stadium.

Bad Bunny and Lady Gaga perform during this year's Super Bowl half-time show at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images)

Jay-Z has built a career as an executive and entrepreneur. The Brooklyn rapper co-founded Roc-A-Fella Records and founded Roc Nation in 2008, building it into an entertainment company that works with artists and athletes.

He became the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017 and joined the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

He is also a four-time Emmy winner.

Kendrick Lamar performs during the 2025 Super Bowl half-time show at Caesars Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Getty Images: Patrick Smith)

Roc Nation will executive produce the half-time show, with Hamish Hamilton directing.

The half-time show has collected Emmys in recent years. Bad Bunny's performance in February won a record seven, including best live variety special, while Kendrick Lamar's show last year won for music direction.

AP

World.title: AFL abandons Opening Round for season 2027
World.content:
The AFL has abandoned the Opening Round fixture from the past two seasons, with all 18 clubs now set to play in Round One in 2027.

The previous seasons saw the four teams based in New South Wales and Queensland play home games, while this year's draw also included one game at the MCG.

The split fixture meant each of the teams that played in the Opening Round — also referred to as round zero — subsequently had an early season bye.

Marcus Bontempelli of the Bulldogs during Opening Round in 2026 in Brisbane. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Russell Freeman)

Critics say the fixturing caused distortions in the draw, giving an advantage to the teams that played in Opening Round.

"We have listened to feedback and are pleased to be able to deliver a Round One for all our 18 clubs and fans as we bring back a traditional nine-game opening weekend across the country," AFL chief Andrew Dillon said in a statement.

Andrew Dillon announced the codes in-principle agreement to a new Illicit Drugs Policy in March. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Former premiership coach with West Coast and Collingwood and now ABC analyst, Mick Malthouse, said Opening Round compromised the fixture.

"We don't need it and it's a blessing now that we don't have it," he told ABC Sport.

"Let me say that 'zero round' was appropriately named.

"It had zero impact on the public; in fact, I'll go in the reverse and say it had a completely negative impact."

Malthouse said the early season byes caused by the Opening Round meant the ladder was not meaningful until all teams had played the same number of games, which in the season just passed did not happen until the end of Round 4.

"All round zero did was compromise the ability of sides to be ready for the next game," Malthouse said.

Mick Malthouse said Opening Round compromised the AFL draw. (Getty Images: Mark Dadswell)

"If you've got a game tucked under your belt, you're ready; you're miles in front of the next side.

"And don't worry about the results of those games; it's more important about the long-term effect on players.

The president of the AFL Fans' Association, Ron Issko, welcomed the move to reinstate a full Round One.

"Credit to the AFL for listening," he told ABC Sport.

"When you start a season after waiting six months for the season to start and not all teams are playing, it's sort of like a soft launch.

"It just didn't have that energy.

"We're a national competition and what's better than having all teams playing on Round One."

The AFL's move to highlight games in NSW and Queensland was seen as a response to the National Rugby League's move to stage that competition's opening games in Las Vegas.

Opening Round was seen as a response to the NRL starting its season in Las Vegas, in the United States. (AAP: Supplied/NRL Photos)

"We've looked over the border and so seeing that there's games played in Las Vegas, [said] 'Wow, if that's the way they operate, let us do something similar,'" Malthouse said.

"Forget about what's happening over the border and in fact embrace what's over the border and applaud them," he said.

Round One of the 2027 season will be played from March 17-21, with matches in NSW, Western Australia, South Australia and Victoria.

Hawthorn will play triple-premiers Brisbane in Round One of the 2027 AFL season. (Getty Images: Steve Bell)

It has been delayed one week from the usual season start time by the test cricket 150th anniversary match between Australia and England at the MCG.

The season will kick off with a match between the Sydney Swans and Geelong at the SCG on Wednesday, March 17.

The following night, losing grand finalist Fremantle will play the Western Bulldogs at home.

Three-time reigning premiers Brisbane will play on the Friday night against Hawthorn at the MCG.
