The platform is also working on improved discovery features for Live video and a hub on a creator’s profile for episodic Reels, meaning a series of connected Reels similar to TikTok’s playlist feature.

“The thing that the team has been working on that we’re excited to share with you is trying to make it so that the short-form and the long-form video can be symbiotic,” Mosseri said. “We’re going to try to support these different types of formats, both in the mobile app, but also on the TV app, which I think is … going to take some time to get right. But I’m actually very excited about it, and we’re very committed to it long term.”

Tech.title: Uh-oh, it sounds like the iPhone Duo keeps cracking and users aren’t happy about it
Tech.content:
In Brief

The launch of the iPhone Duo, Apple’s hotly anticipated foldable phone, is off to a rough start. The phone was announced at this year’s Surprise and Shine event, with Apple promising that it had finally gotten a notoriously tricky form factor right.

Now, however, Bloomberg reports that early Duo users have been complaining about screens cracking “after just hours or days of use.” Some users have reported hearing a loud crunching noise, followed by the appearance of a crack. Others have reported display malfunctions.

404 Media has also reported that early adopters are dealing with “big fat creases down the middle of the [$2,000] folding screen.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for comment and will update this story if it responds. The company told Bloomberg that it was “aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units.”

Creating a functional foldable phone has long been an ambition in Silicon Valley, but many of the models released so far have suffered from similar maladies. Apple promised that it had cracked the code, but these early complaints suggest it may not have solved the problem after all.

Tech.title: Fusion startups are giving the government shares in exchange for awards. Is it worth it?
Tech.content:
The U.S. government has long had an on-again, off-again relationship with the fusion power sector. As of last week, it’s definitely back on.

Helion and Commonwealth Fusion Systems (CFS) received awards totaling $260 million from the Department of Commerce under the CHIPS and Science Act, the 2022 law that funds domestic semiconductor development, to develop advanced semiconductors used to help power and control their reactors. Helion landed $175 million, while CFS reeled in $85 million.

But as with many recent government awards, these come with strings attached. Helion and CFS have agreed to give the government nonvoting shares in return. With these awards, the fusion industry is finally getting the government’s attention, though maybe not the sort it envisioned.

In the past, government support for a startup meant nondilutive capital, meaning money that doesn’t shrink existing investors’ ownership percentages, while giving the company a bigger war chest. Investors loved the deals because it meant their startups got more money without them having to pony up. The government doled out the cash to boost American innovation, though it also meant that, in most cases, the government didn’t directly benefit when it picked a winner.

The Trump administration has been pushing to change that calculus.

Small awards with big consequences?

For both companies, the total dollar amount pales in comparison to how much each has raised. CFS has raised about $4 billion, while Helion is close behind with $3.2 billion in committed capital. The awards are perhaps more important as signals that, after years of cutting and then trickling out fusion funding, the U.S. government is back in the game.

Fusion, which generates power by fusing atoms together as the sun does, is an expensive endeavor, requiring exotic materials, sophisticated computer modeling, and complex manufacturing. Progress over the last decade has attracted private investors who have bet more than $14 billion that one or more companies will be able to put a power plant on the grid.

Yet according to the Fusion Industry Association, the sector’s trade group, that’s still not enough to beat other countries in the race. Last year, the trade group called on the federal government to inject a one-time infusion of $10 billion into the sector, with $5.4 billion intended for fusion startups.

“Other nations are moving aggressively to accelerate their commercial fusion industries, pouring billions in state-backed efforts to win the race to fusion power,” a spokesperson for CFS told TechCrunch. CFS is a member of the Fusion Industry Association. “The $10 billion ask is designed to build out the research infrastructure in the DOE’s Fusion Roadmap and be catalytic for the U.S. domestic fusion industry to compete with China.”

Until recently, the federal government had been dribbling out dollars for fusion. The Biden administration introduced the Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program, a Department of Energy program that pays companies as they hit technical goals, but the dollar amounts were paltry; less than $50 million was distributed in the first couple years. More recent awards were a little bigger, but still well shy of money the Fusion Industry Association has called for.

Now, with two companies getting $260 million, it looks like the lobbying may be starting to pay off, though not quite as planned as it comes from Commerce rather than the research budget the Fusion Industry Association sought, and it carries equity strings.

The Fusion Industry Association’s lobbying campaign did not include conversations about equity stakes in exchange for awards, a person familiar with the matter told TechCrunch. Yet Helion said the government will receive $175 million in nonvoting equity based on its Series G round, which valued the company at $15.5 billion. That works out to a stake of roughly 1%. The government’s stake in CFS will also be nonvoting and based on the company’s most recent valuation, which CFS has not shared publicly. That means the size of the government’s stake in CFS is not known.

“This type of structure has become more common in large U.S. government investments in recent years,” David Kirtley, co-founder and CEO of Helion, told TechCrunch in a statement. “This approach aligns the interests of Helion and the U.S. taxpayer around our commercial success.”

The CFS spokesperson echoed those comments. “This U.S. equity stake will enable the U.S. taxpayer to participate in the upside of our commercial success in exchange for investing in important research and development that supports the growth of an American commercial fusion industry.”

Not alone

Helion and CFS are the latest in a series of companies that have seen the government take a stake in exchange for federal dollars.

Last year, critical minerals supplier MP Materials gave the government a 15% stake in exchange for a $400 million investment coupled with a $150 million loan, offtake agreements (which are guaranteed purchases of its output), and profit sharing. Another critical minerals company, USA Rare Earth, gave up a 10% stake for a $277 million award and a $1.3 billion loan. And Intel set an even more awkward precedent. The Biden administration had already awarded the company $8.9 billion that hadn’t yet been paid out. Last year, the Trump administration turned that money into a roughly 10% stake in Intel. The list goes on.

Outside the U.S., Germany-based fusion startup Proxima Fusion confirmed to TechCrunch that the German government and the European Union are on its cap table. It also has received equity investments from German government-backed funds, including SPRIND (Germany’s federal agency for disruptive innovation) and DCTF (Deutsche Climate Tech Fonds).

Not every fusion startup that has worked with the government has given up equity. Thea Energy and Avalanche Energy, which have received federal awards and contracts, and Pacific Fusion, which has partnered with federal labs, confirmed to TechCrunch that they have not given the government a stake. Inertia Enterprises also told TechCrunch that it had not given the government any equity; the startup has a public-private partnership with the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory to commercialize the fusion technology developed there.

So far, it’s just a handful of startups that have agreed to government stakes in exchange for awards. Still, it could set the tone for the industry.

By directly investing in fusion startups, the Trump administration is signaling that fusion power is a strategic priority for the U.S. Such backing could boost investor confidence, though it could just as easily have a chilling effect on private investment. VCs will now have to weigh whether the dilution from a government stake is worth the trade-off. And what happens to cap tables in case of pay-to-play rounds or wind-downs? Who gets priority?

The fusion industry may have raised billions of dollars in recent years, but it will need billions more to deliver on its promises. Federal awards used to be no-brainers when it came time to scale up. Now they’ve grown more complicated. Will the new bargains be worth it?

Tech.title: AI Agents Are Media’s New Favorite Audience
Tech.content:
Every morning, Michelle Seo receives a morning briefing from Chattiana, her Muse artificial intelligence agent.

Chattiana’s briefing lists Seo’s agenda and to-do list, and plucks water-cooler topics from the headlines in her various newsletters along with links to the sources.

“I'm kind of challenging myself as an introvert to start more conversations,” Seo, a San Diego-based public relations consultant, tells WIRED. The newsletter, she says, gives her a sense of the daily news and options for filling an awkward silence on a Zoom call.

Seo is far from the first person to consume her news with an AI assist. In fact, the trend has become so common that some news outlets are starting to produce content that treats AI agents—not human readers—as the intended audience. This can look like anything from feeds optimized for AI to pieces structured to allow agents to create personalized articles.

“We believe that the media ecosystem is changing,” says Axios chief revenue officer Jacquelyn Cameron. ”We see this with open web deteriorating. We see that search is shrinking. We see that hyperpersonalization is surging, that LLMs are becoming more important in the way that people are consuming” their news.

Major publishers have responded to that change in a variety of ways. Many, including WIRED’s parent company Condé Nast, have signed deals to allow AI platforms to surface their content. Outlets are grappling with “generative engine optimization,” or GEO, strategies to ensure articles appear in responses to AI prompts. Last year, AIOSEO, a SEO plug-in for WordPress sites, launched a feature that provides websites with LLM.txt files, which help AI discover and interpret sites’ content.

Others have taken a more defensive posture: The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft in 2023 for copyright infringement, alleging that the companies illegally trained models on reporting. That case is still ongoing.

What Axios and a handful of others are trying, though, represents a more foundational shift in how the media operates—and who its stories are for.

“We have always said,” Cameron says, “that we want to be where the audience is.”

At the Digiday Publishing Summit in September, Axios announced the upcoming launch of Axios Direct: feeds designed for AI agents.

“We do believe that a significant portion of news consumption will move into AI systems, LLMs, and devices,” Cameron says. She describes the feeds as a more efficient way for agents to access Axios content, cutting back on narrative to prioritize structured data—more similar to a Bloomberg terminal than a series of articles.

Tech.title: NASA’s Oldest Martian Spacecraft Have Been Running for Decades. Here’s How
Tech.content:
NASA’s Mars Odyssey spacecraft has been operating for so long, it can rent a car without any fees. The spacecraft arrived at the Red Planet on October 24, 2001. It, along with its 20-year-old sibling, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO), have operated longer than anyone watching their launches could have dreamed possible.

Having such a long record of observations from above the Martian surface has rewritten the story of water on the planet, past and present alike. Keeping the wizened orbiters going for so long has been possible only thanks to great engineering and constant problem solving—and a little luck. But scientists wonder whether, despite their storied legacies, Odyssey and MRO will be the last of their kind, at least for the Red Planet.

“Both Odyssey and MRO are some of the most productive spacecraft that have ever existed,” says Briony Horgan, a planetary scientist at Purdue University who isn’t affiliated with either mission, calling them “critical” to NASA’s overall Mars research program. Odyssey’s observations of the planet’s ice, for example, and MRO’s ability to see surface features change over time have each given scientists unprecedented insight into Mars as a vibrant planet rather than a lump of rock. Odyssey and MRO also connect humans to every NASA rover, which can’t communicate with Earth directly. It’s an impressive legacy for a pair of orbiters that were only meant to last just a few years.

Space is a notoriously harsh environment that takes luck and resilience to survive for decades. Particularly tricky is the barrage of high-energy particles hitting machinery; a powerful enough strike to a delicate enough apparatus can be fatal. And whereas engineers can keep constant tabs on satellites orbiting Earth, bandwidth to Mars is more limited—science spacecraft might only check in once or twice a week, says Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, who has worked on a range of more recent Mars orbiters.

“A Mars craft has to be able to manage by itself,” he says.

Tech.title: Instagram Is a Streaming Service Now
Tech.content:
I’ve never listened to a full episode of the Happy Wife Happy Life podcast, hosted by Jordan Myrick and Kendahl Landreth, but I’ve sure seen all the clips.

My Instagram Reels algorithm recently served me, along with 5 million other viewers, a brief rant from Myrick about feeling bamboozled by the health care system. Then, I spent the next hour scrolling through the show’s other snippets on Reels, loving the couple’s snarky banter. Still, I never followed the duo to a different platform to watch the full-length podcasts.

On Monday, Instagram announced plans that might have turned me into a regular listener of the show. Instagram will expand tests in the US that let creators upload long-form content up to 90 minutes and flip a video’s orientation to horizontal. Creators can also link their short clips directly back to full-length videos.

Tech.title: Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls
Tech.content:
The Franklin County board of elections building at 1700 Morse Street in central Columbus, Ohio, is an early voting site for next week’s midterms. It is also located in the middle of the large Somali American community that was targeted by the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency’s Operation Buckeye last December. The campaign was designed, the agency said, to find “the worst of the worst criminal illegal aliens.”

The result was a paltry number of arrests, months of sustained harassment, and a lingering feeling that ICE agents could return at any minute, especially around election time.

“Here in central Ohio, our early voting location is located in a neighborhood that's been the hardest hit by ICE, and it's an immigrant community neighborhood,” Liliana Rivera Baiman, an organizer with the 614 ICE Watch group and the Ohio Good Neighbor Network, tells WIRED. “So we knew that that neighborhood was at risk and that people were going to be going to vote there, and a lot of the community there, like our Somali community that can vote, our Latino community, they walk to the location.”

Baiman’s group is responding to the threats from the Trump administration to target immigrant communities during the midterms. Dozens of volunteers are already patrolling near early voting sites in Columbus every day, Baiman says, and the figure will rise to around 250 on Election Day. They have been trained to document, record, and report any sightings of federal immigration agents, sharing the information in dozens of Signal and WhatsApp groups.

“We teach people that they have to observe the behavior. We show them what to look out for, what does ICE look like, this is the type of uniform that agents wear, these are the types of vehicles that they drive,” Baiman says. “We show them examples so that they can get familiar with what they might see.”

These efforts are being repeated in towns and cities across the country. WIRED spoke to a dozen people taking part in this effort, whose groups are working together to combat what they see as an existential threat to American democracy. Central to this response are training sessions run by massive national groups like Common Cause, the American Civil Liberties Union, and Indivisible, as well as local groups like Living United for Change in Arizona and NorCal Resist, that have created massive groups of people who can document and record what ICE is doing, understand voters rights, and in many cases, prepare for worst-case scenarios.

Tech.title: How to Hide Your Baby From the Government
Tech.content:
At first blush, Kristin LaHargoue’s social media resembles that of many thirtysomething moms espousing aspirational lifestyles. To her 88,000-plus followers on Instagram, LaHargoue—a crunchy blonde living in central Utah—routinely posts her children, her husband, and herself traipsing around the globe on her account @veda.revival. There they are, standing before the Sagrada Familia, striking silly poses on a busy Tokyo street, or dancing beachside in the Philippines. In an April 2026 post soundtracked to a version of Taylor Swift’s “The Fate of Ophelia,” LaHargoue wrote that she and her family have thus far traveled to over 40 countries.

Flying around the world at such a clip isn’t unusual for influencers. But LaHargoue says her children, although born in the US, travel without birth certificates or Social Security numbers. Her thinking is aligned with the sovereign citizen movement: an ever-expanding group of anti-government activists that, for almost half a century, have operated on the belief that they aren’t subject to US law. “Hot take: You don’t actually need a birth certificate to raise a thriving, traveling, fully functional child,” she writes in the same post. “Yeah … I said it. Because we are living proof of it.” By virtue of not registering her two young children’s births, she says her sons are “sovereign babies”—an oft-used hashtag, on accounts such as LaHargoue’s, to describe a child bearing alternative identification documents.

With her brand Veda Revival, LaHargoue offers a white-glove concierge service to new and expecting parents, rooted in the belief that obtaining requisite birth documents is tantamount to entering one’s children into “the jurisdiction of the US corporation.” A larger sovereign citizen movement has existed in the US for decades, with its practitioners similarly eschewing traditional government documents; acts of protest can also include tax evasion, driving without a license, and in the case of Terry Nichols—domestic terrorism. But the rise of influencers selling an alternative means of obtaining a passport, and the idea that babies can be sovereign, represents a new, digitally native outgrowth of this ideology.

For $497, LaHargoue sells a bundle that includes videos and templates for parents to obtain passports for their children based on “nationality” versus “citizenship,” with detailed instructions so they might respond confidently during “interactions with agents of the matrix.” Those seeking something more intensive can pay $997 for “hand-holding,” meaning that LaHargoue will personally guide them in navigating this divergent route. (LaHargoue declined WIRED’s request for an interview, citing the forthcoming birth of her third child.)

WIRED Ghost Stories Five hauntings from the other side of technology. Have a ghost story of your own? Share it in the comments below.

LaHargoue, who says she has worked with over 1,000 parents to obtain passports for their sovereign babies, is one of a growing cohort of influencers working in the unregulated industry that’s now selling this self-taught knowledge. One “family legacy architect” named Minister Dionne, known for broadcasting missives to her 125,000 Instagram followers about how registering one’s child makes them “wards of the state,” offers “Status Correction FastTrack Bundles” for securing noncitizen national passports (for as much as $555). LaHargoue also offers an affiliate program for those who want to make a commission of 15 to 20 percent by successfully selling her sovereign baby services.

It’s impossible to quantify how many sovereign babies currently live in the US, given their parents’ feelings about record-taking. (According to one oft-cited estimate, 100,000 to 300,000 people identify as sovereign citizens, although it's hard to know exactly because of the nature of the movement.) But Adam Bojak, a family law attorney in western New York who is currently on the ballot for the New York state legislature, says that he’s seen an uptick in cases involving sovereign children. In decades past, he’d have maybe one client per year who’d vacate or even try to reject formal identification documents for their children; lately, that’s increased to a half dozen a year, a phenomenon he suspects is linked to the “psychic break” that happened during Covid. “So many of these things are downstream from the aftereffects of that,” he says. “Just where people were ripped apart socially and physically from each other, emotionally. [It’s a rupture] that leads into this idea that everybody’s out for themselves.”

Remote learning during the pandemic also transformed education. Homeschooling rates surged in the early 2020s and remain high: The National Home Education Research Institute estimated earlier this year that 3.4 million children in the US are homeschooled—a number that is almost certainly underreported—compared to 1.4 million back in 2003. Tess Ulrey, executive director of the Coalition for Responsible Home Education, is unsurprised that the sovereign baby movement has risen in tandem with homeschooling rates, as homeschooling can become an inadvertent gateway into sovereign thinking. Some parents might pull their child out of school and “get tied up in this ideology of like, ‘Well, it is my right to do whatever I want. Well, why would the government be tracking that?’” she says.

Tech.title: Is an Under-Sink Reverse Osmosis System Worth It? Benefits, Costs, and Drawbacks
Tech.content:
That funny taste in your tap water may be a harmless nuisance—or it may be cause for serious concern. Either way, you can do something about it by installing a reverse osmosis (RO) water filtration system in your home.

Stand-alone RO systems and pitchers sit on your countertop and generally require manual refilling from the tap. You’ll save space and avoid the hassle of constantly refilling the unit by installing an under-sink or under-counter model that connects directly to your plumbing lines. Either way, RO systems aren’t cheap. But for some homeowners, they may be an invaluable investment.

What Is Reverse Osmosis?

Osmosis is the movement of molecules—usually water—through a semipermeable membrane that blocks larger particles like salts and sugars from passing through. After osmosis, the concentration of particles on both sides of the membrane ends up in equilibrium. It’s how plants get water from the soil, and it’s how your kidneys filter junk out of your blood.

While osmosis is a spontaneous phenomenon that happens naturally, reverse osmosis requires pressure to force water through a membrane in the other direction, effectively removing all of those compounds from the water to render it pure. It’s how salt is removed from seawater to make it drinkable, and it’s one way tap water can be purified in your home.

RO differs considerably from traditional filtration systems, which rely on physical barriers, typically activated carbon, to manually capture particles that pass through. Eventually, these filters become saturated with sediments and other matter and have to be replaced. While carbon filters are fairly blunt, able to capture larger particles of at least 0.1 microns in size, RO systems have a much finer-grained membrane that captures contaminants on a microscopic level (typically down to 0.0001 microns).

Photograph: Matthew Korfhage Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Brita Everyday Elite Water Filter Pitcher $45 Amazon

Carbon filters can make your water taste and smell better, but with RO you are getting much, much cleaner water than what that inexpensive Brita filter can muster. (That said, RO can’t capture everything, and carbon filters are still useful for capturing certain volatile organic compounds through adsorption. Most RO systems also have an additional carbon filtration system included.)

Note that two types of RO systems are available: Tanked RO systems filter water slowly (albeit passively, without electricity) and sequester it in a (rather large) tank under your sink. Today, tankless RO systems are more popular, processing water on demand but requiring electricity to keep things flowing expeditiously. Tankless systems are considerably more expensive due to their inherent complexity.

What Are the Real Risks of Contaminants in Water Today?

“US tap water is safe for most people most of the time,” says John Voll, an industrial water treatment veteran and the founder of Tap & Air, a website that monitors water and air quality for hundreds of municipalities. “The problems are local, not universal.”

The first step to understanding your personal risk is to gauge whether your own water is up to snuff by simply looking up its most recent data report online. The Safe Drinking Water Act requires community water systems to publish an annual report on the quality of water they’re delivering, due by July 1 each year.

These are heady documents, so to keep things simple, Voll says to keep your eye on three key pollutant metrics: lead, nitrate or arsenic, and PFAS (so-called forever chemicals popular in nonstick cookware and other products). While the first two are serious issues, they’re fairly rare today. PFAS, however, are a particularly significant problem across the country. Voll says that 98 of the 200 largest US cities have at least one PFAS compound detected in their water supply. Reverse osmosis systems can handle them—as well as lead and other compounds. Carbon filters usually can’t.

Tech.title: I Tested Every Major AI Agent for a Day. Here’s the Best One
Tech.content:
Last year, I remember sitting in WIRED’s office, complaining to my colleagues nonstop about how much AI agents suck. They were just bad at everything.

As a software reporter, I sat through meeting after meeting where tech bros—mostly men—demonstrated how their new agent would revolutionize my everyday life and automate away the tedium. The catch was that none of these so-called “agents” actually worked.

Fast-forward to today, and always-on AI agents are booming, with major players racing to release their own versions to attract early adopters. The key reason these personal agents are hitting the larger zeitgeist, beyond Silicon Valley nerds, is that they work. Well, at least more reliably than last year. AI agents still make mistakes, but I also see significant improvements in following through on tasks and controlling a browser. These little guys got their glow-up.

It can be hard to know where to start with AI agents and which one best fits your automation needs. So I spent a day experimenting with every major AI agent to understand their strengths and weaknesses. Before going to bed on Wednesday last week, I set up six always-on agents on my iPhone: Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Instinct, Anthropic’s Claude Duet, Google’s Gemini Spark, and xAI’s Grok Bot.

Each agent differs slightly in price and function. Muse is free to use and has dominated the smartphone app download charts since its September release. Instinct is also free, but you need an invite code from a user; it’s operated through your texts rather than an app. OpenAI’s Dots are behind a $100-a-month paywall, the most expensive I tested, and built inside of ChatGPT. Google’s Gemini Spark is a beta inside the Gemini app and costs $20 a month. xAI’s Grok Bot costs $30 a month and is in its own app. Lastly, Anthropic’s Claude Duet costs $20 a month and is the newest of the bunch—released as a wait-listed research preview the night before my tests.

OpenClaw isn't on my list. Despite the AI agent sparking much of this innovation earlier this year, it’s too clunky for the average person to set up. Maybe it will be in a future ranking, where I could also include smaller players like Hermes by Nous Research and Poke.

What Exactly Is an AI Agent?

If you’ve never used an AI agent—I have zero judgment for the holdouts—it's like texting a digital assistant to complete tasks: scan your email for important missed messages, track vacation flight deals, and help with daily shopping decisions.

Compared to a chatbot’s turn-based experience, these tools are more proactive and will nudge you first when they detect an opportunity to be helpful. All of your messages with these agents are often stored in a single thread that feels like a group text. The AI agents complete many of these tasks by controlling a virtual browser, essentially their own computer for internet access.

The Rubric

I’ve tested AI software from a nontechnical perspective for the last few years, so I feel especially qualified to help guide you through this moment. I designed five basic tests to run each agent through, enacting all this chaos over 24 hours to gauge their proactivity, direction following, and browsing abilities. (Somehow, my iPhone didn’t melt into a puddle.) I scored each attempt on a scale of 1 to 5, and tallied the results at the end to crown a winner—and hand out an award for most annoying.

This is not an endorsement of any of these AI agents. The software remains nascent and often fraught with privacy and security concerns. These agents work best when connected to your personal data, like email and calendars, but require a level of trust that could ward off some users. For example, an X user claimed he recently connected AI agents to his bank account and work Slack, and then was mortified when an agent posted how much money he had for his colleagues to see.

Additionally, these tests are a limited sliver of what the tools can do. All of the agents will improve over time, as you share more data about yourself and how you like to complete tasks. I only shared my personal Google Calendar and Gmail with the tools, so I didn’t fully expose the AI agents, Billy Evans–style, to everything.

Morning Briefing

On Thursday mornings, WIRED’s Gear desk meets to chat about current coverage plans and sometimes pitch ideas for the next week. So, I wanted to see which AI agent put together the best tech news briefing and could use that information to generate a compelling headline. Companies often tout these tools as being great for compiling morning dossiers that keep you up-to-date on important events and breaking news.

I sent each AI agent an extensive prompt detailing my areas of coverage at WIRED, along with context about how this pitch would be used. Even though I asked the AI agents to take 30 minutes and really do deep research before answering, only Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots actually kept researching for most of the allotted time. The other AI agents either instantaneously spit out a pitch or sent me the headline after a couple of minutes of searching. While not a major mistake, it suggests that in this instance Muse and Dots were a bit better at following my instructions—a critical function of an AI agent.

Tech.title: Grok Says Its AI-Generated Version of ‘The Odyssey’ Is ‘Not Historically Accurate’
Tech.content:
You don’t hear the defenders of so-called Western civilization talk much about The Odyssey these days.

Maybe that’s because their rabid denunciations of Christopher Nolan’s film adaptation of Homer’s epic were buried in an avalanche of money. The July blockbuster has grossed nearly $1.8 billion worldwide, silencing the right-wingers who predicted a massive flop due to diverse casting and deviations from the source material.

Perhaps the loudest of these preemptive critics was Elon Musk. The world’s richest man spared no vitriol for what he considered a desecration of the ancient Greek narrative; four days after its release, he vowed to produce a superior version. “Before this year ends,” Musk wrote on X, “Grok Imagine will make a full-length movie of The Odyssey that is historically accurate and true to the art of Homer.”

A little more than three months later—long after the discourse moved on—the public finally has a first glimpse of what we might call the Grodyssey, an Odyssey rendered through prompts fed into xAI’s video and image generation model. Rather than a “full-length movie,” it’s a seven-minute “episode” of an apparently ongoing series, depicting how Odysseus, king of Ithaca, resists a call to war against Troy but is ultimately compelled by an oath of loyalty to sail there with his army.

“Odyssey with Grok Imagine,” Musk announced Friday on X when sharing the clip, produced by AI entertainment company Wonder Studios X. The subdued post received just 18,000 likes, notably less engagement than other recent posts in which Musk cast doubt on the results of Brazil’s elections, complained about pronouns, and disparaged “legacy news.”

Tech.title: Daylight Saving Time Ends This Weekend. Here’s When (and Why) the Clocks Go Back
Tech.content:
Daylight saving time ends this weekend, with the clocks officially changing at 2 a.m. on Sunday. While it’ll still be light enough for trick-or-treating on Halloween, the time change will hit the day after, when most of the US adjusts back one hour.

The time shift is notorious for disrupting sleep patterns and schedules. Some politicians are advocating for the abolition of time changes and the permanent adoption of daylight saving time, or DST. The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act in July, but it still needs Senate approval and the president’s signature to become law — meaning that, for now, we still have dark winter hours coming.

If you, too, dislike how early it gets dark each day through winter, just remember that brighter evenings will return in mid-March.

More from CNET

When does daylight saving time end?

Daylight saving time in the US ends at 2 a.m. local time on Sunday. It will return at 2 a.m. local time on March 14, 2027. The end of DST is when we “fall back,” whereas in March, we “spring forward.”

The US isn’t alone in observing daylight saving time. Check out this list of other countries that use DST, along with their start and end dates.

Daylight saving time vs. standard time

The official US time website shows where time zone boundaries are located. Time.gov/Screenshot by CNET

The exact start dates for daylight saving time and standard time float a little. DST kicks off on the second Sunday of March and ends on the first Sunday of November with the return of standard time.

We spend about eight months of the year in DST. We can thank the Uniform Time Act of 1966 for bringing some order to what had been a complicated history of time changes in the US.

“Motivated by transportation improvements, this act mandated standard time within the existing time zones and established a permanent system of uniform DST, including the dates and times for twice-yearly transitions,” the Bureau of Transportation Statistics states in a history of time zones.

The country’s time zones date to the railroad boom of the late 1800s. DST formally entered the chat in 1918, but its application was inconsistent until 1966. The country tried year-round daylight saving time in January 1974 under President Richard Nixon to address the energy crisis. It didn’t go over well. Congress and President Gerald Ford restored standard time in October 1974.

If you truly hate time changes, then consider moving to Arizona (except for the Navajo Nation) or Hawaii. Those states are on standard time all year long, and their residents don’t have to deal with the physical and mental health impacts of the change. Puerto Rico, Guam, the Virgin Islands, American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands also skip DST.



Sleep experts seek year-round standard time

Organizations such as the National Sleep Foundation, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the Society for Research on Biological Rhythms are united in calling for permanent standard time, saying it’s better for human biology.

“There’s a mismatch between the outside world and our internal clocks during daylight saving time that can result in some negative health consequences,” says Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation.

Dzierzewski cites mental health concerns and upticks in cardiovascular events and drowsy driving. He also calls out safety issues with young children walking to school or sitting at bus stops in the dark. Those safety issues were a big reason why permanent DST didn’t last in 1974.

Will we ditch these time changes for good?

Time changes aren’t popular. An October 2024 YouGov poll (PDF) of more than 1,100 US adults found that 63% would like to see the changing of the clocks eliminated. Only 17% wanted to keep time changes, and 20% weren’t sure.

Efforts to end the time changes have so far failed to pass into law. The bipartisan Sunshine Protection Act, which would have made daylight saving time permanent, passed the Senate in 2022 — the new version of the bill passed the House earlier this year and was sent on to the Senate to review in July.

While many people agree on eliminating time changes, the schism between daylight saving time and standard time remains. Standard time may have a bit of an image issue compared to DST.

“Part of the issue is that people associate daylight saving time with summer. People love summer, right?” Dzierzewski said. “But the simple fact of the matter is, it would still be summer if we were on permanent standard time.”

President Donald Trump criticized time changes in a 2024 Truth Social post: “The Republican Party will use its best efforts to eliminate Daylight Saving Time, which has a small but strong constituency, but shouldn’t! Daylight Saving Time is inconvenient and very costly to our Nation.”

Bills and resolutions at the state level haven’t had real-world impacts yet. Politicians are still split on whether they want permanent daylight saving or standard time. Dzierzewski is hopeful that permanent standard time will win out.

“This is the first time in several years where I’ve seen more legislation introduced at a state level in support of permanent standard time as the solution,” he said.

If you’d like to see time changes end and want to advocate for either daylight saving or standard time, contact your state and national representatives and express your opinion.

"You're in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally." Joseph Dzierzewski, senior vice president of research and scientific affairs at the National Sleep Foundation

Adjust your body clock to daylight saving time

Daylight saving time is happening, so now it’s a matter of figuring out how to deal with it. It’s not just about the day of the time change.

“You’re in a better situation to cope with the effects of the clock change if you have good sleep health generally,” Dzierzewski said. He recommends exposure to bright light in the morning, physical activity during the day, eating meals at regular times and practicing a relaxing wind-down routine at night.

The majority of Americans struggle to get the National Sleep Foundation’s recommended 7 to 9 hours of sleep for most adults. A CNET survey found that more than half of US adults use some method to cope with sleep-related challenges. Check out some expert-backed tips for improving your sleep quality.

“If you’re doing these healthy sleep behaviors, you’re probably more resilient to some of these changes,” Dzierzewski said. “If you have poor sleep to begin with, you’re probably going to feel it a little bit more.”

Establishing a better sleep routine can take time. There are two things you can do in direct response to the time change. Dzierzewski suggests adjusting your bedtime and wake-up time gradually ahead of the change. For example, you could shift your schedule by 15 minutes per day and ease yourself into DST. He also recommends getting a good dose of bright morning light on the day of the time change to help set your internal body clock.

Think of DST as another kind of wake-up call, one that can motivate you to evaluate your sleep routine and quality and make positive changes. Start with these six simple habits. And don’t forget to change your clocks. Do it the night before, and you won’t have to worry about it later.

Tech.title: Walter Koenig, Star Trek’s Original Chekov, Dies at 90: ‘He Loved You Too’
Tech.content:
Walter Koenig, known as the cheeky and endearing Russian navigator Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek television series, died on Sunday at 90, The New York Times reports. Koenig played the tart-tongued character for the iconic show’s second and third seasons, and also reprised the role in six Star Trek movies featuring the original cast.

Koenig had a memorable stint in another space-themed show, Babylon 5, playing telepath Alfred Bester. He worked as a screenwriter on shows including Land of the Lost and Family. He voiced Chekov in numerous video games and also wrote several books.

But for many, he’ll forever be remembered as the likable ensign with a Monkees mop-top hairdo and distinct accent. Chekov’s Russian heritage was important to a show that displayed a unified future, where a diverse crew, even including the half-Vulcan Spock, explored the stars together. His Russian accent on words such as “wodka” for vodka and, most famously, “nuclear wessels” for “nuclear vessels” in 1986’s Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, resulted in fan-favorite quotes. Chekov even once told proud Scotsman and fellow Enterprise crew member Montgomery Scott that “Scotch was invented by a little old lady in Leningrad.”

More from CNET

Koenig was born in Chicago to Russian Jewish immigrant parents from Lithuania. According to his obituary in The New York Times, Star Trek creator Gene Roddenberry was told that young viewers thought the stars, William Shatner as Captain Kirk and Leonard Nimoy as Mr. Spock, were too old. Producers hoped younger viewers would be drawn to Koenig and his Davy Jones-esque hair. Be that as it may, Koenig was 30 when cast, only five years younger than Shatner and Nimoy.

Walter Koenig, second from left in the back row, is seen with the cast of the original Star Trek series. Sunset Boulevard/Getty Images

Koenig’s wife, Judy Levitt Koenig, died in 2022. They had two children. In 2012, Koenig was honored with a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame.

In 2008, he served as best man at fellow Star Trek cast member George Takei’s wedding to Brad Altman, with fellow cast member Nichelle Nichols also standing up for the couple. Takei remembered Koenig with a touching Instagram post.

“Walter was more than Chekov,” Takei wrote. “He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend. To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too.”

Tech.title: Rivian Halloween Update Turns R1, R2 Into Ghostbusting EVs Through Nov. 2
Tech.content:
Halloween is one of my family’s favorite holidays, a sentiment clearly shared by somebody at Rivian. Every October, owners of its electric trucks and SUVs can activate Halloween Mode, which changes the exterior lights, sounds and graphics on the infotainment display to match the spookiest season. It’s pretty fun.

This year, Halloween Mode on the R1S, R1T and R2 EVs has become a Ghostbusters–themed experience that Rivian says changes each of its EVs “into a ghost-hunting machine.” The over-the-air update adds lights and sounds, easter eggs and hidden clues in the digital infotainment system, a tie-in with the Rivian Assistant voice control system, and an arcade-style Halloween game that can be played while parked.

The update, developed in collaboration with Sony Pictures, is available now and runs through Nov. 2.

More from CNET

The seasonal mode features custom lights and sounds while parked. Rivian

Who ya gonna call?

A new in-vehicle Ghostbusters app bundles the seasonal features into a single red toggle, accessible while parked. Tapping it syncs the EV’s interior and exterior lighting and themed audio to match the Ghostbusters’ car, the Specialized Electronical Vehicular Device (or Ecto-1). Second-generation R1 and R2 owners can also choose from Proton Pack, Slimer, Ghost Trap, or Peter Venkman themes. R1 Gen 1 owners only get the main Ecto-1 theme, but each option pairs a unique exterior LED sequence with a matching audio track. The EV can also be set to automatically trigger a random themed light-and-sound show whenever someone walks past, giving trick-or-treaters a fun surprise.

Inside, the dashboard and rear displays transform to match Ecto-1’s control panels, playing a version of the iconic Ray Parker Jr. Ghostbusters theme song. The Rivian mobile and smartwatch apps also update to match the vehicle’s controls, allowing owners to trigger Ecto-1’s siren and flashing lights from outside the vehicle.

Inside, the various displays are transformed to match the controls and instruments of the Ecto-1 car from the films. Rivian

In addition to putting on a show for passersby, the spooky infotainment mode features clues hidden throughout the EV’s menus that can be tapped to reveal secret characters — like Slimer and Rivian’s Ghost Guard — triggering animations, audio and easter eggs. Even the Rivian Assistant voice command system gets in on the act, taking on an eerie tone for the season, triggering light shows with spoken commands, reading clues for the in-dash scavenger hunt and playing sound effects on request.

Rounding out the update is Mallow Mash, an arcade game accessible from the main touchscreen where players race against the clock to pop mini Stay Puft Marshmallow Men. The full creature feature set — including the scavenger hunt, the arcade game and most of the lights and sounds — is only available when the vehicle is in park. However, the touchscreen’s visual theme will remain active if switched before driving, so you can take the show on the road.

The update also themes the Rivian mobile and smartwatch apps to match the Ghostbustin’ theme. Rivian

To get in on the fun, both the vehicle software and the Rivian mobile app need to be up to date. Once updated, look for a prompt on the driver display that asks whether you’d like to “hunt some ghosts” and opens the Ghostbusters app.

The real Ecto-R1

In addition to the seasonal software, Rivian also built a few physical homages to the original Ecto-1 based on its R1S. Dubbed the Ecto-R1, the full-size electric SUV features white paint on the body and 22-inch Aero wheels, red graphics running the length of the chassis, and the No-Ghost logo on its hood and front doors. Rivian has loaded the EV’s roof rack with a custom frame filled with screen-accurate sirens, spotlights, a radar dish and side tanks, as well as vintage emergency lights sourced and restored to complete the look. It’s so cool.

I couldn’t convince Rivian to sell me one of its custom Ecto-R1s — though that hasn’t stopped me from asking repeatedly — but the builds will be on display for fans to check out in person at Rivian retail spaces in Austin, Miami, San Francisco, New York, and Laguna Beach and Venice, California. The full list of events is on Rivian’s Halloween page.

Tech.title: Apple’s ‘Pro and Tell’ Event: Everything Announced So Far This Week
Tech.content:
Apple’s Pro and Tell experience week is here, and it’s already off to a strong start, with the new iPad Mini unveiled on Monday morning. But there’s more to come: We’re also expecting refreshes and changes to the iMac and MacBook Pro lineups, including a long-anticipated touchscreen laptop.

Apple’s had a busy few months, launching the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September alongside the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5, followed by the iPhone Duo launch at the end of last week. Apple’s smart home lineup, revealed during its recent Welcome Home event, is up next: the HomePod Mini 2 will launch on Friday; the Apple HomeView and Apple TV 4K on Nov. 13; and availability for the Home Collection products begins in December.

This week will culminate with Apple hosting a special event on Wednesday, and CNET will be on the ground capturing all the latest details. But ahead of that, here’s what we’re expecting to see from the tech giant, and we’ll update this piece as more details are revealed.

More from CNET

Apple’s new iPad Mini

Announced on Monday, Apple’s new iPad Mini is available to preorder on Wednesday and will go on sale Nov. 6. It starts at $699 for 128GB of storage, $799 for 256GB and $999 for 512GB.

Setting it apart from the last iPad Mini, which came out two years ago, the new tablet has an 8.5-inch OLED screen (versus an LCD), IP67 water and dust resistance, an Apple A20 processor, a repositioned front-facing camera and a through-screen speaker system called Acoustic Display, as well as being thinner and lighter than before.

A new iMac

We don’t yet know what’s coming for the rest of this week, but one heavily rumored product is a new iMac, which we’re expecting to be updated with an M6 chip, just like the Mac Mini. The current generation of iMac was last updated in 2024.

It’s likely the new iMac will be announced Tuesday morning.

MacBook Pro refresh

We’re anticipating several MacBook Pro updates this week, including an OLED touchscreen version.

“I’m expecting a 14-inch MacBook Pro to get updated with the M6 chip,” CNET Managing Editor Josh Goldman says. “I’m not sure the 16-inch will get that, since it usually doesn’t get a base M-series chip. My feeling is they’ll probably hold off on that until next year, when they can add the M6 Pro/Max chips.”

Goldman added that he’s expecting the 14- and 16-inch OLED touchscreen models will still be based on the M5 Pro/Max chips, however.

The MacBook Pro chip upgrade announcement could hit Tuesday morning, to be followed on Wednesday by the new touchscreen versions of Apple’s highest-end laptop.

And as for the iPhone Duo launch last week, check out CNET’s ongoing folding test — you can watch Day 1 of the livestream here and tune in on Tuesday as we continue testing how many times the iPhone Duo can fold without cracking in the CNET lab.

Tech.title: AI Killed the Homework Era
Tech.content:
Grading homework and providing feedback to students is arguably the toughest part of being an educator. During my tenure as a professor, reviewing the results of carefully crafted assignments was at best a barometer of how well I was relaying the concepts and crucial elements of the course. In the era of AI, it’s become an infuriating exercise in futility.

Discussion posts littered with complex references to materials outside the course’s accepted reading. Students who were instant masters at the subject matter from day one, taking a page from the classic tactic of “forge your mom’s signature the first time so you can keep forging it forever.”

After reading a story last week about a UC Berkeley math professor who no longer bothers grading his students’ homework because they’re all using AI, I couldn’t help reflecting on my own experience as a professor of practice at the Walter Cronkite School of Journalism and Mass Communication at Arizona State University. With the proliferation of AI tools once ChatGPT launched in late 2022, and tech giants worldwide started following suit, launching increasingly sophisticated chatbots and now AI agents, grading homework became deeply depressing.

More from CNET

In advanced communications courses like the ones I taught, reviewing homework turned into a hypervigilant hunt for the hallmarks of AI-generated text and ideas. The beast was cunning, quick and never slept. My tools for catching it were sorely lacking.

Despite there being no way to verify it, I was fairly certain there were online students in my classes who had never done any of the work themselves the entire course. When those students were given work they could not outsource to AI, like simulations and recorded oral presentations, they reliably struggled to maintain the perfect standard they had set. But when you get A’s all semester, one C or D doesn’t really matter. The AI cheating math still shakes out.

In an effort to keep myself alert to the use of AI tools in completing homework, I always ran a smattering of assignments through a few widely available AI chat tools to compare against student-submitted work.

Most of the time, this method was inconclusive, but by the time I left teaching earlier this year, I suspected that at least 90% of the students I had online were using AI to do all or part of their work.

In my very small in-person classes, I had several confrontations over the unauthorized, clandestine use of AI to complete assignments. One in particular made me rethink the purpose of my work.

A student gave a presentation early in the semester, and when asked a few basic questions in front of the class about how they came up with their ideas, the student was flummoxed, unable to explain the circumstances that led to their own creative output.

We had a talk privately later that day about AI use, and the student admitted to using ChatGPT to create part of their assignment. They agreed to never use it again in my class. On the next assignment, we ended up having the same discussion, and I was given the same promise. It didn’t stick.

When I went to my supervising dean about the use of AI in my classroom and inquired as to whether this case should be referred to the academic integrity board, they told me it was at my discretion and that, candidly, the university and college were grappling with what stance to take in the face of wide AI adoption. ASU’s stance on AI currently reads, in part: “Our focus is on using AI not only to address educational challenges, but to do so in a way that respects and uplifts all learners.”

Education is about the journey, not the outcome

Some might argue that cheating is a natural impulse. On your taxes, on the Monopoly board. Sometimes putting a thumb on the scale is the only way we feel we can win at a game that looks rigged or too hard to beat.

But education isn’t a game. Even though school environments can be competitive, learning is not something at which you “win.” It’s a personal journey meant to unlock fluency you can call on at will, like knowing how to speak a language or effortlessly opening a door.

AI may be viewed as a skeleton key by the students of today, granting instant access to great grades and passable answers that a busy, bored teacher can’t flag as 100% fake. Students who outsource the work of learning take for granted the value in being able to perform expertise with ease, and also risk ruining their credibility at their own peril.

Until our brains are plugged into our computers 24/7, it’s a crutch that educators can’t afford to quibble about any longer.

Tech.title: Download iOS 27.2 Now to Bring These Features and More to Your iPhone
Tech.content:
More than a month after Apple released iOS 27 to the general public, the tech giant released iOS 27.2 on Monday. While iOS 27 brought Siri AI and more to your device, iOS 27.2 expands Siri AI to other languages, and the update brings a few upgrades in other apps, such as FaceTime and Apple Music.

If you’re wondering what happened to iOS 27.1, the foldable iPhone Duo launched on 27.1 on Friday. That is the only device that will run iOS 27.1, and all devices can update to 27.2 now.

CNET/Apple

Here are some of the features you can try in iOS 27.2. Don’t forget, Apple Intelligence features are only available on Apple Intelligence-compatible devices, like the iPhone 18 Pro.

More from CNET

Siri AI in more languages

Siri AI is available on iOS 27 now. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

In iOS 27.2, Siri AI comes to French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish in beta. Siri AI was initially only available in English.

Apple previously said Siri AI would expand to these additional languages, so this shows the company moving quickly on that promise.

Use front and rear cameras simultaneously in FaceTime

In iOS 27.2, you can use your front and rear-facing cameras at the same time in FaceTime calls. This allows you to FaceTime with a larger group of people — you don’t have to squeeze everyone into a single frame to see the person on the other end of the call. However, everyone on the call needs to be on iOS 27 or later for this feature to work.

Apple Music gets a new color scheme

The old Apple Music logo (left) next to the logo introduced in iOS 27.2. Screenshot by CNET

The iOS 27.2 update also brings a new look to the Apple Music app. The app icon is now black and white, as opposed to the reddish hue it had in previous iOS versions. Tapping into the app also reveals new blue menu items throughout, rather than the same reddish tone as the older app logo.

Refreshed Podcasts options

The Podcasts app also gets an update in iOS 27.2. The update introduces two rows to the top of the Home tab within the app: New Episodes and Continue Playing. This can help you keep track of which podcasts are new and which you still have to finish.

It’s a small, pleasant addition to the interface, and I appreciate how it helps keep my podcasts organized.

Apple TV profile expansion

In iOS 27.2, you can create TV Profiles in your Apple TV app. You can assign a profile to your child or someone else and ensure your preferences aren’t messed with.

So if you’re tired of being recommended kids’ shows after letting your child watch the series Shape Island, you can create a profile for your child and let them watch those quirky little shapes all they want. (But also, it’s possible that I like Shape Island more than my son does, so you should check it out.)

Apple TV multiview on iOS

Another Apple TV update in iOS 27.2 is Multiview. If you subscribe to Apple TV you can watch up to four live sports streams, including streams from Major League Soccer and Formula 1, at once. That way, you don’t miss an important game, or you can look at a map of the racetrack while watching feeds from driver-view cameras.

The updated Health app is gone

The refreshed Health app isn’t available in iOS 27.2. Apple

Apple removed the redesigned Health app before releasing iOS 27.2 to the general public. Developers and beta testers could explore the refreshed app in early iOS 27.2 betas and see things like a new Longevity tab and your Health Age.

The redesign was always expected to launch sometime later this year. So it’s not surprising this feature isn’t included in the general release of iOS 27.2. It’s also not unusual for Apple to include features in early beta versions of software, then remove or change them in later betas or upon the release of an iOS update.

Here are the full release notes for iOS 27.2.

Siri AI (All iPhone 16 models and later, iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max)

Siri Al can recall your past conversations, so you can ask Siri about something it told you before, like the restaurants it recommended last week.

Siri Al can draw from more sources to give you a great answer, including photos attached in Messages, Calendar event attendees, your voicemails, and better results from Safari history and Reading List.

Excluded Apps lets you choose which apps Siri, Search, and suggestions can access, all from one setting.

Granular text selection lets you select and copy just the part of a Siri response you need.

Siri Al is available in more languages, with support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, and Spanish. Siri Al is not available in the EU or mainland China.

Other

Suggestions in Messages help you take action based on the context of your conversations, such as adding a Calendar invite for dinner.

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, avoid adding duplicate photos and display a reminder before albums expire, so participants can save important photos and videos.

Support for SynthID watermarking to help identify whether an image was generated or modified with generative tools in Photos and Image Playground.

The Home tab in the Podcasts app offers two separate sections for New Episodes and Continue Playing, letting you find the latest updates from your shows and then pick up where you left off.

The Friends tab in the Games app provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages.

Simple Profiles in the Apple TV app lets everyone in your household have their own profile, with recommendations that fit what they like to watch.

FaceTime supports adding a third-party sign language interpreter or live captioner to a call.

For more, here’s what to know about iOS 27 and why your battery might be draining faster after updating. You can also check out why the iPhone Duo will launch with iOS 27.1 and our iOS 27 cheat sheet.

Tech.title: Are We All Maxxed Out? Dictionary.com Names ‘Maxxing’ Its 2026 Word of the Year
Tech.content:
Are you focusmaxxing today? Knowledgemaxxing? Maybe fibermaxxing? Dictionary.com has chosen “maxxing,” which can seemingly be attached as a suffix to any other English word, as its Word of the Year for 2026.

Dictionary.com defines maxxing as “the practice of pursuing an activity to the fullest or optimizing a certain aspect of your life.” It’s not a lot different from older expressions such as taking it to the max, maxing out a credit card or feeling maxed out. Words like max, maximum and maximize have their roots in the Latin maximus — meaning “greatest” or “largest.”

But maxxing takes it to another level. The word has an additional x and can be tacked onto the back of seemingly any word. Dictionary.com said that two of the most common of these in 2026 have been looksmaxxing and tokenmaxxing.

More from CNET

Looksmaxxing — maximizing one’s physical appearance — was the most popular internet search term in 2026 for derivations of maxxing, according to Dictionary.com. Certain internet content creators popularized the term and have gained large followings with their sometimes extreme approaches to improving their looks.

Tokenmaxxing is another frequently searched term. In the world of AI, token refers to a small bit of written text that AI language models process to formulate responses. The term tokenmaxxing generally refers to using AI as much as possible at work, as companies integrate AI more and more into workflows. It’s no joke: Some companies are tracking and evaluating their workers on how much and how effectively they use AI in their jobs.

Maxxing can also be used on its own, such as, “Have you been maxxing on anything lately?”

Dictionary.com said the popularity of “maxxing” in all its various uses indicates how much we value optimization, as does the rising use of prefixes super- and ultra- in 2025.

“Whatever we’re doing, we want to push it further,” Dictionary.com reports. “But its expanding uses also reveal how people are responding to that impulse. Some embrace it. Some exaggerate it for laughs. Others flip it on its head to describe stepping away from the relentless pursuit of more. The open question is whether this need for optimization has peaked or if we’ll push even harder next year.”

If you let your imagination fly, you can maxx on anything — dietmaxxing to lose weight, bookmaxxing to read more, bingemaxxing for all that streaming.

Data center among the top 5

Dictionary.com’s shortlist of top words this year included affordability, data center (spelled as two words), odyssey and unc. Affordability has been one of the most common words in politics in the lead-up to the midterms — can people pay for what they need? Data centers are sprouting up all over the US and are either gateways to economic prosperity or harbingers of doom, depending on whom you talk to.

Unc, short for uncle, refers to someone who’s out of touch with Gen Z and Gen Alpha culture; and odyssey cracked the top five thanks to the popularity of The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan’s 2026 film adapted from Homer’s Greek epic about Odysseus’ journey home after the Trojan War.

Tech.title: OpenAI Has a Surprising Defense Against Election Deepfakes
Tech.content:
One of the biggest problems of the AI age is that AI deepfakes are now so realistic that they’re practically indistinguishable from real photos. That matters a lot during election season, when voters are looking for reliable, truthful information on their candidates and polling sites. OpenAI is implementing a new safeguard to prevent people from making political deepfakes.

The US midterm election is only a week away on Nov. 3. Tech issues are taking center stage in many races, especially as AI and data center concerns rise for folks across the country. (Check out CNET’s guide to spotting political scams.)

If you were to go into ChatGPT today and ask it to generate an image “depicting election interference or that may discourage voting,” as OpenAI put it in an Oct. 20 update, the chatbot would create the image, given it doesn’t violate any other content guidelines. But it will be in an illustrated or cartoon style — all requests to have the image appear photorealistic should be ignored.

More from CNET

For example, CNET asked ChatGPT to create an image of Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers standing outside a polling location. Every such prompt generated an image in a cartoon style. A photorealistic version of this kind of image would likely spark anxiety, if not outright panic, for voters.

Every edit request for ChatGPT to make an image of ICE officers outside a polling location generated a picture in a cartoon style to avoid confusion for people who see it. Screenshot by Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

The idea is to make it harder for bad actors to create realistic political deepfakes that could interfere with or question the integrity of an election without stymying people’s ability to create political content in general. In another example, CNET Managing Editor Jon Reed couldn’t trick ChatGPT into creating a photojournalist-style image that showed a voting machine recording the wrong choice.

Voting machines recording results other than a voter’s selection is a common election myth. Screenshot by Jon Reed/CNET

“The problem with deepfakes isn’t social commentary, it’s deception. So our aim is to degrade the evidentiary value of an image, while preserving room for illustrations and social commentary,” Josh Lawson, OpenAI’s head of elections, told CNET. The goal is to “make our platform less useful to bad actors by adding another layer of friction,” he said.

This cartoonification of AI images is a practical way to make political deepfakes a little harder to create. Improving AI image models, like ChatGPT Images 2.5, is a double-edged sword. Newer models make fewer errors or hallucinations, making better content for creators. But removing those flubs makes it even harder for everyone else to identify AI-created content with the naked eye. Verification or AI labeling methods have tried to help, but those methods aren’t industry-wide nor foolproof.

When I asked Gemini maker Google about any precautions it is taking specifically for AI images, a spokesperson pointed me to its midterm election policy, which says the company is “rolling out additional protections to limit the creation of misleading election-related images” but doesn’t include any details on how.

Anthropic doesn’t have a traditional image or video generator, and a spokesperson told CNET that any attempts to use Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections violate its policies. The company also posted this general election guidance earlier this month.

Claude refused to make a photorealistic image with potentially “sensitive election-related” content. Screenshot by Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET

There’s no guarantee that OpenAI will keep this system in place once the election cycle is over. But it’s a solid sign from one of the biggest AI labs that it is taking its role in safeguarding American elections’ integrity at least somewhat seriously.

For more, check out what to do when you’ve been deepfaked and everything to know about the Take It Down Act.
